template_adherence.title: 3. Continuing to Leverage Python 2
template_adherence.context:
Attempts were made to upgrade all usage of Python from an older EOL'd version to Python 3. This presented a number of issues as we also use Ansible and Amazon Linux. The combination of these showed difficulty around how we use Ansible to install packages (`yum` module currently). The Ansible `yum` module is reserved specifically for Python 2. Python 3 requires usage of the `dnf` module. However, according to statements and current evidence, AWS has no intention to support a `dnf` extra for the life of Amazon Linux 2. It was also stated [in this forum post](https://forums.aws.amazon.com/thread.jspa?threadID=317863) "We are committed to keeping Python 2.7 secure for the life of Amazon Linux 2".

Another attempt was then made to replace our underlying OS with CentOS 8 perhaps to see how heavy of a lift this could be. With a bit of tweaks, we were able to at least run the automation that creates encrypted base AMIs. However, this is only the surface of everything that would have to be tested/changed for this move to happen. The referenced tweaks were as follows (for tracking purposes):
- Change the default value for the `bake_ami` variable found [here](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/applications/config/default.yml#L3) to a CentOS AMI ID (ami-0f5f21f0f86d11d6e was used for testing which is a "hardened" CentOS 8 image maintained / distributed by Frontline).
- Change all usage of the `yum` module to the `dnf` module in this [role / configuration file](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/build/roles/common/base-os/tasks/amazon.yml).
- Create a task to set symbolic links after installing Python 3 for `/usr/bin/python -> /usr/bin/python3` and `/usr/bin/pip -> /usr/bin/pip3` since Python 3 installations follow the `<package>3` naming convention by default.
- Comment out / remove the task for [installing, starting, and enabling the NTP daemon](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/build/roles/common/base-os/tasks/amazon.yml#L27-L37) as that package was not found with default repositories on the CentOS image and it also already comes with `chrony` installed and enabled.
- Comment out / remove Amazon Linux distro based conditional for the install of the `epel-release` package as well as an additional task that currently exists specifically for usage of Amazon Linux 2 image ([both outlined here](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/build/roles/common/base-os/tasks/amazon.yml#L44-L48)).
- Comment out / remove task that [removes yum lock](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/build/roles/common/base-os/tasks/amazon.yml#L53-L56) since `dnf` was the package manager / module used in this scenario.
- Addition of a task to install the ssm-agent as it would no longer come by default if we stopped leveraging Amazon Linux distributions.
- Drop the usage of `unicode` type in some of our custom Ansible related Python files within the `filter_plugins` directory [here](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/filter_plugins/aws_finders.py#L25) and [here](https://github.com/department-of-veterans-affairs/devops/blob/master/ansible/filter_plugins/resource_tags.py#L404). More on the "why" of that change/dynamic can be found in [this article](https://medium.com/better-programming/strings-unicode-and-bytes-in-python-3-everything-you-always-wanted-to-know-27dc02ff2686).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to upgrade from Python 2 (EOL) to Python 3 for security and support reasons.
- Compatibility issues with Ansible modules (`yum` vs `dnf`) and Amazon Linux 2 support.
- Operational challenges and testing effort required to switch OS or package managers.
- Security considerations from the Operations and Security teams.
- Potential future changes in Amazon Linux or infrastructure that might enable Python 3 usage.
template_adherence.decision:
After multiple days of testing, analysis, troubleshooting, and presenting these numerous issues to the Operations team as well as a chat with Joe to gather thoughts from a security perspective, it has been decided at this time to "accept risk" on the continued usage of Python 2 at this time. At this time, our Python code is not end-user-facing (frontend is Ruby) and the bulk of it exists in internal scripts, lambdas, and our CI/CD pipeline.

Intentions to revisit this issue would largely hinge on one of the following scenarios:
- Amazon Linux 3 is released with full Python 3 + dnf support
- Amazon Linux 2 changes direction to fully support Python 3 + dnf
- Through the work of our infrastructure recommit, if we can get to a fully containerized environment, we will ensure the images used do not leverage the end of life'd version of Python if at all possible.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Using a end of life'd version of Python internally.
- Lack of development / support for currently used Python 2 packages.
- Potential compatibility issues.
- Potential dependency issues.

alternatives.description: Upgrade all usage of Python from Python 2 to Python 3, including changing Ansible modules from `yum` to `dnf` and possibly changing the underlying OS to CentOS 8.
pros: Aligns with supported and secure Python version.
Future-proofs the infrastructure and codebase.
Removes dependency on deprecated Python 2.
cons: Significant operational challenges due to Ansible module compatibility.
Amazon Linux 2 does not support `dnf` module, requiring OS change.
Requires extensive testing and changes to automation scripts.
Potentially large effort and risk in migration.

alternatives.description: Continue using Python 2 despite it being end-of-life, accepting the associated risks for now.
pros: Avoids immediate operational and compatibility issues.
Leverages existing stable environment and automation.
Allows time to revisit when better support or infrastructure is available.
cons: Security risks due to using unsupported Python version.
Potential future compatibility and dependency issues.
Lack of development and support for Python 2 packages.

template_adherence.title: 4. Return Uninflected VA Keys in vets-api
template_adherence.context:
Using the Rails 6 zeitwerk file loader requires strict naming conventions of files. So without a Rails inflection, `va_something` class files are expected to have the class name of `VaSomething`. With an inflection, that class name would be `VASomething`. `vets-api` uses a mix of `VA` and `Va` in class names. To make things consistent, as well as support instances of `humanize` outputing `VA` in caps as an acronym, the inflection will be introduced.

However, using this inflection has a downstream affect on json responses transformed into camelCase by the [olive_branch](https://github.com/vigetlabs/olive_branch) gem. Previously keys structured like `the_va_something` were transformed into `theVaSomething`, but with inflection they will now be `theVASomething`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to comply with Rails 6 zeitwerk file loader naming conventions.
- Consistency in class naming between `VA` and `Va`.
- Support for `humanize` outputting `VA` as an acronym.
- Impact on JSON responses transformed by the olive_branch gem.
- Desire to minimize breaking changes and tech debt.
template_adherence.decision:
Create a patch implemented for the olive_branch middleware that returns keys containing `VA` as if "VA" was not an acronym.

In the future vets-api should introduce a version that doesn't support olive_branch.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Introducing some technical debt by patching an external gem.
- Low risk of olive_branch gem changing since it has had no changes in over a year.
- Hope that the patch remains stable until vets-api can move to a version without olive_branch.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative would be to not patch olive_branch and accept the changed key naming or to refactor vets-api to avoid the issue.
pros: Avoids patching an external gem, reducing technical debt.
cons: Leads to inconsistent key naming in JSON responses.
May break existing clients expecting the old key format.

template_adherence.title: 11. Persistent User Identity Proposal
template_adherence.context: Currently, users who log onto va.gov during repeat visits have potentially inconsistent behavior from the site, especially if they switch the credential they login with. This is most stark with aspects of the site that leverage persistent data, such as forms that the user has partially filled out, and which must be matched up to the user. The Accounts table is used today to aid in this, it creates a table entry that links an idme_uuid, icn, sec_id, to different data in our schema, and which we can retrieve even after a user session has been ended and a new one started. There are some issues with the current implementation, however, which make the intended experience inconsistent. The Accounts table relies on a matching idme_uuid, first and foremost. Then will attempt to match with an ICN or a sec_id, depending on the retrieval method. If a user logs in with different credentials, such as ID.me from va.gov, and then later DS Logon from MyHealtheVet (then navigates to VA.gov), they may see different forms and other persistent data depending on the credential. My Proposal involes refactoring the work done for the Accounts table into something more along the lines of how we actually deal with our users. This involves the concept of a 'credential_user', and a 'real_user', and tables to represent each of these: `user_verifications` and `user_accounts`. A 'credential_user' is our perspective of a user simply as information we get from a specific credential provider. For example, if a user logs in with MHV, we would expect to have an MHV uuid representing their account uuid. When a user authenticates, we would store the 'credential_user' by finding or creating an entry in the `user_verifications` table. This table would store the uuid from whatever credential provider they logged in with, whether or not the user was verified (LOA3/IAL2) and a link to an entry in the `user_accounts` table. A 'real_user' is our perspective of an actual human behind the entity logging in, regardless of how they logged in. These are reflected in a `user_accounts` table, and would only have an optional icn value (if icn is set, we know they are a real, verified human. Because we can make an MPI call with only an icn, this value represents all of the 'real' data we have on the 'real_user'. If an icn is not set, we know there is a human behind the entity logging in, but we cannot verify it to any human in our records). Every 'credential_user' will have a link to a single 'real_user', and every `user_verifications` entry will have a link to a `user_accounts` record. If a user was not verified and then becomes verified, the `user_accounts` entry may either simply be updated with the new icn, or, if an existing `user_accounts` record exists with that icn, it will be replaced by the existing `user_accounts` entry, and the unverified `user_accounts` entry will be moved into a `deprecated_user_accounts` table. Every persistent table on the backend will point to a `user_accounts` uuid, as we want to correlate these to a 'real_user', not to the specific credential. By organizing things this way, we will have consistent behavior for the end user, regardless of whatever credential combination they often use.

template_adherence.title: 7. Use arduino-cli in offline mode
template_adherence.context:

This might not be desirable at some institutions because they restrict Internet access or because many people using arduino-cli at the same time might saturate the available bandwith.
Using arduino-cli in offline mode also means that we know which version of libraries are used, which simplifies troubleshooting.
Arduino-cli supports multiple platforms.
Each of these platforms has platform-specific tools that need to be downloaded.
It is not possible to download the tools needed for a Windows host on a Linux host.
We have to manually download the tools for the different platforms.

- Tools must be manually downloaded for each platform as cross-platform downloads are not possible.

May introduce complexity and potential bugs.
Delays initial implementation.

}

template_adherence.title: ADR 1: Bootstrap Sentinel
template_adherence.context:
Connaisseur's main components are a MutatingWebhookConfiguration and the Connaisseur Pods. The MutatingWebhookConfiguration intercepts requests to create or update Kubernetes resources and forwards them to the Connaisseur Pods tasked, on a high level, with verifying trust data. The order of deploying both components matters, since a blocking MutatingWebhookConfiguration without the Connaisseur Pods to answer its requests would also block the deployment of said Pods.

In [#3](https://github.com/sse-secure-systems/connaisseur/issues/3) it was noted that prior to version 1.1.5 of Connaisseur when looking at the `Ready` status of Connaisseur Pods, they could report `Ready` while being non-functional due to the MutatingWebhookConfiguration missing. However, as stated above the MutatingWebhookConfiguration can only be deployed _after_ the Connaisseur Pods, which was solved by checking the `Ready` state of said Pods. If one were to add a dependency to this `Ready` state, such that it only shows `Ready` when the MutatingWebhookConfiguration exists, we run into a deadlock, where the MutatingWebhookConfiguration waits for the Pods and the Pods wait for the MutatingWebhookConfiguration.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid deployment deadlock between MutatingWebhookConfiguration and Connaisseur Pods.
- Desire for Connaisseur Pods' `Ready` status to accurately reflect functional readiness.
- Avoid complexity and non-Kubernetes-like solutions.
- Ensure deployment failures are consistent and observable.
- Security considerations regarding potential adversary actions.
- Ease of monitoring and operational clarity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to choose Option 1: At the start of the Helm deployment, create a Pod named `connaisseur-bootstrap-sentinel` that runs for 5 minutes (the Helm installation timeout). Connaisseur Pods report `Ready` if they can access notary and either the MutatingWebhookConfiguration exists or the sentinel Pod is still running. If both access and MutatingWebhookConfiguration exist, the sentinel Pod is killed early. This approach allows a glance at the Namespace to judge if Connaisseur is running properly, avoids deadlocks, and maintains Kubernetes-like readiness semantics.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include consistent deployment failure detection after the sentinel timeout if deployment fails, and sufficient monitoring by observing Connaisseur Pods' readiness. Negative consequences include potential adversary exploitation if they can deploy a sentinel Pod, deployment failure if notary healthcheck fails during sentinel lifetime, and minor complexity in deployment cleanup.

alternatives.description: Create a sentinel Pod during Helm deployment to manage readiness and avoid deadlock.
pros: Allows Connaisseur Pods to report `Ready` accurately during deployment.
Avoids deployment deadlock between MutatingWebhookConfiguration and Pods.
Enables consistent failure detection after timeout.
cons: Adds complexity with sentinel Pod management.
Potential security risk if adversary can deploy sentinel Pod.

alternatives.description: Let Connaisseur Pod readiness be non-indicative and require manual monitoring of MutatingWebhookConfiguration.
pros: Simpler deployment without sentinel Pod.
Avoids complexity in readiness logic.
cons: Readiness status does not reflect actual functionality.
Requires manual monitoring, increasing operational burden.

alternatives.description: Deploy MutatingWebhookConfiguration when Pods are healthy instead of ready, using health status for readiness.
pros: More accurate readiness semantics based on health.
Avoids sentinel Pod complexity.
cons: Health status requires querying each Pod individually.
Considered non-Kubernetes-like and ugly solution.

template_adherence.title: ADR 2: Release Management
template_adherence.context:
During its initial development Connaisseur was more or less maintained by a single person and not released frequently. Hence, the easiest option was to just have the maintainer build and push at certain stages of development. With the influx of more team members, the number of contributions and hence the number of needed/reasonable releases went up. Also since publication, it is more important that the uploaded Connaisseur image corresponds to the most recent version referenced in the Helm chart.

A single person having to build, sign and push the images whenever a new pull request is accepted is hence unpractical for both development and agility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle increased number of contributions and releases due to more team members.
- Importance of ensuring the uploaded image corresponds to the latest version referenced in Helm chart.
- Avoid exposing credentials to GitHub Actions due to security concerns.
- Desire to automate release process while maintaining control.
- Need to balance development agility with release process overhead.
template_adherence.decision:
For choice 1, the decision was to maintain two branches: `master` for the latest release code tagged with release versions, and `develop` for current development state merged into `master` for releases. This reduces the pain of releasing with every pull request at the cost of some overhead.

For choice 2, the decision was that whoever merges a pull request tags the commit on `master` with the new version, builds, signs, and pushes the release image manually, then triggers pipeline integration tests. This avoids exposing credentials to GitHub Actions and supports repository openness to pull requests, with automation via a shell script to ease manual steps.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Development can proceed without immediate shipping of changes.
- Release process does not expose credentials to GitHub Actions.
- Code is tagged with Git tags.

Negative consequences:
- The process from code to release is more cumbersome than before.
- Release still requires human intervention.

alternatives.description: Continue with PRs from personal feature branches to `master`.
pros: Simple workflow, no additional branches to manage.
cons: Releases happen with every pull request, which is impractical with more contributors.

alternatives.description: Have a development branch against which to create pull requests, either a continuously existing `develop` branch or version-specific development branches.
pros: Allows separation of development and release code.
Supports more controlled release process.
cons: Adds complexity with branch management.

alternatives.description: Have the pipeline build, sign and push the images.
pros: Automates the release process fully.
Reduces human intervention.
cons: Exposes credentials to GitHub Actions, posing security risks.
May limit repository openness to pull requests.

alternatives.description: Have a maintainer build, sign and push the images.
pros: Avoids exposing credentials to CI/CD pipelines.
Supports repository openness to pull requests.
cons: Requires manual steps, increasing human intervention.
Potentially slower release process.

template_adherence.title: ADR 3: Multiple Notary Configuration
template_adherence.context:
Previously Connaisseur only supported the configuration of a single notary, where all signature data had to reside in. Unfortunately this is rather impractical, as one doesn't create all signatures for all images one uses in a cluster. There is a need to access signature data from multiple places, like in a setup where most images come from a private registry + notary and some from Docker Hub and their notary.

There is also the problem that a single notary instance could use multiple root keys, used for creating the signatures, like in the case of Docker Hub. Connaisseur also only supports a single root key to be trust pinned, thus making it impractical.

That's why the decision was made to support more than one notary and multiple keys per notary, which leads to the question how the new configuration should look like. This also has implications on the notary health check, which is important for Connaisseur's own readiness check.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support multiple notaries to handle images from different sources.
- Need to support multiple root keys per notary.
- Configuration should minimize duplication and complexity.
- Readiness probe behavior needs to be reconsidered with multiple notaries.
- Default notary/key selection behavior must be defined.
- Maintain operational stability even if some notaries are unreachable.
template_adherence.decision:
- For Choice 1, Option 1 was chosen: The `notary` field becomes a list `notaries`, each with multiple public root keys.
- For Choice 2, Option 4 was chosen: Use a `name: "default"` field to indicate default notary/key if none specified in image policy.
- For Choice 3, Option 3 was chosen: Decouple Connaisseur readiness from notary health checks but log unreachable notaries.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Configuration supports multiple notaries and multiple keys per notary, improving flexibility.
- Default notary/key selection is explicit via naming, reducing ambiguity.
- Connaisseur remains operational even if notaries are unreachable, improving availability.
- Readiness probe no longer blocks deployments due to notary health, which is a breaking change but improves usability.
- Slight increase in configuration complexity due to multiple notaries and keys.
- Logging of notary health issues allows monitoring without blocking operations.

alternatives.description: Choice 1: How to configure multiple notaries and keys.
pros: Option 1 (Per Notary): Minimizes duplication by grouping keys under each notary.
Option 2 (Per Notary + Key): Simpler image policy without key field.
cons: Option 1: Image policy must specify both notary and key, more complex.
Option 2: Duplication of notary entries for each key, more configuration overhead.

pros: Option 1 (First item): Simple, no extra config needed.

Option 4 (Default name): Clear and explicit default via naming.

template_adherence.title: ADR 4: Modular Validation
template_adherence.context: With the upcoming of notaryv2 and similar projects like Cosign, the opportunity for Connaisseur arises to support multiple signing mechanisms, and combine all into a single validation tool. For that to work, the internal validation mechanism of Connaisseur needs to be more modular, so we can easily swap in and out different methods.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to support multiple signing mechanisms; flexibility to swap validation methods; handle sensitive configuration values properly; provide powerful and explicit configuration options; maintain core functionality and avoid unnecessary complexity.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a modular validator configuration structure with a 'validators' list containing different validation methods identified by name and type. Hard-code sensitive fields per validator type to prevent misconfiguration. Change image policy to reference validators by name with additional fields as needed, including special 'allow' and 'deny' static validators. Validator interface returns a digest, and Connaisseur creates JSON patches accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: The system gains flexibility to support multiple validation methods and signing mechanisms. Configuration is explicit and manageable, with sensitive data handled securely. The validator interface remains focused on core functionality, returning digests to avoid unnecessary complexity. Users have more powerful configuration options with explicit allow and deny validators.

template_adherence.title: ADR 6: Dynamic Configuration
template_adherence.context: The configuration of validators are mounted into Connaisseur as a configmap, as it is common practice in the Kubernetes ecosystem. When this configmap is upgraded, say with a `helm upgrade`, the resource itself in Kubernetes is updated accordingly, but that doesn't mean it's automatically updated inside the pods which mounted it. That only occurs once the pods are restarted and until they are the pods still have an old version of the configuration lingering around. This is a fairly unintuitive behavior and the reason why Connaisseur doesn't mount the image policy into its pods. Instead, the pods have access to the kube API and get the image policy dynamically from there. The same could be done for the validator configuration, but there is also another solution.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for dynamic configuration updates without pod restarts
- Kubernetes native approaches preferred
- Minimizing network requests for configuration access
- Simplification of configuration resources
template_adherence.decision: Two decisions were made: 1) For accessing configuration, Solution 1.2 (Restart pods with updated configmap annotations) was chosen for its Kubernetes native approach despite losing "on the fly" changes. 2) For the number of configmaps, Solution 2.2 (One combined resource) was chosen for simplicity.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Configuration changes require pod restarts to take effect
- Avoids use of CustomResourceDefinitions for validators
- Simplifies configuration management by merging resources
- Loses ability for dynamic "on the fly" configuration changes
- Aligns with Kubernetes native practices

pros: Kubernetes native approach.

pros: Separation of concerns.
Clear resource boundaries.
cons: More resources to manage.

alternatives.description: Merge image policy and validator configurations into one resource.
pros: Simpler management with a single resource.
cons: Potentially less modular and flexible.

template_adherence.title: 0002 - API Design Framework/Documentation
template_adherence.context:
Planning and documenting an API is critical to its success. Poorly planned and undocumented APIs are difficult for end-users to build against and make building a front-end application that uses the API more difficult as well. Choosing a good API modeling should not impose a heavy burden on development, but ideally provide a strong set of tools that can be used to produce documentation, testing, and producing scaffolding for software development kits (SDKs)

There are primarily two options for a framework that are worth evaluating:
- Swagger
- RESTful API Modeling Language (RAML)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section, but the context and decision sections imply drivers such as ease of use, community support, tooling quality, and prior experience.
template_adherence.decision:
Raster Foundry will use Swagger to design and document its API instead of using RAML for a few reasons.
- Azavea has used Swagger successfully on a few projects already and has experience using it
- The community around Swagger is larger and rooted in open source (Swagger has been donated to the Open API Initiative) and is currently at version 2.0
- The tooling around Swagger is better documented and supports a more diverse set of languages compared to RAML
template_adherence.consequences: As a consequence to choosing Swagger for documenting the API we will need to develop a Swagger specification for Raster Foundry. Ideally, we should design the API first and build it second to ensure that it is easy to use and intuitive. Additionally, we should deploy a version of the Swagger UI alongside the application to serve as documentation for end-users and to help with testing.

pros: Azavea has used Swagger successfully on a few projects already and has experience using it
The community around Swagger is larger and rooted in open source
Tooling around Swagger is better documented and supports a more diverse set of languages

template_adherence.title: Web Backend Language and Framework
template_adherence.context: A backend web framework is needed to handle web requests and coordinate with other backend components, such as database interaction and batch processing workflows. The team has experience with Django (Python), but Scala frameworks like Play and Akka HTTP are also considered, especially due to integration with a Scala tile server using GeoTrellis. The decision involves weighing the benefits of Python's ease of use against Scala's type safety and better refactoring capabilities. The choice also considers the specific needs of the project, such as API creation without HTML templating and third-party authentication.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a backend web framework to handle requests and coordinate backend components
- Team experience primarily with Django (Python)
- Potential benefits of using Scala frameworks due to tile server integration with GeoTrellis
- Trade-offs between Python's dynamic typing and Scala's static typing
- Specific framework features needed (API creation, no HTML templating, third-party authentication)
- Desire to minimize inter-server communication complexity
- Importance of compile-time error checking and easier refactoring
- Team's willingness to learn Scala and adopt best practices
template_adherence.decision: The project will use Scala as the backend language with Akka HTTP as the framework. Despite less team experience with Scala, the advantages of unified backend language, compile-time checks, and reduced inter-server communication outweigh the cons. Akka HTTP is preferred over Play due to its lightweight nature and alignment with project needs. This choice also aligns with the existing Scala tile server and GeoTrellis integration.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Team members must invest effort to gain Scala expertise through training, best practices, and collaboration with the GeoTrellis team.
- Akka HTTP, being relatively young, may present bugs, but fallback to Spray is possible.
- Unlike Django, Akka HTTP lacks built-in features like ORM and migrations; additional libraries like Slick and migration tools (Scala Forklift, slick-migration-api, Flyway) will be needed.
- The decision may increase initial development effort but aims for long-term maintainability and reduced errors.

template_adherence.title: 0006 - Workflow/Task Manager
template_adherence.context:
This ADR has been superseded by `ADR-0019`.

Some actions and features of Raster Foundry require a way to manage asynchronous tasks and workflows.
For instance, user uploads of imagery or tools may start workflows in an ad hoc manner, while in
contrast imports of imagery from NASA or partners may need to happen on a schedule. The nature of
these tasks could vary from bash scripts and python functions to spark jobs and ECS tasks.

The ideal tool will provide some means to monitor task progress, retry on some failures, and
notify personnel if necessary. There are a few options of tools we can use: celery, SWF, Luigi, and Airflow.
Azavea has experience working with both celery and SWF; however, due to our past experience with these
tools it seemed prudent to explore additional options as well.

| Workflow Tool   | Pros | Cons |
|-----------------|------|------|
| Celery          | Familiar, written in python, flexible | Provides poor primitives for workflows, many open issues, difficult to monitor workflows |
| SWF (botoflow)) | Familiar, now written in python, maintaining state is not our responsibility (HA by default), great primitives for workflows and tasks | Difficult to monitor, relatively immature tools and projects, not many others using it |
| Luigi           | Mature, seems to be stable, written in python | Unfamiliar execution model, primarily designed for scheduled, recurring task |
| Airflow         | Mature, stable, fits into our execution model, written in python, excellent UI | Requires celery (for what we want to do)), requires managing the scheduler and a cache
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage asynchronous tasks and workflows with varying nature (bash scripts, python functions, spark jobs, ECS tasks).
- Requirement for monitoring task progress, retry on failures, and notification.
- Familiarity and past experience with some tools (celery, SWF).
- Desire for a tool with good primitives for workflows, stability, and good UI.
- Integration with existing infrastructure components (Postgres, redis).
template_adherence.decision: Raster Foundry will use Airflow as a task manager. The decision is based on Airflow's large and active user base, its status as an Apache incubator project indicating high quality, excellent UI for monitoring tasks and workflows, support for both scheduled and ad hoc tasks, and architectural compatibility with existing infrastructure components like Postgres and redis.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to become more familiar with Airflow, though documentation is good and improving.
- Potential need to extend Airflow's functionality if lacking in some areas, though unlikely in the short term.
- Some limitations in Airflow out of the box, such as lack of a best practice for versioning tasks/workflows.
- Requirement to manage task dependencies within worker containers or develop custom Airflow operators or queue management strategies.

template_adherence.title: Operating System and Containers
template_adherence.context:
We have used Docker containers, in various ways, on previous projects and our experience has been mixed but overall positive. Containers help to speed up CI builds and deployments, at the cost of added complexity and usage frustrations, especially for non-Linux users (most notably designers). We've decided that the best way to use Docker containers for local development is inside of a Vagrant VM, which lessens some of their benefits for local development but also improves the experience for non-Linux users.

For the past three years or so, we have used Ubuntu as the basis for every new project which required an operating system.

There are other container specifications, such as Rocket, and obviously, other Linux distributions. However, we do not have major complaints about either Docker containers or Ubuntu.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include prior experience with Docker and Ubuntu, the benefits and drawbacks of using containers (speeding up CI builds and deployments vs. added complexity and frustrations for non-Linux users), the need to maintain a positive development experience for non-Linux users, and the flexibility to change container or OS technologies if needed in the future.
template_adherence.decision: We will continue to use Docker containers to encapsulate running applications, and to use Ubuntu as our host operating system. This decision is based on our accumulated experience and satisfaction with both technologies, and the theoretical isolation containers provide to allow swapping technologies later if necessary. We will consider other Linux distributions or base images on a case-by-case basis, especially for deployment, but anticipate continuing to use Ubuntu locally for development.
template_adherence.consequences: We will need to develop a Docker-centric system architecture and development environment, and determine how best to integrate Docker and Spark. We will need to continue to be vigilant about maintaining a positive development experience for non-Linux users.

alternatives.description: Use other container specifications such as Rocket or other Linux distributions instead of Docker and Ubuntu.
pros: Potentially smaller base images for containers.
Possibility to optimize for specific deployment environments like AWS ECS.
cons: Lack of experience with alternatives.
No major complaints about current technologies, so change may introduce unnecessary risk.
May complicate local development experience, especially for non-Linux users.

template_adherence.title: 0011 - Framework for Tool UI
template_adherence.context:
Within the Tools section, Raster Foundry needs to provide an interface that allows for the linking of the user's resources with Raster Foundry's various processing tools to easily create an imagery processing pipeline from their browser. Through dragging-and-dropping components into the diagramming interface, the user will be able to specify which sources are fed into which processing tools and whether the output from these tools will be routed into another processing tool or used as a new source of imagery.

Using an already existing robust and well-maintained open-source framework will allow us to focus efforts on building the interface built around the diagramming framework rather than re-invent the wheel.

Previous research from phase 1 of ModelLab evaluated several frameworks and recommended JointJS. This ADR builds on that research to re-evaluate and finalize the decision given the current architecture of Raster Foundry.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a robust, well-maintained open-source diagramming framework
- Ability to integrate with Raster Foundry's architecture
- Features such as interactive elements, custom shapes, smart routing, JSON (de)serialization, event-driven and touch-enabled support
- Availability of a straightforward API and useful open-source features
- Avoiding reinventing the wheel by leveraging existing research and frameworks
- Consideration of commercial extensions and their necessity
template_adherence.decision: JointJS remains the best choice as the diagramming framework for Raster Foundry's Tool UI. Its straightforward API, useful open-source features, and high-quality documentation make it optimal for our use-case. The mechanisms for ingesting JSON to initialize graphs will ease integration aspects.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to build layout logic for diagrams as JointJS does not provide automatic layouts
- Design and build the interface allowing users to add sources and tools to their processing flow
- Familiarization with the JointJS API, mitigated by its high-quality documentation
- Integration approach similar to Leaflet, encapsulating the library in a component with event listeners and a workflow service

template_adherence.title: Map component ADR
template_adherence.context:
The current leaflet map implementation was intentionally made as a very thin wrapper. We've developed enough code around it to quantify what we need leaflet to do in raster foundry, as well as the shortcomings of our current approach.

The initial approach tries to control the leaflet map exclusively thorugh bindings to callbacks and properties. We've found that this creates a lot of complexity in the components and controllers due to the way that data must flow through components.

Ideally, components should use one-way data bindings where possible, and call bound functions in order to change data in a parent. The current way we have things set up requires all of the important state to be centralized in a parent controller, and modified through two-way bindings in child components.

Adding layers which need to be controlled by a child attribute has necessitated creating a separate binding for each type of interaction, and this has resulted in a bloated leaflet map component.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce complexity in components and controllers caused by two-way bindings and multiple bindings for interactions.
- Desire to use one-way data bindings and function callbacks for state changes.
- Need for efficient management of geojson layers and map events.
- Requirement to support multiple use cases with different map interaction needs.
- Maintainability and scalability of map interaction code.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a new architecture where most map interaction happens through a centralized MapService and MapWrapper classes rather than through Angular bindings. The leaflet map component will self-register with the MapService and expose a MapWrapper instance. Map layers and events will be managed via this service and wrapper, reducing the complexity of bindings and improving efficiency. The component will consolidate toggles into an 'options' attribute to simplify configuration.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Reduced complexity in Angular components by limiting map interaction to service and wrapper calls.
- Centralized management of map state and events.
- Easier to support multiple maps and complex interactions.

Negative:
- Additional manual management of synchronization between map state and Angular context.
- Potential for the MapWrapper to become bloated if not carefully managed.
- Need to ensure proper lifecycle management of listeners and state.

alternatives.description: Continue using two-way bindings and multiple bindings for map interactions in Angular components.
pros: Fits naturally with Angular's binding system.
No need to introduce new service or wrapper abstractions.
cons: Leads to complex and bloated components.
Difficult to manage state and interactions efficiently.
Hard to scale and maintain as features grow.

alternatives.description: Use a fully external map library with its own state management, minimizing Angular bindings.
pros: Potentially cleaner separation of concerns.
Leverages existing map library capabilities.
cons: May require significant refactoring.
Less integration with Angular lifecycle and data flow.
Could complicate synchronization with Angular components.

template_adherence.title: 0013 - Spark Execution Environment
template_adherence.context:
Part of the Raster Foundry processing workflow requires a source imagery ingest into a GeoTrellis Catalog. GeoTrellis depends on Apache Spark to parallelize work during an ingest, and that work typically occurs on an Apache Spark enabled compute cluster.

Prior iterations of Raster Foundry attempted ingests with an Apache YARN managed compute cluster via Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) on a per-request basis. Unfortunately, that didn't perform well due to the overhead of bootstrapping an EMR cluster.

Our goal for the this iteration aims to keep some Spark cluster components active at all times through a combination of spot pricing and usage based cluster auto-scaling. This approach should help minimize cluster bootstrapping durations and keep cost-incurring cluster resources at a minimum.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to keep costs low
- Desire to ship quickly
- Minimize cluster bootstrapping overhead
- Maintain shared cluster resources between environments
- Isolate environments at the VPC level
- Build on top of Amazon EMR platform
- Use spot pricing and auto-scaling aggressively to keep costs low
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to have a shared (across staging and production) Amazon EMR cluster with the infrastructure split across three Amazon VPCs (Staging, Spark, Production). The Staging and Production VPCs will be peered with the Spark VPC to allow private network access if necessary. Public facing APIs like Amazon EMR's Step API or Raster Foundry API will be used for communication between systems. This approach balances cost, speed of delivery, and operational overhead.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Modifying CIDR ranges requires destroying and recreating almost all resources in the VPCs.
- EMR Master instance group requires an on-demand instance from specific instance families, possibly requiring Reserved Instances to keep costs low.
- Terraform has limited support for Amazon EMR; CloudFormation or direct AWS EMR API access will be needed for features like spot bidding and auto-scaling.
- Auto-scaling should be based on cluster-level YARN metrics published to CloudWatch; tuning is required.
- The best EMR job submission method is unclear; Step API is preferred for integration and security reasons.
- Direct spark-submit invocations are brittle and lack built-in job tracking, making them less desirable.

alternatives.description: Use a per-request EMR cluster via Apache YARN managed compute cluster (previous approach).
pros: Isolated clusters per request
Potentially simpler resource management per job
cons: High overhead due to cluster bootstrapping
Poor performance due to startup delays
Higher cost due to frequent cluster creation and teardown

alternatives.description: Use direct spark-submit invocations from EC2 nodes.
pros: Direct control over job submission
Avoids some API complexities
cons: Brittle and requires complex configuration
Security group and service discovery issues
Lacks built-in job tracking mechanisms

template_adherence.title: API documentation ADR
template_adherence.context:
The goal isn't to make this super complicated, but give us a basis for building out more full-fledged documentation as the project goes -- beyond just listing API endpoints (see Auth0's docs section as inspiration https://auth0.com/docs). There are javascript libraries that can assist us with parsing the swagger spec, so a good amount of the work will be purely presentational.

Of significant import is that the framework that we choose here gives us an opportunity to test out design practices and frameworks before we apply them to our primary applications. Choosing a framework here that we don't plan on using elsewhere would have significant opportunity costs. We also need to consider that Raster Foundry is almost certainly going to be transitioned over to Angular 2, and this is the only chance we will have to learn about Angular 2 before we do so. Additionally, other projects at Azavea that the Raster Foundry team work on, such as Hunchlab, are considering moving from Angular 1.X to Angular 2.X
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to choose a framework that supports building more full-fledged documentation beyond just listing API endpoints.
- Desire to test design practices and frameworks before applying them to primary applications.
- Consideration of future transition of Raster Foundry to Angular 2.
- Opportunity to learn Angular 2 before transitioning main projects.
- Need for a CMS-lite type system where code and API documentation can coexist.
- Maintenance and ecosystem considerations of frameworks.
- Performance and debugging concerns with Angular 1.X.
- Desire to align with team objectives and use maintained frameworks.
template_adherence.decision: We will write the API documentation as a traditional SPA using Angular 2, using either Webpack or Angular CLI as a build tool. This approach allows us to accomplish our flexibility goals while also allowing us to test Angular 2 before transitioning the main Raster Foundry app over to it.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Maintaining a second application is a significant cost.
- Static site generators do not meet our needs, so maintaining a standalone website is preferred over maintaining a fork of a static generator.
- Angular 2 solves many issues present in Angular 1.X, offering higher performance and more maintainable code.
- Angular 2 is a younger framework; some libraries available in Angular 1.X may not exist or be less stable.
- Component frameworks for Angular 2 are less mature, but custom components are feasible.
- Spin-up cost for this application is incurred to test Angular 2 before larger project transitions.
- Angular design practices learned will carry forward due to backporting from Angular 2 to Angular 1 over the last 6 months.

template_adherence.title: 0019 - Workflow/Task Manager
template_adherence.context:
This ADR supersedes `ADR-006`.

Back in August of 2016, we went through an extensive evaluation process for a workflow manager. After looking at a number of open source and hosted solutions, we settled on Apache Airflow. Since then, we've had some success with Airflow, but also a number of setbacks.

First, we've encountered a number of deeply rooted issues with Airflow's scheduler. At times it would lock up and cease scheduling queued jobs, emitting cryptic error messages in the process. Other times, it would consume a large percentage of an instance's CPU while emitting many valueless log messages.

Second, Airflow's UI was a big differentiator in our initial decision making process. In practice, the UI proved confusing to use, and hasn't lended itself well to running in a distributed environment (e.g., task log centralization, real-time log reporting).

Lastly, our troubleshooting processes often led us to community supported help resources, like the Airflow mailing lists and issues. The more time we spent reading through these entries, the lower our confidence in Airflow became. Leadership was in a constant state of turmoil around releases, and a presence of production grade users became less and less visible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly titled or sectioned, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections: issues with Airflow's scheduler reliability, UI usability problems, lack of confidence from community support, and desire for a more stable, hosted solution with better operational characteristics.
template_adherence.decision:
We are replacing all of the following Airflow components with AWS Batch:

- Scheduler
- Web server
- Worker
- Executor (Celery)

AWS Batch is a hosted service produced by Amazon Web Services (AWS). When used in `MANAGED` mode, it assists in scheduling, executing, and reporting status on submitted jobs. In addition, it provides a minimal UI for visually tracking job status. Under the covers, its execution environment is Amazon ECS.
template_adherence.consequences:
- By running Airflow in production for almost a year, we've gained a signifiant amount of expertise in troubleshooting issues associated with it, and the tasks it executes for us. A portion of this expertise will be lost, and will need to be rebuilt for AWS Batch.
- AWS Batch aggregates its logs in CloudWatch Logs. The is a departure from our approach of centralizing logs in Papertrail.
- The Airflow migration to AWS Batch has consumed, and will continue to consume engineering resources. Those resources could have been spent in other areas of the product.
- Because AWS Batch is a hosted service, depending on it makes it harder to make Raster Foundry a platform that can be deployed on-premise.
- We will also have to engineering a solution for enabling local development because no mechanisms exist to simulate AWS Batch locally.
- AWS Batch has no support for scheduling jobs on a recurring schedule (e.g., nightly jobs). This support will have to be engineered outside of the hosted service.

template_adherence.title: Handling Anti-meridian Artifacts in Polygon Display
template_adherence.context: Polygons crossing the anti-meridian present ambiguity in display. Various heuristics exist to address this, but none are universally correct. The problem involves determining which polygons need fixing and how to fix them.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a practical, implementable solution that handles most cases encountered, especially for imagery sources that do not cover wide global areas. The solution should balance correctness and complexity, and be applicable to current data constraints.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a hybrid approach combining the smallest area and degree difference threshold heuristics, applied only to scene footprints. This approach is a temporary solution suitable for current imagery sources that do not cover wide global areas.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision provides a practical fix for most polygons encountered, avoiding issues with small polygons near the anti-meridian. However, it may still have issues with very large polygons and does not address all possible cases due to the mathematical ambiguity of the problem.

alternatives.description: Smallest area heuristic: Calculate polygon area two ways and assume the smaller is correct.
pros: Relatively simple to implement
Likely correct for most imagery
cons: Fails for polygons covering more than half the world horizontally

alternatives.description: Degree difference threshold: Use a threshold on the absolute sum of westmost and eastmost coordinates.
pros: Only affects polygons close to the meridian
cons: Doesn't fix polygons outside threshold
Can have false positives
Threshold tuning required

alternatives.description: Assume no polygons cross the anti-meridian.
pros: Easy to implement
Relies on polygon sources splitting into multipolygons
cons: Does not address the problem if polygons do cross the anti-meridian

alternatives.description: Combine smallest area and degree difference threshold, applied only to thumbnails.
pros: Better than individual solutions
Avoids issues with small polygons near anti-meridian
cons: Still issues with very large polygons
Both eastmost and westmost points must be near anti-meridian

template_adherence.title: 0023 - Object ACRs in text array
template_adherence.context: This ADR supersedes ADR-0020 concerning the implementation of Access Control Rules (ACRs) in Raster Foundry. The existing ACR mechanism stores access rules in a large table, which has grown significantly, causing slow and timed-out queries, especially for scenes. Despite some optimizations, a more sustainable and faster approach is needed to handle access control queries efficiently as the data grows.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers are the need to improve query performance on access control rules, especially for scenes, to handle the growing size of the ACR table and avoid slow or timed-out queries. The solution should maintain the existing access control semantics while improving scalability and query speed. It should also be compatible with existing data models and endpoints, and allow for manageable migration and adaptation.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add text[] fields to all first-class objects to store ACRs at the object level, migrate ACRs from the centralized access_control_rules table to these object-level text arrays, create GIN indices on these fields, drop the original ACR table, and adapt all related endpoints, data models, SQL commands, and tests to use this new structure. This approach has been experimentally shown to improve query performance significantly.
template_adherence.consequences: The ACR strings will be reformatted to exclude object information and stored as strings of the form "<subject type>;<optional subject id>;<action type>" in the text arrays. Serialization and deserialization will be handled via doobie mappings and custom data models. Access control data will not be returned in listing endpoints but only via specific permissions endpoints. CRUD operations will be adapted to work with the new text array fields. Querying will leverage PostgreSQL array functions and operators for efficient filtering. Migration will require careful handling, possibly involving temporary tables and table replacements. Examples and code snippets illustrate data models, CRUD operations, and queries adapted to the new approach. This change improves query speed but introduces complexity in migration and requires updates to multiple system components.

alternatives.description: Continue using the centralized access_control_rules table with query optimizations and hardware scaling.
pros: No major changes to data models or endpoints.
Leverages existing infrastructure and codebase.
cons: Query performance issues persist as data grows.
Scaling hardware is costly and may not fully solve performance problems.
Complex queries with JOINs and UNIONs remain slow.

alternatives.description: Use a NoSQL or specialized access control system to manage permissions separately.
pros: Potentially better scalability and performance for access control queries.
Decouples access control from main relational database.
cons: Requires significant architectural changes.
Increases system complexity and maintenance overhead.
Data consistency and integration challenges.

template_adherence.title: 0025 - User Access Scopes
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to control user permissions on a different axis for the Raster Foundry API, beyond specific object instance permissions. It highlights the current limitation where access control rules are tied to specific object IDs and do not support broader access control across object types, such as preventing users from creating projects or deleting annotations.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include minimizing performance overhead when evaluating user scopes per request, preventing certain users from creating new objects, and ideally developing a flexible approach to handle unforeseen access control scenarios.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt 'The More Granular Variation' solution, which treats scopes as positive permissions (presence of a scope grants access) rather than access reductions. This approach supports granular control, promotes consistency, and is more intuitive at the endpoint level, despite potential complexity in encoding/decoding scopes or requiring additional columns.
template_adherence.consequences: The chosen solution allows for easy addition of new scopes, promotes consistency by narrowing scope types, and encourages granular access control. However, it may require additional columns or complex encoding/decoding mechanisms. It also implies changes to the data model and endpoint authorization logic.

pros: No possible conflicts as it only handles read-only restrictions
Minimal effect on current data models, requiring only one additional field on User
cons: Only supports read-only scoping
Requires machinery to encode/decode scopes to/from the database

alternatives.description: The Wild West Solution allows a list of scopes per user with minimal constraints, e.g., 'ProjectReadOnly' or 'ProjectNoDelete'.
pros: Easy to add new scopes as needed

cons: Lack of constraints can cause conflicting rules requiring programmatic resolution
Requires machinery to encode/decode scopes to/from the database

alternatives.description: The Civilized Solution uses multiple columns per user for each object type with a single scope value to prevent conflicts.
pros: Easy to add new scopes as needed

Promotes consistency by narrowing ScopeType members
cons: Requires many columns to be added to User data model/table
Requires machinery to map ObjectTypes to columns

alternatives.description: The More Granular Variation treats scopes as positive permissions per domain, allowing granular access control.
pros: Easy to add new scopes as needed
Promotes consistency by narrowing ScopeType members
Encourages granular scoping versus broad scope types
More intuitive at the endpoint level
cons: May require many columns or complex encoding/decoding process

template_adherence.title: ADR 0026 - Post-hoc Metrics Scripting
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to track metrics for events and non-events in Raster Foundry servers, including metrics from third party services and ongoing usage data for querying and visualization. template_adherence.decision: For external events, the decision is to use scheduled metric event aggregation with Lambda and Step Functions, abandoning the webhook approach due to feasibility issues. For non-events, the decision is to gather information directly from S3 rather than extending the database schema, to avoid complexity and potential inconsistency.
template_adherence.consequences: For external events, the consequences include the need to create multiple Lambda functions, Step Functions, and API endpoints, as well as mechanisms to prevent duplicate metric insertion. For non-events, consequences include creating a new usage_data table, asynchronous backfill jobs, and Lambda functions to respond to S3 SNS events to maintain usage data accurately.

template_adherence.title: 0027 Annotate Project STAC Export
template_adherence.context:
This is an ADR documenting decisions made on MVP features of exporting Raster Foundry/Annotate label data and scenes in STAC-compliant catalogs. This aims to make us one step closer towards integrating STAC to the path of interoperability among Azavea’s Machine Learning workflow.

In Raster Foundry, we support creating geospatial labels based on images and scenes added to project layers. This feature is further extended in Annotate App, which is an application backed by Raster Foundry APIs, so that teams can work on an image labeling projects simultaneously within status-tracked tasks. To enable downstream Machine Learning work better in interoperating these ground truth labels, we have decided to implement a feature for exporting images and labels in STAC catalogs in an asynchronous manner. The following sections will go into details about the export process, the structure of the exported catalog, and where they are stored.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to export Raster Foundry/Annotate label data and scenes in STAC-compliant catalogs.
- Support asynchronous export process.
- Ensure access control and permissions for export operations.
- Structure exported catalogs to reflect project layers, scenes, and labels.
- Store exported catalogs on S3 for environment-specific access.
- Facilitate interoperability with Machine Learning workflows.
- Plan for future enhancements such as relative links and notifications.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement CRUD endpoints for STAC exports under `api/stac`, create a STAC catalog builder that structures exports into Layer, Scene, and Label collections, and use AWS batch jobs to build exports asynchronously. Exported catalogs are stored on environment-specific S3 buckets with absolute links currently, with plans to move to relative links. Access control is enforced for export operations, and the export process includes filtering by task statuses.
template_adherence.consequences:
- STAC endpoints, export builder, and batch jobs transform Raster Foundry data into STAC resources stored on S3.
- Enables asynchronous export of label and scene data.
- Provides structured STAC catalogs reflecting project layers and tasks.
- Access control restricts export operations to authorized users.
- Current use of absolute links may require future updates to relative links.
- Future work includes notifications and enhanced export features.

alternatives.description:
Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implied alternatives include:
- Synchronous export instead of asynchronous batch jobs.
- Storing exports locally or in a different storage system instead of S3.
- Different API design or no CRUD endpoints.
- Different catalog structure or no use of STAC standard.

These alternatives are not detailed with pros and cons in the ADR.
pros: Not applicable as alternatives are not explicitly discussed.
cons: Not applicable as alternatives are not explicitly discussed.

template_adherence.title: Use scala-opentracing for initial tracing implementation
template_adherence.context: Our tile servers are under constant load, making it difficult to analyze logs and gather useful metrics. We want to assess tracing libraries in the Scala ecosystem to improve logging and eventually integrate with external tracing services like Jaeger, AWS X-Ray, or Honeycomb.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: We need a tracing library that is maintainable, easy to start with, integrates well with our stack, and supports exporting traces to external services. Risk of abandonment, ease of setup, and compatibility with existing infrastructure are key concerns.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to use scala-opentracing for our initial tracing implementation because it is maintained by someone responsible for a production system, is relatively easy to set up, and supports logging and exporting traces to Jaeger. Other options like natchez and http4s-tracer had significant drawbacks or were not ready for production use.
template_adherence.consequences: We will add scala-opentracing to our codebase and start with a logging tracer. Infra work will be needed to integrate third-party tracing services. We must choose a trace repository, possibly AWS X-Ray or Jaeger, and decide on tracing granularity and sampling rates to balance performance and observability.

alternatives.description: Use natchez tracing library.
pros: Promises nice integration with TypeLevel ecosystem.
Has examples for database tracing.
cons: Difficult to implement required ConcurrentEffect for Kleisli.
Example does not cover webservice use case.
Recommended not to use in production by a known expert.
Ongoing work to improve integration is incomplete and has no timeline.

alternatives.description: Use scala-opentracing library.
pros: Maintained by someone responsible for production system.
Easy to set up logging tracer quickly.
Supports extensions for custom trace IDs and Jaeger integration.
Can wrap OpenTracing compliant tracers for other sinks.
cons: Logging tracer does not print or store tags by default.
Requires adding repository to resolvers.
Some Scala warnings in Jaeger integration code.

alternatives.description: Use http4s-tracer library.
pros: Encourages better design by requiring tracing algebra throughout code.
Tagless final implementation.
cons: Lacks notion of spans and tagging as per OpenTracing spec.
Tracing has to be integrated deeply, making it less of an afterthought.
No out-of-the-box support for exporting traces to external services.
Not implemented in demos due to complexity.

template_adherence.title: Create Observation Repository Sort
template_adherence.context: Researchers may require methods for sorting the lists of Whale Observations to extract key information regarding whale migration, population, etc. Through Observation's available comparison methods the proposed sorting is possible.
template_adherence.decision:
Create `sortByDate` and `sortById` methods in ObservationRepository.

`sortByDate` uses the comparator `compareByDate` from the `Comparator<Observation>` interface and `Collections.sort()` to sort the list of observations by field `sightingTime` (Date).

`sortById` uses the default `compareTo` method from the `Comparable<Observation>` interface and `Collections.sort()` to sort the list of observations by field `ObservationId` (long).

`Collection.sort()` implements the abstract strategy of the `Comparator` interface using the concrete strategy `compareByDate` and returns an integer referring to the order of the objects.
template_adherence.consequences: Whale Observation lists are sortable. Future iterations of the program can easily add new comparators for sorting since we have implemented the strategy design pattern with the `Comparator<Observation>` interface.

template_adherence.decision: Create `getByDate` and `getById` methods in ObservationRepository. `getByDate` uses an iterator to find all observations matching a given date, while `getById` uses `Collections.binarySearch()` to find an observation by its ID. Sorting and comparison strategies are used to support these methods.
template_adherence.consequences: Searching for Whale Observation objects with the same `sightingTime` or for a particular `ObservationId` is now possible.

alternatives.description: Use only iterator-based search methods for both date and ID searches.
pros: Simple implementation.
No need for sorting or comparator strategies.
cons: Potentially slower searches for ID as binary search is more efficient.
Less optimized for large datasets.

alternatives.description: Use `Collections.binarySearch()` for both date and ID searches after sorting.
pros: Efficient searches for both date and ID.
Consistent search approach.
cons: More complex implementation.
Requires sorting by date and ID, which may be costly or complex if multiple observations share the same date.

template_adherence.title: Model for transformations: Build own
template_adherence.context: The computation result of the winery yaml parser is a `TServiceTemplate.java`. The problem is whether plugins should deal with this model directly or if there is a more convenient way for plugin developers to access the TOSCA topology.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a convenient, type-safe, and clean data model for plugin developers, ease of use, maintainability, and the complexity or overhead introduced by alternative approaches such as EMF.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen alternative is to build own data model instead of reusing the TServiceTemplate or describing the metamodel with Eclipse EMF. This approach offers a cleaner data model, better object-oriented design, type safety, and convenience for plugin developers.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a clean data model, cleaner OO design, convenient usage for plugin developers, type safety, less code duplication, central definition of node types, and easier troubleshooting. Negative consequences include the need to maintain both UML diagrams and Java classes.

alternatives.description: Inherit from `TServiceTemplate` and extend it in some way, creating a new model with all classes in a different package inheriting from all model classes, adding new methods.
pros: `org.eclipse.winery.model.tosca.yaml` reused
cons: EMF Resource Set handling is implemented manually
Plugin developers have to deal with the model in an inconvenient way: types are not expressed via java classes leading to ugly OO design
Each plugin would have to define own classes of the supported node types and map contained elements individually

alternatives.description: Build own data model, modeling normative Node Types as Java classes and instances as NodeTemplates, accessible via a graph using jgrapht.
pros: Clean data model
Cleaner OO design
Convenient usage for plugin developers
Type safety
Less code duplication in plugins
Central definition of specific supported node types
Easier to troubleshoot due to strong typing
cons: Both UML diagram and Java classes need to be maintained

alternatives.description: Describe metamodel with Eclipse EMF and generate instance model, leveraging Resource Sets handling for transparency and synchronization of UML and code.
pros: Resource Sets handling provides transparent solution
UML and code stay synchronized
cons: Changing all the model to EMF causes huge overhead
Getting EMF into non-OSGi projects is hard
Team lacks knowledge of technology leading to high risk

template_adherence.title: Use Project Lombok in order to avoid writing boilerplate code
template_adherence.context:
The implemenation of the EffectiveModel must make use of the builder pattern (many optional parameters required for object construction).

Without the builder pattern, the model has approx. 2.5k loc. With the builder pattern, it grows to approx. 4k loc, due to the boilerplate nature of the pattern.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to reduce boilerplate code and maintain readability and maintainability of the EffectiveModel implementation, which uses the builder pattern with many optional parameters. Consideration of developer experience and tooling requirements.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen alternative is to use Lombok. This option was selected because it results in a significantly smaller code base, better maintainability and readability, and the ability to remove Lombok easily if needed. The downside is that every developer must install the Lombok plugin in their IDE and understand the annotations used.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a smaller and more maintainable code base, improved readability, and flexibility to remove Lombok if necessary. Negative consequences include introducing some 'black magic' to the codebase, requiring developers to learn Lombok annotations, and the need for IDE plugin installation.

alternatives.description: Use Lombok, an annotation-based framework to eliminate boilerplate code, supporting builder pattern, getters/setters, and more.
pros: Significantly smaller EffectiveModel code base
Better maintainability due to smaller code base
Better readability due to smaller code base
The 'delombok' feature allows easy removal of Lombok if needed
No boilerplate that can get out of sync if class changes
cons: Introduces more 'black magic' to the codebase
Developers have to know what each annotation does
Every developer has to install a plugin for their IDE (IntelliJ, Eclipse supported)

alternatives.description: Write boilerplate code manually.
pros: Pure vanilla Java
cons: Boilerplate code that might get out of sync when class changes

alternatives.description: Use Kotlin instead of Java.
pros: Lean language design
Similar positive effects as Lombok in terms of maintainability and readability
cons: Team (besides one member) doesn't know Kotlin
Kotlin is much harder to learn than Lombok

template_adherence.title: Implement own tosca parser
template_adherence.context: The project initially integrated the winery parser from the eclipse winery project to parse TOSCA YAML templates. However, the data structure provided by the winery parser, TServiceTemplate, was inconvenient due to its design around syntax rather than semantics, lack of type safety, and unresolved symbolic names. To address this, a new data structure, EffectiveModel, was created focusing on semantics, along with a converter from TServiceTemplate. Further complexity led to the vision of a ServiceGraph to better represent the model as a graph. Eventually, the idea emerged to bypass TServiceTemplate and parse directly into ServiceGraph using SnakeYAML, simplifying the workflow.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers were the inconvenience and complexity of using the winery parser's data structures, the need for semantic clarity and type safety, the desire to simplify the parsing workflow, and to reduce code complexity and maintenance burden. Concerns included the effort required to implement a new parser and the risk of missing aspects of the TOSCA specification.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to implement their own parser instead of reusing the winery yaml parser. This choice was made because the custom parser allowed for a simpler, more semantic-focused data structure, eliminated the need for converter logic, and resulted in a smaller code base. The winery parser is still used for syntax validation, but the main parsing is done by the custom parser.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a simpler and more semantic data model, reduced code complexity, and better maintainability. Negative consequences include the effort and risk involved in implementing and maintaining a custom parser. The winery parser remains in use for syntax validation, so some dependency remains.

template_adherence.title: 2. Adopt DDD approach
template_adherence.context:
`menu-generation` application's scope is not well defined and may cover a lot of concepts around the Menu generation features, such as:

- managing a recipes catalog
- searching in this catalog for recipes based on multiple criteria
- collaborating on this catalog
- handling allergies and tastes
- generating shopping lists

All above concepts may be complex to model and should not be considered as simple data in a CRUD system. Other new features may emerge in the future. In addition, all those features are related but should not be treated as a whole in a big ball of mud architecture.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to model complex and related concepts in the `menu-generation` application, the potential emergence of new features, and the desire to avoid a monolithic, tangled architecture (big ball of mud). The solution should support adaptability, clear separation of concerns, and maintainability.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt Domain-Driven Design (DDD) as defined by Eric Evans to model the different concepts, maintain adaptability, and split the application into bounded contexts to avoid mixing concepts in a large, messy codebase.
template_adherence.consequences: Focus on domain modeling with aggregates and services, using object-oriented programming to design domain objects. Domain objects will be kept infrastructure-agnostic to avoid mixing concerns. Aggregates will be isolated in dedicated packages with unidirectional dependencies to avoid cyclic dependencies. Different bounded contexts will emerge, potentially leading to splitting the application into different modules or services.
