template_adherence.title: Automate Metadata generation and signing
template_adherence.context:
The [eIDAS interoperability specification][eidas-interop] requires member states (MS) that are exporting identities to host a SAML metadata file for their proxy node so that requesting member state's connector node(s) can establish trust.

The SAML metadata contains the proxy node's entity ID and the public key used to sign its SAML responses. The metadata in turn needs to be signed by a private key and the public counterpart provided to the requesting MS. The metadata is only valid for a limited period of time and every time its contents change, for example if the signing key has been rotated, the metadata needs to be regenerated and resigned.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to establish trust between member states via signed SAML metadata, the use of a hardware security module (HSM) for key management, the requirement to automate metadata generation and signing to handle key rotations and metadata validity periods, and the desire to use the same signing key for both metadata and SAML responses.
template_adherence.decision: Automate the generation and signing of the metadata using the HSM for signing, performing this every time a new proxy node instance is spun up and at regular intervals according to metadata validity duration. Use a custom Kubernetes service to automate this process, issuing an X509 certificate for the private key in the HSM to be published in the metadata and provided out-of-band to requesting member states.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Introduction of another application that interacts with the HSM.
- Need to determine the duration of metadata validity.

alternatives.description: Manually generate and sign metadata without automation.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need for additional services or automation.
cons: Prone to human error and delays.
Difficult to maintain consistency and timely updates.
Not scalable for multiple proxy node instances.

alternatives.description: Use a third-party service or tool to handle metadata generation and signing.
pros: Leverages existing solutions.
Potentially reduces development effort.
cons: Dependency on external service reliability and security.
May not integrate well with existing HSM setup.
Less control over signing keys and process.

template_adherence.title: Deploy a proxy node per connector node
template_adherence.context:
The eIDAS specification states that member states (MS) requesting an eIDAS identity can operate one or more connector nodes. The MS exporting the identity, us in this case, should only operate one proxy node from the point of view of the requesting MS.

Trust between the connector node and proxy node is established by the connector consuming and verifying the proxy node's SAML metadata and vice versa. Verification of the metadata is accomplished using public keys exchanged by both parties out of band.

Therefore, from every MS that wishes to consume UK identities we will need:
- the URL from which to fetch their metadata
- a certificate which can be used to verify the signature of their metadata

In turn, we will provide our URL and certificate to the requesting MS.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to comply with eIDAS specification regarding proxy and connector nodes.
- Security concerns about key management and trust boundaries.
- Operational complexity and cost of managing services.
- Desire to limit impact of compromise to individual MS.
- Ease of implementation and maintenance.
template_adherence.decision:
Running a single instance of the proxy node services and infrastructure to handle requests from all potential requesting MS would need some way of aggregating their metadata. An additional service would most likely be required to do this, bringing with it the added cost of having to secure and administer that service, as it would end up being the root of trust for _all_ requesting MS. In our current implementation, a single proxy node would also mean a single signing key being used to export all UK identities to every requesting MS, making that key all the more valuable.

Instead, we will run one instance of the proxy node services and infrastructure isolation _per_ requesting MS connector node. They will share a single hardware security module (HSM) but will each have independent credentials to access the HSM and an independent signing key held by the HSM.

Having multiple instances running, one per requesting MS, would be fairly easy to implement and provides additional benefits, such as:
- a compromise to the infrastructure of one proxy node should not easily affect another
- the damage of compromising one proxy node's signing key is limited to a single requesting connector node
- signing key and metadata rotations can be performed on an individual connector node basis, removing the need to coordinate with multiple requesting MS
template_adherence.consequences:
- Having to maintain multiple entries in Terraform
- More complex deployment rollouts

alternatives.description: Run a single instance of the proxy node services and infrastructure to handle requests from all potential requesting MS.
pros: Simpler infrastructure with only one proxy node instance to manage.
Potentially easier deployment and maintenance due to fewer instances.
cons: Requires an additional service to aggregate metadata from all requesting MS.
Additional service would be the root of trust for all requesting MS, increasing risk.
Single signing key used for all UK identities, increasing value and risk if compromised.

template_adherence.title: Add service mesh for traceability
template_adherence.context:
eIDAS project has been challenged with some security concerns provided by National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). One of these concerns was a possibility for a connector application or the connection between given connector and the user being compromised and allow for stolen request IDs impersonate or create new identities.

Sadly, it's out of our control. We do however, have an obligation to monitor actions that are going through the system, in order to prove our innocence.

We have made a presumption, that Hardware Security Module (HSM) logs would be able to tell us when it has been used to sign a thing and attach it to some of the logs that we're currently holding.

This isn't however true for the version of HSM that is provided to us by AWS. We have managed to raise a feature request, which will not be coming for a while.
template_adherence.decision:
Reliability Engineering has proposed to implement tracing through the system with the use of Service Mesh. This requires our services to pass around a header in the requests. Cyber Security team, will then create some monitoring around these logs and alert when a path of the request is not performed in a correct order indicating the request is being injected. These logs would then be compared with a size of a body sent through to the HSM and back, to establish when that exact request has been signed.

This doesn't solve the problem entirely, but is good enough for now before we receive an appropriate solution from AWS.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Complexity around networking
- Additional burden to maintain

template_adherence.title: Separation of concerns
template_adherence.context: The SAML profile used by the eIDAS scheme requires that SAML messages are sent directly to the receiving proxy node via a user's browser. This introduces a host of security concerns, especially when we take the history of SAML exploits and XML security in general into account. Due to many of the attacks being centred around breaking XML parsing, the main concerns raised were of SAML being parsed by a public-facing service or the service responsible for communicating with the hardware security module (HSM). This suggests we can't implement the proxy node with a monolithic architecture.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Security concerns related to SAML message parsing, especially risks of XML parsing attacks; need to limit attack surface by separating responsibilities; desire to prevent a single compromised service from compromising vital services; use of Kubernetes to isolate sensitive microservices.
template_adherence.decision: The proxy node is split into a series of microservices, each with limited responsibilities. Kubernetes is used to ensure sensitive microservices do not run on the same node. This limits damage from compromising a single service and prevents compromising vital services via malicious XML.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Improved security by separation of concerns and limiting attack surface; Kubernetes isolation of services.
Negative: Increased maintenance overhead due to running multiple microservices.

template_adherence.title: Hashing the identity information
template_adherence.context:
The SAML profile used by the eIDAS scheme requires that SAML messages are sent directly to the receiving proxy node via a user's browser. This introduces a host of security concerns, especially when we take the history of SAML exploits and XML security in general into account. Due to many of the attacks being centred around breaking XML parsing, the main concerns raised were of SAML being parsed by a public-facing service or the service responsible for communicating with the hardware security module (HSM). With all this considered, the role of the SAML parsing has been assigned to the Verify Service Provider (VSP).

We need to have confidence that the identity information we are sending back to the Member State is the same as the identity information which was originally issued by the identity provider (IDP). The Gateway service will receieve a SAML response back from the Hub which is sent to the Translator service, before being passed onto the VSP which will parse the response. Due to the exploits surrounding XML parsing, we need to be confident that the VSP hasn't been compromised, as it could result in manipulated attributes being sent to the Translator which would ultimately result in fraudulent identities being sent back to a Member State.
template_adherence.decision: To ensure that we are confident that the identity information we are sending back to the Member State is the same as what was originally issued by the IDP, we will LOG to monitoring a secure one-way SHA-256 hash of the user attributes in the Verify Hub and within the Translator service in the eIDAS Proxy Node. Any mismatches between the two Hashes will trigger an alert.
template_adherence.consequences: - This would be more beneficial to be implemented as a technical control, to have a higher confidence that no malicious transactions are approved.

template_adherence.title: Allow dynamic loading of Yetibot plugins via config
template_adherence.context:
Yetibot currently resides across two primary repos:

- github.com/yetibot/yetibot
- github.com/yetibot/yetibot-core

template_adherence.decision:
Switching to a plugin system allows us to split up the code base into much more
fine grained, logical units. For example, we may split the `github` command into
its own plugin.

The first plugin is [yetibot-kroki](https://github.com/yetibot/yetibot-kroki).

template_adherence.title: Handle `print` CSS rules in ECL
template_adherence.context:
- There is currently no `print` stylesheets on ECL.
- `print` display is the same as `screen` display, i.e. the CSS is applied for both media.
- Users should be able to print ECL components — and pages built with ECL — if needed. `print` display should only contain relevant content with the minimum styling, in order to facilitate a better printing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support printing of ECL components and pages.
- Keep `print` CSS minimal and relevant.
- Maintain separation of `screen` and `print` styles.
- Ease of maintenance and clarity in CSS structure.
- Performance considerations in loading stylesheets.
template_adherence.decision:
We generate `screen` and `print` styles in 2 separated files.
We don't create any global reset for `print`.
We apply `print` CSS per component, using the component's classes.
We aim to keep the `print` CSS as small as possible.
We create design tokens for `print` display.
template_adherence.consequences:
- A dedicated stylesheet has to be created. Each component (or at least most of them) will have a dedicated SCSS file or mixin used to generate the `print` styles.
- The existing ECL stylesheets should only be loaded for the `screen` media; the `print` stylesheets should only be loaded for the `print` media. The way the stylesheets are loaded on the ECL website needs to be updated.

alternatives.description: One stylesheet for everything: `screen` and `print` CSS rules in a single CSS file with `@media print` sections.
pros: Single CSS file to manage.
Simpler HTML includes.
cons: Mixes `screen` and `print` styles, potentially harder to maintain.
All styles loaded regardless of media, possibly impacting performance.

alternatives.description: Two separated stylesheets: separate CSS files for `screen` and `print` media.
pros: Clear separation of styles.
Only relevant styles loaded per media, improving performance.
cons: More files to manage.
Requires changes in stylesheet loading logic.

alternatives.description: Separate `screen` and `print` CSS rules grouped separately.
pros: Clear separation of styles.
cons: Need to define CSS rules for each component for `print` media.

alternatives.description: Define common rules and override for `print`.
pros: Less duplication, only override needed rules.
cons: Overrides can be complex and harder to track.

alternatives.description: Separate all styles into common, `screen`, and `print`.
pros: Clear separation and no duplication.
cons: Harder to read and maintain.
Requires updating existing CSS.

alternatives.description: Start without CSS for `print`, relying on default display and global CSS rules.
pros: Simpler initial implementation.
cons: Less control over `print` styles.
May require global CSS rules and later per-component additions.

template_adherence.title: Define which browsers we support
template_adherence.context: The main tools we use (babel-preset-env for the JavaScript, autoprefixer for the CSS) rely on browserslist in order to derive the list of browsers they are supposed to support. Before creating this decision record, our browserslist configuration file contained a certain set of queries which roughly translated to a list of browsers. The latest version of the IPG defines a set of minimum browser versions that must be supported, and also specifies that all European Commission websites must offer an optimal browsing experience on every browser which has been used by at least 2% of its total users in the last 12 months. Since we can't build a specific version of ECL for every website, we expand the scope to target browsers with > 0.5% usage in European countries in the last month. We also know that EC computers can use Firefox ESR, so we include that in the configuration. If a project needs a different configuration, it will have to create a custom build of ECL.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support minimum browser versions as requested by the IPG.
- Need to support browsers with more than 0.5% usage in Europe according to StatCounter.
- Need to support Firefox ESR used by EC computers.
- Tools like babel-preset-env and autoprefixer rely on browserslist configuration.
- The configuration should be maintainable and reflect real usage.
- The decision should allow for updates as browser usage and IPG requirements evolve.
template_adherence.decision: The final decision is a mix of alternatives 1.1 and 2.1. We support the minimum browser versions requested by the IPG and all browsers with more than 0.5% usage in Europe according to StatCounter. We also support Firefox ESR. The browserslist configuration is explicitly defined with these criteria. This approach balances fixed minimum versions with dynamic usage-based selection.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to keep caniuse-lite up-to-date.
- Need to update the configuration whenever the IPG updates its requirements.
- Need to properly communicate which browser versions are covered at the time of the build.
- The configuration will evolve over time as browser usage statistics and IPG requirements change.
- Projects needing different configurations must create custom builds.
- The approach ensures a balance between predictability and adaptability to real usage.

alternatives.description: Base configuration with a list of fixed versions (e.g., ie 11, Chrome 55, safari 12, iOS 7).
pros: Predictable and consistent list of supported browsers.
cons: Maintaining a static list can be cumbersome.
Does not adapt automatically to changes in browser usage or versions.

alternatives.description: Dynamic queries based on usage statistics (e.g., > 1%, > 1% in alt-EU).
pros: Easy to understand and automatically updated when caniuse-lite is updated.
cons: Stats may not reflect the true audience of EC websites.

alternatives.description: Alternative 1.1: "BROWSER > VERSION" - support all versions greater than a fixed version.
pros: Ensures coverage of all versions above a certain version.
cons: Requires manual updates when older versions are no longer supported.

alternatives.description: Alternative 1.2: "last X BROWSER versions" - support last X versions of browsers.
pros: Automatically drops old browsers.
Useful for evergreen browsers.
cons: Some browsers might get dropped inadvertently.
Does not make sense to combine with "BROWSER > VERSION" queries.

alternatives.description: Alternative 2.2: Based on custom stats from Matomo or other analytics.
pros: Reflects true audience of EC websites as a whole.
cons: Requires work to adapt stats to browserslist.
Requires maintenance and frequent updates.

template_adherence.title: Handle `editor` CSS rules in ECL
template_adherence.context:
- Content editor of sites using ECL may have to use basic html markup instead of custom CSS classes (example: wysiwyg editor) - A global class `ecl-editor` was provided in ECL1, with adapted design for default html tags (`

`, `

    `, ``, etc.) - `ecl-editor` rules are only provided for a few components on ECL2 (blockquotes and links), and missing for some others As we have to add missing editor rules, we could take some time to think about the best way to handle them. Currently these rules are added the same way it was done in ECL1: - a mixin file containing the CSS rules - a CSS file for component - a CSS file for editor rules related to this component) All editor CSS rules are part of the `dev` preset, and so are integrated in all other presets
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle missing editor CSS rules for ECL components
- Desire to keep components small and maintainable
- Consideration of BEM compliance and CSS duplication
- Ease of use for developers
- Clear separation between core ECL and editor-specific styles
template_adherence.decision:
- All editor CSS rules are put in a new package `@ecl/ec-editor`.
- CSS is duplicated from component (no SASS mixins).
- A new preset `ec-preset-editor` is created to store these rules.

- Clear separation of editor CSS rules from core components
- Components remain small and unmodified
- Duplication of CSS rules may increase maintenance effort

template_adherence.title: Handle `themes` in ECL v3
template_adherence.context:
- ECL v2 was made in order to generate two independent design systems, EC and EU.
- ECL V3 starts from the assumption that there is only one source template and one design system with multiple `themes`.
- The number of themes to accommodate is not set as of the time of the document writing, thus the magnitude could vary between 2 (previous systems) to 20+.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR is driven by the need to manage multiple themes in ECL v3 efficiently, reduce code duplication, handle resource organization, and address uncertainties in publishing and tooling (e.g., Storybook). The drivers include scalability, maintainability, complexity reduction, and clarity in package and resource management.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to manage themes as separate packages (Option 4) and resources as separate packages (Option 1). This approach was chosen over other options due to complexity and limitations in SASS, and to better organize code and resources.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Ongoing discussions about the definition of "theme" and its overlap with presets.
- Need for improved CSS source code organization to scale and reduce complexity.
- Changes required in release packages and uncertainty about publishing themes.
- Potential changes in Storybook applications, with unclear approach to multiple themes.
- Uncertainty in managing other assets like JavaScript, markdown, icons, templates, and environment variables.

template_adherence.title: Apply ECL 3 styling to some HTML tags
template_adherence.context:
- Styling of some HTML tags (without CSS class) has been a redundant request from some ECL users
- In ECL 2, package `ecl-editor` was provided as a workaround. It worked quite well, but ended up raising some CSS conflict issues like [FRONT-1697](https://citnet.tech.ec.europa.eu/CITnet/jira/browse/FRONT-1697)
- In ECL 3 we shoud come with a more robust way to handle this, without disturbing the recommanded way to use ECL (by adding CSS classes)
- We have no control over the final markup of pages. So we can't rely on any markup based selectors (like `>`, `+`, ...)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to provide styling for some HTML tags without CSS classes
- Avoid CSS conflicts and leaks
- Maintain compatibility with ECL recommended usage (CSS classes)
- Support utilities usage
- Provide an optional CSS or preset
- Avoid frequent code updates for new components/utilities
template_adherence.decision: Option 4: global namespace excluding ecl components, but including utilities was chosen because it prevents CSS leaks, does not override components, and still works with utilities, despite producing a more verbose CSS file.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Robust styling solution that avoids CSS leaks and conflicts
- Positive: Compatible with utilities and components
- Negative: More verbose CSS file
- Negative: Slightly more complex CSS rules

alternatives.description: Style elements directly, e.g., h1 { ... }, button { ... }
pros: Easy to override for components due to very low specificity
cons: No easy way to prevent CSS leak to other elements on the page
Not robust, likely to cause unwanted side effects

alternatives.description: Global namespace, e.g., .ecl h1 { ... }, .ecl button { ... }
pros: No CSS leak
cons: All components must use `.ecl` namespace, breaking BEM structure
Impacts all ECL users

alternatives.description: Global namespace excluding ecl components, e.g., .ecl h1:not([class*="ecl-"]) { ... }
pros: No CSS leak
No override of components
cons: Targets elements using utilities, preventing default styling when utilities are added

alternatives.description: Global namespace excluding ecl components, but including utilities, e.g., .ecl h1:not([class*="ecl-"]), .ecl h1:is([class*="ecl-u-"]) { ... }
pros: No CSS leak
No override of components
Works with utilities
cons: More verbose CSS file

- profound understanding of the domain and required functionality
- generalized business entities / resources, i.e. avoidance of use case specific APIs
- clear separation of WHAT vs. HOW concerns, i.e. abstraction from implementation aspects — APIs should be stable even if we replace complete service implementation including its underlying technology stack

pros: Enables early review feedback

template_adherence.title: Notifications - Email Service
template_adherence.context:
PIMS requires a way to send email notifications to agencies throughout the workflow of disposing properties.

Use Cases;

- Whitelist of agencies who will receive emails
- Inform all agencies of a new properties in the Enhanced Referral Program (ERP)
- A way for agencies to show interest, or to opt out of further notifications
- Inform all agencies of status change or progress of properties in ERP
- Inform owning agency of status change of disposal project
- Notify owning agency of requirement or information

The **Common Hosted Email Service (CHES)** is a free service offered and supported by the **Exchange Lab**.

Additional Information here;

- [Common Services Showcase](https://bcgov.github.io/common-service-showcase/)
- [Common Hosted Email Service](https://bcgov.github.io/common-service-showcase/#CHES)
- [GetOk](https://getok.pathfinder.gov.bc.ca/getok/about)
- [GetOk - PIMS](https://getok.pathfinder.gov.bc.ca/getok/apps/PIMS)
- [ReDoc](https://ches-master-9f0fbe-prod.pathfinder.gov.bc.ca/api/v1/docs)
- [GitHub](https://github.com/bcgov/common-hosted-email-service)
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need for a reliable email notification system for PIMS.
Desire to leverage existing supported services to reduce development and maintenance effort.
Requirement to support features like attachments, scheduling, bulk email, HTML/plain text, and tracking.
Need to handle asynchronous notifications and failure management.
Requirement to maintain message tracking and template management within PIMS.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to integrate with the Common Hosted Email Service (CHES) for email notifications rather than building a new solution.
This includes leveraging CHES features such as sending emails with attachments, scheduling, bulk email merges, and tracking.
Additionally, PIMS will develop features to maintain message IDs, handle asynchronous notification failures, and manage message templates.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include not having to build or support an email notification system, and benefiting from internal support and knowledge sharing as CHES is used by other projects.
Negative consequences include lack of SLA and no UI application support for CHES.

alternatives.description: Build a custom email notification system within PIMS instead of integrating with CHES.
pros: Full control over features and SLA.
Custom UI and support tailored to PIMS needs.
cons: Higher development and maintenance effort.
Requires building and supporting infrastructure from scratch.
Lack of existing internal support and knowledge sharing.

alternatives.description: Integrate with another third-party email service instead of CHES.
pros: Potentially better SLA or features.

template_adherence.title: ADR 0001: Multiple Roots Under the Tendermint Application Hash
template_adherence.context: Currently the Tendermint ABCI application hash is equal to the consensus state root for a specific height. In order to allow additional uses, like proving to light clients that specific events have been emitted in a block, we should make the application hash be derivable from potentially different kinds of roots.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support additional uses such as proving to light clients that specific events have been emitted in a block, requiring the application hash to be derived from multiple roots rather than a single consensus state root.
template_adherence.decision: The proposed design is to derive the Tendermint ABCI application hash by hashing all the different roots using SHA-512/256, concatenating a context string and all root hashes. Implementation changes include updating the ABCI multiplexer and consensus API to handle multiple roots.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Enables inclusion of different kinds of provable data as part of consensus-layer blocks.
Negative: Breaking change for consensus layer; all roots must be included in signed headers.
Neutral: Consensus state checkpoints need to handle multiple roots.

alternatives.description: Merkelize the roots in a binary Merkle tree to handle multiple roots.
pros: Potentially more scalable for a large number of roots.
cons: Adds complexity.
Likely requires more round trips for common use cases.

template_adherence.title: Go Modules Compatible Git Tags
template_adherence.context: Projects that depend on Oasis Core's Go module need a way to depend on its particular version. Go Modules only allow Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 for versioning of the modules which makes it hard to work with Oasis Core's CalVer (calendar versioning) scheme. The currently used scheme for Go Modules compatible Git tags omits the MICRO version if it is zero, which only works for versions with MICRO zero, thus incompatible with Go Modules versioning requirements.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to support Go Modules versioning requirements, compatibility with Go tools, and ability to depend on specific bugfix/patch releases. Avoid treating versions as pre-release to ensure proper update notifications and version resolution.
template_adherence.decision: Tag Oasis Core releases with Go Modules compatible Git tags in the format go/v0.YY0MINOR.MICRO, where YY is the short year, 0MINOR is the zero-padded minor version, and MICRO is the patch segment. This scheme ensures compatibility with Go Modules versioning requirements and enables users to use Go tools effectively.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Allows users to depend on bugfix/patch releases in a Go Modules compatible way without pinning to commits. Negative: The connection between ordinary Git tags and Go Modules compatible tags is not obvious, and zero-padding minor version limits releases per year to 100.

alternatives.description: Use Go Modules compatible Git tags with a -MICRO suffix to denote patch versions, e.g., go/v0.YY.MINOR-MICRO.
pros: Simple to implement.
Follows a straightforward extension of existing versioning.
cons: Go treats such versions as pre-release versions.
Go tools would not notify users of updates properly.
go get @latest would not fetch the real latest version if it has a -MICRO suffix.

template_adherence.title: ADR 0003: Consensus/Runtime Token Transfer
template_adherence.context: Currently each runtime can define its own token (or none at all) and there is no mechanism that would support transfer of consensus layer tokens into a runtime and back out. Introducing such a mechanism would allow the consensus layer tokens to be used inside runtimes for various functions. This ADR proposes such a mechanism.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to enable consensus layer tokens to be used inside runtimes, the requirement for secure and controlled token transfers, and the necessity to prevent token loss or misuse by malicious or faulty runtimes.
template_adherence.decision: The proposal adds support for consensus/runtime token transfers by allowing staking accounts to set allowances for beneficiaries and by assigning each runtime an account in the consensus layer. Transfers are controlled via messages emitted by runtimes during rounds, with mechanisms for discrepancy detection and message execution results. This design balances flexibility, security, and operational constraints.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling token transfers into and out of runtimes and controlled token availability. Negative consequences include risks of token theft by malicious runtimes, token locking due to runtime suspension, and potential user errors causing token loss. Neutral consequences involve the runtime's responsibility to handle message results properly.

alternatives.description: Do not implement a mechanism for transferring consensus tokens into runtimes, leaving runtimes to define their own tokens independently.
pros: Simpler system without added complexity of token transfer mechanisms.
No risk of tokens being locked or stolen due to runtime issues.
cons: Runtimes cannot leverage consensus layer tokens, limiting functionality.
No unified token management across consensus and runtimes.

alternatives.description: Allow direct transfers into runtime accounts without allowance controls or message-based execution.
pros: Simpler transfer mechanism without allowance management.
Potentially easier for users to transfer tokens.
cons: High risk of tokens being locked if transferred incorrectly.
No control over token spending by runtimes, increasing security risks.

template_adherence.title: Runtime Compute Node Slashing
template_adherence.context:
The runtime compute nodes make updates to the runtime state by submitting commitment messages to the roothash service in the consensus layer where discrepancy detection and resolution are performed.

Currently, the compute nodes are never slashed even if they commit incorrect results. While integrity is guarded by discrepancy detection and resolution, compute nodes should be disincentivized to behave incorrectly.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to disincentivize misbehaving compute nodes by introducing slashing mechanisms; ensure integrity and correctness of runtime state updates; handle evidence of misbehavior; maintain system performance and state management; consider impact on runtime determinism and node liveness.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a slashing mechanism for punishing misbehaving compute nodes with per-runtime configurable slashing parameters, new runtime-specific slashing reasons, failure-indicating executor commits, updated runtime descriptor and staking parameters, evidence submission and verification methods, and consensus parameters for evidence expiry.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Compute nodes can be disincentivized to submit incorrect results.
Negative: Additional state and processing overhead for storing and expiring evidence; risk of slashing due to runtime non-determinism.
Neutral: No slashing for liveness or freezing misbehaving nodes introduced.

alternatives.description: Do not introduce slashing for runtime compute nodes and rely solely on discrepancy detection and resolution to maintain integrity.
pros: Simpler system without additional slashing complexity.
No additional state or processing overhead for evidence management.
cons: No direct disincentive for misbehaving compute nodes.
Potentially weaker enforcement of correct behavior.

alternatives.description: Introduce global slashing parameters only, without per-runtime configurable parameters.
pros: Simpler configuration and management.
Uniform slashing policy across all runtimes.
cons: Less flexibility to tailor slashing to specific runtime needs.
May not adequately address runtime-specific behaviors or risks.

template_adherence.title: ADR 0012: Runtime Message Results
template_adherence.context: Currently, the results of emitted runtime messages are `MessageEvent`s, which only provide information whether the message execution was successful or not. For various use-cases additional information about message results would be useful. One of such is supporting staking by runtimes. Currently, a runtime can emit an `AddEscrow` message, but is unaware of the actual amount of shares it obtained as a result of the added escrow. For some use-cases (e.g. runtime staking user deposited funds) this information is crucial for accounting. Similarly, for `ReclaimEscrow`, the runtime doesn't have the direct information at which epoch the stake gets debonded. The only way to currently obtain this data is to subscribe to consensus events, something which runtime doesn't have access to. Adding results to `MessageEvent` solves both of the mentioned use cases: - for `AddEscrow` the result should contain amount of shares obtained with the escrow - for `ReclaimEscrow` the result should contain the amount of shares and epoch at which the stake gets debonded
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to provide additional information about message execution results beyond success/failure, especially for staking use-cases. The limitation that runtimes cannot subscribe to consensus events directly. The desire to keep the solution simple and integrated with existing message event mechanisms. The requirement to support arbitrary result data in message events to cover various message types.
template_adherence.decision: Implement support for arbitrary result data in `MessageEvent` runtime message results by adding a `Result` field to the `roothash.MessageEvent` struct and updating relevant interfaces (`MessageSubscriber`, `MessageDispatcher`) to propagate execution results. This enables runtimes to obtain detailed message execution results via `MessageEvents` in `RoundResults`.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Enables runtimes to support staking functionality by accessing detailed message execution results. Negative: Introduces breaking changes to message event structures and interfaces. Neutral: None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Add support to runtimes for subscribing to consensus events.
pros: Provides direct access to consensus events data.
cons: More heavyweight and complex solution.
Not currently accessible to runtimes.
Less simple than message events solution.

template_adherence.title: Marain Service List and Instance Manifests
template_adherence.context: The desire to define formally and unambiguously what are the component parts of a Marain instance. (An 'instance' is one deployed set of services operating in isolation from any other instance. We maintain a dev instance separate from any production use. Where customers use Marain services but are not using endjin's hosted production instance, they have their own instance.)
template_adherence.decision:
The `Marain.Instance` repo (this repo) includes a master service list, `Solutions/MarainServices.jsonc`. This JSON (with comments) file contains an entry for each service that can be part of a Marain instance. This gives a name to the service (e.g. `Marain.Tenancy`) and identifies the GitHub project in which the service is defined. It also defines an API prefix, for use in scenarios where all services are made available behind a single API management layer—the API prefix indicates what the first part of the URL should be at the API gateway for accessing the relevant service.

Whereas `MarainServices.jsonc` is common to all instances, each instance also defines a manifest. This determines whether particular services are deployed to a particular instance, and if so which version.
template_adherence.consequences: By putting this information in JSON (or JSONC) files with a narrowly defined purpose it is very easy to see exactly what services can go into a Marain instance, and which particular versions are deployed to a particular instance. It also drives the automaticed deployment process implemented by `Deploy-MarainInstanceInfrastructure.ps1`.

template_adherence.title: Services use ARM and AAD indirectly through common mechanisms
template_adherence.context:
Historically, our automated deployment scripts have tended to include a large amount of common boilerplate. This is partly because they are self-contained—they can typically be run on their own to perform a deployment. And it is partly just because they originate from what the Visual Studio tooling creates.

The problem with this is that it makes the project-specific details hard to spot. When looking at a sea of code that's almost identical to every other project, it's hard to see what it's doing that is in any way different from everything else.
template_adherence.decision:
With `Marain.Instance`, deployment scripts in individual services do not communicate directly with either ARM or Azure AD. (They should not even be aware of what mechanisms are being used to perform this work—they should not need to know whether we are using the PowerShell Az module, the az CLI or even custom library code to talk to Azure, for example.)

Anything that needs to be done either in Azure or AAD must be done through operations provided by the shared `Marain.Instance` code. It passes in an object that provides various methods that provide the necessary services.
template_adherence.consequences:
The amount of deployment code required in individual services is drastically reduced. What remains expresses the particular requirements of the service in question.

The main downside is that if a service has unusual requirements, `Marain.Instance` needs to be modified to make the necessary new capability available.

template_adherence.title: PowerShell Core 6 Deployment Scripts
template_adherence.context: Deployment requirements need to be expressed somehow—either declaratively or in a programming language.
template_adherence.decision: Individual Marain services express their deployment requirements in the form of a set of PowerShell scripts. These will be run in PowerShell core v6.
template_adherence.consequences:
The advantage of a programming language over data structures is deployment scripts can make decisions if they need to. There's an automatic level of flexibility. PowerShell is a scripting language, meaning that there's relatively low complexity when it comes to getting things runnable—services don't need to build their deployment code, they just need to make script files available. Using PowerShell Core means we have the option to run on Linux.

The downside is that PowerShell gets a bit messy for anything non-trivial. You end up wanting to create modules, at which point you now need a means of installing the module (which also tends to complicate the development of the code that gets installed as a module).

template_adherence.title: Azure pipeline security model
template_adherence.context: This ADR defines an approach for a pipeline security management process. It enables application deployment pipelines to perform all tasks associated with the deployment of typical Azure PaaS-based solutions, in a way that adheres to the principle of least privilege and supports oversight and audit requirements. The process allows teams to manage their own configuration with minimal friction, while facilitating centralized oversight when needed. It outlines common tasks pipelines need to perform and how these are typically achieved today.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to adhere to the principle of least privilege, support oversight and audit requirements, enable teams to manage their own configuration with minimal friction, and facilitate centralized oversight. The solution must support typical pipeline tasks such as resource creation, role assignments, querying and managing Azure Active Directory applications and service principals, and must integrate with Azure DevOps pipelines and service connections.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a configuration model maintained in a Git repository that defines security requirements for Azure DevOps service connections. A security management pipeline reads this configuration and ensures least privilege service connections per application and environment. The pipeline maintains resource groups, custom roles, AAD service principals, role assignments, and permissions. The pipeline runs with high-level permissions but is tightly controlled via Azure DevOps project restrictions, branch protection, and pull request review policies.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include autonomous pipelines for development teams, security teams having review and approval responsibilities without direct operational support, correction of configuration drift, and a full audit trail via version-controlled configuration. Negative consequences include potential long pipeline run times with large configurations, the pipeline becoming a single point of failure, complexity in handling deletions and renames in configuration, and lack of support for credential key-rotation synchronization.

pros: Simple and does not require automation.

pros: Supports automation with controlled elevated permissions.

template_adherence.title: 7. Barcode Querying
template_adherence.context: We've been using Barcode values that have been recorded as either private (associated only with an organization) or global (available to all organizations). The idea was that Essentials Banks could decide to "Share" a barcode with everyone by making it global, and that this barcode could then be used by others. The implementation, as well as the actual use-cases by Essentials Banks in beta testing, has contraindicated this utility. Additionally, it's unclear how Barcode lookup happens with regard to Base Items.
template_adherence.decision:
"Global" barcodes are associated with Base Items. Doing a Barcode lookup now does a cascade retrieval.

1. First, it checks if the organization has defined a barcode with that value.
2. If that exists, then it uses that record.
3. If it doesn't exist, then it checks to see if that barcode value exists as a global barcode.
4. If it exists there, it gets the base item associated with that, and then looks at the organizations items and finds the oldest item with that base item type, and applies it to that.
5. If it can't find one for that, then it prompts the user to create a new barcode record.

When we get EAN13 numbers for major products, we can enter those as global barcodes, associated with the generic base items; eg. 48x Pampers 3T and 48x Huggies 3T will both map to the 48x 3T record.
template_adherence.consequences: The primary benefit is that the barcodes will just magically work for most major products (when we get EAN13s entered), while still allowing the organizations to customize to their liking. It's possible since the inference is just assuming the oldest item of that base item type, that it will point to the "wrong" record, but we've yet to encounter that bug report.

template_adherence.title: Secure JSON Output
template_adherence.context:
We are working on a new feature of Form Builder where a form creator (user) can opt to have submissions (citizen answers) sent as JSON to an endpoint of their choosing. These endpoints can be any url, but will likely be CMS or case management systems.

The first use case of this is the HMCTS complaints form. This form requires an integration to HMCTS' Optics system. We will be creating a custom adapter that receives the JSON output from Form Builder, and then generates the complaint in Optics. This adapter will live outside the Form Builder infrastructure. In the future, the hope is that teams will create their own adapters in order to integrate Form Builder with various external systems.

This ADR is regarding how to secure this JSON output from Form Builder to the endpoint set by the user.

Threats
- Payload may be intercepted, exposing sensitive user answers.
- Payload may be modified in transit, with potentially damaging consequences.
- POST requests could be made to the receiver (adapter) from sources other than Form Builder, creating records in their systems that don't reflect user submissions.

Risks
- Reputational damage due to data breaches
- Security threats from modified payloads

Mistakes from the User
- Users could potentially enter an incorrect endpoint, which would deliver sensitive data to an incorrect endpoint.
- Users could share security information accidentally, allowing malicious actors to receive payloads.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to secure JSON output from Form Builder to user-defined endpoints.
- Protect sensitive user data from interception and modification.
- Prevent unauthorized POST requests to adapters.
- Minimize management overhead.
- Ensure ease of use for non-technical users.
- Compliance with MOJ security standards.
- Validation of user-entered endpoints to ensure HTTPS and domain restrictions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use TLS over HTTP (HTTPS) combined with encrypted JSON payloads using JWE and a shared secret for encryption/decryption. Mutual TLS was rejected due to management overhead. A shared secret is preferred over certificates for ease of use by non-technical users. The shared secret will be system-generated and set as an environment variable. The Form Builder system will validate user-entered endpoints to ensure they are HTTPS and within the '*.gov.uk' domain. The solution involves Form Builder connecting to adapters via HTTPS, encrypting JSON payloads with the shared secret, and adapters decrypting the payloads accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: The chosen solution achieves the desired level of security with an easy implementation for users building future adapters. It ensures encrypted data in transit and payload encryption to protect sensitive data even within internal networks. The approach balances security with usability by avoiding complex certificate management and relying on shared secrets. Endpoint validation reduces risks from user mistakes. Overall, it mitigates reputational and security risks associated with data breaches and unauthorized data modification.

alternatives.description: Use mutual TLS for authentication and encryption between Form Builder and adapters.
pros: Provides strong authentication and encryption.
Ensures only authorized clients can connect.
cons: High management overhead for certificate issuance and renewal.
Complexity for non-technical users.
May be overkill for the use case.

alternatives.description: Use TLS alone without payload encryption.
pros: Simpler implementation.
Standard security practice for data in transit.
cons: TLS is often terminated at network edges, leaving data unencrypted inside networks.
Does not protect against internal network threats or impersonation.

alternatives.description: Use certificates for signing and de-serializing payloads instead of shared secrets.
pros: Strong cryptographic assurance.
Widely used in secure communications.
cons: Requires users to generate and upload certificates.
Too complex for non-technical users.
Management overhead.

One category of data which can be present is that of files in the form of documents, images and other files users may upload as part of their form submission. The ADR discusses considerations such as security, ease of implementation, and integration, and explores various options for including files in JSON output.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include security concerns (encryption at rest and in transit), ease of implementation and maintenance, integration ease for receiving systems, scalability, reliability, and constraints related to file retention and access (e.g., S3 signed URL expiry). Also considered are the responsibilities of Form Builder versus external adapters, and the trade-offs between pushing files versus letting receivers pull them.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt option 6: Store and serve PSK-encrypted files directly from S3. This approach expects the receiver to retrieve files, moves files to a separate S3 bucket with different permissions, encrypts files with a pre-shared key, serves files encrypted with native S3 signed URLs valid for one week, and places responsibility for decryption on the receiver. This option balances security, scalability, and maintenance concerns without requiring a proxy application.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include risks that unintended audiences could access files if information is leaked, but benefits include making files in form submissions available outside Form Builder via a JSON API, facilitating integration with other systems. Files remain encrypted throughout the Form Builder ecosystem except at certain processing points, enhancing security. The approach clarifies responsibilities and avoids building a proxy application, aiding feasibility within project timescales.

template_adherence.title: 4. Microservice authentication
template_adherence.context:
There are currently 3 different ways that microservices talk to each other in the form builder platform JWT, JWE and API keys.

Consistency can benefit the service by keeping a minimum of protection across all endpoints and help developers better understand the system.

Constraints:

- Backend services should not be allowed to make arbitrary calls with each other without the authorisation of a `runner` form submission.
- The `runner` should be the only service able to authorise new submissions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for consistent authentication method across microservices.
- Security constraints preventing arbitrary calls between backend services.
- Desire to leverage JWT features such as signed tokens and claims.
- Maintain existing user data protection while integrating with JWT.
template_adherence.decision: JWT was chosen as the authentication mechanism for microservices. The frontend `runner` holds the private key to sign JWT tokens, which are included in request headers. Backend services verify these tokens using public keys obtained from a token API, ensuring requests originate from active forms. This approach prevents backend services from making arbitrary calls as they do not hold private keys. User data protection continues via encrypted tokens incorporated into the JWT `sub` claim.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Arbitrary requests between APIs are prevented, enhancing security.
- Future permission restrictions can leverage JWT claim headers, such as token expiry.
- Requested data is not inside the JWT token and thus not signed, which may have implications for data integrity verification.

alternatives.description: Continue using multiple authentication methods (JWT, JWE, API keys) as is.
pros: No immediate changes required.
Existing systems continue to function without modification.
cons: Inconsistency in authentication methods can cause confusion.
Potential security risks due to varied protection levels.
Harder for developers to understand and maintain the system.

alternatives.description: Use API keys exclusively for microservice authentication.
pros: Simplifies authentication to a single method.
API keys are straightforward to implement and manage.
cons: API keys can be less secure if not managed properly.
Lacks the flexibility and features of JWT such as claims and expiry.
Does not prevent arbitrary calls between services effectively.

template_adherence.title: 6 Reduce the number of emails per submission
template_adherence.context:
Form Builder sends one email per file uploaded for each application. For those forms that allow multiple files to be uploaded this generates a lot of email noise for both form owners and the applicants. This can result in additional work to sift these emails or even create unforced errors in workflows that are manual in nature.

The use of AWS SES as the email service means that there is a 10MB upper limit on the size of each email that is sent.

Options discussed:

1. Attach as many files as possible to a single email up to the 10MB limit.

2. Hard cap limit on 10MB in total accross _all_ the files uploaded per form.

3. Admin interface for form owners to log in and retrieve file uploads per submission.

4. Email a link to the form owner allowing the ability to download all attachments in one go.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Reduce email noise for form owners and applicants; minimize manual workflow errors; respect AWS SES 10MB email size limit; minimize code changes and architectural impact; avoid increasing threat surface.
template_adherence.decision: Option 1 (Attach as many files as possible to a single email up to the 10MB limit) was chosen as it is the most reasonable solution at this time, requiring the least amount of code change and not changing the architecture or increasing the threat surface of Form Builder.
template_adherence.consequences: Recipients will receive fewer emails per Form Builder submission, typically a single email with multiple attachments, though sending more than one email remains possible. This change applies across all forms using Form Builder.

template_adherence.title: 7. Replacing the storage
template_adherence.context:
The center of the Form Builder Platform is the form metadata, which is a collection of json files. These files are created by the Editor application and stored into Github using Git to version and transfer. The Editor does not interact with any of the services instead it produces a collection of files which is finally stored into Github. A link to Github is then used by the Publisher to obtain the files and create the form online.

Github was chosen due to it giving transparency, versioning, some form of collaboration, data ownership and it could be integrated to the local services easily being built. Another reason was that the user base for Form Builder would be Developers who would have an understanding of version control and git and therefore be beneficial.

Why the change

There is a shift in the product proposal moving from a supported model to a full self service model, this has shown that using git and github is a blocker or at least friction point for new users. Also, to facilitate this move to being a true Self Service platform the method of user intervention between the editor and the publisher.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Shift from supported model to full self service model; git and github usage is a blocker for new users; need to reduce user intervention between editor and publisher; maintain form builder principles; ensure data availability only through authorized applications; ensure versioning and disaster recovery.
template_adherence.decision: Remove the use of git and github to store the form metadata and move saving the form metadata from github to a database with an API to manage it.
template_adherence.consequences: The form data will not be stored in public by default, which improves data privacy. This can be mitigated in a future release if needed.

alternatives.description: Continue using git and github for storing form metadata.
pros: Provides transparency, versioning, and collaboration.
Integrates easily with local services.
Familiar to developer user base.
cons: Acts as a blocker or friction point for new users.
Not suitable for a full self service model.
Requires user intervention between editor and publisher.

alternatives.description: Move saving form metadata to a database with an API.
pros: Supports self service model better.
Removes git/github as a blocker.
Allows data access through authorized applications only.
Supports versioning with version numbers.
Enables scheduled backups and disaster recovery plans.
cons: Requires development and hosting of new service.
Changes existing workflows.
Potential initial migration effort.

template_adherence.title: 10. Testing the Editor Pipeline
template_adherence.context:
Our pipeline follows a continuous delivery method with the manual gate to release to production.

![alt text](0010-release-pipeline-context.png "Diagram of how the editor is released through the pipeline.")

We have one Editor in test which causes issues when the rest of the team want to test a feature. Also, while the Editor is tied up in testing the pipeline is blocked for deploying to live-production.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but inferred from the context and decision sections: need for multiple testable editors to allow wider team testing, limitations of running locally due to locked down Macbooks, need for clean removal of test editors, and authentication considerations.
template_adherence.decision:
Changing the pipeline to create an Editor (all plugged in to the dev and test environments). This will involve, building and deploying the editor code into a pod and attaching to a unique URL. Not every branch will need to create a new test editor, the developer will need to add "testable-" to the beginning of the branch name (i.e. `testable-my-really-awesome-feature`).

The Editor will use the current auth mechanism unless the effort outweighs the investment. At a minimum, basic auth of a set username and password must be added.

Test Editor must be cleanly removed after it has fulfilled its purpose. This should ideally be automated either triggered by merging the branch or via commandline.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Each testable editor will have its own URL
* PR's are raised after QA by the rest of the team
* Main will continue be the single source for deploying through the pipeline
* Acceptance tests will still run against the main branch and at a later date look at running them against a testable editor
* Clean removal of the testable editor will keep the namespace managed

pros: Allows developers to test features locally without pipeline changes.

template_adherence.title: Build Nimbus Console As Part Of The Experimenter Code Base
template_adherence.context: Experimenter is a web application developed solely for the purpose of managing product experiments at Mozilla. It was originally designed to manage the Shield experimentation workflow, and has expanded to include a comprehensive workflow for managing Normandy experiments. Project Nimbus is being developed with very different core assumptions than the previous experimentation platforms, and it is unclear whether building on top of the existing Experimenter infrastructure or creating a new purpose specific application will best suit the project's needs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Meeting Project Nimbus' needs in a rapid, continuous fashion with minimal downtime
- The impact to (a) near-term goals of launching our first real set of feature experiments (b) mid-term goals of deprecating and replacing existing experimentation channels (Normandy pref-flips, leanplum) (c) long-term developer productivity and maintenance costs.
- Contributability by a large, distributed group of people with different backgrounds (web engineers, data engineers, data scientists)
- Fitting cohesively into the FXA engineering pipeline/culture
- Continuing to support the existing experimentation (Normandy) workflow until Normandy experiments can be deprecated and transitioned to Nimbus
template_adherence.decision: After careful consideration of both options, the decision was made to build on top of Experimenter and invest in improvements. This includes creating new models, improving and documenting a development workflow usable by all team members, and writing a new front end in React. The alternative to start a new application in Node/Typescript was rejected due to risks around time to parity and operational overhead of maintaining parallel systems.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include reusing much of the existing Experimenter infrastructure, maintaining a single source of truth for experiments, and leveraging existing APIs and integrations. Negative consequences include the need to refactor some database schemas, potential complexity supporting both Normandy and Nimbus, and some constraints due to existing core design decisions. The decision also commits the team to improving the existing codebase and workflows to better fit Nimbus needs.

High unit test coverage and automated integration tests.
Continuous deployment and dynamic risk mitigation.
cons: Existing workflow/UI not applicable to Nimbus needs.

template_adherence.context:
Currently, Jetstream is responsible for daily processing experiment data for analysis after enrollment has completed. We're also interested in processing experiment data for monitoring purposes. Monitoring data is a little different from analysis data in that it is live (updated every few minutes) and needs to be available immediately when an experiment starts collecting data. Also, unlike analysis data, monitoring data sacrifices absolute accuracy for timeliness in order to detect big problems early. Jetstream is only responsible for generating analysis data and we need an alternative approach to access monitoring data from Experimenter.

Currently, Grafana is used to display monitoring data. It works by querying live tables from BigQuery on-demand and does not have any caching. We would like to eventually replace Grafana capabilities with custom visualizations inside of Experimenter. The goal is to have more flexibility than Grafana gives for how to display the data as well as less overhead for users when context switching from one visualization platform to another.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Data needs to be displayed "live", updating within minutes
* Cost needs to stay low
* Have flexibility with how the data is visualized
* Data loading speed
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is "(2) Query Data On-Demand from Experimenter short term and (4) Optimize the ETL long term". Option (3) was dismissed due to too many cons compared to others. Option (1) is fast but expensive. Option (2) is slower but cheaper and comparable to current Grafana performance. Option (4) has potential to be cheapest but requires further breakdown. The plan is to implement option (2) immediately for basic monitoring and continue working on option (4) for long term.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision allows for immediate implementation of user-friendly monitoring in Experimenter with option (2), while working towards a more optimized and potentially cheaper ETL solution (option 4) in the long term. This balances cost, speed, and flexibility. However, option (2) requires building complex data fetching and caching logic in Experimenter, increasing maintenance burden. Option (4) needs more detailed proposal and cost confirmation before implementation.

alternatives.description: Periodic ETL Output in GCS bucket: Add ETL in biguqery_etl to process live data periodically and output results to a GCS bucket accessible by Experimenter, running every 5-10 minutes.
pros: No additional complexity for data processing in Experimenter
Allows flexibility for how data is visualized in Experimenter
Data will load faster coming from a bucket than needing to wait for a BigQuery query to run
cons: May be much more expensive than other options due to running full ETL queries every 10 minutes

alternatives.description: Query Data On-Demand from Experimenter: Add a background celery task that fetches data on-demand from BigQuery and stores it in Redis cache, which is invalidated periodically.
pros: Not slower than current Grafana graphs
Allows flexibility for data visualization in Experimenter
Caching layer makes it same price or cheaper than other options
cons: May be slower from user's perspective compared to precomputed ETL data
Requires building complex data fetching, processing, and storage logic in Experimenter, increasing maintenance burden

alternatives.description: Embed Existing Grafana Graphs: Embed existing Grafana graphs directly.
pros: Simplest and quickest solution
cons: Does not allow flexibility in data visualization in Experimenter
Slower compared to periodic ETL
Could be more expensive unless caching is added

alternatives.description: Option (1) + ETL Optimizations: Add an hourly job to aggregate 5-minute intervals of live data, append to a table hourly, and create a python script to generate queries for graphs and experiments with aggregation granularity.
pros: No additional complexity for data processing in Experimenter
Allows flexibility for data visualization
Data loads faster than waiting for BigQuery queries
Potentially cheaper than other options
cons: Needs more detailed proposal and cost confirmation before implementation

template_adherence.title: Location for the new Experiment "Docs Hub" codebase + docs
template_adherence.context:
ADR #5, ["Use Docusaurus + GH Pages for the Nimbus User Doc Hub"](https://github.com/mozilla/experimenter/blob/main/experimenter/experimenter/docs/adrs/0005-doc-hub.md), determined that our approach to setting up a new central location for Experimenter/Nimbus and related project documentation would use [Docusaurus](https://v2.docusaurus.io/), a static site generator, with the static files being served from [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/). While we knew we would be introducing a new set of code we didn't explicitly decide where it would live and what the process for deploying would look like, beyond suggesting it could live in the existing Experimenter repository.

In investigating how to set all of this up we realized there would be certain caveats to hosting and deploying this code from the Experimenter repository, and this lead to the consideration of using a dedicated repository. This ADR outlines our options and end decision.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- How much setup work is involved, both for the code _and_ for integrations or other non-code processes?
- How much overhead and complexity is involved in maintaining this setup, as well as keeping our processes and tools in sync with Experimenter?
- Not everyone who contributes to these docs is a programmer; how much of a learning curve does this present?
template_adherence.decision:
Set up a new, dedicated repository

Editor's note, 2021-03-12 - This ADR was written after a separate repository was already set up, worked on, and put into use. We've decided to, for approximately one month, use it and see if there is any major fallout. This ADR should be amended with the result of that experiment.
template_adherence.consequences:
The decision to set up a new, dedicated repository provides a fresh repository allowing greater initial and long-term flexibility in code setup, organization, and deployment. Deployments can be done independently, potentially with simpler CI/CD workflows, reducing complexity and failures compared to integrating with the existing Experimenter repository.

However, it introduces cultural overhead with another repository to learn and manage, requires setting up permissions and integrations anew, and contributors must clone and install dependencies separately. It also precludes merging documentation and Experimenter code changes in the same pull request.

alternatives.description: Use the Experimenter repository, main branch
pros: Everything is under one roof with no new repositories or branches to manage.
Existing integrations like code analysis Actions, Dependabot, Jira, and Sentry can be reused with minimal setup.

cons: Higher learning curve for contributors only interested in documentation.
CircleCI jobs run on all PRs and merges, potentially wasting resources and requiring config changes.

The hub is intended for multiple services, so housing it inside Experimenter may be conceptually odd.

cons: Effectively a new repository hidden inside an existing one, increasing learning curve.

Mixed PRs would be confusing as they relate to distinct source paths.

template_adherence.title: Front-end web development with HTMX
template_adherence.context: Nimbus UI uses GraphQL to fetch data from the backend and it highly depends on the three packages i.e. graphene-django, graphene and apollo-client and we have seen these packages not getting released new versions for a while. We have found out that using GraphQL significantly hinders the performance of the Experimenter as it adds extra overhead while making the call and the benefit of using GraphQL is not something we are making use of. We also have to significantly maintain the burden to implement most of the API in both DRF (Django Rest Framework) and GraphQL, and additional testing and tools are required to support that. As our application is growing so what steps we should take to improve the performance and better maintainability of the application?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Improve performance which leads to better UX Experience
- Reduce dependency on extra packages
- Better easier development tooling
- Better maintainability of the application
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: After careful consideration, we have decided to choose the option - Designing new pages with HTMX, and keep the existing UI (React and GraphQL), and eventually moving to HTMX. Moving to HTMX is simpler in terms of backend compatibility as we can use our existing code without any major modifications. Work includes creating new pages using HTMX, setting up test cases to test HTMX pages, and evaluating the success/failure of HTMX on the Experimenter platform, so that if we are successful we can start the transition from React to HTMX completely. Whereas in option 1 we need to actively work on the backend and frontend to transit from GraphQL to REST Apis. This can only work once we have converted everything to Rest Api's i.e. both frontend and backend. Particular V5 API of the experimenter is not used anywhere else apart from the front end, so if we switch to HTMX, we will be not dependent on any kind of APIs and will be closer to the server. The main benefit of choosing option 2 is that it can co-exist with React/GraphQL, meanwhile, we will update to the latest dependency packages to improve performance and can slowly progress towards 100% HTMX.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- All web pages using HTMX!
- Better performance
- Learn new tool HTMX

Negative Consequences:
- We'd be looking for to determine whether the new pages aren't successful. The one possible solution would be to re-write those pages in Typescript/React and instead of GraphQL and transition to Rest API.

template_adherence.title: Nimbus Web SDK Architecture
template_adherence.context: This is part of a body of work necessary to support the use of Nimbus within web applications. The current Nimbus SDK is written in such a way that it supports client-oriented experimentation — experiments are downloaded, evaluated, and stored on the client, and a feature store is exposed with the experiment branches applied. In previous decisions (not in this repository), we've already decided that in order to support web experimentation the Nimbus SDK will need to be updated to be stateless, to support a more statically defined set of helper methods, and to have additional support for Python. Ultimately, the problem we're trying to solve can be boiled down to one question — how can we update the Nimbus SDK to support web applications while continuing to support the existing clients? As an example of what the Cirrus API might look like, we can likely expect endpoints to perform the following: Enroll a user into available experiment(s), This would return the enrolled experiments as well as the feature values given the enrollments, Fetch the default feature values, Fetch the feature manifest, Fetch a specific feature value given enrolled experiments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Architecture decisions for Nimbus on the web
* The core logic of the existing SDK (Rust) will be re-used for the Nimbus web service (Cirrus)
* The SDK needs to support Python via UniFFI
* The SDK needs to be stateless
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to move forward with option number 2, "Cargo features, one library". This option, like the others mentioned, meets the key decision drivers. We believe using this option will be the most maintainable long-term, despite the added complexity of using cargo features. In addition, implementing this option has a similarly short timeline and amount of work necessary as compared to the "Cargo features, separate library" option, without the additional overhead of more complex typing.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Meets all decision drivers.
* Small amount of work necessary with a very limited amount of code churn.

Negative Consequences:
* It will be difficult to draw boundaries between Cirrus and Nimbus code.
* We could run into unexpected issues with UniFFI, as multiple UDL files in a single crate has not yet been tested.

alternatives.description: Separate `nimbus-core`, `nimbus-sdk`, and `cirrus-sdk` libraries: Move core Nimbus business logic to a new `nimbus-core` library, with `nimbus-sdk` and `cirrus-sdk` depending on it.
pros: Separate libraries allow for strong separation of concerns.
Changes in the `cirrus-sdk` library will not require changes the `nimbus-sdk` library.
Certain Nimbus-only features (such as the event store) will not available in the Cirrus library.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
RKV dependency only included when `nimbus` feature is enabled.
Will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
All code relating to core Nimbus business logic remains in one place.
cons: Defining and using types becomes more difficult.
Traits will be needed to extend functionality in the Nimbus Core library, which is complex.
Would result in a significant amount of code churn.
Many methods and structs would need to move and have call signatures updated.

alternatives.description: Cargo features, one library: Use cargo features for conditional compilation within a single library.
pros: Feature configurations are familiar to Rust developers.
All Nimbus business logic remains in one place.
UniFFI bindings can be conditionally generated for each feature with different UDLs.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
Will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
cons: Onboarding developers to Rust features may be harder.
Cirrus and Nimbus logic in the same crate may blur boundaries.
First time including multiple UniFFI UDLs in a single crate; potential unexpected issues.

alternatives.description: Cargo features, separate library: Use features differently with a `stateless` feature to disable state-oriented features, and have Cirrus as a separate library.
pros: All benefits of "Cargo features, one library" option.
Minimal churn required.
Better separation of concerns between Nimbus and Cirrus.
Dependencies can be excluded based on enabled features.
Will not increase the size of the existing Nimbus SDK binary.
cons: Onboarding developers to Rust features may be harder.
Cirrus calling Nimbus methods may blur boundaries.
Changes in Nimbus method signatures could cause unexpected changes in Cirrus.

alternatives.description: Expose a stateless API alongside the stateful API (Do nothing): Add static/stateless methods for experiments alongside existing stateful API.
pros: Simple and mostly additive.
cons: Increases risk of developer error.
Stateless methods would be visible in Android and iOS where they shouldn't be used.
Increases binary size for both Cirrus and Nimbus.
