template_adherence.title: Layer Level Deployments
template_adherence.context: We want a way to define and manage the deployment of resources which are shared across multiple solutions. A number of services offered by cloud providers, namely AWS have services which can only be deployed once per AWS Account or enable a service across an entire account. How should we manage these resources to scale with our plugin support and to support the features we have introduced for our other deployments
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Support required for multi region deployments to allow global image registry
* Deprecation of the fragment and case style template processing which is currently used for account level deployments
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "Extend occurrence support to work at any layer", because this allows for greater flexibility over the resources we can deploy and aligns with our other deployment processes
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

* Occurrences will be the approach we use for all deployments
* Opens support for any occurrence features that we have in place already or develop in the future
* Makes our existing deployment model easier to follow ( our current tiers deployments will belong to the Segment and show that relationship )

### Negative Consequences

* Complexity in extending the occurrence building process
* May introduce some complexity in managing default and required singleton instances of deployments. We can manage this and could potentially be a useful feature

alternatives.description: Add support for a layer level component like deployment option
pros: Good, because it aligns with our existing concepts around distinct deployment units which are standalone deployments
Good, because it is similar to own component style deployment process
Good, because we can use standardised naming and state querying ( resources, attributes etc. )
cons: Bad, because it adds complexity in our processing and requires the implementation of a new occurrence structure ( one which supports singleton deployments )

alternatives.description: Refactor existing services to use a similar approach to extensions and apply extensions to layers
pros: Good, because it is simple and simplifies the management of layer based deployments, i.e. add the layer level extensions you want and deploy
Good, because it aligns with the current approach and would require less work to implement
cons: Bad, because it wouldn't gain the benefits of state sharing and would require global naming functions to support
Bad, because it could create conflicting resources as part of a shared single deployment

alternatives.description: Extend occurrence support to work at any layer
pros: Good, because it reuses a lot of what we already have
Good, because it unlocks the occurrence work we have done for use across the whole hamlet tenancy
Good, because it standardises all resource deployments into a single conceptual model ( components and occurrences )
cons: Bad, because it will require significant redevelopment of our occurrence process and could introduce bugs across the board
Bad, because it could potentially create some complexity or "lowest common denominator" issues that impact the implementation of the occurrence

template_adherence.context: Hamlet Deploy is not a compiled binary file nor is it written in a single programming or scripting language. It is a combination of all of the above; Java for the Freemarker wrapper, Freemarker has its own DSL, the original Hamlet Deploy Executor is presently primarily Bash scripts and the "Click" CLI Executor is written in Python. When a handled exception occurs, there is no consistency in the error information provided. A handled error in Freemarker is likely to provide a large JSON object for review, whilst an error in the Bash Executor will provide a brief summary of the problem. Because these summaries are not always unique-per-error, many provide only a generic error message.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for consistent and meaningful error information across multiple components and languages in Hamlet Deploy. Desire to improve error reporting and communication, maintainability, extensibility, and community accessibility. Concerns about maintenance overhead, enforceability, and specificity of error messages.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is to introduce logging classes that group together messages of a similar kind. This approach provides a framework for tailoring messages with reusability and community accessibility, with minor maintenance overhead. It allows for future extension or upgrade and re-evaluation for more specific error handling if necessary.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved consistency across error sources, accessibility to community content, and a maintainable framework for error messaging. Negative consequences include less specificity compared to unique error messages and the need to re-evaluate the approach later for potential enhancements.

alternatives.description: Create a manually-maintained library of error codes and assign one to each handled error.
pros: Provides a method for tailored error messages and possible fixes to the user.

Improves reporting and communication around errors.
Ensures consistency across potential error sources.
cons: Increases maintenance overhead.
May be challenging to enforce consistently.
Difficult to make extensible by community content.

alternatives.description: Introduce logging classes that group together messages of a similar kind.
pros: Allows tailoring messages with reusability.
Accessible to community content.
Ensures consistency across error sources.
Framework can be extended or upgraded later.
Minor maintenance overhead once established.
cons: Less specificity compared to unique error messages.

template_adherence.title: Hamlet Engine distribution through docker image layers
template_adherence.context: The hamlet engine is made up of a collection of software components which are based on a number of different platforms ( bash, freemarker, java ). Our current distribution process collects these components into a multipurpose docker image that can handle most build and deploy tasks. The collection process uses git to pull down the code from the software components and includes this in the image. The problem with this process is that it really only works in a controlled docker environment, making this image multipurpose has resulted in a large docker image and installing other versions of hamlet requires pulling a new image.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Having a simple installation process for user local installations or integration in existing processes
* Simple version management support with a focus on handling the usage of features under active development within deployment pipelines
* A tested and verified release process
template_adherence.decision: Chosen `Docker image layer as component artefacts with support for installing these images` as this is the most flexible option and provides a foundation for managing the distribution of hamlet code
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Establishes a process for distributing packages which supports the different platforms we use
* Opens up support for enhancing our release process to be safer and more flexible
* Doesn't add too much overhead and is reasonably straightforward to understand

Negative Consequences:
* Is essentially implementing our own package manager which a lot of people already have and implement
* Doesn't necessarily cover off the software platform dependencies but at least makes it get the scripts that can tell us that easily

alternatives.description: Docker image layer as component artefacts with support for installing these images
pros: Docker images are agnostic from their software platform and can handle storing the different file types we want
The images can be retrieved without specific dependencies on other package managers
We can have both immutable and mutable releases, dev, nightly, stable and also have tagged releases
The layers can integrate with our existing docker images as required using the `COPY --from` syntax
cons: It is an uncommon pattern and does require a depth of docker image knowledge to maintain
It requires executor specific implementation of the pull process

alternatives.description: Include all software components in the hamlet-cli python package
pros: This would provide a single command to install the cli and all the components
It uses a standard known installation method ( pip ) for installation processes
cons: It wouldn't allow for different version of the engine components independent from the cli to be used. They could be done through virtual envs but would require publishing packages on each push to a component
It doesn't accomodate the idea of different executors running the engine. This would need to be implemented in each executor

template_adherence.title: 3. OPG-Data API Specification
template_adherence.context:
We need to arrive at an API spec that is fully formed, without spending an inordinate amount of time creating something from scratch, when other mature specifications exist and can be leveraged to suit our needs well.

Most major tech corporations have arrived at their own slightly differing proprietary implementations of a RESTful API spec, and none are completely awful or completely successful.

Some are more mature than others, such as JSON:API https://jsonapi.org, which "has been properly registered with the IANA. Its media type designation is application/vnd.api+json."

It is also open-source https://github.com/json-api/json-api.

template_adherence.title: Error Handling And Status Codes
template_adherence.context: When something goes wrong, the API should respond with as meaningful information as possible, to allow developers to pinpoint the source of the problem.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to provide meaningful error information to API consumers, standardize error reporting, support multiple errors in a single response, and align with established standards such as HTTP status codes, JSON-API error format, and RFC 7807.
template_adherence.decision: Use appropriate HTTP status codes combined with custom error codes and messages following the Problem Details for HTTP APIs (RFC 7807) and JSON-API error format. Return multiple errors in an array to provide comprehensive feedback. Adopt the ethos of JSON-API while satisfying application/problem+json requirements.
template_adherence.consequences: Standardized and unambiguous error reporting, improved developer experience by pointing to error sources quickly, support for multiple errors in one response, and adherence to best practices from RFC 7807 and JSON-API.

template_adherence.title: 14. shared services
template_adherence.context:
As we move to a structure where products share services rather than being purely isolated systems, we are moving away from a model where the API Gateway acts solely as a pathway into the Sirius Backend API. Early integrations such as providing LPAs to __Use and LPA__ or passing files from the __Digital Deputies Reporting Service__ were thin layers of translation over the existing Sirius API.

The next phase of our API work is to move to a model where multiple products share and use an API that owns all its data, and encapsulates a need in the OPG domain. Our first example is the Use an LPA codes service, which provides data for both Sirius Case Management and the Use an LPA service, but is independent of both.

This is in parallel to work that is splitting Sirius into smaller services, with the expectation that the two streams of work will eventually converge as a set of isolated services that can be recomposed into new products, our "Service Swarm".
template_adherence.decision:
Shared services will sit behind the OPG Data API Gateway and follow the [0009-api-domain-structure.md](api domain structure decision). Shared services will be isolated and own a particular domain for our applications. That is, they own a particular business process or kind of data, for example the generation and expiry of access codes.

These services currently live within the boundary of the "Sirius" account, but are deployed independently.
template_adherence.consequences:
This new model requires that product teams build and test with known contracts with appropriate mocking of the service during development stages (see [0013-pact-broker.md](Pact Broker decision)).

This approach also means that cross team communication around needs and contracts is essential during kickoff and improvements.

Services must have ownership from a team. This is currently the "Integrations" team, who own, maintain and interate the API as product work.

This model opens up the opportunity for us to reduce the amount of duplication across our products by providing independent services for common patterns (i.e. Authentication).

Use of the [0009-api-domain-structure.md](common domain structure) means that services can live in either Lambdas, ECS tasks or elsewhere depending on the need, with the API Gateway as a stranglepoint for moving
implementations as needed.

template_adherence.title: Use a version tag to make updating WordPress easier
template_adherence.context:

We want to automatically update minor and patch versions but not major versions. We have created a `v5` tag in our snapshot repo that will point to the latest released version of version 5.

template_adherence.decision: Set the revision of WordPress in `config/application.json` to be `v5`
template_adherence.consequences: We will be able to update WordPress within a major version easily but upgrading to a new major version will still be quite manual.

template_adherence.title: Use Roave/SecurityAdvisories to help protect against vulnerable packages
template_adherence.context:
We often use third-party Composer packages in our themes. We should review these packages via libraries.io before installing them, and should receive GitHub security alerts on repos using composer packages that have known vulnerabilities.

However, Composer does not warn you if you're installing a package that has a known vulnerability - those warnings will, at best, only come after that change has been pushed up to GitHub.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to protect against vulnerable third-party Composer packages.
Current Composer tooling does not warn about known vulnerabilities at install time.
Desire to have an automated way to prevent installing vulnerable package versions.
Maintain manual review as an additional safety measure.
template_adherence.decision:
Add the Roave/SecurityAdvisories package to our template theme as a Composer dev dependency.
This package uses Composer's conflict setting to prevent installation of known vulnerable package versions.
It sources vulnerability data from FriendOfPHP/security-advisories and the GitHub Advisory Database, and is updated regularly.
template_adherence.consequences:
Provides an additional layer of protection against potential vulnerabilities beyond manual review.
Will only throw errors during composer update or require commands, so warnings are not automatic.
Manual review of dependencies should still be performed as per existing RFC.

alternatives.description: Do not add Roave/SecurityAdvisories and rely solely on manual review and GitHub security alerts.
pros: No additional dependencies added to the project.
Relies on existing manual processes and GitHub alerts.
cons: No automated prevention of installing vulnerable packages at install time.
Higher risk of vulnerable packages being installed before detection.

alternatives.description: Use other automated vulnerability scanning tools integrated with CI/CD pipelines.
pros: Potentially more comprehensive scanning and alerts.
Can integrate with existing CI/CD workflows.
cons: May require additional setup and maintenance.
Might not prevent installation of vulnerable packages locally.

template_adherence.title: 8. Use a dependabot.yml file to configure security alert rules
template_adherence.context:
GitHub security alerts can provide us with useful information when there is a vulnerability in a package we use.

However, currently the vast majority of alerts we receive are for vulnerabilities in NPM dev dependencies, which are highly unlikely to lead to any real vulnerability in the production environment. See https://overreacted.io/npm-audit-broken-by-design/ for more details.

This creates so many false positives that we're unable to spot the meaningful security alerts we need to act upon amongst the noise.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to reduce noise from security alerts caused by NPM dev dependencies, which are unlikely to affect production.
The desire to focus on meaningful security alerts that require action.
The limitation that Dependabot does not support glob/wildcard-based rules, requiring manual maintenance of configuration files.
template_adherence.decision: We will use a `dependabot.yml` file to configure the security alerts so that alerts are raised for all composer packages, but only production NPM packages.
template_adherence.consequences:
This should filter out most of the noise of alerts we don't need to act on, and leave us with a manageable number of meaningful security alerts. It will also control what dependencies Dependabot automatically opens PRs for.

Because Dependabot does not currently allow for glob/wildcard-based rules, we will need to manually maintain the file for each repo.

A PR template should help ensure we keep the `dependabot.yml` files up to date, and a separate ADR will be opened to that effect.

alternatives.description: Not using a dependabot.yml file and continuing to receive all security alerts including many false positives from NPM dev dependencies.
pros: No additional configuration or maintenance required.
All alerts are received, so no risk of missing any vulnerability alerts.
cons: High volume of false positives making it difficult to identify meaningful alerts.
Wasted effort in triaging irrelevant alerts.

alternatives.description: Using glob/wildcard-based rules to configure alerts if Dependabot supported it.
pros: Easier to maintain configuration with less manual updates.
More flexible and scalable alert configuration.
cons: Dependabot does not currently support glob/wildcard-based rules.
Not feasible at this time, requiring manual maintenance instead.

template_adherence.title: Artifacts Deployment
template_adherence.context:
Deploying artifacts to nexus was done with this plugin before, but a bug was reported.
When reading a child pom without `version`, for example, it does not retrieve the information inherited from the parent pom.
We have to investigate alternatives.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to deploy artifacts to Nexus reliably without bugs, handling credentials securely, and adhering to the build-once principle.
template_adherence.decision:
`Nexus Artifact Uploader` is chosen, because:
- `Maven lifecycle phase: deploy` does not meet our build-once principle.
- `Nexus Artifact Uploader` has the same situation regarding parameters as `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`, but can handle credentials as a Jenkins plugin.
template_adherence.consequences: Using `Nexus Artifact Uploader` will simplify credential handling as a Jenkins plugin and avoid issues with the build-once principle that arise with the Maven lifecycle deploy phase. However, it still requires preparing a list of parameters similar to the Apache Maven Deploy Plugin.

alternatives.description: Apache Maven Deploy Plugin (deploy:deploy-file)
pros: Official maven plugin for deployment, which is perfect for any maven projects if you only care whether your artifacts are deployed correctly.
cons: A list of parameters has to be generated before using the plugin, including `artifactId` and `version`, which is the same case as the `Nexus Artifact Uploader`.
Credential info has to be stored in the `settings.xml`, which introduces additional implementation.

alternatives.description: Maven lifecycle phase : deploy
pros: Same as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`.

You don't have to pass the parameters as `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` and `Nexus Artifact Uploader`, because `package` phase is executed implicitly and makes the parameters ready before `deploy` phase.
cons: Same case as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` for handling credentials.
A list of phases is triggered implicitly before this phase, including `compile`, `test` and `package`.
It's not possible to skip some of the maven goals binding to certain phases, e.g., `jar:jar` goal of the Apache Maven JAR Plugin cannot be skipped.
This violates the build-once principle, which is the main reason this option is rejected.

alternatives.description: Nexus Artifact Uploader
pros: Without the pain of handling the credentials, which was mentioned above in `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin` section.
It's promising, when the plugin is used properly.
cons: A list of parameters has to be prepared, same as the `Apache Maven Deploy Plugin`.

template_adherence.title: Automatic Versioning and Release of Cloud Applications
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the context of providing a Continuous Delivery (CD) pipeline for SAP Cloud Platform applications that adheres to the "build once" principle. It explains the problem with the current Maven Release Plugin approach, the meaning of "release" and "to release," and the issues with SNAPSHOT versions in artifact repositories.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include auditability (uniquely identifying deployed software versions), automation (supporting multiple daily releases without manual intervention), and compatibility with existing build tools (Maven). The need to avoid SNAPSHOT versions due to their ambiguity and potential deletion by artifact repositories is also a driver.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement an automated versioning schema where each commit to the productive branch (master) is treated as a new release. The version number includes a human-readable build timestamp (ISO 8601 format, UTC, without colons) and the git commit id, e.g., "2.7.3-2018-03-02T114757UTC_ff46bb0f00a663018f3efea697b2fb5e86fe6d41". Automatic versioning is enabled by default but can be disabled. Git tags are not created automatically to avoid clutter, but can be created manually.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include improved auditability by having unique version identifiers per build, enabling automated releases on each commit to master, and avoiding the use of ambiguous SNAPSHOT versions. The approach supports manual tagging for noteworthy versions and avoids cluttering git tags. It also allows disabling automatic versioning for builds that do not follow this approach.

alternatives.description: Use the Maven Release Plugin as is for versioning and releasing.
pros: Standard tool widely used in Maven projects.
Integrates with Maven build lifecycle.
cons: Does not satisfy auditability requirements due to SNAPSHOT versions.
SNAPSHOT versions are ambiguous and may be deleted by artifact repositories.
Manual release process not feasible for multiple daily releases.

alternatives.description: Manual versioning and tagging by developers.
pros: Full control over version numbers and releases.
Can use semantic versioning and manual tagging.
cons: Not feasible for multiple releases per day.
Prone to human error and delays.
Does not support automation requirements.

template_adherence.title: Move Cx Server Script in Container
template_adherence.context:
We have a bash script (`cx-server`), which orchestrates the Docker containers used by our Cx Server.
Using bash is inconvenient for Windows users, as Windows does not include bash by default.
There is options for running bash on Windows, such as the Windows Subsystem for Linux, but this is not trivial to setup and requires switching Windows to Developer Mode.
Other options include running a virtual machine locally, or connecting to a remove Linux system, but both are not always possible and have too much overhead.

Recently, we added a "companion" Docker image which is used by `cx-server` to run scripts.
Unrelated, the idea was born to move `cx-server` into this image, so the remaining `cx-server` is a very thin wrapper which can also be added as a Windows compatible script file.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support Windows users who do not have bash by default.
- Avoid complex setup like Windows Subsystem for Linux or virtual machines.
- Maintain CLI compatibility and smooth upgrade path.
template_adherence.decision:
We move the bash script inside the `s4sdk/cxserver-companion` Docker image.
The old `cx-server` script just delegates the command to the script inside the companion container.
A new `cx-server.bat` script is added, doing the same for Windows.
We don't use PowerShell to increase compatibility with Windows.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Improved Windows compatibility by providing a Windows batch script.
- Maintains CLI compatibility and smooth upgrade path.
- Slight increase in complexity by adding delegation scripts and containerized script execution.

alternatives.description: Keep the bash script as is and require Windows users to set up bash environments (WSL, VM, remote Linux).
pros: No changes to existing scripts.
No additional maintenance overhead for new scripts.
cons: Inconvenient for Windows users.
Requires complex setup for Windows users.
Potentially limits adoption or usability on Windows.

alternatives.description: Rewrite the script entirely in a cross-platform language or tool (e.g., PowerShell, Python).
pros: Native cross-platform support.
No need for container delegation.
cons: Requires rewriting and testing the script.
PowerShell might reduce compatibility with some Windows versions.
Adds dependency on runtime environments.

template_adherence.title: Treatment of application with a frontend that don't have a package lock file
template_adherence.context:
The node package manager (npm) creates a so called ["lock file"](https://docs.npmjs.com/files/package-locks) when running `npm install`. The recommended action is to commit this file to version control, as stated by the command itself:

```
$ npm install
npm notice created a lockfile as package-lock.json. You should commit this file.
```

Some npm commands, which are part of the pipeline, such as `ci` and `audit` require that a package lock file exists.

Thus, if a project lacks the package lock file, there are tree options:

* Refuse to build the project, which enforces the recommended practice of committing the lock file
* Silently create a package lock file as part of the pipeline
* Avoid npm commands which require a package lock
* Would disable the npm audit stage
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle projects that lack a package lock file in the build pipeline
- Ensure npm commands that require a package lock file can run without failure
- Maintain build reliability and developer workflow
- Warn developers when package lock file is missing
template_adherence.decision: If a project has a `package.json` file, but no package lock, we create a package lock file as part of the pipeline and warn the user about this. The created package lock file is not archived as part of the pipeline build artifacts.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Jenkins builds don't fail when developers forget to commit the package lock
- If the developers chose not to commit the package lock long term, the build is less reliable
- npm audit can run always on projects with a frontend component

alternatives.description: Refuse to build the project if the package lock file is missing, enforcing the recommended practice of committing the lock file.
pros: Enforces best practice strictly
Prevents builds with inconsistent dependencies
cons: Builds fail if developers forget to commit the lock file
May disrupt developer workflow

alternatives.description: Avoid npm commands which require a package lock file, effectively disabling npm audit stage.
pros: Simplifies pipeline by skipping problematic commands
Avoids build failures due to missing lock file
cons: Disables npm audit, reducing security checks
May lead to inconsistent builds

template_adherence.title: Structure of SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven Projects
template_adherence.context:
SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK encompasses components such as Java libraries, Maven archetypes, a Virtual Data Model and a Continuous Delivery Toolkit.
The Continuous Delivery Toolkit must be able to build, test and deploy arbitrary SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven projects developed by teams within and outside of SAP.

Based on best practices gained when developing cloud-native applications, we learned that it should be possible to separate unit- and integration tests to run them in isolation.
Reasoning for requiring running them in isolation are:

* Dependencies for unit tests might not be required for integration tests and vice versa, or even conflict with them
* Unit- and integration test can be run independently and parallel, locally and on CI/CD

Alternative options to separate unit- and integration tests:

* Use [Maven profiles](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-profiles.html)
* Use [Maven multi-module](https://maven.apache.org/guides/mini/guide-multiple-modules.html) projects

Archetypes for generating valid projects are provided.
[Example projects](https://github.com/sap/cloud-s4-sdk-examples) are available.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to build, test, and deploy SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Maven projects reliably.
- Best practices for cloud-native applications suggest separating unit and integration tests.
- Tests should be runnable independently and in isolation.
- Avoid conflicts and unnecessary dependencies between unit and integration tests.
- Simplify usage for users, including inexperienced Maven users.
- Enforce conventions and structure for projects to ease pipeline processing.
template_adherence.decision:
Projects built by SAP S/4HANA Cloud SDK Pipeline need to be Maven multi-module projects.
Required modules are `application`, `integration-tests` and `unit-tests`.
Additional modules are **not** allowed.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Users don't need to select Maven profiles for running tests.
- For inexperienced Maven users, selecting profiles for running tests might be more confusing compared to choosing the right module.
- There would need to be a common convention which profiles need to exist with fixed names if profiles were used.
- Fine grained dependency selection for each module is possible.
- Different versions of a dependency in productive and test code can be used easily in separate modules.
- Less likely that test dependencies leak into production code.
- Forces separation of unit- and integration tests.
- Easier to check adherence to the testing pyramid.
- Enforce that typical integration test dependencies are not used in unit tests.
- Allows easier implementation of the build once principle.
- Avoids rebuilding application artifact unnecessarily in CI/CD.
- Existing projects need to adapt to this structure.
- Tests in the application module are ignored by the Pipeline.
- Developers must put tests into the correct module.
- Pipeline can assume which Maven modules exist, simplifying scanning.
- Without this, module discovery would be fragile.

alternatives.description: Use Maven profiles to separate unit and integration tests.
pros: Allows separation of tests without multi-module structure.
Might be simpler for some Maven users familiar with profiles.
cons: Users need to select profiles to run tests, which can be confusing.
Requires common convention for profile names.
Potential conflicts or dependency issues between profiles.
Less fine-grained dependency control compared to modules.

alternatives.description: Use Maven multi-module projects to separate unit and integration tests.
pros: Clear separation of tests into modules.
Fine-grained dependency management per module.
Simplifies pipeline assumptions and scanning.
Supports build once principle and avoids unnecessary rebuilds.
Reduces risk of test dependencies leaking into production code.
Enforces testing pyramid adherence.
cons: Existing projects need to adapt to this structure.
Developers must correctly place tests into modules.
Additional complexity of multi-module project structure.

template_adherence.title: Support autoscaling using Kubernetes
template_adherence.context: The pipeline can leverage certain Kubernetes features to support dynamic scalability.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support dynamic scalability in the pipeline using Kubernetes features, while considering overhead, isolation, and support for pipeline extensions.
template_adherence.decision: Use the approach of creating a pod per stage to balance overhead and isolation, and create a pod per step for pipeline extensions to support dynamic configurations.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision allows for efficient scalability with acceptable overhead and maintains isolation between stages. However, it requires managing pod creation per stage and handling extensions with pod per step, which may add complexity.

pros: Addresses overhead problem of per step pods.

cons: Requires knowing dockerImages used in each stage in advance.

alternatives.description: Create pod per pipeline: create a single pod for the entire pipeline.
pros: Simplifies pod management.
cons: Contradicts isolation principle between stages.

template_adherence.title: 3. Author validation
template_adherence.context:
Currently users are provided with very little useful feedback as to any errors in the questionnaire they are building. This change aims to provide a way for the users to see feedback on the changes they are making by exposing the validation errors to them.

There are multiple types of validations:
- Intra-entity. These are validations on fields within an entity itself e.g. a question page must have a populated title.
- Inter-entity validations. These are validations across entities. e.g. an answer validation that references an answer can only reference a previous answer.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to provide useful feedback on questionnaire errors to users; support both intra-entity and inter-entity validations; performance considerations for validation speed; maintainability and extensibility of validation approach; integration with existing JSON questionnaire format and GraphQL API.
template_adherence.decision: Use JSON schema with AJV library to validate questionnaires on the API side and expose validation results via GraphQL types to the UI. Validation is performed on every request using Express middleware for simplicity, with re-validation after every mutation to keep errors up to date. Validation errors are provided at the entity level in GraphQL types with detailed error information.
template_adherence.consequences: UI will have all necessary data to display validation errors within the questionnaire. The responsibility for how errors are shown or hidden lies with the UI, which may involve complexity handled by prototypes. Validation approach is performant and maintainable, but running validation on every request may be suboptimal if performance degrades in the future, requiring potential caching or other optimizations.

template_adherence.title: 3. Replace Postgres RDB with JSON
template_adherence.context:
A point of repeated discussion within the development team has been whether or not a relational database is the most appropriate persistence option for the Author product.

The GraphQL specification and the documentation of associated libraries do not prescribe any one best method for the persistence of data. Rather, they suggest thinking of GraphQL as an abstraction layer that can be wrapped around any type of backend persistence.

In the early stages of development on the Author product, a decision was taken to start with a relational database, which has served us well until this point.

Over time, the database specific code in the API has added to the complexity of the API and have made some requirements more difficult to implement than they ought to be. Examples of such features include Duplication, Moving and Ordering.

The team has some new requirements to implement a permissions model around Author's questionnaire data. Due to the the relational nature of our data model, we estimate that in order check if an author has permissions to perform a mutation at one of the lower levels of the relational tree (say, update a validation rule) several joins would need to happen just to get back up to the root of the data model (i.e. Questionnaire) just so that permissions could be checked.

Moreover, this check would likely need to happen on every request, resulting in increased complexity.

Another motivating factor for revisiting our persistence mechanism is our current inability to easily port questionnaires between environments.

At present, there isn't an easy way of taking a questionnaire built in one environment e.g. pre-prod and migrating that data into another environment e.g. local/dev/test/prod. There are a few reasons for this, but one of the primary reasons is that database autogenerated Ids make it more difficult to ingest data from other environments and data would need to be migrated from many tables to do this successfully.

### Motivations

We hope making this change will make it:

- Easier to make changes to the API going forward, as there is less complexity and less code to maintain.
- Easier to write tests (most functionality can be tested by unit tests on pure functions).
- Easier to move data between environments (for example from pre-prod to prod)
- Easier to implement permissions checking.
- Easier to keep versioned history of changes and restore to point in time.
- Cheaper to run cloud infrastructure (serverless), and overall more performant.
- More portable if we need to migrate to another cloud provider.
- Require significantly less calls to the datastore per request.

We also believe that we will see improvements to our CI and Cypress test execution times since it will be possible to load in a questionnaire in a pre-configured state rather than having to build up scenario in each test.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce complexity and code maintenance in the API.
- Desire to improve testability through unit tests on pure functions.
- Requirement to easily move data between environments.
- Need to implement a permissions model efficiently.
- Desire to keep versioned history and enable point-in-time restore.
- Cost and performance considerations for cloud infrastructure.
- Portability concerns regarding cloud provider dependency.
- Reduce the number of datastore calls per request.
- Improve CI and test execution times.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision taken is to refactor the API to use a JSON document database as a persistence mechanism.

Initially our implementation will be focused on targeting DynamoDB, with the ability to run the application locally using either an in-memory or containerised local DynamoDB instance. However we're striving to not become dependent on any one cloud provider and so we should have a very thin layer of integration with Dynamo and rely on reading and mutating an in-memory JSON document for the most part.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Benefits of making the change

We believe that we will see benefits/improvements in the following areas after making this change:

- Performance improvements (single read operation for queries, single write operation for mutations)
- Simplified duplication logic.
- Simplified ordering/moving logic.
- Simplified author validation logic (we could leverage JSON schema validation for some of it).
- Simplified code base (can probably delete most of the API code (repositories, data entities, migrations etc)
- Since we would no longer rely on numeric autogenerated Ids from the database it will allow us to provide human-readable URLs which has been noted as being important for analytics.
- We will have the ability to support point-in-time restore of data by assigning each schema change a new version.

### Risks and mitgations

This is a large change to the API and so the main risk to delivery is ensuring that no functionality and/or data is lost as part of this change.

We plan on mitigating this risk by ensuring that we keep a high level of test coverage, particularly around the API which is it main contract between the backend and the UI and ensuring that we test data migrations thoroughly in a dev environment before switching over to this new mechanism in our pre-prod and prod environments.

The team aims to unblock other development tasks as soon as possible, so we will seek to merge code back into master as soon as it is stable and has sufficient test coverage. We expect that some of the code will be sub-optimal at the beginning, but are committed to improving this over time with subsequent pull requests.

cons: Increased complexity in API code due to relational joins.
Difficulties implementing new features like permissions, duplication, moving, and ordering.
Hard to port questionnaires between environments due to autogenerated IDs.
Potentially more calls to the datastore per request, impacting performance.

cons: Additional evaluation and integration effort.
May not have as mature local development support as DynamoDB.
Could introduce new complexities or limitations not yet understood.

template_adherence.title: The GCS Library represents optional parameters as variadic function arguments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are not explicitly titled or separated, but can be inferred from the context and consequences sections. They include ease of use of optional parameters, avoiding the need to create new handles for parameter changes, compilation concerns, API overloading complexity, and integration with other optional parameters like timeouts.
template_adherence.decision:
The parameters are passed as variadic arguments into any function that needs them. That is, all APIs look like this:

```C++
class Bucket /* or Object as applicable */ { public:
template <typename... Parameters>
ReturnType ApiName(
FixedArgument1 a1, FixedArgument2 a2,
Parameters&&... p);
```

and are used like this:

```C++
void AppCode(Bucket b, FixedArgument1 foo, FixedArgument2 bar) {
b.ApiName(
foo, bar, storage::IfMetagenerationMatch(7), UserProject("my-project"));
```
template_adherence.consequences:
The advantages of this approach include:

- It is easier to use parameters in an API, it does not require to create a new bucket or object or client handle just for changing the parameters in one request.

The downsides include:

- All APIs become templates, we should be careful not to create massive header files that are slow to compile.
- It is harder to overload APIs.
- It is not clear how other optional parameters of the APIs, such as timeouts, fit with this structure.

alternatives.description: Use per-request parameters as properties modified in the client or object, creating new handles with applied modifiers.
pros: Allows grouping optional parameters in a handle, potentially cleaner API usage for multiple requests.
cons: Requires creating new bucket or object handles for changing parameters.
May be less convenient for single requests.

alternatives.description: Pass optional parameters as variadic function arguments directly in API calls.
pros: Easier to use parameters in an API.
Does not require creating new handles for parameter changes.
cons: All APIs become templates, potentially increasing compile times.
Harder to overload APIs.
Unclear integration with other optional parameters like timeouts.

template_adherence.title: Do not duplicate validation performed by the server-side.
template_adherence.context: many APIs impose restrictions on their parameters. Names may have length limits, or strings may need to conform to specific formats, or ranges must be non-empty. It is tempting to validate these arguments in the client-side, since we *know* the API will fail if it is allowed to continue with the invalid parameters. However, any such validation is redundant, since the server is going to validate its inputs as well. Furthermore, any such validation is wasteful: most of the time the application will pass on valid arguments, checking them twice is just wasting client-side CPU cycles. Moreover, the server-side is the source of truth, so having the validations performed on the client side will require extra work if the server restrictions are ever modified.

template_adherence.title: The GCS Library uses optional fields only for sub-objects.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- The underlying protocol is JSON, which allows fields to be absent.
- The application can filter fields using the `fields` query parameter.
- Need to decide how to represent optional fields in the client library.
- Desire to balance ease of use with semantic correctness regarding presence or absence of fields.
template_adherence.decision:
- For string fields where there is no semantic difference between an empty string and the field not present we just use `std::string<>`.
- For array fields where there is no semantic difference between field not present and an empty array we just use `std::vector<>`.
- For integer and boolean fields we default to `0` (and `false`) if the field is not present.
- For object fields we default to wrapping the field in `optional<>`.

For fields wrapped in `optional<>` we offer convenience functions to make it easier to operate on these fields. For a field called `foo` these are:

- `has_foo()` returns true if the field is set.
- `foo()` returns the field value if set, the behavior is undefined if the value is not set.
- `foo_as_optional()` returns the optional field.
- `reset_foo()` resets the field (for writable fields).
- `set_foo()` sets the field (for writable fields).
template_adherence.consequences:
The advantage of this approach is that most fields are easy to use most of the time. The disadvantage of this approach include:

- The ambiguity when the application filters the returned fields, the value may be the default value because the client did not get the field.
- As applications change over time and they start filtering different fields the code may assume that the value of a field is valid, but it has a default value. With optionals the application should crash during testing, or may be programmed defensively since the start.
- It also requires more thought designing the classes a field has different semantics for "not there" vs. "the default value".

alternatives.description: Use `optional<T>` for all fields regardless of type.
pros: Uniform representation of optionality across all fields.
Clear semantic distinction between 'not present' and 'default value'.
cons: More cumbersome to use for simple types like strings and arrays where empty or default values are acceptable.
Increased complexity in client code.

alternatives.description: Use native types with default values for all fields, no optionals.
pros: Simpler client code, easier to use.
No need to check for presence explicitly.
cons: Cannot distinguish between 'field not present' and 'field present with default value'.
Potential semantic ambiguity when filtering fields.

template_adherence.title: Functions should report errors using `StatusOr<T>` instead of throwing exceptions.
template_adherence.context: We know there will be users of these C++ libraries who want to use C++ exceptions as well as those who are not able to. Our C++ libraries must work for all of our users, regardless of their ability to use exceptions.
template_adherence.decision: None of our APIs will throw exceptions to indicate errors. Instead, our APIs will typically report errors to callers by returning a `Status` or `StatusOr<T>` object, unless the library we're using has another non-throwing way to report errors (e.g., [badbit][badbit-link] in the standard I/O library).
template_adherence.consequences:
This decision will result in a single set of APIs and a consistent vocabulary for all users, whether or not they choose to compile with exceptions. This decision does not prevent callers from using exceptions in their own code.

A downside of this decision is that our APIs will not be natural or idiomatic for the [50+%][survey-link] of users who might prefer exceptions for error reporting.

Changing existing APIs from throwing exceptions to returning `StatusOr<T>` is a breaking change. As of this writing (Jan 2019), this project has a [Google Cloud Storage][gcs-link] component that is at the Alpha quality level, and a [Google Cloud Bigtable][bigtable-link] that is already at the Beta quality level. We plan to immediately change the API for Google Cloud Storage. We have no immediate plans to change the API for Cloud Bigtable. We will communicate a timeline to change this API in a separate document.

template_adherence.title: Deprecated functions do not have examples.
template_adherence.context:
we write examples for all important functions, typically the ones
that result in one or more RPCs. From time to time we need to deprecate a
function, maybe because the function has a serious defect that cannot be
resolved without changing its API, or because the function represents an
experiment that "failed", or because we found a better way to do things.
template_adherence.decision:
when we deprecate a function we will remove the examples to that
function. If the function is being replaced, we will reference the replacement
in the "Examples" paragraph. If the function is being removed, we will simply
remove the examples before the function itself. Unit tests and integration tests
are preserved. While a function might be deprecated, it is expected to work.
template_adherence.consequences:
customers will be directed to the improved replacement,
customers will not be misguided by examples that point to a deprecated approach.
Developers of `google-cloud-cpp` will have fewer examples to maintain. Customers
that cannot migrate to the new approach will not find examples of the approach
they are currently using, this is mitigated by (a) they already are using the
old approach, and (b) they can find the examples in the documentation
accompanying old releases.

template_adherence.title: Credential refresh failures participate in retry loop.
template_adherence.context: many credential types require fetching tokens from a remote service. For example, service account impersonation credentials must obtain an access token (which are time limited) by contacting the [IAM service account credentials] service. Likewise, for services without [self-signed JWT] support (e.g. GCS) the access tokens must be obtained via a separate service. The question arises: should we use a retry loop to refresh the credentials? Or should rely on the retry loop of the RPC that triggers a token refresh?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the complexity of managing multiple retry loops, the behavior of token refresh failures especially in non-idempotent operations, and the desire to minimize surprises for customers by having a single retry loop. Additionally, considerations about background token refreshes and caching tokens to reduce failures influence the decision.
template_adherence.decision: No separate loop to refresh credentials; the failures participate in the overall retry loop.
template_adherence.consequences: For customers, this means one less retry loop to think about. A separate refresh loop would be surprising as some random RPCs could take longer (or shorter) to fail than configured by the main retry loop. The downside is failures on a token refresh triggered by a non-idempotent operation. Token refreshes are retryable even if the operation that triggered the refresh is not. Problems can be minimized by using background threads to refresh tokens before they expire, and these background refreshes should be retryable.

alternatives.description: Retry the token refresh but only use remaining time: run the retry loop for the token refresh, using the existing retry strategy (and consuming its "time" or "error count").
pros: Feasible approach to handle token refresh retries.
Uses existing retry strategy.
cons: Requires changing all stubs and decorators to consume a retry policy.

template_adherence.title: Use micro frontends
template_adherence.context:
We designed the API layer (known as the backend) to be a custom set of services. This allows the user to tailor it to their own requirements, and introduce custom code as needed.

The original plan was to make the presentation layer (known as the frontend) a monolith. That is, a single service that generates all the HTML pages.

As a monolith, it is hard, if not impossible, to change or replace parts without having to replace the whole. This would mean a lot of configuration options to support differing requirements. It would also limit adoption of the platform as it can't meet them.

We investigated the use of micro frontends in [#371][Spike].
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow customization and flexibility in the frontend layer, avoiding the limitations of a monolithic frontend that is hard to change or replace. Desire to support differing requirements and increase adoption by making the frontend modular and optional.
template_adherence.decision: We will create separate services for individual, and groups of, pages. The user will use a proxy to make them appear as a single service. The frontends are independent of each other, and are always optional.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The frontends will need to share knowledge of authentication.
- Each frontend will have its own assets.
- The user will need to configure each frontend so it knows how to generate links to other frontends.
- The user can choose which frontends to use.
- The user can add their own frontends as needed.

alternatives.description: Keep the frontend as a monolithic service generating all HTML pages.
pros: Simpler deployment as only one service to manage.
Easier to maintain consistency across pages since all are generated by the same service.
cons: Hard or impossible to change or replace parts without replacing the whole.
Would require many configuration options to support differing requirements.
Limits adoption as it can't meet diverse user needs.

template_adherence.title: 2. Use component-level micro frontends for the header and footer
template_adherence.context:
Having [separate micro frontends for pages] requires duplication of the header and footer.

We expect users will want to change the content of both, as well as their styling and behaviour.

We investigated the use of micro frontends in [#371][Spike].
template_adherence.decision:
We will create dedicated services for the header and footer.

We will use [Edge Side Includes (ESIs)], limited to `<esi:include>`, to transclude them into pages.

Each component will have 2 ESIs: 1 for the `<head>` and 1 for the `<body>`.
template_adherence.consequences:
- It is compatible with popular ESI processors (e.g. Varnish, Fastly).
- Not all popular CDNs are ESI processors (e.g. AWS CloudFront). If there is no trusted proxy that can do so, each
page-level micro frontend will need to process the ESIs itself. They can detect this through the
[`Surrogate-Capability`][Surrogate-Capability] request header.
- Components can add their own CSS and JavaScript in the `<head>` ESI.
- We will need to take care to avoid clashes in styling and behaviour between the page and the components.
- The user can replace header and footer services with their own, or not use them at all.

template_adherence.title: Why Service sign in pages aren't linked to from transaction pages using a content id
template_adherence.context: Currently, when content designers create a transaction page they enter a URL for the service that the start button should link to, and this service is usually an external (to GOV.UK) URL. Service sign in pages however will be GOV.UK content items, and ideally we should not link to specific content item URLs as they could change in future. Instead, the links should reference a content_id, which never changes. However as the field where content designers enter the URL that the start button should link to doesn't support content_ids currently, the only option available to them is to enter the URL for the service sign in page.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid linking to URLs that may change, the current limitation of the content designers' URL field not supporting content_ids, and the risk assessment of linking directly to URLs versus content_ids.
template_adherence.decision: After discussion with the publishing platform team, it was decided that the risk of linking directly to a URL is low because if the base_path of the service sign in page changes, the publishing API will automatically create a redirect. Therefore, the current approach of linking directly to URLs is acceptable for now.
template_adherence.consequences: The current approach carries some risk but is mitigated by automatic redirects. Ideally, future work should enable referencing content_ids instead of URLs to fully mitigate risk.

pros: Simple to implement with current system limitations.
Low risk due to automatic redirects by publishing API.
cons: Links may break if redirects fail.

alternatives.description: Modify the system to support content_id references instead of URLs.
pros: More stable and future-proof linking.

template_adherence.title: Why "Service sign in" is its own format
template_adherence.context:
The Q3 Start Pages mission goal was to make it easier for users to choose a sign in option in order to access a service. It was decided that a page should sit in between the transaction/guide page and the service which allows users to select a sign in option such as GOV.UK Verify or Government Gateway, or to register for a new account (henceforth known as the service sign in page).

template_adherence.title: Represent persistent identifiers (schema:identifier) using schema:PropertyValue instead of Text or URL
template_adherence.context: PropertyValue is more expressive than the Text or URL, and this is helpful when trying to query across data publishers for the same PID. For example, while schema.org/identifier does force the value to be a resource, there isn't consistent use of the same resource URI to define a PID. Using a PropertyValue enables publishers to express the identifier scheme and the value separately while also expressing them together if desired. The ADR also explains common properties of identifiers, references the identifiers.org Registry for disambiguation, maps these properties to schema:PropertyValue fields, and discusses including prefixes in the value to help disambiguate identifiers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for more expressive representation of persistent identifiers to enable effective querying across data publishers; the inconsistency in resource URIs for the same PID causing querying problems; the availability of a comprehensive registry (identifiers.org) for disambiguating identifier schemes; and the desire to include identifier scheme and value separately for clarity and normalization.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to encourage the use of schema.org/PropertyValue when describing persistent identifiers (PIDs) instead of using Text or URL directly. This approach allows expressing the identifier scheme and value separately and supports better querying and normalization.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved expressiveness and querying capability across data publishers, better disambiguation of identifiers, and leveraging existing registries for identifier schemes. Negative consequences are not explicitly stated but may include the need for harvesters to recognize and normalize PIDs accordingly.

alternatives.description: Continue using Text or URL types directly for persistent identifiers without using schema:PropertyValue.
pros: Simplicity in implementation as it uses existing common types.
No need to change existing data publishing practices.
cons: Lack of expressiveness to separate identifier scheme and value.
Inconsistent resource URIs make querying and linking difficult.
Less effective querying across data publishers.

template_adherence.title: Specific Recommendations for Metadata Distribution Information
template_adherence.context:
It isn't obvious how to build a package of related files for a Dataset. To include metadata files in the schema.org description of a Dataset, reusing the `schema:distribution` property doesn't seem correct as it should serialize the actual data. As a result this issue only addresses how to use core schema.org properties to create a link between Metadata files and Datasets.

- https://github.com/ESIPFed/science-on-schema.org/issues/4
- Decision discussed at ESIP Winter Meeting. Notes here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ycG9Dlt6xRr9wxjqkQrPkJQJvm83E34eue_cxkrSGUI/edit?ts=5e1503e3#
- https://schema.org/subjectOf and https://schema.org/about
- https://schema.org/encodingFormat
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to properly link metadata documents to datasets without misusing the `schema:distribution` property, and to describe encoding formats of metadata files accurately, including profiles beyond MIME types. Also, the desire to use core schema.org properties and to have best practices and validation (e.g., SHACL shapes) for these relationships.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to link metadata documents to datasets using `schema:subjectOf` or `schema:about` properties, and to describe encoding formats of metadata files using `schema:encodingFormat` with multiple values to specify MIME types and profiles. This approach uses core schema.org properties and allows for detailed metadata description.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a clear and standardized way to link metadata files to datasets and to describe their encoding formats, facilitating interoperability and clarity. Negative consequences include the broadness of `schema:subjectOf` and `schema:about` which may include other relationships, necessitating SHACL shapes and best practices to ensure conformance and correct usage.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative is to reuse `schema:distribution` property for metadata files, which is deemed incorrect because it should serialize actual data, not metadata.
pros: Simpler model by reusing existing property.
cons: Misuses `schema:distribution` property, leading to confusion.
Does not clearly distinguish metadata files from data files.

template_adherence.title: Use PROV-O, isBasedOn, and ProvONE for provenance information
template_adherence.context: High level relationships that link datasets based on their processing workflows and versioning relationships are critical for consumers to differentiate versions of a Dataset, to clarify when a dataset is derived from one or more source Datasets, and to specify linkages to the software that created these derived Datasets. The PROV-O recommendation provides the widely-adopted vocabulary for representing this type of information, and should be used within Dataset descriptions, as most relevant properties are missing from schema.org. The main exception is schema:isBasedOn, which provides a predicate for indicating that a Dataset was derived from one or more source Datasets. Producers and consumers should interpret schema:isBasedOn to be an equivalent property to prov:wasDerivedFrom (in the owl:equivalentProperty sense). Either is acceptable for representing derivation relationships, but there is utility in expressing the relationship with both predicates. When other PROV predicates are used, it is preferred to use prov:wasDerivedFrom. Workflow relationships among processing software and both source and derived data files shoudl be described with prov:used and prov:generatedBy predicates, and by using workflow classes from ProvONE.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to represent provenance information about data processing workflows, data derivation relationships, and versioning information clearly and consistently. Use of widely adopted vocabularies and standards (PROV-O, ProvONE, schema.org) to ensure interoperability and clarity. Support for reproducible research through detailed workflow descriptions. Clarity in versioning and derivation relationships for consumers and aggregators.
template_adherence.decision: Provide provenance information about data processing workflows, data derivation relationships, and versioning information using PROV-O, ProvONE, and schema.org predicates. Specifically, use schema:isBasedOn, PROV-O predicates such as prov:wasDerivedFrom, prov:wasRevisionOf, prov:used, and prov:generatedBy, and ProvONE classes like provone:Program and provone:Execution to specify software workflows that create derived products.
template_adherence.consequences: Versioning and derivation relationships will be clearer. Aggregators and search systems should use these properties to cluster versions of Datasets and provide bi-directional linkages to derived data products. Software processing and other processing relationships can be provided via linkages to prov:Activity, particularly provone:Execution and provone:Program for specifying software processes that create derived products. However, these relationships can be complex for multi-step workflows. Providing these relationships supports reproducible research through software workflows.

template_adherence.title: ADR 007: Commit to Shares in Header
template_adherence.context: Only a single data root must be included in the Celestia block header; if more than one data root is included, light nodes will not have any guarantees that the data behind the other data roots is available unless they run a separate sampling process per data root. PayForMessage transactions include a commitment of roots of subtrees of the Celestia data root, which is required for compact proofs that a message was or was not included correctly. Over the wire, PayForMessage transactions include multiple signatures for the same message with different sizes of Celestia block to allow for non-interactive message inclusion. Rollup blocks must follow a similar strategy, specifically the data root in rollup block headers must commit to subtree roots in the Celestia data root, otherwise rollup nodes would not have any guarantees that the data behind the data root in a rollup block header is available.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to ensure data availability guarantees for rollup blocks similar to Celestia's approach, the requirement to commit to subtree roots in the rollup block header, the challenges of message inclusion and commitment in PayForMessage transactions, and the networking overhead concerns related to multiple messages per witness.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to commit rollup transactions in share form and layout in the rollup block header, similar to PayForMessage commitments. Rollup transactions begin aligned with power of 2 shares, and a new rollup block header and commitment is constructed for each possible block size. The rollup block header is appended after the transactions as a footer, changing the download pattern for rollup nodes. The WirePayForMessage structure is modified to include a new 'footers' field equal to the number of witnesses, allowing verification by appending the associated footer to the message.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive, negative, and neutral consequences are marked as TODO, so the impact is not fully detailed yet. The decision will affect message inclusion logic, data commitment, and network message structure.

alternatives.description: Don't commit to data root in rollup block header and use the MessageShareCommitment field in PayForMessage transaction to commit to both rollup block header and data.
pros: Simpler approach without modifying rollup block header structure.
cons: May only work securely under certain scenarios, not general case.
Rollup block data not committed in header, so can be malleated by rollup block producers.

alternatives.description: One message per layout, having rollup block header commit to subtree roots but different message per witness depending on data square size.
pros: Maintains commitment to subtree roots.
Allows for different layouts.
cons: Leads to unacceptably high networking overhead due to multiple messages per witness.

alternatives.description: Auction off rows instead of shares, only a single message per row, simplifying code paths.
pros: Simplifies code paths by removing multiple messages per row.
Potentially easier message inclusion logic.
cons: Does not solve the problem of changing square size.
Represents a design pivot not yet decided upon.

template_adherence.context:
* We will be storing a very small amount of data in the session.

* Cookie size will be smaller.
* One package can provide both the secrecy and authentication.
* The overall risks are considered to be less than using JWT.

template_adherence.title: 17. Brute force protection of application endpoints
template_adherence.context:
This ADR details the mitigation of brute force attacks on certain endpoints - other types of protection are out of scope.

We have a need to mitigate brute force attacks on certain endpoints in the application. Currently these are:

* Actor Login
* One Time Passcode (adding an LPA)
* Viewer Code (viewing an LPA)

Brute force can be defined as multiple failed attempts to carry out these actions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context and decision sections imply drivers such as the need to reliably identify users and track attempts to protect against brute force attacks on specific endpoints.
template_adherence.decision:
Protecting against these kinds of attacks is a problem in two parts; reliable identification of users and the recording of attempts by that user against protected endpoints.

Identification: The bare minimum of information that we can use to identify a user is their originating IP address. This is not without issue as it can be spoofed, or more likely the user is behind a NAT or proxy layer (as will likely be the case with our corporate users). We can couple the browser sent headers that offer extra user identifying information (such as 'Accept' 'DNT', 'User-Agent' etc) in a hashing function to generate an ID that should more uniquely identify a user.

We will identify users using a hash calculated using the incoming IP and associated headers.

We will track this identity in the session to guard against changing headers within a session.

Attempt Tracking: We will use a cache service (AWS Elasticache) to track failure attempts at each of the three endpoints defined above.

We will use a per-endpoint moving window rate-limit to reduce brute force impact - these will be individually configurable in terms of window size and request limit.
template_adherence.consequences:
This will introduce a new piece of technology to the stack - a Redis based Elasticache.

Identification of users is a tricky issue and prone to abuse. Further refinements on the approach will need to be made.

template_adherence.title: 18. Session lifetime and session based cookies
template_adherence.context: We need to supply the user with prompts that they have been logged out due to inactivity. This is not currently possible due to our session lifetime being dictated by the expiry of our session cookie (currently 20 minutes). Once a cookie has expired we do not recognise a user in order to tell them that they have been logged out.
template_adherence.decision:
* We will lengthen the cookie expiry to be as long as the business requires to display a _"logged out due to inactivity"_ message. Somewhere in the region of 1 day - 1 week will likely be acceptable.

template_adherence.consequences: This will increase the size of the session cookie but we believe it is still below the size where we would consider moving to different infrastructure (session information stored within AWS). We will revisit this issue when any further additions are made.

template_adherence.consequences:
A nice feature of Typeorm is that it will automatically migrate your database schema to match what's defined in your entities. This looks great for development but once we have production users we'll probably need to turn this off and move over to explicit migrations.

Typeorm encourages you to put database column definitions on "entity" classes. We need to make careful use of interfaces to prevent these details leaking where they shouldn't.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use bare git repos
template_adherence.context: When we create git repos we can either use `git init --bare` or we can clone them. A cloned repo has one main working tree with the git directory inside it. You can add additional worktrees. A bare repo does not have a default worktree, but we can still check out branches using the `git worktree` command.
template_adherence.decision:
We should create a folder structure for each repo, something like

```
- git-repos
- <hash of repo ID>
- git # main bare git repo
- branches # worktrees go under here
- master # a worktree for the master branch
```

This folder structure will also allow us to store other data about the repo in files
template_adherence.consequences:
Using bare repos allows us to re-use code from Jam, and it also looks like it will make things less confusing when we start committing files, since multiple clients can work on separate branches independently. It feels cleaner somehow than having a non-bare repo.

Once we start cloning people's repos it will be hard to change this decision, but not impossible.

template_adherence.title: 8. Hexagonal architecture / CQRS
template_adherence.context: We have just enough features in the repo to see the shape it will need to take.
template_adherence.decision:
We'll aim our refactoring towards a hexagonal architecture, using commands and events as the way to communicate with the core domain.

Something like this:

![diagram](./0008-hexagonal-architecture.jpg)

Key to the diagram:

- Each box represents at least one yarn/npm package.
- Arrows, where drawn, indicate a dependency.
- Green indicates where we've already created and are building this package.
- Amber indicates where we have code for this, but it still needs to be factored out into this design.
- Hand-drawn lines indicate a bounded context.

Other agreements:

- Communication into / out of the core domain will be via commands and domain events.
- Commands going into the domain will all be asynchronous. The application layer (client port) can abstract this away by watching for domain events that indicate when the command has completed.
- We won't use event sourcing for the domain models, but we will probably persist domain events in a log.
- The client port will mediate queries to go straight into git, e.g. for streams of files.
- The web may keep its own cache of read models, shaped in the representation needed for its API. Hence the separate bounded context.
template_adherence.consequences:
This design enables us to handle known and anticipated future requirements cleanly and quickly.

We will need time to move the existing code into this design before we're ready to absorb new features.

We still need to figure out:

- How to shape the abstraction around the task scheduler - use a specific port? Or just build someting around the events?

template_adherence.title: use command/query-based API for git repos
template_adherence.context:
Interacting with git repos involves many fine-grained operations, each of which is independent from the others - there's no shared state between them, other than what lives in the repo itself on disk. So they can be handled by independent functions rather than being modelled as methods on a class.

We anticipate that as the application grows, the number of these operations is likely to grow too. To maintain the open/closed, principle, we need a way to add new operations whithout modifying too much existing code.

It's also useful to be able to test each operation independently, since some of them will need quite involved test cases, and a single test of tests for one class would get pretty lengthy.

Finally, would be helpful to be able to compose fine-grained operations into higher-order ones, such as combining the operations of creating a branch, making a commit, and pushing to origin into a `PushCommit` operation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle many fine-grained, independent git repo operations.
- Desire to maintain open/closed principle as operations grow.
- Need for independent testing of operations.
- Ability to compose fine-grained operations into higher-order ones.
- Ease of reading tests and client code.
- Potential complexity for newcomers in setup code.
template_adherence.decision: Implemented a command-bus package providing a TypeScript-friendly single `dispatch` function that takes different types of message objects and dispatches them to appropriate handler functions.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Tests that set up git repos are easier to read.
- Potential to serialize/deserialize messages for background task scheduling.
- Mocking the repo interface may be more tricky, possibly requiring a facade.
- Pattern might confuse newcomers due to less nice setup code for `dispatch` function.

template_adherence.title: 11. Remove task scheduler (for now)
template_adherence.context:
The current design of task scheduler creates one queue per repo. We can't see how this can work with an out-of-process worker, since the worker needs to know in advance which queues to listen on, and the list of repos could change.

This design was primarily influenced by needing a way to synchonise the acceptance tests at the point where the jobs for a repo had all finished.

As we work to implement feedback when repo connections fail, this design was causing friction.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly titled or separated, but can be inferred from the Context and Consequences sections discussing design limitations, synchronization needs, and performance impacts.
template_adherence.decision: Its simpler for the time being to remove the task scheduler, so repo connections and fetches will be immediately consistent, for the time being.
template_adherence.consequences:
The upside is simplicity - it's one less moving part as we try to model the state transitions as we try to connect a repo.

The major downside is that a connect HTTP request to the service will currently not respond until the `git fetch` has completed, where previously it responded immediately, while the `fetch` happened in the background. We should not deploy until this is resolved, as it would have performance impacts on CucumberStudio, which makes these calls during a user request.
