template_adherence.title: Always use value objects in the core
template_adherence.context:
We've historically used primitives for things like, say, a RepoId. We've also sometimes used interfaces, exported by the core package, to represent the shape of some values being passed in.

We've found that using primitives doesn't make the most of Typescript, and also makes the code less expressive. Value Objects attract behaviour, and where we've used a value object, we've been able to move functions onto it.

Where we've mixed interfaces and full-blown objects to represent values, we've found the interfaces confusing. It's better to standardise on one or the other.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve expressiveness and leverage TypeScript capabilities.
- Desire to standardize on a single approach for representing values to reduce confusion.
- Maintain use of interfaces for polymorphic API surfaces.
- Encourage behavior encapsulation by using value objects.
template_adherence.decision:
As of issue #164, all types passed into the interfaces of the core package are value objects.

Interfaces will continue to represent API surfaces that might have polymorphic implementations, but value object classes, exported by the core package, will represent values.

This applies even to single attributes like a commit author's name.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Slightly increased effort in setting up test data.
- Potential need to revive or adopt tools like 'tdb' to assist with testing.

alternatives.description: Continue using primitives and interfaces as before without standardizing on value objects.
pros: No additional setup or changes required.
Familiarity with existing codebase maintained.
cons: Less expressive code.
Missed opportunity to leverage TypeScript's strengths.
Interfaces mixed with objects can cause confusion.

alternatives.description: Use only interfaces to represent values, avoiding value objects.
pros: Consistent use of interfaces.
Potentially simpler type definitions.
cons: Interfaces lack behavior encapsulation.
Less expressive than value objects.
May not fully leverage TypeScript capabilities.

template_adherence.title: 16. Handle concurrent git operations
template_adherence.context: Concurrent git operations can fail because git is locking the repo. The current implementation is waiting for jobs to finish, but multiple workers in different containers can still take jobs in the queue and proccess them in parallel.
template_adherence.decision: Reduce worker concurrency to 1 by using a single container (for now).
template_adherence.consequences:
1. The system cannot process multiple jobs in parallel which could make depending services slower.
2. We'll have to consider a better way of handling queues and workers in the future:
- We'll need workers handling jobs in parallel but in sequence for each repositories. i.e. jobs cannot be run in parallel for a single repo.
- Ideas to do that: Mutex, one queue per repo, allocate jobs for a repo to a dedicated worker using some sort of supervisor.

template_adherence.title: 4. Application architecture
template_adherence.context:
We are starting to build a beta of the 'Apply for postgraduate teacher training' service. This service will have 5 distinct user groups, who will have their own interface in the service.

1. Candidates are people who would like to become a teacher.
2. Provider users work for an organisation that provides teacher training, like a school or university
3. Vendors make software that universities use for administration
4. Referees will be provided by candidates and the service will ask them to provide a reference
5. Users within DfE need information about the performance of the service and solve problems

For the architecture of the system, we've discussed 2 options: a microservice architecture and a monolith.

In the microservice architecture, we might split up the service into 3 or more applications - for example an API, a frontend for candidates and a frontend for the provider users. In the monolithic architecture, all components live together in a single application.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to choose an architecture suitable for a small team (less than 20).
- Consideration of benefits typically associated with microservices (independent teams, scaling, reuse).
- Anticipated traffic patterns and team size.
- Desire for ease of development and deployment.
- Awareness of potential downsides of monoliths (complexity, slow tests).
template_adherence.decision: Chosen to go for a monolith architecture because the microservice benefits are not significant for this project given team size, traffic patterns, and reuse needs. Monolith approach simplifies development and deployment.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to structure the application well using modules and separation to maintain boundaries.
- Need to invest in making tests fast to avoid slowdown.
- Potential risk of complexity and difficulty understanding the monolith over time.

alternatives.description: Microservice architecture splitting the service into multiple applications (API, frontend for candidates, frontend for providers).
pros: Allows teams to work independently.
Enables independent scaling of components.
Facilitates reuse of components across the organisation.
cons: Team size is small, so independent teams less critical.
Traffic spikes are similar across components, so independent scaling less useful.
No current need to reuse components elsewhere.

alternatives.description: Monolithic architecture with all components in a single application.
pros: Simpler to run for developers.
Easier to deploy.
Better suited for small team and similar traffic patterns.
cons: Can lead to complexity with growth of classes and files.
Tests may become slow over time, causing frustration and development slowdown.

template_adherence.title: 8. API extensions mechanism
template_adherence.context:
With the first alpha version of our API released and the first vendor integrations on the the horizon, we need a plan around minor and major revisions to our API. Our API baseurl is already versioned ('/api/v1') but it was suggested we should explore 'extension' mechanisms to the API so that we are able to release previews of API changes to vendors or supply custom fields to specific vendors, if needed, without creating problems for everyone else. There is some concern that the tools or libraries vendors may use to integrate with our API break when they encounter a new/unknown attribute, instead of just ignoring it.

The main idea explored was giving vendors the ability to request optional fields as URL query parameters (e.g. `/?extensions=key1,key2`), which would ensure:

- only vendors who explicitly requested optional fields would receive them, and
- the set of optional fields requested would always stay the same, unless vendors update the URL they use for their API requests

Therefore, we tried to come up with a plan which would provide such functionality while consistent with the API choices made so far.

An ideal 'extensions' mechanism would provide:

- an update path for API changes,
- which does not obstruct API use for vendors who expect payloads never to change,
- while allows enough customisation for vendors with more agile teams

### Findings

Although our API is not advertised as a [JSON:API](https://jsonapi.org/), it follows many conventions of the spec, so we tried to plan an 'extensions' mechanism consistent with JSON:API guidelines. JSON:API allows the use of `/?fields=` and `/?include=`.

However, the JSON:API spec contains:

> If a client requests a restricted set of fields for a given resource type, an endpoint MUST NOT include additional fields in resource objects of that type in its response.

and

> A resource object’s attributes and its relationships are collectively called its “fields”.

This would work fine for vendors not specifying `/?fields=` but would result in very long URLs for vendors requesting optional fields, as they would need to specify all fields they need (unless we use something like a non-standard `/?fieldset=` grouping).

We could, in theory, use `/?include=` to specify groups of attributes to be included in a separate part of the response (JSON:API provides an `included:` section), but strictly speaking these extra fields are not really additional resources. There would also be some complexity around mapping data between the main attributes block and the `included:` section, even more for one-to-many associations/lists, especially in the absence of ids.

If we wanted to proceed with either `/?fields`= or `/?include=`, we would probably need to consider changing the presentation of resources to make use of the `relationships:` and `included:` blocks, as is good JSON:API practice. This, in effect, would mean we start advertising our API as a JSON:API one, as parsing relationships and associations properly would then require the use of JSON:API consumer library, for practical purposes. JSON:API libraries exist in many languages and ecosystems, but their level of maturity varies.

#### Pros

- implementing an extensions API would allow us to pre-release features to specific vendors
- agile vendors could optimise their requests, by requesting exactly the fields that they need
- we would not need to increment our API version with every minor field addition

#### Cons

- it is unclear what the best approach for adding this extensions mechanism is (`/?fields=` vs `/?include=` vs `/?fieldset=`, plus do we merge fields in main attributes block or do we add to the `included:` section)
- if we were to follow JSON:API recommendations and put associations in `relationships:` and `included:` blocks, it would be easier to add `/?fields=` and `/?included=` support, but this would make our responses hard to parse by vendors that do not have JSON:API libraries.
- implementing such an 'extensions' mechanism may be overkill for a small number of vendors and minor API revisions a year
- an 'extensions' mechanism could, actually, be introduced as part of a minor release at any point, does not need to be implemented now
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support minor and major revisions to the API without breaking existing vendors
- Desire to allow preview or custom fields for specific vendors without impacting others
- Concern about vendor tools breaking on unknown attributes
- Desire to keep API usage simple for vendors expecting stable payloads
- Consideration of JSON:API conventions and their implications
- Trade-offs between URL complexity, response structure, and vendor parsing capabilities
- Frequency and scale of API changes and vendor needs
template_adherence.decision: We have decided to not to implement an 'extensions' mechanism at this point because there is no immediate need and we are likely to make a better choice of implementation when and if such a need does arise. If additional fields need to be released, we shall take the traditional route of a minor version release, ensuring no breaking changes are included in the release. The current advertised API versioning strategy can be found here: https://apply-for-postgraduate-teacher-training-tech-docs.cloudapps.digital/#versioning
template_adherence.consequences: None, unless the rate of minor releases becomes too frequent, at which time we will be in a better position to decide on how to implement that extension mechanism - fields, include or something else.

alternatives.description: Implement an extensions API using URL query parameters such as `/?fields=`, `/?include=`, or a custom `/?fieldset=` to allow vendors to request optional fields.
pros: Allows pre-release of features to specific vendors
Enables agile vendors to optimize requests by requesting exactly needed fields
Avoids incrementing API version with every minor field addition
cons: Unclear best approach among `/?fields=`, `/?include=`, or `/?fieldset=`
Following JSON:API recommendations would require changing response structure to use `relationships:` and `included:` blocks

Could be introduced later as part of a minor release

template_adherence.title: 13. Course Option Validity
template_adherence.context:
We define a course option as a specific combination of (course, study mode, site). A course has several sites, and each site may offer the course in full time or part time modes. Every course option we create for a course covers one of the combinations.

We've recently completed a series of iterations that deal with:

- course options falling into a state that means they are no longer valid choices for an application
- how to deal with options that fall into this state after they've already been added to a candidate's application

This ADR summarises the design choices made during this phase of work and provides an overview of how various course option states are handled.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly state decision drivers as a separate section or heading. However, the context and decision sections imply drivers such as handling invalid course options, preventing submission of applications with invalid options, and managing course option states effectively.
template_adherence.decision:
The service currently stops an application being submitted (via error messages on submission) in the following cases:

- The course is full (ie - it has no vacancies at any of its course options)
- The course has been withdrawn by the provider from Find.
- The course has been closed by us on Apply.
- The specific course option chosen by the candidate is full (but other course options have vacancies).

There's a fifth state we handle as well:

- Upon syncing, the Find API tells us that a specific site is no longer related to a course.

For these cases, we:

- try and delete the course options for this site/course combo, OR
- if the course option is part of a candidate's application we set the field `site_still_valid` to `false` and notify support instead.
template_adherence.consequences:
- We now handle the majority of known 'invalid' course option states.
- There is further analysis underway to decide if, when stopping app submission, it's worthwhile distinguishing between site vacancy and study mode vacancy.

template_adherence.title: 14. Alerting and Monitoring
template_adherence.context:
The team have recently discussed Apply's approach to alerting. By alerting we mean that we are notified when:

1. There's is an outage
2. The service is partially down, like DfE Signin or a specific feature
3. Candidates cannot make applications, though no errors are thrown. For example because of a bug.
4. The system is performing so slowly that it's not usable
5. Before there's an outage

We currently have the following setup for alerting us that something is wrong:

- Azure availability alerts. Azure checks the healthcheck endpoint. This checks if the application has database connectivity and is processing background jobs correctly. Azure availability tests records failure only on the third failed attempt and we are notified ~5 minutes after a failure.
- Smoke tests run after each deploy. These tests sign in to the service and make sure that the service is usable.
- Sentry tells us when exceptions occur.

We've discussed expanding the things we alert for. For example, we could alert on lower-level technical issues like disk space, memory leaks, or high CPU. These alerts could potentially give us advance warning of infrastructure issues.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to be notified of outages, partial service failures, application issues without errors, performance degradation, and advance warnings before outages. There is a concern about false positives and over-alerting from low-level system metrics. Confidence in existing Azure availability alerts, smoke tests, and Sentry exception monitoring influences the decision. The preference is for symptom-based monitoring over cause-based monitoring, as described by the Google SRE handbook.
template_adherence.decision: We will not add monitoring for low-level system metrics as we have confidence in Azure and our current smoke tests and availability tests to pick up major problems. We acknowledge a small chance that lower-level alerts would alert us sooner but they increase false positives and over-alerting. We choose symptom-based monitoring over cause-based monitoring. We will continue to be alerted in Slack for service availability and Sentry exceptions, and continue to improve our smoke tests.
template_adherence.consequences: We will continue as we do now, improving the availability check, smoke tests, and Sentry setup.

alternatives.description: Add monitoring for low-level system metrics such as disk space, memory leaks, or high CPU to get advance warning of infrastructure issues.
pros: Potentially earlier detection of infrastructure problems.
More granular insight into system health.
cons: Increased chance of false positives.
Risk of over-alerting and alert fatigue.
Additional complexity in monitoring setup.

template_adherence.title: 16. Structured GCSE grades
template_adherence.context: Since the service launched, candidates have been able to enter details about their academic and other relevant qualifications using free text answers for most questions. We’ve seen that free-text answers can often lead to candidates submitting applications with spelling errors, which may reduce their chances of being offered an interview. There is also some complexity around entering GCSE standard equivalent qualifications; there are a number of different English GCSE exams, and science GCSEs can be awarded in a number of different ways. There are two key differences between English and Science GCSEs - for English GCSEs they have different certificates and are considered separate qualifications (eg. English Language and English Literature) - a candidate can enter an 'other English GCSE' qualification and give it a name, eg. Cockney Rhyming Slang. We considered two different options for how we store this data in the database - as separate records, one for each GCSE qualification - as a single record with the different qualifications stored in a JSON blob in a `structured_grades` column Part of the reason for this problem is that the English GCSE form is a single page but is gathering information about multiple qualifications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include reducing spelling errors in free-text answers, handling complexity of multiple GCSE qualifications especially English and Science, database structure reflecting domain structure versus code complexity, and ease of storing 'other English GCSEs' with custom names.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to use the JSON blob approach to store multiple English GCSE qualifications in a single record. This was chosen because the candidate interface treats English GCSEs together rather than separately, and to avoid extra code complexity that would arise from modeling multiple separate records in the database.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include smaller code footprint and encapsulation of serialization logic in the form object, and easy storage of 'other English GCSEs' with custom names. Negative consequence is that the database structure does not reflect the domain structure of multiple qualifications as separate records.

alternatives.description: Separate records for each GCSE qualification in the database.
pros: Database structure closely reflects the domain structure of multiple qualifications.
cons: Increased code complexity to handle multiple English GCSEs in the application form and grade controller.
No obvious way to store the name of 'other English GCSEs' such as Cockney Rhyming Slang without adding new fields.

alternatives.description: Store different qualifications in a JSON blob in a single record's `structured_grades` column.
pros: Encapsulates serialization and deserialization logic inside the form object, reducing codebase impact.
Easily stores names of 'other English GCSEs' such as Cockney Rhyming Slang.
cons: Database structure does not reflect the domain structure.

template_adherence.title: 17. Application Choice Updated At
template_adherence.context:
Consumers of the Vendor API can filter applications by updated_at value, to get a list of applications that have changed since a certain time. They typically use this to avoid processing applications that have already been ingested into their services. If the updated_at values are inaccurate, there is a potential for vendors to process applications twice or miss application changes entirely. For that reason, we set up touch relationships from the application form to the application choice to ensure that changes to the application form touch the application choices.

This approach resulted in false positives (where the updated_at value had changed but the data in the application API response had not). This is because there are fields on the application form which do not appear in the application API response.

For example, when geocoding data was added to applications. Every application was touched, but the data was not included in the response so API consumers could not see any changes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for accurate updated_at timestamps to avoid duplicate or missed processing by API consumers.
- Avoid false positives where updated_at changes but API response data does not.
- Simplicity and maintainability of the solution.
- Ability to explicitly track significant attribute changes affecting API responses.
- Mitigation of risks of false negatives and false positives in updated_at changes.
- Maintainability of specs to ensure correctness of significant attributes list.
template_adherence.decision: For changes to the application form we will specify a whitelist of attributes that, when changed, affect the application API response. This approach keeps an explicit list of significant attributes and uses standard Rails techniques, making it simple and easy to follow. To mitigate risks of false negatives and false positives, specs have been added to check the list of significant attributes against those affecting API responses. For smaller related models, a concern TouchApplicationChoices is added to touch application_choices on create, update, or delete.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The updated_at attribute for ApplicationChoices will now accurately reflect when the last update that affected it occurred.
- New specs need to be maintained when the single application presenter is changed.
- Requires ongoing maintenance of the whitelist and specs to ensure accuracy.
- Addresses false positives and negatives better than previous approaches.

alternatives.description: Render the API response for an application whenever a related model changes and detect if the response changed to decide whether to update updated_at.
pros: Only change updated_at when the API response actually changes.
cons: Sensitive to changes in the shape of the API response, not just data changes.
Adding new fields to the response would cause updated_at to change even if data is not meaningfully changed.
Requires complex logic to ignore certain changes, increasing complexity.

template_adherence.title: Public ids for qualifications
template_adherence.context: The Vendor API exposes candidate qualifications and grades for systems to ingest. Each qualification in the system has an id, which vendor systems use to identify the qualification. It is therefore important that each qualification coming from the API has a unique id. We use the database id for a qualification object for this purpose. An issue arises when we have qualifications that are made up of multiple exams/grades. See [the ADR on structured grades](./0016-structured-gcse-grades.md) for background on the way gcse qualifications are stored. API consumers expect one qualification entity per exam/grade. However, because of the structured grades introduced above, some exams/grades share the same database id. Therefore, not all the ids for qualifications coming through the API are unique.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for unique identification of qualifications in the API.
- Backwards compatibility with existing vendor systems.
- Handling of structured grades vs single grades.
- Avoiding id collisions between database ids and public ids.
- Ensuring API consumers receive unique ids per qualification entity.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to introduce a new public_id column in the application_qualifications table to store the API id for a qualification. For qualifications with simple grades (including triple science gcse), the public_id will be set to the database id initially via a data migration. For qualifications with structured grades, the public_id column will be nil, and public ids will be set inside the structured_grades json, with one id per grade. The first grade inside structured grades will get the database id as its public_id, and other grades will get new unique public_ids generated via a postgres sequence. A new column will be added to replace the structured_grades column to safely change the data structure. This approach maintains backwards compatibility and ensures globally unique ids in the API.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Each qualification entity will have a globally unique id in the API.
- Backwards compatibility with existing vendor systems is maintained.
- The data model is extended with a new public_id column and a new column replacing structured_grades.
- Complexity in handling structured grades is managed by assigning public_ids within the JSON structure.
- Use of a postgres sequence ensures uniqueness of generated public_ids.

alternatives.description: Change the data type of the id field in the API response to a string to support ids like '123', '123_1', '123_2'.
pros: Allows unique ids by appending suffixes to the base id.
Simple to implement in the API response.
cons: Vendors were not able to support this change.
Breaks backwards compatibility with existing integer id expectations.

template_adherence.title: Version API via URI path
template_adherence.context:
Versioning APIs can be controversial. Ideally, APIs don't need to change, or be additive so as not to break backwards compatibility. Occasionally, some changes require bigger changes.

We will do our best to be open w/ what we accept and strict w/ what we return

There are lots of ways an API can change:
* Breaking changes across the entire API (all endpoints change from REST to GraphQL for example)
* Breaking changes at a resource level (/v1/booking) needs to change
* Breaking changes in behavior

This decision currently applies to the 1st bullet.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use Okta as Identity provider
template_adherence.context:
Okta is an Identity as a Service provider (similar to Auth0) that can provide authentication and authorization support to an application.  They have a forever free developer account that allows up to 7000 active users/mo (well below our anticipated usage).

Okta provides the ability to authenticate against a variety of providers (okta, social (facebook, github, microsoft azure, etc), SAML, AD/LDAP).  We would use the Microsoft social OpenConnect ID provider.  It will map the Microsoft user into an Okta user, essentially acting as a proxy or facade to Microsoft while providing a more uniform and standards adhering API.

They have integrations into Spring Boot 1.x (via okta spring security starter) and Spring Security 5.x (via Spring Boot 2.x) supports Okta out of the box.

They have a React client SDK instead of using our handrolled client code for Microsoft Azure AD.

The real value add comes when we need to add roles/groups (admin level users).  You get admin screens/dashboards "for free" to add/remove users etc.

Later on, we could add additional social logins (or support AD directly if needed).

Spike can be found at: https://github.com/buildit/bookit-api/tree/okta-spring-boot-1.x
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a reliable Identity as a Service provider with support for multiple authentication providers.
- Desire to have a uniform and standards-adhering API for authentication.
- Integration support with Spring Boot and React client.
- Requirement for admin level user management (roles/groups).
- Consideration of future extensibility (additional social logins, direct AD support).
- Concerns about local user table necessity and synchronization.
- Limitations of free developer account and SLA concerns.
- Uncertainty about acquiring MS Graph access tokens for user data access.
template_adherence.decision:
- Delay implementation for now due to the need for a local user table.
- Use Okta as the Identity Provider (IdP) for Bookit.
- Use Okta's React client for client-side code.
- Use Okta's Spring Boot 1.x starter.
- Use Okta Access Tokens as Bearer tokens.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Spring Boot 2.x support for Okta is not yet released and lacks support for @EnableResourceServer.
- Likely need to maintain a local user table for efficient queries.
- Okta provides a layer of abstraction for potential future changes.
- Access Tokens enable support for third-party API access.
- Need to determine how to obtain user details via access token or userinfo endpoint.
- Synchronization challenges between Okta and local users.
- Free developer account limitations: no SLA, no customizable verification emails.
- Uncertainty about acquiring MS Graph access tokens for email/calendar access.

alternatives.description: Continue using Microsoft as the identity provider with id_token as Bearer token.
pros: Already in use, so less initial setup.
Direct integration with Microsoft services.
cons: Less uniform API compared to Okta.
Lack of admin dashboards for user management.
Potentially more custom client code needed.

alternatives.description: Use another Identity as a Service provider like Auth0.
pros: Similar features to Okta.
Potentially different pricing or SLA options.
cons: May require additional evaluation and integration effort.
Unknown compatibility with existing Spring Boot and React setup.

template_adherence.title: 7. Use Pac4J to validate tokens
template_adherence.context:
http://www.pac4j.org

While exporing alternatives to our custom filter and token validator, we came across pac4j which can deal with Azure AD out of the box.

The driver for this alternative is to have a library where we can point it to the discovery url (https://login.microsoftonline.com/organizations/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration) and have it "just work."  Microsoft is a bit off standard where they add {tenantId} to the Issuer URL because this is a multi-tenant endpoint.  While it's not hard, openid connect libraries need to be adjusted to handle this.  Pac4j does this for free.
template_adherence.decision: * Use Pac4J to validate MS id_tokens instead of our current custom filter code
template_adherence.consequences:
* Less unit testing on our end
* Pac4J only supports the Authorization Code flow which is not what we would be using
* Unless we went with the hybrid flow (id_token + code)
* Pac4J is an additional layer on top of Spring Security (as it can be used with a variety of other frameworks)
* As such we would have to learn yet another framework to configure security
* There is a HeaderClient that would work with the JwtAuthenticator to handle Bearer tokens but can't hook into the AzureAdClient that we're seeking

template_adherence.title: 10. JPA manages schema
template_adherence.context: Originally, we used Spring Boot's Database Initialization support to automatically create and intialize our database via schema.sql and data.sql scripts.  Each deployment (application initialization) would execute these scripts.  Our implementation would drop the database and recreate it each time.  While this accelerated our development (avoid data migrations), it's not sustainable
template_adherence.decision:
* Leverage Hibernate's (our JPA implementation) ddl-auto feature to update the staging/production databases (we will continue to drop/recreate all other databases....local, integration).
* recreating in integration ensures a clean database for each run.  In addition, it validates that we can recreate a database from scratch
template_adherence.consequences:
* Hibernate does warn against utilizing this feature "in production."
* We can "test" the update in staging.  There is a risk that Hibernate updates a schema naively which may result in dropped data
* This approach won't address how we can add static data (locations & bookables for now) over time.
* Hibernate won't drop columns that are no longer used.  Add only.
* Also won't migrate data for you.  Schema only.
* If any of the above prove onerous, we can address by introducing a database migration tool such as Liquibase or Flyway.
* This did cause us to hit a memory limit (previously set to 256MB).  Had to bump to 512MB.

template_adherence.title: Contain and manage state
template_adherence.context:
The hardest part of debugging Page Previews issues (especially those related to EventLogging) was understanding the state of the system (the "state") and how it's mutated given some interaction(s). This was in no small part because the state was defined, initialized, and mutated in various parts of the codebase.

The state required for Page Previews to function isn't actually overly complicated. To keep things easy to debug/easy to reason about we should endeavour to isolate the state and its mutations from the various other parts of the system.
template_adherence.decision: Use [Redux](http://redux.js.org).
template_adherence.consequences:
* Newcomers will have to familiarise themselves with the library (especially it's nomenclature).
* All changes will have to be broken down into: the additional state that they require; actions that are dispatched; and how the state is mutated as a result of those actions. This requires discipline.
* We benefit from using a tool that is part of an increasingly rich ecosystem, e.g. see [Redux DevTools Extension](https://github.com/zalmoxisus/redux-devtools-extension).

template_adherence.title: 3. Keep enabled state only in preview reducer
template_adherence.context: There is global state for determining if the previews are enabled or disabled. It lives in the `preview` reducer as the `enabled` key. The problem arises when the settings reducer also needs to know about the previous `enabled` state to decide how to handle changes triggered by a `SETTINGS_CHANGE` action. Several options to handle this state duplication and synchronization issue were considered.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers include avoiding duplication of state and logic, maintaining clarity and maintainability of the codebase, preventing confusion about which state to use, and minimizing the risk of state getting out of sync. Also considered were the implications on action creators being synchronous or asynchronous (Redux Thunk).
template_adherence.decision: Option 3 was chosen: Keep the `enabled` flag in the `preview` reducer as the canonical source of `enabled` state, convert `saveSettings` to a Redux Thunk to query global state and dispatch current and next state in the action. This choice was made for clarity and maintainability, despite the con of using a Redux Thunk in a synchronous action creator context.
template_adherence.consequences: The `saveSettings` action creator is now a Redux Thunk that queries the enabled state from the `preview` reducer and includes it in the `SETTINGS_CHANGE` action. This allows the `settings` reducer to perform its business logic based on accurate state. The approach reduces duplication and confusion but introduces the use of Redux Thunk in a synchronous action creator scenario.

template_adherence.title: Frontend sources directory structure
template_adherence.context:
With the addition of a frontend bundler, there are now assets that are the source, and assets that are for distribution.

Before, all assets were distribution ones stored in `resources/`, just a configurable convention used by the Reading Web team for using MediaWiki's ResourceLoader.

In order to facilitate the CI checks and understanding where sources are and where compiled sources are, we need to chose two distinct paths for storing sources and distribution files.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but implied drivers include ease of understanding to the wider development community and good mapping between the name and what they contain.
template_adherence.decision:
After some discussion, because of ease of understanding to the wider development community and the good mapping between the name and what they contain, we chose to:

* Put unbundled frontend sources in `src/`.
* Put bundled distribution files in `dist/` under `resources/` in `resources/dist/`.
* Files directly distributed by ResourceLoader remain under `resources/*` to follow Reading Web Team's conventions around assets used by ResourceLoader.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Frontend sources will be under `src/`.
* After `npm start` or `npm run build` the bundled sources will be under `resources/dist`.
* Jenkins will check in continuous integration that the sources under `src/` are actually compiled when commited under `resources/dist`.
* If the `src` path where to become inconvenient because we wanted to add other types of sources in it, we'll move the frontend assets to `src/js` or something more specific.

template_adherence.title: 6. Factories
template_adherence.context: Given that the majority of the codebase is going to be rewritten, there's a need for a consistent style for building the system anew. The Reading Web team has historically taken an object oriented approach, resulting in classes with many varied concerns and inheritance issues, leading to testing difficulties. The team uses underscore prefixes for private members due to lack of visibility modifiers. The decision to use Redux means much code will be written as functions returning objects (factories). A general rule is needed to produce maintainable and familiar code, acknowledging exceptions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for consistent style in a major codebase rewrite; historical issues with object-oriented approach leading to complex, hard-to-test classes; lack of language/tooling support for visibility modifiers; adoption of Redux requiring factory-style functions; desire for maintainability, familiarity, and flexibility; trade-offs between inheritance and composition.
template_adherence.decision:
1. Favor factories over classes by default.
2. Favor classes only when performance benefits of prototypal inheritance outweigh consistency and simplicity benefits.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Easier portability without framework dependencies; replacement of 'new' with factory functions; encourages composition over inheritance leading to more flexible systems.
Negative: More effort required to share behavior via composition; 'instanceof' operator becomes useless; requires careful interface design.
Overall, should result in easier to test and maintain components.

alternatives.description: Favor classes over factories, continuing the traditional object-oriented approach with inheritance.
pros: Familiar to developers used to classical OOP.
Potential performance benefits from prototypal inheritance.
cons: Leads to classes with many varied concerns.
Harder to test components in isolation.
Encourages inheritance over composition, which has known drawbacks.

alternatives.description: Use a mixed approach without clear preference, choosing factories or classes as needed without a guiding rule.
pros: Flexibility to choose the best approach per case.
No strict constraints on design style.
cons: Lack of consistency across codebase.
Potential confusion and maintenance difficulties.
Harder to enforce best practices and testing strategies.

template_adherence.title: 8. Enable minification of bundle with UglifyJS
template_adherence.context:
Sources are currently minified by JSMin producing a bundle bigger than necessary. We want to produce a JS bundle as small as possible to ship less code to clients.

Given we have a pre-compilation step in Popups, we can leverage node based tooling without penalty, so using UglifyJS to minify the code is an option.

We performed some analysis to see the differences in asset size between the two tools. See:

* [Minifying assets with uglifyjs][1]

Results with the current codebase as of today 12th of May 2017 are that uglify produces a 40% smaller bundle, and a 25% smaller bundle when using gzip.

This results are stable through the last 3 months, the same test has been performed multiple times. See [Compressed JS comparison][2]
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Produce a smaller JS bundle to reduce client code size and improve performance.
Leverage existing pre-compilation step to use node-based tooling.
Empirical evidence showing UglifyJS produces significantly smaller bundles than JSMin.
template_adherence.decision:
Webpack's production mode has been enabled for `npm run build`, and thus the compiled bundle will be minified in production with UglifyJS.

See [Enable production settings for the production bundle][3]
template_adherence.consequences: The Popups bundle served in production is 40% smaller, 25% when using GZIP.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSMin for minification.
pros: Already in use, no changes needed.
Stable and known process.
cons: Produces larger bundles compared to UglifyJS.
Less efficient minification leading to more data sent to clients.

alternatives.description: Use UglifyJS for minification.
pros: Produces 40% smaller bundles, 25% smaller with gzip.
Leverages node-based tooling in pre-compilation step.
Improves client performance by reducing bundle size.
cons: Requires enabling Webpack production mode.
Introduces new tooling dependency.

template_adherence.title: 9. Utilize browser caching
template_adherence.context: We needed to make sure we're not overloading the servers with excessive requests. We wanted to find a way to serve fresh resources while keeping the back-end happy.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but inferred from the context: need to reduce server load, serve fresh resources, avoid complexity of custom caching.
template_adherence.decision: Page Previews will leverage the browser's cache rather than maintaining its own. We rely on Grade A browsers implementing HTTP caching correctly and their vendors making accessing them as efficient as possible in order to avoid incurring the incidental complexity of writing our own cache in JavaScript. We'll set appropriate `Cache-Control` HTTP headers for both the MediaWiki API and the RESTBase page summary endpoint with the help of the Services team.
template_adherence.consequences: Resources fetched from the MediaWiki API will be cached for 5 minutes in public caches and the browser's cache. Resources fetched from the RESTBase endpoint will be cached for 14 days in public caches.

template_adherence.title: Replace Mustache.js with Template Literals
template_adherence.context: UI HTML templates are currently populated with variables by the mustache.js template system, which adds an 8.1 KiB dependency used only in a few places. ES6 template literals provide similar readability and are part of JavaScript itself, making them a favorable and sustainable alternative. Transpiling with Babel enables other ES6 features and reduces dependency size. Manual HTML escaping is now required, replacing mustache.js's built-in escaping.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Reduce dependency size, enable modern JavaScript syntax (ES6), maintain compatibility with grade A browsers, and improve code sustainability and readability.
template_adherence.decision: Transpile ES6 template literals using Babel to replace mustache.js templates, resulting in a net size reduction and enabling modern JavaScript features while maintaining compatibility.
template_adherence.consequences: ES6 syntax is enabled without changing existing device support, and 7.8 KiB less of minified uncompressed JavaScript is delivered. Manual HTML escaping is required, but this is acceptable given the benefits.

alternatives.description: Continue using mustache.js templates without change.
pros: No need to add transpilation step.
No manual HTML escaping required.
cons: Maintains 8.1 KiB dependency.
Does not enable modern ES6 syntax.
Less sustainable and less readable code.

alternatives.description: Use a UI library like Preact with JSX to handle templates.
pros: Automatic HTML escaping.
Modern syntax and better integration.
cons: Adds complexity and dependency.
Uncertain if Extension:Popups will adopt a UI library.
Potentially larger bundle size.

template_adherence.title: Use Terraform for Infrastructure Definition and Deployment Instead of Serverless
template_adherence.context: Serverless framework limits functionality compared to CloudFormation, which itself has limitations such as a maximum of 200 resources per stack. template_adherence.title: AWS RDS permissions
template_adherence.context:
AWS RDS are managed database servers.

eLife uses RDS to alleviate the task of database management tasks like
distribution, fault tolerance, monitoring.

eLife uses PostgreSQL RDS instances for several projects.

eLife provisions these RDS instances, their databases and database users using
Cloudformation.

Because RDS is a *managed* database server, there are constraints in it's usage.

Commonly encountered constraints are:

* no ssh access to the machine(s) hosting the database server
* no 'root' user access within the database
* [a similar-to-but-not-really 'root' user called 'rds_superuser'](http://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/UsingWithRDS.MasterAccounts.html)

During the life of an application, the database provisioned by Cloudformation
may be deleted and re-created, losing the permissions the original database was
created and successfully provisioned with.

If the new owner of the database is not the 'root' user or a member of the 'rds_superuser' role, some non-application activities such as backups and testing may fail with permission errors.

Re-instating permissions in a PostgreSQL database is an involved process.
template_adherence.decision:
The RDS *root* user provisioned shall always be the `owner` of the application database.

The RDS *application* user will have enough permissions to read and write to the application database.

The RDS *application* user will not have permission to drop/re-create the application database *in continuumtest, end2end and prod environments*.
template_adherence.consequences:
Applications that depend on creating or destroying their database will fail with permission errors.

Backups and restore can be done purely by using the root user and without the application's knowledge.

template_adherence.title: Supported PHP Versions
template_adherence.context:
eLife has several microservices (and larger projects) written in PHP.

In order to provide language version consistency across projects we need to get a consensus on which versions we are going to support.

There is an exception, `crm` not being upgraded on PHP 7 (using 5.6 instead) but supporting it.

Staying up to date with the major and minor versions of PHP is important:

- to be able to use new features and libraries (nice to have)
- to keep working on a version that receives bug fixes and security updates (must have)

All infrastructure is currently based on:

- Ubuntu 14.04 (doesn't have PHP 7.x by default)
- Ubuntu 16.04 (does have PHP 7.0 by default)
- a popular [PPA](https://launchpad.net/~ondrej/+archive/ubuntu/php) filling in the blanks, supporting 7.0, 7.1, and 7.2.
- official [PHP Docker images](https://hub.docker.com/_/php/) supporting 5.6, 7.0, 7.1, and 7.2.

PHP 7.0 has ceased active support, but has [security support](http://php.net/supported-versions.php) until 2018-12-03.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for language version consistency across projects.
- Importance of staying up to date with PHP versions for new features and security.
- Infrastructure constraints (Ubuntu versions, PPAs, Docker images).
- Exceptions like the `crm` project.
- Timing of security support ending for PHP 7.0.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use PHP 7.0 on all existing and new PHP projects bar exceptions that do not support it (`crm` if needed).

We will upgrade to PHP 7.1, PHP 7.2 and similar minor versions as a concerted effort on all libraries and projects, before the end of the security support.
template_adherence.consequences:
- No libraries or projects should require PHP >= 7.1 until it is provided by approved builder-base-formula states or base images.
- A single epic should capture all necessary upgrades when switching to a new minor version.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative would be to not standardize on PHP 7.0 or to upgrade immediately to newer versions without coordination.
pros: Could allow faster adoption of newer PHP features.
cons: Lack of consistency across projects.
Potential for compatibility issues.
Security risks if older versions are used without support.

template_adherence.title: 5. Routing protocol data formats
template_adherence.context:
We need a standard format for messages to be exchanged by the routing protocol.
This format would be used by routers on different implementations.
template_adherence.decision:
We use the following formats:

For a message:

```
{
onward_route: Route,
return_route: Route,
payload: Any
}
```

Where

`Route` - an ordered list of addresses.


For an address:

```
{
type: Integer,
data: Any
}
```
template_adherence.consequences:
Applications can use the same format to implement handling code.

Transports between different implementations would have to agree on a certain
format to exchange payloads and addresses.

Different nodes have to agree on address types to exchange messages with such types
in the routes

`fread` from the data.table R package, provides reading in of large datasets with the option of chunking the data into smaller, more managable pieces. Chunks are defined by row numbers. `fread` will take precise row numbers, or will throw an exception if the row number it has been told to delimit by does not exist.
template_adherence.decision:
Tests showed that reading in a chunk whereby the row number to read-in was outside the possible number of rows for a file, was slower to throw an exception, than first counting the number of rows, by selecting only a single column to read-in, and reading every row, and using that count to inform the loop function which iterates over the file to be read in.

As this data is being read-in we have chosen to make use of it, by selecting the column to read in as the encrypted HES IDs. A unique list of these IDs will be compiled and will form an initial master patient index.
template_adherence.consequences:
A file is read in an additional time in order to do a row count.

Some data files are small and do not require this row count and chunking, but are being treated equally.

A large vector is created and appended to, each time a new file is read in, adding to the processing time.

template_adherence.title: Defining an inpatient spell
template_adherence.context: A continuous inpatient spell (CIPS) is defined as a sequence of inpatient spells with different hospital providers, from the patients admission to discharge to the usual place of residence. Spells are considered to be part of the same CIPS up to three days, equivalent to two nights, have passed between discharge from one provider and admission to another provider. Each patient can have multiple inpatient spells and/or multiple continuous inpatient spells.
template_adherence.decision: All spells within a CIPS have to have the same ENCRYPTED_HESID. Within each group of spells belonging to the same ENCRYPTED_HESID, rows are then ordered by ADMIDATE_FILLED. A spell is considered to be part of the same CIPS as the previous spell if EPISTART is not more than 3 days later than EPIEND of the previous spell and one of the following is true: The discharge destination of the previous spell is another hospital (DISDEST is 51, 52 or 53), The source of admission of the current spell another hospital (ADMISORC is 51, 52 or 53), The method of admission of the current spell is a transfer (ADMIMETH is 2B, which recoded to 67 during cleaning, or 81). Two derived variables correspond to CIPS information: NEW_CIPS (TRUE if the episode marks the beginning of a new CIPS, FALSE otherwise) and CIPS_ID (CIPS identifier, unique in combination with ENCRYPTED_HESID). A new CIPS table (APCC) is created, containing one row per CIPS (or per unique combination of ENCRYPED_HESID and CIPS_ID), populated using information derived from the first spell within each CIPS (excluding certain columns) and information derived from the last spell within each CIPS (including certain columns).

template_adherence.title: Defining an inpatient spell
template_adherence.context: A hospital spell is defined as a period of care with one hospital provider (trust), from admission to discharge or transfer. A spell can be made up of one or more Finished Consultant Episodes (FCE), which is a continuous period of care under one consultant. Most spells consist of one episode or one row in the APC dataset but some spells contain multiple episodes. Each patient can have multiple episodes and/or multiple spells.
template_adherence.decision: An episode is considered "valid" for creating a spell when it is finished (EPISTAT equals 3) and the following are not missing: ENCRYPTED_HESID, ADMIDATE_FILLED, PROCODE3, EPIKEY, EPISTART, EPIEND. All episodes within a spell have to have the same ENCRYPTED_HESID and PROCODE3. Episodes are ordered by EPISTART, EPIEND, EPIORDER, TRANSIT, EPIKEY. An episode is part of the same spell as the previous episode if one of the following is true: ADMIDATE_FILLED is the same, EPISTART is the same, or the discharge method of the previous episode is a transfer and the current episode start date matches the previous episode end date. Two derived variables, NEW_SPELL and SPELL_ID, are created to identify spells. A new spell table (APCS) is created with one row per spell, populated using information from the first and last episodes within each spell, with specific columns included or excluded as detailed.
template_adherence.consequences: NEW_SPELL and SPELL_ID are set to NA for episodes which are not valid.

template_adherence.title: How will data be stored and accessed?
template_adherence.context:
The raw HES data is large, complex, unweildly and potentially dirty. A way to clean, store and later easily access the data for analysis required, which means that repeated cleaning and prep of the raw data is avoided.

There are multiple datasets (with different variables), which once cleaned, will be accompanied by additional derived variables, and additional derived datasets.
template_adherence.decision:
The raw data will be read into a SQLite database through R. R is The Health Foundation's open-source language of choice, and is well equiped to handle later analysis of said data. An SQLite database is not stored in memory, avoiding holding very large datasets an R session. It is a standard database format which can be easily queried with SQL which can in turn be written within most other common languagses, including R.

In an SQLite database the database consistents of all the data, and within that there are tables; here each table corresponds to a HES dataset or a derived dataset.
template_adherence.consequences:
Some additional learning is required in how to query an SQLite database. This requires some additional documentation (to come).

An SQLite database still occupies quite a large amount of storage space.

Reading large files into R is always going to somewhat slow, but through testing we have optimised the process using (`fread`)[link to come] from the data.table package, to read in the data in chunks and write directly to SQLite.

template_adherence.title: use of both RabbitMQ (bunny) and Redis (Sidekiq) queuing systems
template_adherence.context:
In order to simplify the search infrastructure we are moving to using the publishing API as the source of data. This allows us to reduce the amount of code duplication across projects, as currently each publishing app has to implement a write interface into rummager.

We expect this will give us a number of improvements, including:

* rebuild the search index more easily
* reduce the load on the publishing API - rummager currently needs to retrieve tagging data from the publishing API when it indexes documents

The publishing API currently uses rabbit MQ to tell downstream apps that a new publishing event has occurred, with the key specifying the publishing app and the publishing event type.

Rummager currently processes `link` events from the rabbit MQ stream, this works by reading the message off the rabbitMQ stream, doing a small amount of manipulation and then creating a Sidekiq worker task to perform the data update.

When processing messages off the queue it is important that the process can provide the following features:

* Concurrency
* Failure/Queue side tracking
* Retry logic
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for concurrency, failure and queue side tracking, and retry logic in message processing; desire to reduce code duplication and load on publishing API; maintainability and future flexibility in message distribution system.
template_adherence.decision:
We initially looked at two options, either reading the data from the rabbit MQ stream and processing inplace, or writing the message to a Sidekiq worker and then have it perform the required processing.

While it is possible to implement all the above features using just the rabbit MQ system there is currently no simple way to do this and all the logic would need to be manually coded.

For this reason we have opted to use the Sidekiq queue library alongside rabbit MQ as it provides all the functionality that we require out of the box in a fully tested and mantained system.

This also means we are not locked into rabbit MQ as the distribution system of publishing API messages, this is esspecially import as Tijmen suggested this may be changed in the future.
template_adherence.consequences:
This means we have additional points of failure in the system, as we are reading from one queue and writing to second one. This is especially important when debugging and we have a clear diagram for the data flow through the system as well as a documented way to determine the status of a message within the system.

In addition to this it is important to differentiate the different components and ensure that new developers are clear which gems/libraries are associated with which queuing system.

alternatives.description: Reading the data from the rabbit MQ stream and processing inplace.
pros: Possible to implement all required features using just rabbit MQ.
cons: No simple way to do this.
All the logic would need to be manually coded.

template_adherence.title: use versioning to handle race conditions when updating the govuk index
template_adherence.context:
We are in the process of creating a new 'govuk' index to replace the existing mainstream, government and detailed indexes. The new index will be populated by rummager using publishing and unpublishing event messages pulled from a queue controlled by the publishing API.

Rummager cannot rely on messages from the queue being processed in the order that they were generated. This means that either rummager should handle edge cases such as these or we will need to accept the consequences:

- A document is published twice in quick succession. The second publishing event arrives in rummager first. The later, stale message should not overwrite the more recent data in the index.
- A document is unpublished and then immediately republished. The republishing message is processed first. The later, stale unpublishing message should be ignored and the published document should remain in the search index.
- A document is published and then immediately unpublished. The unpublishing event is processed first. The later, stale publishing message should not re-add the document to the search index. It should remain unpublished.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to handle out-of-order message processing from the publishing API queue, to prevent stale or out-of-date messages from overwriting more recent data in the search index, and to handle race conditions especially around publishing and unpublishing events. Desired qualities include data consistency in the search index, robustness against race conditions, and maintainability of the solution.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Elasticsearch's external versioning feature, leveraging the publishing event number as the version to ensure optimistic locking and prevent stale updates. For unpublished documents, the simplest approach is to delete them from the index, accepting some rare race conditions until tombstone records can be implemented later. Additionally, a regular reindexing job will be scheduled to fix any inconsistencies caused by race conditions.
template_adherence.consequences: Most race conditions should be handled correctly by the versioning system, but race conditions in unpublishing may lead to occasional unpublished documents appearing in the search index until the next reindexing. This could cause users to see unpublished pages in search results, leading to 404 errors or redirects. The support team has options to remove such documents manually or wait for reindexing.

alternatives.description: Handle race conditions by storing unpublished documents as tombstone records temporarily to prevent stale republishing messages from recreating deleted documents.
pros: Prevents race conditions related to unpublishing more robustly.
Ensures the index state accurately reflects unpublished documents until cleanup.
cons: Adds complexity to the system.
Requires additional implementation effort and maintenance.
Postponed due to resource constraints.

template_adherence.title: Incremental popularity updates
template_adherence.context: In ADR 003, the process for bulk loading data into Rummager's search indexes was changed to update the existing index in place rather than creating a separate index, which required locking. The main reason for bulk loading is to update the popularity field every night, affecting every document in the search index. After switching to the new index, there were spikes in 503 errors coinciding with the nightly task, with elasticsearch queries timing out. The goal is to have reads unaffected by bulk indexing, prioritizing user search ability over content freshness. Investigation considered limiting the popularity update task to a small number of documents each night.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain search availability and performance during bulk indexing, the observed spikes in errors and query timeouts during popularity updates, and the desire to reduce impact on search performance without significantly increasing indexing time.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to not make technical changes to the popularity update process at this time. Instead, the number of sidekiq processes indexing into elasticsearch simultaneously was reduced, which lowered the impact on search performance without noticeably affecting indexing time.
template_adherence.consequences: The popularity update still impacts search response time. Bulk loading into an empty index remains possible via the migrate_schema rake task. The elasticsearch cluster is not optimally tuned for bulk-indexing performance; experiments with settings did not improve impact on search performance, so configuration was left unchanged.

alternatives.description: Implement incremental popularity updates by updating only a small number of documents each night.
pros: Potentially reduces load and impact on search performance during updates.
Could limit the number of documents updated, reducing indexing time.
cons: Rank values change significantly day to day, making partial updates unreliable.
Difficult to maintain accurate relative rankings with partial updates.
Would require significant changes to Rummager to use different popularity metrics.

alternatives.description: Store vc_14 in the search index and update popularity only when vc_14 changes beyond a threshold.
pros: Could reduce unnecessary updates for documents with minor changes.
Might allow partial updates based on actual page view changes.
cons: Neglects updating ranks of documents overtaken by more popular ones.
Introduces bias towards older content for less viewed documents.
Complexity added without guaranteed improvement in ranking accuracy.

alternatives.description: Change Rummager to use vc_14 directly for popularity boost, enabling partial updates.
pros: Allows partial popularity updates based on actual page views.
Potentially reduces indexing workload and impact.
cons: Requires significant changes to Rummager.
Needs careful measurement to avoid breaking queries.
Not feasible as an immediate solution.

template_adherence.title: Transition whitehall documents to a Publishing API derived search index
template_adherence.context: Publishing applications used to directly communicate with rummager to index documents, using the `/documents` HTTP API. We've removed this integration for all publishing apps except for whitehall publisher. The publishing API now notifies rummager of every update, using a RabbitMQ message queue. Rummager responds to these messages by updating the `govuk` index. This has allowed us to remove the old `mainstream` index, which contained all sorts of documents beyond what we normally think of as "mainstream" content. The `govuk` index can be rebuilt from scratch by resending the content from publishing API. See [ADR 006](adr-004-transition-mainstream-to-publishing-api-index.md) for more details about moving mainstream content to the govuk index. This leaves two indexes that are populated the old way: `government` and `detailed`. `detailed` contains detailed guides and `government` contains everything else published by Whitehall publisher. We also have a separate worker (`publishing-queue-listener`) that listens to `*.links` notifications from publishing API, and *updates* the old indexes (but doesn't add any new content).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to consolidate indexing to a single process to simplify maintenance and improve data quality.
- Remove old indexing code and infrastructure to reduce complexity.
- Enable better use of available data for search improvements.
- Support running Rummager in the draft stack for preview and draft taxonomies.
- Consider impact on search scoring due to changes in document frequency statistics.
template_adherence.decision: We intend to get rid of the `government` and `detailed` indexes. Rummager should index Whitehall Publisher documents into the `govuk` index. All search indexing code should be removed from Whitehall Publisher. The old indexing code should be removed from Rummager: anything in `lib/indexer` and the `publishing-queue-listener` worker. The infrastructure to log indexing requests to disk can also be removed, since data from the publishing API can be resent at any time.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Over 200,000 documents published by Whitehall Publisher will be affected.
- Improved ability to use additional content metadata (state, publishing history, applicability, services, entities) for search.
- Simplified and unified indexing process.
- Dependency for running Rummager in the draft stack.
- Changes in document frequency statistics affecting search scoring.
- Need to carefully manage transition to avoid missing documents or search regressions.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing multiple indexes (`government` and `detailed`) alongside the `govuk` index, maintaining old indexing code.
pros: No immediate changes to existing indexing processes.
Avoids risk of missing documents during transition.
cons: Maintains complexity with multiple indexes.
Old indexing code remains, increasing maintenance burden.
Limits ability to improve search using unified data.

alternatives.description: Gradually migrate document types one by one to the new `govuk` index, while keeping old indexes operational until migration is complete.
pros: Allows incremental testing and validation.
Reduces risk of data loss or search regressions.
Provides clear migration path.
cons: Requires maintaining both old and new indexing code during transition.
Longer migration period.
Potential for inconsistent search results during migration.

template_adherence.title: Batch processing of rabbit MQ messages
template_adherence.context: As a result of ADR 004, we now process data from rabbit MQ and insert them into our search index. We have scaling issues when large volumes of messages arrive and sit in our sidekiq queue waiting to be processed. Two scenarios cause large queue sizes: republishing from the publishing API and changes to reference material requiring document updates. Currently, messages are processed individually, causing a bottleneck with Elasticsearch (ES). Bulk insertion is recommended by ES documentation. Initial testing of batch processing shows improved queue size and CPU usage without increased errors, though some unexpected SigTerm exceptions were observed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle large volumes of messages efficiently
- Avoid bottlenecks in Elasticsearch due to individual document inserts
- Support republishing and reference material changes
- Maintain system stability and avoid blocking consumer applications
- Address unexpected worker process errors (SigTerm exceptions)
template_adherence.decision: Adopt batch processing of messages from rabbit MQ to reduce processing time and improve throughput. Implement batching in the Rummager processor and govuk_message_queue_consumer. Continue investigating SigTerm errors and validate document republishing correctness before full rollout.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Reduced processing time for indexing documents
- Closer to ability to rebuild search index regularly, preventing drift from publishing API
- Potential risk from observed SigTerm exceptions requiring further investigation
- Improved system throughput without increased 500 errors on dependent applications

alternatives.description: Continue processing messages individually as before.
pros: Simplicity of current system
No new code or testing required
cons: Scalability issues with large message volumes
Bottleneck in Elasticsearch due to individual inserts
Longer processing times
Does not support rebuilding search index efficiently

alternatives.description: Implement batch processing of messages as described in the decision.
pros: Improved throughput and reduced processing time
Supports rebuilding search index
Aligns with Elasticsearch bulk insertion recommendations
No increase in 500 errors observed in dependent apps
cons: Observed unexpected SigTerm exceptions needing investigation
Requires changes to message processing code and testing

template_adherence.title: 4. Check in Copilot Dependencies That Were Already Vendored
template_adherence.context:
Previous packaging of Copilot in istio release relied on the fact that you would be building copilot on the local machine (bosh pre-packaging). This meant that you could reliably fetch all of your dependencies using dep (which was included as a blob in the release).

When we moved to get rid of pre-packaging and instead do all packaging on a bosh vm (just known as packaging) we ended up missing one key external dependency for dep to work (git). Including git as part of release would have meant adding another blob and packaging step just for git.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to remove the dependency on external tools like git during packaging, to avoid adding extra blobs and packaging steps, and to make building copilot more consistent and less dependent on the user's machine.
template_adherence.decision: We removed the .gitignore of the vendor directory and checked-in all of the source code that dep was placing in that directory at build time.
template_adherence.consequences:
- No team member should have to fuss with dep when trying to build copilot.
- Team members will need to remember to check in their vendor dir changes when upgrading / adding / removing dependencies
- Removal of pre-packaging means that building of copilot got more consistent as it cannot vary depending on the user's external machine that is running the bosh deploy
- Dep has been removed as a blob for releases going forward since it is no longer required to build copilot

We may have to reconsider this approach when go.mod becomes an actual thing but that isn't until at least go 1.12.

alternatives.description: Continue relying on dep and including git as a blob in the release to fetch dependencies during packaging.
pros: Maintains current workflow without checking in vendor directory.
No need to check in vendored dependencies, keeping repository size smaller.
cons: Requires adding git as a blob and packaging step, increasing release complexity.
Builds depend on external tools being available, which can cause inconsistencies.

alternatives.description: Switch to go.mod for dependency management once it becomes stable.
pros: Modern dependency management approach.
Potentially cleaner and more efficient than vendoring dependencies manually.
cons: Not available until at least go 1.12, so not an immediate solution.
Requires migration effort and tooling updates.

template_adherence.title: Using Machinist for Factories
template_adherence.context: [machinist][] is a ruby library that makes it easy to create objects for use in test. [Factories tend to be preferable to fixtures][factories-not-fixtures]. We decided to try switching over from [machinist][] to [factory_bot][]. Our primary decision behind switching was because machinist is unmaintained. The last commit to _master_ is from 2013. factory_bot is well maintained and is very popular. We had converted roughly a dozen factories over from machinist to factory_bot, starting from the leaf nodes of our object graph. As we moved to objects with associations, we encountered increasing degrees of friction. The differences in how [sequel][] and [active_record][] handle associations mean that factory_bot was not well suited. In active_record, associations are created by placing a foreign key on one of the two records. Specifically, the record with the `belongs_to` contains the foreign key for the record with the `has_one`. This means that any factory library can create the `has_one` record, generate its primary key 'A', then create the `belongs_to` record with a foreign key of 'A'. In our usage of sequel, some associations have mutual foreign keys on both of the two records. So, a factory library has to create the first record, generate its primary key 'A' with no association, then create the second record with primary key 'B' and foreign key 'A', then update the first record so that its foreign key is 'B'. This "create-create-update" workflow is tricky (but possible) in factory_bot and is clean in machinist.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a maintained and popular factory library.
- Compatibility with the database ORM's association handling (sequel vs active_record).
- Ease of creating complex associations in factories.
- Maintenance status of the libraries.
- Developer familiarity and onboarding considerations.
template_adherence.decision: We have reverted the conversion commits, remaining with machinist. We will switch to a maintained fork of machinist. (It turns out that other people use machinist too.)
template_adherence.consequences:
- New team members will have to learn machinist, whereas rubyists would probably be familiar with factory_bot.
- There will no longer be a state where both machinist and factory_bot are used while converting.

alternatives.description: Switching from machinist to factory_bot, a well-maintained and popular factory library.
pros: factory_bot is well maintained and popular.
Likely more familiar to new ruby developers.
cons: factory_bot is not well suited for sequel associations due to complex create-create-update workflow.
Encountered increasing friction with associations when converting.

alternatives.description: Remaining with machinist and switching to a maintained fork of machinist.

Avoids the complex create-create-update workflow.
Maintains consistency without partial conversion.
cons: Machinist is originally unmaintained (last commit 2013).
