template_adherence.title: 15) Use PSR-11-compatible MediaWiki service container as extension basis
template_adherence.context: WikibaseRepo and WikibaseClient classes act as top level factories for services required inside of the respective extension. The methods to create/retrieve them do not follow a standardized interface, and as many of them are required to build other services, the classes also hold a substantial amount of code to keep and pass references to the created instances once created. This code is low in conceptual value but highly repetitive and a burden on developers. Services which are required in WikibaseRepo and WikibaseClient alike, e.g. FormatterCacheFactory, may also exhibit redundant implementations of their instantiator function as there is no ability to reuse them. MediaWiki supports a concept called ServiceWiring which allows for the registration of services, is an important building block of recent MediaWiki and implements the well-known PSR 11 container interface.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR text does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section or explicitly list the drivers. However, from the context and decision sections, the drivers can be inferred as: the need to reduce repetitive and low-value boilerplate code, the lack of a standardized interface for service creation/retrieval, the desire to reuse service instantiator functions, and the availability of MediaWiki's ServiceWiring implementing PSR-11 container interface as a standard solution.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use MediaWiki ServiceWiring to describe and connect the services on which the wikibase repo and client extensions rely.
template_adherence.consequences: The services described in the wikibase repo and wikibase client extensions will be migrated to respective service wiring files. Boilerplate code holding references to instances of services inside WikibaseRepo and WikibaseClient can be removed. The WikibaseRepo and WikibaseClient client classes will remain as type-safe accessors to the services governed by the service container. The ability to make joint registration of services possible is not immediately implemented but the standardized interface eases future decisions in that direction.

template_adherence.title: 16) Use GitHub Actions as secondary CI system for Wikibase
template_adherence.context:
The Wikibase CI which runs on WMF Jenkins is currently "augmented" by running php unit tests in a variety of additional configurations (e.g. non-English wiki, repo/client-only environment, etc) on legacy Travis CI infrastructure, via the GitHub mirror of our Gerrit code repository, see https://travis-ci.org/github/wikimedia/Wikibase.

The Travis CI features we currently use include:
* PHP installed (multiple versions),
* MySQL running,
* notifications via
* email,
* IRC,
* composer cache.

Due to a change in their business model, the travis-ci.org service is being phased out and replaced by (paid) travis-ci.com. Since we have no intention of dropping the extended CI testing, there are several options how to handle the situation:
* migrate additional CI for Wikibase to some other CI infrastructure, e.g. _GitHub Actions_,
* negotiate with the WMF changing the Travis CI plan to a paid one which would have unlimited/less limited resources available,
* migrate additional CI for Wikibase to additional jobs on WMF Jenkins CI.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to replace the deprecated Travis CI service, maintain extended CI testing for Wikibase, availability of required features on alternative CI platforms, and resource considerations such as cost and effort of migration.
template_adherence.decision:
We will migrate the additional CI for Wikibase to the GitHub CI infrastructure, using _GitHub Actions_.

Reasons: The GitHub mirror of the Wikibase repository exists already and all of the Travis CI features we have been using so far, are available on _GitHub Actions_:
* setup-php,
* MySQL pre-installed on the runner or use MySQL service container (to be investigated),
* notifications via email (built-in),
* notify-irc + failure() condition,
* cache.
template_adherence.consequences: Since most of our Travis CI is a collection of shell scripts, it will mostly work the same under GitHub Actions and migrating is a relatively low-effort solution for the short or mid term; in the long term, the Wikimedia migration to GitLab will presumably change a lot in our CI processes.

template_adherence.title: 18) Keep Wikibase master compatible with last stable MediaWiki Core
template_adherence.context:
Wikibase is currently only tested to be compatible with MediaWiki core and other MediaWiki extensions for:
- sets of commits that are the HEAD of the master branch at one point in time
- cut releases: either for the alpha, weekly train releases (i.e. releases delivered on WMF wikis), or the twice-yearly(ish) official MediaWiki releases

We want to give 3rd party Wikibase users regular 6 monthly releases.

MediaWiki release are currently not that regular; in part due to delays caused by the Covid-19 pandemic.

We intend to produce new Wikibase features on a more regular basis than 6 monthly and we want these to be available to users
as soon as possible. Both for users to benefit from new features but also to shorten our development feedback cycles.

To be able to release Wikibase at any point in time such that it remains possible to apply security patches to MediaWiki core and to
any extensions that are not maintained by WMDE these releases need to be compatible with a "cut release" of MediaWiki.

To ensure this compatibility there are two options:
- Backport Wikibase features, and any dependent patches to the last stable release of MediaWiki before releasing.
This was performed for the upcoming wmde1 release of Wikibase where patches made against master (i.e. 1.36 alpha releases) were backported to the Wikibase 1.35 branch
- Keep Wikibase `master` compatible with the last stable release of MediaWiki

Doing the backporting results in leaving a possibly unknown amount of work for whoever is to make the release and adds lots of uncertainty.
The additional backporting effort will need to be repeated for all upcoming Wikibase releases.
This approach also means maintaining two different (even if only in the sense of git history) versions of the same functionality.

Keeping Wikibase compatible with last stable MediaWiki adds to every developer's workload.
It may result in having to delay using new features in MediaWiki or having to write a compatibility layer in order to use them.
It may result in developers inadvertently using a new feature and then discovering they need to either
write some backwards compatibility layer for it or put that new feature behind a flag.

Doing so may result in being more decoupled from MediaWiki in the long run.

The overhead of the additional development effort will possibly be increasingly lower
the more code has been written that way, and the more Wikibase releases have been published following this approach.

Keeping Wikibase compatible with last stable MediaWiki would likely mean avoiding the "double work" effort
of developing the feature against the master branch, and "backporting" it to be compatible with the last stable version of MediaWiki
needed for the Wikibase release for non-WMF users.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to provide regular 6 monthly releases to 3rd party Wikibase users.
- MediaWiki releases are irregular, partly due to external factors like the Covid-19 pandemic.
- Desire to produce new Wikibase features more frequently than every 6 months.
- Need to maintain compatibility with a "cut release" of MediaWiki to allow security patches.
- Two main options: backporting features or keeping master compatible with last stable MediaWiki.
- Backporting adds uncertainty and repeated effort.

template_adherence.title: 19) Add source information to Property IDs for Federated Properties v2
template_adherence.context:
The Federated Properties MVP introduced a [federatedPropertiesEnabled] setting which enables a Wikibase instance (local wiki) to read all Properties from a remote Wikibase (source wiki). A wiki with this setting enabled can only use federated Properties and disallows the creation or use of any local Properties.
Federated Properties v2 aims to make it possible for users to enable Federated Properties even if their Wikibase already contains data, so that they can choose to use both remote & local Properties to make statements.

To achieve that we need to be able to differentiate between local and federated Properties.

### Considered Actions

We considered two options:

1. Build source information into the Property IDs via repository prefixes.
2. Build source information into the Property IDs via Concept URIs.

#### Prefixes

The administrator of the local Wikibase needs to configure a prefix for the source wiki, which will be used only for federated properties. Local properties will not have a prefix.

**Pros**:
- Easier to parse
- Easier to type

**Cons**:
- Ambiguous without knowing the config

#### Concept URIs

Concept URIs can be set for any Wikibase and also have a default value. An example of referencing a federated property from Wikidata is `http://www.wikidata.org/entity/P31`.
The administrator of the local Wikibase needs to configure the concept URI for the source wiki in case it's not Wikidata.

Since concept URIs guarantee to end in the entity's ID we can think of them as prefixes. In the above example `http://www.wikidata.org/entity/` is the prefix. This way we don't need to worry about parsing them to extract the entity ID.

**Pros**:
- Unambiguous
- Standard practice in the linked data world

**Cons**:
- Typing urls in the browser when containing e.g. '&' is not nice. People might not remember to url encode.
We think having symbols like '&' in the URL in unlikely. Also, API Sandbox can be used to test the API requests and figure out the right format if needed.
- Hard to change / Out of “our” control if they change
If we use the URI only as a prefix to the entity, and not as an actual URL that will be used as such, then this shouldn't be a problem. We acknowledge it's possible for people who use the API to treat it like an URL.
We feel responsible only if Wikidata's URI changes, as we anticipate shipping an example configuration for Wikidata which would then need updating. URIs configured for a source wiki different than Wikidata will have to be updated by the administrator of the local wiki in case they change.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are the need to differentiate between local and federated Properties in a way that is unambiguous, easy to parse, and standard practice. Considerations include ease of typing, ambiguity, standardization, and control over the identifiers used.
template_adherence.decision: Build source information into the Property IDs via Concept URIs, treating them like a prefix.
template_adherence.consequences: It's out of our control when/if URIs change. We acknowledge that this is a real problem and can potentially be reported by people who use the API and treat the URIs as URLs.

alternatives.description: Build source information into the Property IDs via repository prefixes.
pros: Easier to parse
Easier to type
cons: Ambiguous without knowing the config

alternatives.description: Build source information into the Property IDs via Concept URIs.
pros: Unambiguous
Standard practice in the linked data world
cons: Typing urls in the browser when containing e.g. '&' is not nice. People might not remember to url encode.
Hard to change / Out of “our” control if they change

template_adherence.title: 21) Make all Federated Properties-relevant services source and type dispatching
template_adherence.context:
Federated Properties v2 aims to make it possible for users to enable Federated Properties even if their Wikibase already contains data, so that they can choose to use both remote & local Properties to make statements.

Dispatching by entity type is a widely used mechanism in Wikibase that allows the dispatching service to handle entity ids of different types by delegating to the service implementation defined in the [entity type definitions], thus enabling entity type specific behavior within a single service. With Federated Properties v2 the entity type ("property") no longer uniquely identifies the desired service implementation, since local Properties' services need to be handled by database-backed implementations, whereas Federated Properties use API-backed services. In order to work with local and remote Properties, dispatching services need to be aware of the entity's source as well as the type.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support both local and remote Properties in Federated Properties v2.
- Existing dispatching by entity type is insufficient because the entity type alone does not uniquely identify the service implementation.
- Desire to avoid confusing multiple dispatching steps that are not co-located.
- Future-proofing for anticipated Federated Items using the same mechanism.
- Maintainability and clarity by having dispatching happen in a single class.
template_adherence.decision: Make all relevant services source and type dispatching.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Type dispatching services that behave differently for local and Federated Properties become source and type dispatching.
- Creation of EntitySourceLookup to find EntitySource object from entity id.
- Creation of EntitySourceAndTypeDefinitions class to map source + entity type to service callback.
- Added a "type" field to EntitySource to distinguish local (db-backed) vs remote (API-backed).
- EntitySourceAndTypeDefinitions uses entity source type to get service creation callback from appropriate files.
- This approach centralizes dispatching and supports future extensions.

alternatives.description: Keep dispatching by entity type, and build source dispatching only into the Property services.
pros: Less invasive change, only requires adding a second dispatching layer to Property services.
cons: Splitting dispatching into multiple steps that are not co-located can be confusing.

alternatives.description: Make all relevant services source and type dispatching.
pros: Dispatching happens in a single class, improving clarity.
Future-proofing for anticipated Federated Items.
Supports both local and remote Properties uniformly.
cons: More invasive change as multiple services need to be updated to support source and type dispatching.

template_adherence.title: Create a Property ID interface
template_adherence.context:
Federated Properties v2 aims to make it possible to use both federated and local Properties on a single Wikibase instance. We introduced a `FederatedPropertyId` class to refer to Federated Property IDs in the code. `FederatedPropertyId` objects are different from `PropertyId` objects in a few aspects since the former are intended to be used for data access of Properties via an API while the latter are used to get Properties directly from a database.

There are a few service interfaces such as `PropertyDataTypeLookup` which are used throughout Wikibase and need to work for Federated Properties and local Properties alike. To keep these type hints meaningful the two Property ID classes need to share a common parent type.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to support both federated and local Properties on a single Wikibase instance, maintain meaningful type hints in Property-related services, and avoid conceptual mismatches in class inheritance. The solution should allow specific implementations to contain logic for their use cases and avoid loosening type hints too broadly.
template_adherence.decision: Create a Property ID interface that will be implemented by local and federated Property ID implementations. This approach keeps meaningful type hints and allows specific methods for each implementation, despite requiring more changes.
template_adherence.consequences: Introducing the new interface requires major changes to WikibaseDataModel, WikibaseDataModelServices, and all code bases using these packages. Further decisions on naming and rollout plans are needed.

alternatives.description: Make `FederatedPropertyId` extend `PropertyId` after all.
pros: Easiest solution to make all the code work.
cons: Conceptually wrong as `PropertyId` contains methods not fitting `FederatedPropertyId`.
Reducing `PropertyId` to be more generic might exclude specific logic for concrete implementations.
No way to exclude federated IDs when type hinting for local IDs if inheritance is used.

alternatives.description: Loosen the type hints of all Property-specific services to an existing common parent type, e.g. EntityId.
pros: Some precedence in Wikibase for this pattern.
cons: Not a great pattern as it allows types that do not make sense (e.g., non-PropertyId in data type lookup).
Allows anything other than `PropertyId` which is not semantically correct.

alternatives.description: Create a Property ID interface.
pros: Cleanest option.
Keeps meaningful type hints in Property-related services.
Allows implementations to contain methods specific to their use cases.
cons: Requires the most changes.

template_adherence.title: 2. Use aws-eks terraform module
template_adherence.context: A fully configured EKS cluster requires many AWS resources and a lot of configuration. Defining each resource in our own Terraform module maximises flexibility but also requires a significant level of effort. We could instead make use of the existing Terraform registry EKS module to optimise for speed of delivery.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections: need for speed of delivery, flexibility, ease of configuration, and potential future maintainability concerns.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt the existing Terraform registry EKS module.
template_adherence.consequences:
A fully configured EKS cluster can be defined quickly and easily, as many module defaults will be fine for our purposes for the foreseeable future.

The EKS module has comprehensive support for many of the options for EKS cluster config (e.g. worker node types). This will allow us to make changes more easily, and to experiment with different options quickly.

It is possible that we will in future discover some areas of the module that don't work for our needs. Potential options in that instance include contributing to the module, forking it, or moving to our own module (likely with large chunks of code taken from the EKS module).

We must be careful to avoid errors and issues that may be caused by the module's default use of a terraform `kubernetes` provider that is configured by AWS resource outputs. The behaviour of providers derived from other providers' resources is non-deterministic and can lead to intermittent and unpredictable issues - see the warning callout in the Kubernetes provider docs. The approach for handling this limitation will be covered in a subsequent ADR.

template_adherence.title: 3. Split terraform state into separate AWS cluster and Kubernetes resource phases
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle Terraform providers `aws` and `kubernetes` correctly due to dependency issues.
- Avoid non-deterministic behaviour and race conditions in Terraform provisioning.
- Ensure clear separation of concerns between cluster infrastructure and in-cluster resources.
- Facilitate potential future changes to Kubernetes cluster providers.
- Prevent issues during cluster teardown related to AWS load balancers and Terraform state.
template_adherence.decision:
Split Terraform resources into two separate states and phases:

1. cluster-infrastructure - EKS cluster and associated AWS resources. No `kubernetes` provider should be defined.
2. cluster-services - Kubernetes resources and in-cluster configuration, with the `kubernetes` provider configured via TF remote state after `cluster-infrastructure` has been applied. No `aws` provider should be defined unless needed for AWS data sources in k8s resources.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The EKS module's `manage_aws_auth` input variable must be set to `false` to prevent conflicts.
- Prevents potential issues when tearing down an EKS cluster with deployed workloads due to Terraform's lack of awareness of AWS load balancers.
- Introduces a clear boundary and separation of concerns between cluster provisioning and in-cluster configuration.
- Provides flexibility to switch Kubernetes cluster providers in the future.
- Establishes a baseline EKS cluster usable for other purposes beyond GOV.UK.

template_adherence.title: 4. Use AWS Load Balancer Controller for edge traffic services
template_adherence.context: We require a method of managing and directing external internet traffic into the cluster. Kubernetes provides several options for handling inbound traffic. We do not want to expose the cluster directly to the internet, and so require an AWS load balancer in front of the cluster. The load balancer must support TLS termination and integration with our DNS provider (AWS Route 53). Historically Kubernetes has supported provisioning of ALBs and NLBs for Service resources of type=LoadBalancer via the in-tree (built-in) AWS cloud provider, with out-of-tree controllers required for Ingress resources. Built-in cloud providers are now considered deprecated overall, in favour of out-of-tree providers, so an Ingress Controller with support for Service resources is required. The primary and recommended ingress controller for AWS/EKS is the AWS Load Balancer Controller, which can provision and manage ALBs for Ingress resources and NLBs for Service resources. We must also consider how Kubernetes edge services and AWS load balancers will interact with the existing GOV.UK Router service, as there is significant overlap in their functionality and responsibilities. This will require further investigation and likely experimentation, and so that end we should ensure that we're able to use both Ingress and Service Kubernetes resources so that we have the flexibility to support a wide range of use cases in the immediate term - L4 & L7 traffic, name-based routing, HTTP->HTTPS redirection, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to manage and direct external internet traffic into the cluster securely without exposing the cluster directly. The requirement for TLS termination and DNS integration with AWS Route 53. The deprecation of built-in AWS cloud providers in Kubernetes in favor of out-of-tree providers. The need for flexibility to support various use cases including L4 & L7 traffic, name-based routing, and HTTP->HTTPS redirection. Compatibility and integration with existing GOV.UK Router service. Support for AWS WAF and Shield. Considerations for access control and namespace usage in Kubernetes.
template_adherence.decision: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller as the ingress controller for managing edge traffic services in the Kubernetes cluster.
template_adherence.consequences: TLS certificates must be managed via AWS Certificate Manager as the controller supports TLS certificates only through it. DNS management for ingress hostnames is not handled by the load balancer controller and will require a future solution. The default provisioning of one ALB per Ingress resource may not be optimal; grouping of ingresses is possible and may be necessary. Support for AWS WAF and Shield is available and aligns with current usage on GOV.UK. Access control for Ingress rules needs further investigation, especially regarding Kubernetes namespace usage and multi-user access to Ingress objects.

alternatives.description: Continue using the built-in AWS cloud provider for provisioning ALBs and NLBs for Service resources of type=LoadBalancer.
pros: Familiarity with existing built-in provider.
No need to adopt new controllers immediately.
cons: Built-in cloud providers are deprecated in Kubernetes.
Lack of support for Ingress resources provisioning.
Less flexibility and future-proofing.

alternatives.description: Use a different third-party Ingress controller other than AWS Load Balancer Controller.
pros: Potentially different features or integrations.
May better fit specific use cases or preferences.
cons: Less official support or community adoption for AWS/EKS.
May lack integration with AWS services like WAF, Shield, and Certificate Manager.
Additional complexity in management and compatibility.

template_adherence.title: 5. Use EKS managed node groups
template_adherence.context: EKS supports three different types of EKS worker node groups: managed, self-managed, and Fargate. The options are not mutually exclusive and can be combined within a single cluster. Managed and self-managed node groups are EC2 instances with autoscaling groups, while Fargate is a managed service with fewer configuration options but less management overhead. Cluster upgrades are frequent due to Kubernetes' 4-month release cycle, requiring a robust node upgrade process. Requirements for worker nodes are not fully known, so flexibility is important. Managed and self-managed node groups have equivalent functional capabilities, but Fargate has limitations. The main difference between managed and self-managed node groups is the upgrade process, with managed node groups handling upgrades automatically.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for a robust and mature node upgrade process due to frequent Kubernetes upgrades, the importance of maintaining flexibility given unknown requirements, and the functional equivalence of managed and self-managed node groups with differences in upgrade handling.
template_adherence.decision: Use managed node groups for EKS worker nodes.
template_adherence.consequences: Retain maximum flexibility over node configuration without managing the complexity of rolling out node updates. Choosing managed node groups does not preclude future use of self-managed node groups or Fargate, which can be added later without discarding work on managed node groups.

alternatives.description: Use self-managed node groups or Fargate instead of managed node groups.
pros: Potentially more control over node configuration (self-managed).
Fargate offers less management overhead.
cons: Self-managed node groups require orchestrating the update process manually.
Fargate has limitations such as inability to run DaemonSets, specify alternative CNI providers, or attach persistent EBS volumes.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use Helm for application package management
template_adherence.context:
We require something more sophisticated than handcrafted YAML when defining an application's Kubernetes resources, to ensure that applications can be defined once, and deployed to multiple targets with differing configurations. At a high level, we require a means to define an application's Kubernetes resources as an installable package, with configuration options passed in at deploy time.

There are many options for packaging Kubernetes applictions, including but not limited to:

- [Helm](https://helm.sh)
- [Terraform](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/kubernetes/latest/docs)
- [Kustomize](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-kubernetes-objects/kustomization/)
- [Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/intro/cloud-providers/kubernetes/#pulumi-kubernetes-provider)
- [Skaffold](https://skaffold.dev)

While we are currently using Terraform for AWS infrastructure management, we should maintain a strict separation of concerns between managing cloud infrastructure and the software applications that run on top; using a single tool for both will inevitably lead to blurred lines between the two. In addition, [Terraform's kubernetes support is still quite new](https://www.hashicorp.com/blog/beta-support-for-crds-in-the-terraform-provider-for-kubernetes), and can lag behind Kubernetes itself.

While Kustomize has been adopted into the main Kubernetes project, that decision has [not been without controversy](https://goteleport.com/blog/kubernetes-kustomize-kep-kerfuffle/). Kustomize has also not yet seen wide adoption within the industry, and offers little beyond the basic functions of interpolating values into YAML files.

Helm by comparison has widespread industry adoption, a [large number of existing packages](https://artifacthub.io/packages/search), and widespread support in the wider devops and development ecosystem (e.g. [Github Actions](https://github.com/helm/chart-releaser-action), [CircleCI Orb](https://circleci.com/developer/orbs/orb/circleci/helm), [VS Code extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-kubernetes-tools.vscode-kubernetes-tools), [Terraform provider](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/helm/latest/docs)).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a sophisticated, reusable, and configurable packaging solution for Kubernetes applications.
- Desire to separate concerns between infrastructure management and application deployment.
- Consideration of maturity and adoption of available tools.
- Industry adoption and ecosystem support.
- Avoiding tool overlap and confusion between application and infrastructure management.
template_adherence.decision: Use Helm v3+ for application package management.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Ability to leverage existing Helm charts for supporting tools and services.
- Potential future introduction of a Helm chart repository.
- Access to Helm features like release history and rollback, with caution around database migrations.
- Need to manage versioning distinctions between Helm charts and applications.
- Awareness of YAML idiosyncrasies and templating complexities.
- Adoption of Helm does not preclude use of other tools like Kustomize or Skaffold by development teams.

alternatives.description: Use Terraform for Kubernetes application packaging.
pros: Currently used for AWS infrastructure management, so familiarity exists.
cons: Blurs lines between infrastructure and application management.
Kubernetes support is still quite new and may lag behind Kubernetes itself.

alternatives.description: Use Kustomize for Kubernetes application packaging.
pros: Adopted into the main Kubernetes project.
Offers basic functions of interpolating values into YAML files.
cons: Has been controversial.
Not yet widely adopted in the industry.
Offers limited functionality beyond basic interpolation.

pros: Supports Kubernetes and other cloud providers.

Potentially less mature or less widely adopted compared to Helm.

alternatives.description: Use Skaffold for Kubernetes application packaging.
pros: Supports Kubernetes application deployment.
cons: Not discussed in detail in the ADR.

template_adherence.title: 10. Use Dex IdP for user web auth
template_adherence.context:
We want to implement user authentication on the monitoring stack's web applications (Grafana, Prometheus, Alertmanager).

We also want to use Github as the identity provider (IdP), as that provides a means for us to control access based on GDS Github organisation and team membership; the alternative option, GSuite, does not currently have the granular role/group structure that we would require to effectively control access, and introducing that group structure would be out of scope for this project, and would likely replicate the Github group/team structure that currently exists.

Grafana supports many authentication methods, including [Github OAuth2](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/auth/github/) and [OIDC (via generic OAuth2)](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/auth/generic-oauth/).

Prometheus and Alertmanager do not support any form of web-based user authentication, so this must be handled via a proxy or load balancer in front of the application.

We are currently using ALBs in front of Prometheus and Alertmanager, via the [AWS Load Balancer Controller](0004-use-aws-load-balancer-controller-for-edge-traffic-services.md), which supports [authentication via AWS Cognito or OIDC-compliant identity providers](https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/aws-load-balancer-controller/v2.3/guide/ingress/annotations/#authentication).

Github as an IdP does not support OIDC, only OAuth2, so cannot be used with ALB auth. AWS Cognito [does not support OAuth2, only OIDC](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-identity.html), so cannot be used with Github as an IdP.

ArgoCD, our current CD tool, also [implements authentication via OIDC](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/user-management/#existing-oidc-provider), and [includes an OIDC-compliant identity broker](https://argoproj.github.io/argo-workflows/argo-server-sso-argocd/), [Dex](https://dexidp.io).

In summary, OIDC is the only auth protocol supported universally by both our current web-based UIs that support authentication internally, and by ALBs for apps that do not. Github however does not provide an OIDC-compliant IdP.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for user authentication on monitoring stack web applications.
- Desire to use Github as the identity provider for access control based on organisation and team membership.
- Limitations of alternative IdPs like GSuite lacking granular role/group structure.
- Compatibility requirements: Grafana supports Github OAuth2 and OIDC; Prometheus and Alertmanager require proxy/load balancer authentication.
- AWS ALB supports authentication via AWS Cognito or OIDC-compliant IdPs.
- Github supports OAuth2 but not OIDC; AWS Cognito supports OIDC but not OAuth2.
- ArgoCD uses OIDC and includes Dex as an OIDC-compliant identity broker.
- Need for a universal auth protocol supported by all components (OIDC).
- Security and availability considerations for the chosen solution.
template_adherence.decision: Use Dex as an SSO service and identity provider for all web-based user authentication for user-facing web-based cluster services such as monitoring and CI/CD tools. Dex should not be used for other purposes like AWS or Kubernetes authentication.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Establishes a single signon (SSO) service and consistent identity provider for all user-facing platform UIs.
- Provides a single point of integration with the underlying identity provider (Github), simplifying future changes.
- Dex is currently deployed as part of Argo; it should be deployed as a standalone Helm install as a shared platform service.
- Dex becomes a single point of failure and a potential attack target, requiring high availability, security, and penetration testing coverage.

alternatives.description: Use Github OAuth2 directly for authentication where supported.
pros: Direct integration with Github as IdP.
Simpler setup for components supporting Github OAuth2.
cons: Not supported by all components (e.g., Prometheus, Alertmanager).
Does not support OIDC, limiting compatibility with ALB authentication.

alternatives.description: Use AWS Cognito as IdP for authentication.
pros: Supported by AWS ALB for authentication.
OIDC compliant.
cons: Does not support OAuth2, incompatible with Github OAuth2.
Would require migration or duplication of user management from Github.

alternatives.description: Use GSuite as IdP.
pros: Existing identity provider in some contexts.
Potentially supports OIDC.
cons: Lacks granular role/group structure needed for access control.
Out of scope to introduce required group structure.
Would replicate Github group/team structure.

template_adherence.title: 1. Deployment on-prem & as a SaaS
template_adherence.context:
In global health there are two deployment constraints that push against one another:  the desire for iNGO's, government agencies, multi-laterals, etc to lower the barrier to acquiring software solutions by utilizing a SaaS model, and that of many governments to exercise self-reliance and sovereignty of their software and their data by being able to reasonably deploy software on premise in their own data center.

With regards to SaaS, most customers of the software are able and willing to pay reasonable monthly fees, especially if those fees are predictable over a suitable project timeline.  For organizations that want to offer PCMT as a SaaS they likely will expect the number of instances to be quite low:  likely less than 25 in the next 5 years.  Thus the key attributes for those running PCMT as a SaaS and for those consuming PCMT as a SaaS are reasonable fees and lead-times for signing a new instance on.

When a government agency deploys the software in their own data center a principal concern is that of limited resources.  Limited both in hardware and the maturity of the data center, as well as on the technical staff available. There are few organizations within PCMT's user-base that have extensive experience running highly available services or complicated deployment stacks.

We have a number of choices that are available to us:

1. Multi-tenancy development in theory can achieve the greatest cost-per-customer since the same application code on the same hardware can serve more than one customer.  However it can significantly increase the scope and development of each feature as each needs to consider how many customers would share the same resources without impacting one-another. It can also increase deployment cost and complexity as each instance needs to be configured and monitored for many clients.
1. Multi-single-tenancy is really a single tenancy model that utilizes advances in containerization, oftentimes cloud providers, and deployment tools to manage many single instances, one per customer, in such an automated fashion as to make it nearly indistinguishable from multi-tenancy.
1. Serverless is an approach to reduce overhead for developers by shifting resource management to a provider.  It's included here for completeness, and while it may make development practices easier, the deployment of a serverless architecture on-prem in PCMT's context is non-trivial.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to balance deployment constraints between SaaS and on-premise models, cost considerations, technical resource availability, deployment complexity, and performance/resource requirements suitable for on-premise data centers.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to build PCMT as a multi-single-tenant system utilizing containers as the basic unit of deployment. Each PCMT instance will be served by one or more containers, each serving a single function for one instance. Simple Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools will be developed to provision resources both in cloud and on-premise, configure instances, and aid maintenance lifecycle tasks. The system will be designed to run with minimal resource requirements (2GB RAM, 2 CPU cores, 10GB storage) to suit typical on-premise data centers and target a low cost per instance.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include reduced complexity in feature development by avoiding multi-tenancy scoping, and providing a starting point for SaaS deployment. Negative consequences include constraints on scope and performance due to resource limits, and potential additional investment needed for large-scale SaaS deployments to reduce lead-time and cost per instance.

cons: Increases scope and complexity of feature development to handle multiple customers.

alternatives.description: Multi-single-tenancy model using containerization and deployment tools to manage many single instances, one per customer.

Nearly indistinguishable from multi-tenancy in automation.
cons: May have higher resource usage compared to true multi-tenancy.
Requires robust deployment and management tooling.

alternatives.description: Serverless architecture to reduce developer overhead by shifting resource management to a provider.
pros: Simplifies development practices.
Potentially reduces operational overhead.
cons: Deployment on-premise is non-trivial in PCMT's context.
May not suit resource constraints or deployment models desired.

template_adherence.title: 3. Cloud Provisioning through Terraform
template_adherence.context:
Deploying to the cloud is a fundamental part of increasing software delivery frequency. However once the frequency is increased, it becomes increasingly needed to manage the provisioning and configuration of those cloud resources lest a step is forgotten, a security vulnerability is found, or an instance is corrupted. Following patterns found in software development, such as managing infrastructure as code (IaC) and tracking changes in source control, are widely regarded as good practice today.

Many cloud providers have bespoke tooling that helps manage the creation of resources on their infrastructure. While this tooling is hugely powerful, the context of PCMT is that our cloud resources should be kept as simple as possible, in part due to our constraint to allow for on-prem deployments. Further an organization that chooses to deploy PCMT as a SaaS may not use the same cloud provider as the one the PCMT project uses.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to increase software delivery frequency by deploying to the cloud, while managing provisioning and configuration to avoid errors and security issues. The desire to follow best practices such as infrastructure as code and source control. The constraint to keep cloud resources simple to allow for on-prem deployments. The need to support multiple cloud providers since SaaS deployments may not use the same cloud provider as the project.
template_adherence.decision: We will use Terraform to provision cloud resources: compute instances, storage, DNS, etc.
template_adherence.consequences: Terraform is a newer IaC tool that has support for multiple cloud providers, however not all cloud providers, or all advanced capabilities of the supported cloud providers may be available through Terraform.

alternatives.description: Use bespoke tooling provided by individual cloud providers to manage resource creation.
pros: Powerful and tailored to each cloud provider's capabilities.
cons: May lead to complexity due to multiple tools if supporting multiple providers.
Less suitable for on-prem deployments.
Does not align with the goal of keeping cloud resources simple.

alternatives.description: Manually provision and configure cloud resources without IaC tools.
pros: No need to learn new tools.
Direct control over provisioning steps.
cons: Error-prone and not scalable.
Does not support tracking changes in source control.
Contrary to best practices for infrastructure management.

template_adherence.title: 7. Versioning and Release Mechanism
template_adherence.context:

release.  e.g. is it a patch-release, major new functionality, etc.

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to clearly communicate the project's maturity and suitability to stakeholders, leverage semantic versioning to indicate the nature of releases, mark specific code-base states tied to released assets, and indicate the version of Akeneo from which PCMT is derived.

template_adherence.consequences: Semantic versions must be set carefully and intentionally by those designating releases. Builds, pre-releases, and stable releases are controlled through semantic version settings in SCM and the commits built by the CI server.

template_adherence.title: 13. Use Normalize.css to normalize styles across browsers
template_adherence.context: Browsers often have subtle differences or bugs in their default styles. Traditional CSS resets attempt to clear all styling, creating a baseline style from which to build us custom styles. However, this approach often results in reapplying styles that were already implemented by the browser. Normalize.css, instead, normalizes styles to a common theme across browsers. It precisely targets only the styles that need normalizing.
template_adherence.decision: We will use Normalize.css to normalize browser default styles.
template_adherence.consequences: With style normalization, we can be confident that our styles will be consistent across browsers. This does not replace the need to test in all target browsers.

template_adherence.title: ArgoCD Apps of Apps Structure
template_adherence.context: ArgoCD Applications manifests are used to declaratively manage ArgoCD Applications in git, typically stored alongside ArgoCD deployment manifests. Previously, the team controlled ArgoCD deployment and had merge access to the repo storing applications, allowing easy onboarding of new apps via PRs. However, when another team (e.g., cluster-admins or infra) manages ArgoCD deployments in their own repo, the current practice of storing app manifests in that external repo is problematic because the team may lack merge access and it is not ideal for infrastructure managers to handle unrelated PRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage ArgoCD Applications declaratively in git.
- Avoid burdening infrastructure/cluster-admin teams with PRs unrelated to their responsibilities.
- Maintain clear ownership and access control over application manifests.
- Facilitate onboarding of new applications without requiring access to infra repos.
- Desire to enforce project boundaries and resource deployment restrictions.
- Consideration of existing limitations in ArgoCD project enforcement mechanisms.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is (3): Have a separate repository managed by the Operate-First team, with an ArgoCD App of Apps managing this repo. This allows all operate-first/team-specific ArgoCD Applications to reside in the 'opf-argocd-apps' repo, managed by Operate-First admins, while infra-related ArgoCD Applications remain in the infra repo. This setup enables declarative addition of new applications without PRs to the infra repo, reducing burden on cluster-admins and centralizing application management for Operate-First.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include:
- Infrastructure/cluster-admins are not overwhelmed with PRs for ArgoCD app onboarding.
- OperateFirst maintainers can manage PRs efficiently.
- The 'opf-argocd-apps' repo can be leveraged by other clusters for quick ArgoCD application setup.

Negative consequences include:
- No automatic enforcement that applications in 'opf-argocd-apps' belong to the Operate First ArgoCD project.
- Potential risk of applications deploying resources outside intended project boundaries.
- Current enforcement relies on PR-level checks and possibly CI until upstream solutions are available.

alternatives.description: Just have all ArgoCD manifests in one repo and give Operate-First team members access to infra repo to review and merge ArgoCD Applications.
pros: Simpler setup with a single repo.
Direct access for Operate-First team to manage applications.
cons: Infra team must manage PRs unrelated to their responsibilities.
Potential for access control and ownership confusion.

alternatives.description: Have separate teams handle Applications for their Projects in their own Repos, so tracking Applications is the responsibility of individual teams.
pros: Clear ownership per team.
Infra/Operate-First teams are not responsible for other teams' applications.
cons: Potentially more complex management with multiple repos.
Less centralized control and visibility.

alternatives.description: Have a separate Repo that Operate-First manages, and have an ArgoCD App of Apps that manages this repo.
pros: Centralizes Operate-First applications management.
Reduces infra team burden.
Enables declarative app addition without infra repo PRs.
cons: No automatic enforcement of project boundaries currently.
Requires manual or CI-based enforcement.
Potential risk of resource deployment outside intended projects.

template_adherence.title: Repositories Supporting Multiple Environment Deployments
template_adherence.context:
With the introduction of the app of apps ADR we now have a way to separate application management with infrastructure management. The argocd-apps repo now serves as a central point of managing ArgoCD applications (and in turn our manifests in general) for the operate-first initiative.

As per the App of Apps ADR doc we would like both the argocd-apps repo and the repos that each application in the argocd-apps target to be able to be deployed in multiple environments. Environments here can mean multiple namespaces on the same cluster, or different clusters all together.

For example, I should be able to create a single ArgoCD app, that points to the argocd-apps repo and have it create all the ArgoCD applications that live in this repo, regardless of environment. This is fine if your manifest repo only has one set of manifest deployment that can be deployed in any environment without needing additional tuning. This is rarely the case however, and often times you'll have a common set of manifests, and then your target environments will add additional configurations on top of this. This results in multiple subdirectories with different paths for each target environment. This essentially means we can only use argocd-apps repo for a specific environment only.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support multiple environments (namespaces or clusters) from the same repo
- Desire to avoid proliferation of multiple repos for each environment
- Flexibility to tune configurations per environment
- Avoid organizational bloat and complexity
- Maintainability and onboarding complexity considerations
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Kustomize overlays/bases for the argocd-apps repo and have different overlays that patch the path for each environment. This approach accomplishes the goal of supporting multiple environments without needing multiple repos, thus reducing organizational bloat. The argocd-apps repo will follow a structure with a base directory containing common manifests and overlays directory containing environment-specific patches. This allows ArgoCD instances to deploy applications by pointing to the appropriate overlay for the target environment.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include lots of flexibility in tuning configurations for target environments and accommodating different use cases. Negative consequences include potentially added complexity in onboarding applications due to the overlay structure.

alternatives.description: Keep argocd-apps repo environment specific, and use multiple repos as "app-of-apps" repos for each environment.
pros: Clear separation of environments by repo
Simplicity in repo structure per environment
cons: Proliferation of multiple repos leading to organizational bloat
Harder to maintain common manifests across environments
Less flexible for cross-environment changes

alternatives.description: Use Kustomize overlays/bases for argocd-apps repo and have different overlays that patch the path for each environment.
pros: Supports multiple environments from a single repo
Reduces number of repos and organizational bloat
Flexible tuning of configurations per environment
cons: Added complexity in repo structure
Potential onboarding complexity for new users

template_adherence.title: Application Monitoring in Operate First using Prometheus
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need to monitor multiple services deployed in the Operate First environment using Prometheus. It explains the constraints due to OpenShift's pre-installed Prometheus Operator and the limitations of Operator Groups and User Workload Monitoring, leading to the problem of how to structure Prometheus deployments.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include access to cluster-wide permissions, Prometheus instance resource access, locations of monitoring resources like servicemonitors/podmonitors, responsibility for creating these resources, complexity of Prometheus deployments, number of Prometheus instances to deploy, and namespaces for deployment.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to choose Option 1: a single Prometheus instance in a dedicated monitoring namespace, with servicemonitors/podmonitors kept in that namespace and the Prometheus service account given roles to access services in other namespaces. This option is chosen because it is less complex than Option 2 and does not require clusterroles like Option 3.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequence is a simpler setup with a single Prometheus instance and no need for cluster-wide roles, only namespace-specific roles. This reduces complexity and potential security risks associated with cluster-wide permissions.

alternatives.description: Option 1: Single Prometheus instance in a dedicated monitoring namespace with roles to access other namespaces.
pros: Less complex setup than multiple Prometheus instances.
No need for cluster-wide roles, only namespace-specific roles.
cons: Prometheus service account needs roles to access multiple namespaces, which may require careful role management.

alternatives.description: Option 2: Each namespace has its own Prometheus instance, with a main Prometheus federating metrics.
pros: Isolation of monitoring per namespace.
Potentially better fault isolation.
cons: More complex setup with multiple Prometheus instances.
Management overhead of multiple instances and federation.

alternatives.description: Option 3: Single Prometheus instance with clusterrole to access services and monitoring resources cluster-wide.
pros: Simplifies access by granting cluster-wide permissions.
All monitoring resources can be kept in any namespace.
cons: Requires cluster-wide permissions, which may pose security risks.
Potentially more complex to manage cluster-wide roles.

template_adherence.title: Common Authentication for Applications
template_adherence.context: Applications deployed within Operate First are run on top of OpenShift. Many applications require users to log in in order to be able to enforce RBAC, quotas and sandboxing. It is also essential for auditing. User management of the applications should be unified so the same user can access all the applications with a single set of credentials. The username should be unique, but also utilized across applications. The accepted solution should provide SSO, so the user can cary over the identity across different applications. The identity and authentication should be based on the OpenShift authentication.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- For the same user a single user identity is provided to all applications.
- All users are able to authenticate using the same credentials as they use for the underlying OpenShift platform.
- User identity provided by the SSO allows for similar RBAC settings across different applications.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: _"2. Standalone Dex server in a separate namespace"_, because
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive Consequences

- Each Operate First application can consume user identity for all SSO authenticated users.
- Applications don't have to care about user management.
- SSO allows us to share the RBAC rules between applications in similar contexts since the user identity structure (LDAP groups, etc.) is the same.

### Negative Consequences

- Introduces a single point of failure for all user authentications.

alternatives.description:
ArgoCD embedded Dex server

Lives within the Argo CD deployment. Argo CD implements its own wrapper around Dex configuration and deployment, which may prove to be difficult to adjust to application specific usage.

Dex server can provide OpenID identity, can connect to variety OpenID Connect identity sources connectors (Openshift, Github, Google, SSO providers, etc.) and since it's confined to its own namespace it allows for easier SRE as well as future expansion with client database for identity carry over between applications.
pros: Good, because it is already prepared and available and proved to work with ArgoCD.
Good, because it is a lightweight bridge solution to existing OpenID Connect providers.
cons: Bad, because it's not isolated to a separate namespace and doesn't allow full control over the Dex configuration.
Bad, because the deployed Dex server version depends on what Dex version is packaged for ArgoCD by ArgoCD configurator wrapper.

alternatives.description:
Standalone Dex server in a separate namespace

This option allows us to keep all the benefits of a Dex server without compromising ArgoCD stability/reliability.
pros: Good, because configuration is fully in our control as well as Dex version used.
Good, because of the isolation, can be scaled and restricted by quotas.
Good, because it is a lightweight bride solution to existing OpenID connect providers.

alternatives.description:
Standalone Dex server via an operator

This option allows us to keep all the benefits of a Dex server without compromising Argo CD stability/reliability. It also simplifies management duties, since it can be managed declaratively via custom resources.
pros: Good, because configuration is fully in our control as well as Dex version used
Good, because of the isolation, can be scaled and restricted by quotas
Good, because it is a lightweight bride solution to existing OpenID connect providers
Good, because it is easy to configure via custom resources.
cons: Bad, because there are only 2 community implementation, no official one.
Bad, because neither of the currently available Dex operator implementations are maintained.

alternatives.description:
Keycloak server via an operator

Keycloak is a heavy duty identity provided and access management. It can be installed via a Kubernetes operator and can be managed declaratively via custom resources. It can do all the identity provider bridging provided by Dex as well as many more like provide identity on its own, manage LDAP etc.
pros: Good, because it is easy to configure via custom resources.
cons: Bad, because it is heavy weight, resource intensive solution, requiring external database and other components which may prove to be difficult to use in edge/dev cluster setting.

alternatives.description:
OpenShift Oauth server directly

Use OpenShift Oauth directly. This option provides means to authenticate against OpenShift, however OpenShift itself doesn't provide OpenID identity and relies on external sources.
pros: Good, because it is already available in the platform and no setup is needed.
cons: Bad, because we are lacking the essential - there's no identity provided. Only authentication.
Bad, because applications usually require identity to be provided no matter if user is authenticated.

template_adherence.title: Managing Operators
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the ambiguity in the definition of 'cluster-scope' applications introduced by ADR 0010, specifically in the context of deploying operators using the Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM). It highlights the overlapping resource kinds and the need for clear guidance on how to treat these resources in different contexts and usage variants.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Insufficient guidance from ADR 0010 on 'cluster-scope' applications for OLM.
- OLM resources can have cluster-wide or namespace-scoped effects.
- Permission restrictions and singleton behavior of some OLM resources within namespaces.
- Handling operators not deployed via OLM but behaving cluster-wide.
- Managing meta-operators that deploy other operators cluster-wide.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to find a balance between deploying all operator-related resources within the 'cluster-scope' application and requiring all namespaced resources to be deployed within individual applications. Specifically, resources affecting the cluster level (including some namespace-scoped ones) are deployed within 'cluster-scope', while others are deployed in individual applications. This approach allows tracking of all resources that may affect other users and namespaces, with strict rules for resource placement subject to future updates.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clear guidance on operator-related resources, treating manually deployed operators like normal applications without cluttering 'cluster-scope', and enforcing restrictions to prevent privilege escalation via meta-operators. Negative consequences include a complex set of rules that cluster-admins must understand and follow.

alternatives.description: Deploy all operator-related resources within 'cluster-scope' application.
pros: Easy to implement.
Clear rules for users - operators always live here.
cons: Impossible for meta-operators like ODH.
Hard to maintain due to different team ownership.
Increases resources in 'cluster-scope' drastically.
Does not solve meta-operator access issues.

alternatives.description: Require all namespaced resources to be deployed within individual applications, outside of 'cluster-scope'.
pros: Easy to implement.
No complex rules for users.
cons: Impossible for meta-operators like ODH.
Some namespace-scoped resources must be unique per namespace.
Some namespace-scoped resources grant cluster-level access.

alternatives.description: Find balance between the above two options.
pros: Allows weighting each resource kind separately.
Keeps 'cluster-scope' application size reasonable.
Gives control to individual application/project owners.
cons: Requires complex rules and full understanding by system integrators.

template_adherence.title: Cluster deployment methods for moc-infra cluster
template_adherence.context:
This document suggests options for the preferred deployment method for the **moc-infra cluster** at the MOC(Mass Open Cloud). This hub cluster will be the central OpenShift cluster to manage and deploy other clusters on-demand.

The moc-infra cluster is a bare-metal cluster. Deploying an OpenShift Container Platform on bare metal can be achieved by several methods.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include ease of deployment, availability of tools to the public, automation capability, suitability for disconnected environments, and future benefits of using growing Red Hat tools.
template_adherence.decision: We chose to deploy the cluster using the IPI method because it is a light and easy deployment, available for the public to use, and easy to automate the process for reproducible deployment.
template_adherence.consequences: The cluster was successfully deployed using the IPI installation method, which is lightweight, comfortable, and publicly available. The decision avoids the higher effort of UPI and the risks of using a tech preview tool like Assisted Installer.

alternatives.description: UPI - User provisioned infrastructure: Deploy an OpenShift cluster on infrastructure that you prepare and maintain.
cons: More effort involved in setting up the infrastructure.

alternatives.description: IPI - Installer provisioned infrastructure: Deploy an OpenShift cluster on infrastructure that the installation program provisions and the cluster maintains.
pros: Installation is closer to a disconnected environment, which is good practice.
Uses an external tool available to all.
Lightweight, comfortable, and publicly available tool.

alternatives.description: Assisted Installer: Discovery ISO that makes it easy to connect discovered hardware.
pros: Growing Red Hat tool with future benefits.
Part of ACM deployment of new clusters.
Opportunity to provide feedback to developers.
Easily automated using API calls.
Allows booting bare-metal nodes from an ISO image.
cons: Tech preview tool, not a completed product.

template_adherence.title: Cluster deployment methods
template_adherence.context: From the onset we have used the terms "environment" and "cluster" interchangeably, and our repository structure has been reflective of that. However, there seems to be a clear need for a distinction in certain contexts between environments like "MOC" and "Quicklab" and specific clusters belonging to those environments. For example, before we used to use "MOC" to refer to the original `cnv` cluster, but we now have two clusters that belong to the MOC environment (`infra` and `zero`). Furthermore, since there is no such thing as one defacto "Quicklab/CRC" cluster, when we design for these environments we have to design for a very generic environment without adding configurations tuned for one specific cluster. In consideration of these different factors, we must design with _Multi-Cluster Environments_ in mind and restructure existing repos accordingly.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to distinguish between environments and clusters clearly, the scalability of configuration management, the reduction of redundant configurations, and the ability to handle dev environments effectively.
template_adherence.decision: Option 2, organizing repos at the Environment Level, is chosen as the preferred option because it is more scalable and reduces the number of configurations associated with each environment, despite the initial overhead of deciding cluster groupings.
template_adherence.consequences: The repositories are reorganized with apps configured for clusters belonging to common environments. For dev environments, apps will be configured to be generic and non-cluster specific. This approach reduces redundancy and improves scalability but requires careful consideration of cluster groupings and common resources.

alternatives.description: Organize repos at Cluster level, treating clusters individually without grouping them into environments.
pros: Keeps things simple, no need to consider common resources or environment groupings.
cons: Introduces redundant configurations.
No clear way to include dev environments which are often ephemeral.

alternatives.description: Organize repos at Environment Level, grouping clusters into logical environments like 'MOC'.
pros: Allows a common location for resources/configs for clusters in the same environment.
Reduces work by avoiding duplication across clusters in the same environment.
cons: Requires extra consideration on how clusters are grouped.
Needs decisions on what resources are considered common.

template_adherence.title: Enforcing of Resource Quotas
template_adherence.context: Currently clusters being managed by Operate-First are not enforcing quotas on compute and storage resources. This means that anyone can use their `namespace` to use hog as many resources as they wish. We should use Kubernetes' ResourceQuotas to address this concern. Decisions for declaring quotas for resource `requests` and `limits` should be guided by monitoring current trends and usage via available dashboards. We will also need to add default LimitRanges so current workloads are not prevented from creating resources.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to enforce resource quotas to prevent resource hogging, the desire for user-friendliness, consistency, ease of propagation of changes, and minimizing resource waste and management overhead.
template_adherence.decision: Option 1 (Tiered & Custom Resource quotas) is preferred due to the flexibility it offers. If it comes to the point where everyone is opting for custom quotas anyway, the tier option can be abandoned.
template_adherence.consequences: Adopting the tiered and custom resource quotas approach will provide a user-friendly and consistent way to manage resource quotas, ease propagation of changes, but may result in some resource waste and complexity if custom quotas become too numerous.

alternatives.description: Tiered & Custom Resource quotas: Identify a tier of standard ResourceQuotas distributed to each namespace, with allowance for custom quotas on a need basis.
pros: User friendly. Easier for new-comers to pick from a set of options than specify specific requirements.
Consistency. Tiers ensure all new-comers are treated the same and custom requests are treated carefully.
Easy to propagate changes. Updating one manifest updates all in that tier.
cons: May result in waste of compute resources fitting various use cases into small set of tiers.
Could get convoluted if custom ResourceQuotas manifests outnumber standard options.

alternatives.description: Only Resource quotas: No tier option, every namespace has a resource quota customized for their needs.
pros: Less likely to waste resources if tuned correctly for each namespace.
No confusion over when to use tiered or custom quotas since only custom exists.
cons: Adds overhead to onboarding as new-comers must assess exact resource needs.
More resources to track and manage.
Different admins may have different views on necessary quotas, leading to uncertainty.

template_adherence.title: Declarative Definitions for Cluster Scoped Resources
template_adherence.context: In ADR-0009, a directory structure for organizing cluster scoped resources was defined. However, it did not consider the possibility of name conflicts when resources of the same kind and name but different API groups coexist. This creates a problem in storing these resources in the GitHub repository under the current structure, as they would conflict in file paths.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid name conflicts in the repository structure for cluster scoped resources, maintain compatibility with existing tooling, and keep the structure manageable and understandable.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt the second option: organizing resources using the schema `cluster-scoped-resources/base/<API_GROUP>/<KIND_PLURAL>/<METADATA_NAME>/<KIND_SINGULAR>.yaml`. This approach introduces additional directory nesting but aligns with methods used in other tooling and avoids custom naming conventions. Core API group resources will be stored directly under `cluster-scope/base`.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision results in a directory structure that avoids name conflicts by including the API group as a directory level, which is a tried and tested method. It requires additional nesting of directories and the use of `kustomization.yaml` files at base directories to include resources in overlays without modifying default build behavior. An exception is made for resourcequotas, which are namespaced and stored alongside namespace manifests.

alternatives.description: Use a schema that includes the API group as part of the directory name, e.g., `cluster-scope/base/<API_GROUP>-<KIND_PLURAL>/<METADATA_NAME>/<KIND_SINGULAR>.yaml`.
pros: Avoids additional directory nesting.
Simplifies directory structure.
cons: Introduces a custom naming convention that may be unfamiliar.
Potentially less compatible with existing tooling.

alternatives.description: Use a schema with additional directory nesting by API group, e.g., `cluster-scoped-resources/base/<API_GROUP>/<KIND_PLURAL>/<METADATA_NAME>/<KIND_SINGULAR>.yaml`.
pros: Aligns with existing tooling practices (e.g., must-gather).
Avoids custom naming conventions.
Clear separation by API group.
cons: Requires additional directory nesting.
Slightly more complex directory structure.

template_adherence.context: The Operate First Cloud environment spans multiple data centers and multiple regions. template_adherence.decision_drivers: Previous ADRs decided input conditions such as GitHub as the ultimate identity provider and applications leveraging common authentication as clients. template_adherence.decision: The chosen option is to authenticate OpenShift against Keycloak and provide app authentication via Dex against OpenShift because it is a fully declarative solution that is fully supported and available today. template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include declarative SSO configuration for new clusters and applications and a single centralized Keycloak instance. Negative consequences include the need for per cluster Dex deployment due to Keycloak's current inability to import OpenShift groups.

template_adherence.title: Maintaining GitHub organization as a code
template_adherence.context:
Managing GitHub organizations via UI is restricted to few individuals only and does not offer any review mechanisms. The same apply to repository creation, organization membership management and label management. This ADR focuses on bringing transparency into this aspect of housekeeping within a community and aims to provide a way to individual contributors, so they can influence and propose changes themselves.

ADR seeks a way to manage GitHub organization as a code, declaratively via GitOps as a natural extension of the core paradigm of Operate First movement.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Improve transparency, provide auditing and reviews and allow individual contributors to propose changes.
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: _"1. Prow's Peribolos"_, because it's a declarative solution that is widely embraced in upstream communities like Kubernetes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Repositories can be created declaratively.
* Even external users can request themselves to be added to the organization via a pull request.
* Teams can be created and maintained declaratively.
* Labels can be centrally managed in a unified way as well as updated per repository bases.
* Solution can be easily automated via post-submit Prow jobs.

Negative Consequences:
* Using a declarative configuration may not be as straightforward as clicking buttons in the UI.
* Some users can still do manual changes to repositories they own, these changes are undone by the automation.

alternatives.description: Prow's Peribolos
pros: It's a declarative solution.
Widely embraced in upstream communities like Kubernetes.

template_adherence.title: Use DotEnv for Managing Environment Variables
template_adherence.context: Accessing ENV directly without a wrapper is limited and can introduce problems. We want our tooling to help us guard against missing environment variables. When `nil` is accidentally provided during the start up process it is preferable to fail fast with an explicit message. Without this `nil` can be passed down through the stack and cause strange behaviour where the code has been designed with it as a dependency. Instead of adding `nil` guards throughout the codebase (eg. `ENV.fetch('FOO', 'default')`), this should be managed centrally. We have previously used Figaro for this purpose but it was deprecated in 2016 (https://github.com/laserlemon/figaro). We should only use supported gems to ensure we get support in the form of fixes and security patches. We also want to be able to stub our environment variables in our test suite. An easy example of this is when we use environment variables as a feature flag mechanism. We want to stub the value to test both scenarios without being influenced by real values being loaded. Mutating the actual ENV value (eg. `allow(ENV).to receive(:[]).with('BOX_ID').and_return("1234")`) is possible but may have unexpected consequences where more than 1 part of the same process under test uses the same variable. Figaro used to be a handy abstraction layer that we could stub eg. `allow(Figaro).to receive(:env).with(:foo).and_return('bar')`. We should then consider how we can stub environment variables.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to guard against missing environment variables and fail fast with explicit messages.
- Avoid adding nil guards throughout the codebase.
- Use supported gems to ensure ongoing support and security patches.
- Ability to stub environment variables easily in tests without side effects.
- Avoid overhead of managing multiple environment variable files (e.g., .env* and docker-compose.env*).
template_adherence.decision: Use DotEnv to load our environment variables.
template_adherence.consequences:
- When using Docker and Docker Compose, environment variables will need to be loaded with `docker-compose up --env-file=.env.development` rather than `docker-compose.env`, which is a pattern previously used.
- Having two files for managing environment variables such as `.env*` and `docker-compose.env*` is undesirable due to overhead in keeping these in sync.
- DotEnv loads environment variables but doesn't offer an interface as Figaro did; access is via `ENV['foo']` rather than `DotEnv.foo`.
- A supporting decision will be needed to use Climate Control to support testing.

alternatives.description: Continue using Figaro for environment variable management.
pros: Previously used and familiar to the team.
Provided an abstraction layer that was easy to stub in tests.
cons: Deprecated since 2016, no longer supported.
No security patches or fixes, potential risk.
Does not meet the requirement of using supported gems.

alternatives.description: Access ENV directly without a wrapper.
pros: No additional dependencies.
Simple and straightforward.
cons: Limited and can introduce problems.
Requires adding nil guards throughout the codebase.
Does not fail fast on missing environment variables.
Harder to stub environment variables in tests reliably.
