template_adherence.title: Handling Database Corruption
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of users encountering corrupt SQLite databases, which render the related component unusable. It focuses on identifying corrupted databases and deciding the appropriate action when corruption is detected, aiming to avoid deleting valid user data while resolving persistent corruption issues.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include avoiding deletion of valid user data, the negative impact of keeping corrupted databases, and the current lack of a reliable method to distinguish persistent from transient errors, which could be improved by analyzing telemetry and sentry data.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to check for errors when opening a database and compare against known corruption error types (A2), and upon identifying corruption, delete the database file and recreate it (B1). This approach balances conservatism in error identification with practical resolution, with plans to monitor and potentially enhance the strategy in the future.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision allows users with corrupted databases to regain use of affected components by deleting and recreating the database. However, there is a risk of data loss if corruption is misidentified. The approach is simpler to implement and can be improved over time based on telemetry data.

alternatives.description: Assume all errors when opening a database are from corrupt databases.
pros: Sentry data indicates many errors occur during opening.
Migrations likely trigger corruption errors.
Natural time to delete database before queries or connections.
cons: May delete valid user data due to common errors like migration logic errors, OOM, disk full.

alternatives.description: Check for errors when opening a database and compare against known corruption error types.
pros: Eliminates possibility of deleting valid user data.
Sentry data supports errors during opening time.
Natural time to delete database before queries or connections.
cons: Currently lack a comprehensive list of corruption errors.

alternatives.description: Check for errors for all database operations and compare against known corruption error types.
pros: Sentry data shows errors outside opening time.
Eliminates possibility of deleting valid user data.
cons: Consumer code may not expect database deletion mid-query.
Lack of comprehensive corruption error list.

alternatives.description: Delete the database file and recreate the database.
pros: Allows users with corrupted databases to use components again.
cons: Misidentification leads to data loss.

alternatives.description: Move the database file and recreate the database.
pros: Possibility to recover data if misidentified.
Allows user-initiated data deletion.
cons: Recovery function is complex and error-prone.
Adds complexity to database opening code.
User experience may be confusing with delayed data restoration.

alternatives.description: Have the component fail (return failure code).
pros: No risk of user data deletion.
Simplest to implement.
cons: Component unusable if database is corrupt.
No way for users to delete corrupted data.

template_adherence.title: Running experiments on first run early startup
template_adherence.context: As an experimenter, I would like to run experiments early on a user's first run of the application. However, the experiment data is only available on the second run. We would like to have that experiment data available before the user's first run.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Availability of experiments early on the first run
* No impact on experimentation data analysis
* Flexibility in creating experiments
* Ability to quickly disable experiments
* Simplicity of releases
* Mobile's expectations of Nimbus (The SDK should be idempotent)
template_adherence.decision:
None of the options were feasible, so for now we are sticking with option **(A) Do Nothing** until there are experiments planned that are expected to run on early startup on the first run, then we will revaluate our options.

The **(B) Bundle Experiment data with app on release** option was rejected mainly due to difficulty in disabling experiments and pausing enrollments. This can create a negative user experience as it prevents us from disabling any problematic experiments. Additionally, it ties experiment creation with application release cycles.

The **(C) Retrieve Experiment data on first run, and deal with delay** option was rejected due to the fact it changes the Nimbus SDK will no longer be idempotent,and the possibility of introducing undesirable UI.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to do nothing means that experiments will not run early on the first run, maintaining the current state. This preserves flexibility in experiment creation, allows disabling experiments remotely, and keeps the Nimbus SDK idempotent. However, it does not solve the problem of exposing experiments to users on their first run.

alternatives.description: Keep everything the way it is, preventing us from experimenting on users early on their first run
pros: Good, because it keeps the flexibility in experiment creation
Good, because disabling experiments can still done remotely for all experiments
Good, because it keeps the Nimbus SDK idempotent.
cons: Bad, because it doesn't address the main problem of exposing experiments to user on their first run

alternatives.description: On release, have an `initial_experiments.json` that defines the experiments that will be applied early on the first run. Later on the first run, the client would retrieve the actual experiment data from remote-settings and overwrite the bundled data
pros: Good, because it allows us to run experiments early on a user's first run
Good, because it prevents us from having to wait for experiments, especially if a user has a slow network connection
cons: Bad, because it ties experiment creation with release cycles
Bad, because it prevents us from disabling problematic first-run experiments without a dot release
Bad, because it prevents us from pausing enrollment on first-run experiments without a dot release
Bad, because it requires investment from the console team, and can modify existing flows.

alternatives.description: We can retrieve the experiment data on the first run, experiment data however will not be available until after a short delay (network I/O + some disk I/O)
pros: Good, because it enables us to retrieve experiments for users on their first run
Good, because it keeps the flexibility in experiment creation
Good, because disabling experiments can still done remotely for all experiments
cons: Bad, because experiments may not be ready early on the user's experience

Bad, because it forces the customer application to deal with either the delay, or changing the configuration shortly after startup. e.g. a loading spinner or a pre-onboarding screen not under experimental control; delaying initialization of onboarding screens until after experiments have been loaded.
Bad, because it changes the programming model from Nimbus being an idempotent configuration store to configuration changing non-deterministically.
Bad, because the experimentation platform could force the app to add unchangeable user interface for the entire population. This itself may have an effect on key metrics.

template_adherence.decision_drivers: Key drivers include encouraging configurability, providing good error messages for configuration issues, generating up-to-date documentation, enforcing conventions, enabling validation during config-writing while maintaining production speed, supporting multiple config file types, eliminating boilerplate through defaults, and managing hierarchical configurations effectively.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt the official OpenMRS Microfrontend Config Library as a JavaScript module that provides APIs for defining config schemas, accessing config values, providing config files, validating configs in non-production environments, generating documentation, specifying config file hierarchies, and offering a UI for configuration management. The library mandates default values for all configuration elements.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include standardized configuration management, improved developer experience, better error handling, automated documentation, enforcement of conventions, and support for complex configuration hierarchies. Potential negatives are not explicitly discussed but may include the overhead of maintaining the config library and the learning curve for developers.

alternatives.description: Developers handle configuration how they like, typically using native JSON import mechanisms without standardized validation or documentation.
pros: Flexibility for developers to choose their own methods.
No additional tooling or library maintenance required.
cons: Inconsistent configuration handling across microfrontends.
Likely incomprehensible runtime errors for bad configurations.
Lack of validation and documentation support.

alternatives.description: Provide tooling for configuration management without bundling a runtime module into applications.
pros: Offers some support for configuration validation and documentation.
Does not increase application bundle size with runtime code.
cons: Not meaningfully integrated into applications, leading to low adoption.
Reduces validation and documentation to unenforced best practices.
Developers may ignore tooling due to lack of integration.

template_adherence.title: Contributing guidelines for OpenMRS frontend projects
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses how contributors should make pull requests to frontend projects within OpenMRS, aiming to standardize contribution practices and lower barriers to entry.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to follow widely accepted open source standards, ensure a safe and welcoming community environment, maintain a clean commit history, and reduce barriers to contribution such as mandatory JIRA tickets or single-commit PRs.
template_adherence.decision: The ADR decides to use Github contributing.md and pull_request_template.md files, the OpenMRS code of conduct, the OpenMRS MPL-2.0 license, community-maintained pull request tips, and enable Github squash and merge for frontend projects. It also decides not to enforce linking every PR to a JIRA ticket and allows multiple commits per PR, leveraging squash and merge to maintain commit history clarity.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include alignment with open source standards, a safer community, legal protection, and easier contribution processes. Negative consequences might include some inconsistency in PR ticket linking and commit granularity, but these are mitigated by the squash and merge strategy and community guidelines.

alternatives.description: Continue enforcing that every PR must link to a JIRA ticket and have only one commit.
pros: Ensures all work is tracked via JIRA.
Simplifies commit history by enforcing single commits.
cons: Increases barrier to contribution due to JIRA account and ticket creation requirements.
Destroys incremental commit history and makes review harder.
Discourages contributions that do not fit neatly into JIRA tickets.

alternatives.description: Do not use Github squash and merge, require multiple commits to be preserved as is.
pros: Preserves all commit history as authored.
Allows detailed incremental commits.
cons: Results in a more cluttered master branch commit history.
May confuse reviewers and contributors with many small commits.
Does not align with Github's recommended practices for clean history.

template_adherence.title: Versioning strategy for OpenMRS frontend ESMs using modified Semantic Versioning
template_adherence.context: OpenMRS frontend ESMs require a versioning strategy that respects their unique characteristics, particularly their focus on UI features and configuration schemas, which differ from typical API-centric modules.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to respect backward compatibility of APIs and configuration schemas; need to account for functional UI changes; need to consider backend module dependencies; desire to follow Semantic Versioning principles with necessary modifications.

template_adherence.consequences: Provides clear guidance for versioning frontend ESMs that accounts for their unique characteristics; ensures compatibility and upgrade safety; may require implementers to understand the modified SemVer rules; aligns versioning with both API and UI changes.

template_adherence.title: ADR 001: Coin Source Tracing
template_adherence.context: The specification for IBC cross-chain fungible token transfers (ICS20) requires awareness of the origin of any token denomination to relay packets containing sender and recipient addresses. The problem involves handling token denomination prefixes that grow with each transfer and contain special characters, conflicting with SDK coin denomination validation rules.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to maintain consistent and valid coin denominations within SDK-based chains, handle the increasing length of token denomination prefixes, and ensure compatibility with existing ICS20 specifications without requiring changes to other implementations.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to hash the denomination prefix to produce a consistent-length internal representation for cross-chain fungible tokens, using a SHA256 hash of the denomination trace path and base denomination. This hashed denomination is used internally and stored in a lookup table in the ibc-transfer module, while the full denomination path is still used in packet data to maintain compatibility with ICS20.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clearer separation of source tracing behavior, consistent coin validation, and cleaner denominations. Negative consequences include the need to store denomination traces in the ibc-transfer module, increased client complexity to fetch base denominations, and slightly increased gas usage. Neutral consequences include slight differences with ICS20 spec and additional validation logic.

alternatives.description: Use the full denomination prefix directly without hashing, as per the original ICS20 specification.
pros: Maintains full traceability in the denomination string.
No need for additional storage or lookup tables.
cons: Denomination strings can become excessively long, exceeding SDK coin length limits.
Special characters and uppercase letters in port/channel IDs violate SDK coin validation rules.
Can cause unexpected panics or transfer failures due to invalid denominations.

alternatives.description: Modify the ICS20 specification to allow longer and more flexible denomination strings.
pros: Aligns the specification with practical needs of cross-chain transfers.
Removes the need for hashing and lookup tables.
cons: Requires changes to multiple implementations beyond SDK-based chains.
Potentially breaks compatibility with existing chains and tools.
Longer denominations may still cause UX or performance issues.

template_adherence.title: ADR 006: Secret Store Replacement
template_adherence.context:
Currently, an SDK application's CLI directory stores key material and metadata in a plain text database in the user’s home directory. Key material is encrypted by a passphrase, protected by bcrypt hashing algorithm. Metadata (e.g. addresses, public keys, key storage details) is available in plain text.

This is not desirable for a number of reasons. Perhaps the biggest reason is insufficient security protection of key material and metadata. Leaking the plain text allows an attacker to surveil what keys a given computer controls via a number of techniques, like compromised dependencies without any privilege execution. This could be followed by a more targeted attack on a particular user/computer.

All modern desktop computers OS (Ubuntu, Debian, MacOS, Windows) provide a built-in secret store that is designed to allow applications to store information that is isolated from all other applications and requires passphrase entry to access the data.

We are seeking solution that provides a common abstraction layer to the many different backends and reasonable fallback for minimal platforms that don’t provide a native secret store.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve security protection of key material and metadata.
- Desire to leverage built-in secret stores available on modern desktop OSes.
- Requirement for a common abstraction layer to support multiple backends.
- Need for reasonable fallback on minimal platforms without native secret stores.
template_adherence.decision:
We recommend replacing the current Keybase backend based on LevelDB with Keyring by 99 designs. This application provides a common abstraction and uniform interface between many secret stores and is used by AWS Vault application by 99-designs.

This solution fulfills the requirement of protecting both key material and metadata from rogue software on a user’s machine.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Increased safety for users.

Negative:
- Users must manually migrate.
- Testing against all supported backends is difficult.
- Running tests locally on a Mac require numerous repetitive password entries.

Neutral:
- {neutral consequences}

alternatives.description: Continue using the current Keybase backend based on LevelDB with passphrase encryption and plain text metadata.
pros: No changes required, immediate continuation of current system.
Users and developers are familiar with the existing system.
cons: Insufficient security protection of key material and metadata.
Metadata is stored in plain text, exposing sensitive information.
Vulnerable to attacks via compromised dependencies without privilege execution.

alternatives.description: Develop a custom secret store solution tailored to the application's needs.
pros: Full control over implementation and features.
Can be optimized specifically for the application's requirements.
cons: High development and maintenance cost.
Potentially less secure than mature, tested solutions.
Longer time to delivery.

template_adherence.title: ADR 008: Decentralized Computer Emergency Response Team (dCERT) Group
template_adherence.context:
In order to reduce the number of parties involved with handling sensitive information in an emergency scenario, we propose the creation of a specialization group named The Decentralized Computer Emergency Response Team (dCERT). Initially this group's role is intended to serve as coordinators between various actors within a blockchain community such as validators, bug-hunters, and developers. During a time of crisis, the dCERT group would aggregate and relay input from a variety of stakeholders to the developers who are actively devising a patch to the software, this way sensitive information does not need to be publicly disclosed while some input from the community can still be gained.

Additionally, a special privilege is proposed for the dCERT group: the capacity to "circuit-break" (aka. temporarily disable) a particular message path. Note that this privilege should be enabled/disabled globally with a governance parameter such that this privilege could start disabled and later be enabled through a parameter change proposal, once a dCERT group has been established.

In the future it is foreseeable that the community may wish to expand the roles of dCERT with further responsibilities such as the capacity to "pre-approve" a security update on behalf of the community prior to a full community wide vote whereby the sensitive information would be revealed prior to a vulnerability being patched on the live network.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce the number of parties handling sensitive information during emergencies.
- Desire to coordinate various blockchain community actors effectively.
- Requirement for special privileges like circuit-breaking message paths.
- Governance flexibility to enable/disable privileges.
- Potential future expansion of dCERT roles.
- Need for mechanisms like continuous voting, slashing, and emergency disband.
- Parameters to be governed and adjustable.
- Ensuring security and trustworthiness of dCERT members through staking and slashing.
- Handling emergency scenarios such as collusion or malicious behavior.
- Balancing centralization risks with operational efficiency.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement the dCERT group as a specialization group as defined in ADR 007, including features such as continuous voting, slashing for soft contract breaches, member revocation, emergency disband, and compensation stipends. New governance parameters will be introduced to manage aspects like stipend allowance, member limits, staking requirements, quorum, proposal wagers, stabilization periods, and circuit-break privileges. The continuous voting mechanism will be implemented via an Electionator object with detailed rules for membership changes and stabilization. Staking and slashing mechanisms will ensure member accountability, with governance playing a role in suspensions and slashing. Emergency disband procedures will be enabled through special governance proposals. dCERT members will have specific transaction capabilities including description changes, circuit-breaking message routes, and voting to suspend members. Circuit-breaking will disable message routes temporarily, with unbreaking only possible via hard fork upgrades. Abuse of privileges will be penalized by severe slashing.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include reducing the number of parties to coordinate with during emergencies and lowering the risk of sensitive information disclosure to malicious parties. Negative consequences include centralization risks. Neutral consequences are not explicitly detailed.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text. The ADR focuses on the chosen approach without listing alternative solutions or approaches.

template_adherence.title: ADR 009: Evidence Module
template_adherence.context: In order to support building highly secure, robust and interoperable blockchain applications, it is vital for the Cosmos SDK to expose a mechanism in which arbitrary evidence can be submitted, evaluated and verified resulting in some agreed upon penalty for any misbehavior committed by a validator, such as equivocation (double-voting), signing when unbonded, signing an incorrect state transition (in the future), etc. Furthermore, such a mechanism is paramount for any IBC or cross-chain validation protocol implementation in order to support the ability for any misbehavior to be relayed back from a collateralized chain to a primary chain so that the equivocating validator(s) can be slashed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a flexible and extensible evidence submission and handling mechanism.
- Requirement to support slashing and penalizing validators for misbehavior.
- Support for routing evidence messages to appropriate handlers.
- Ability to modify slashing penalties via governance.
- Support for querying evidence and parameters.
- Integration with other modules like slashing and governance.
template_adherence.decision: We will implement an evidence module in the Cosmos SDK supporting abstractions and interfaces for custom evidence messages, handlers, and slashing methods. The module will route evidence messages to handlers, allow governance to modify slashing penalties, and provide queriers for evidence and parameters. The Evidence interface and routing/handling mechanisms are defined to support flexibility and extensibility.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Enables on-chain processing and penalization of validator misbehavior.
- Allows evidence types and handling logic to be defined by any module.
- Does not rely solely on Tendermint for evidence submission.

Negative:
- No easy way to introduce new evidence types through governance on a live chain due to handler introduction limitations.

Neutral:
- Uncertainty about persisting infractions indefinitely or relying on events.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but alternatives could include relying solely on Tendermint for evidence submission or having a monolithic evidence handling mechanism without extensibility.
pros: Simpler implementation.
Less complexity in routing and handling.
cons: Less flexible and extensible.
Cannot support custom evidence types easily.
Does not support governance modification of slashing penalties.

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Modular AnteHandler
template_adherence.context:
The current AnteHandler design allows users to either use the default AnteHandler provided in `x/auth` or to build their own AnteHandler from scratch. Ideally AnteHandler functionality is split into multiple, modular functions that can be chained together along with custom ante-functions so that users do not have to rewrite common antehandler logic when they want to implement custom behavior.

For example, let's say a user wants to implement some custom signature verification logic. In the current codebase, the user would have to write their own Antehandler from scratch largely reimplementing much of the same code and then set their own custom, monolithic antehandler in the baseapp. Instead, we would like to allow users to specify custom behavior when necessary and combine them with default ante-handler functionality in a way that is as modular and flexible as possible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for modularity and flexibility in AnteHandler design
- Desire to avoid rewriting common antehandler logic
- Compatibility with existing ModuleManager architecture
- Ease of understanding and reasoning about antehandler execution
- Ability to pre- and post-process in antehandler chain

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: State Accessors
template_adherence.context:
SDK modules currently use the `KVStore` interface and `Codec` to access their respective state. While this provides a large degree of freedom to module developers, it is hard to modularize and the UX is mediocre.

First, each time a module tries to access the state, it has to marshal the value and set or get the value and finally unmarshal. Usually this is done by declaring `Keeper.GetXXX` and `Keeper.SetXXX` functions, which are repetitive and hard to maintain.

Second, this makes it harder to align with the object capability theorem: the right to access the state is defined as a `StoreKey`, which gives full access on the entire Merkle tree, so a module cannot send the access right to a specific key-value pair (or a set of key-value pairs) to another module safely.

Finally, because the getter/setter functions are defined as methods of a module's `Keeper`, the reviewers have to consider the whole Merkle tree space when they reviewing a function accessing any part of the state. There is no static way to know which part of the state that the function is accessing (and which is not).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce boilerplate and repetitive code in state access.
- Desire to modularize state access and improve UX for module developers.
- Align with object capability theorem to restrict access rights more granularly.
- Improve code reviewability by making state access scopes explicit.
- Maintain compatibility with existing SDK modules and allow opt-in usage.
template_adherence.decision:
We will define new types `Value` and `Mapping` to represent references to key-value pairs and key-value spaces in the state, respectively. These types will encapsulate state access with core methods for getting, setting, checking existence, and deleting values.

Additionally, we will define derived types from `Value` (e.g., `Boolean`, `Enum`, `Integer`, `String`) with type-specific encoding schemes and from `Mapping` (e.g., `Indexer`) with typed keys.

This approach allows automatic serialization, explicit access scopes, and safer transfer of state access rights. The new accessor types will be opt-in and coexist with the current architecture.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Serialization is automatic, reducing developer effort.
- Code size is shorter with less boilerplate, improving UX.
- State access rights can be transferred safely and explicitly.
- Access scopes are explicit, aiding code review and security.

Negative:
- Serialization format details are hidden, which may reduce transparency.
- The architecture differs from the current one, requiring adaptation.
- Type-specific accessor types must be defined manually.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing `KVStore` interface and `Codec` with manual getter/setter functions in module `Keeper`s.
pros: No architectural changes required.
Developers are familiar with the current approach.
cons: High boilerplate and repetitive code.
Hard to modularize and transfer access rights safely.
Poor UX and code reviewability due to implicit access scopes.

alternatives.description: Use a generic code generation tool to automatically generate getter/setter functions for each module's state keys.
pros: Reduces manual boilerplate code.
Keeps current architecture largely intact.
cons: Adds complexity with code generation tooling.
May not fully solve access rights granularity and modularity issues.
Generated code may be harder to debug or understand.

template_adherence.title: ADR 013: Observability
template_adherence.context:
Telemetry is paramount into debugging and understanding what the application is doing and how it is performing. We aim to expose metrics from modules and other core parts of the Cosmos SDK.

In addition, we should aim to support multiple configurable sinks that an operator may choose from. By default, when telemetry is enabled, the application should track and expose metrics that are stored in-memory. The operator may choose to enable additional sinks, where we support only Prometheus for now, as it's battle-tested, simple to setup, open source, and is rich with ecosystem tooling.

We must also aim to integrate metrics into the Cosmos SDK in the most seamless way possible such that metrics may be added or removed at will and without much friction. To do this, we will use the go-metrics library.

Finally, operators may enable telemetry along with specific configuration options. If enabled, metrics will be exposed via `/metrics?format={text|prometheus}` via the API server.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for telemetry to debug and understand application behavior and performance.
- Support for multiple configurable sinks, initially in-memory and Prometheus.
- Seamless integration of metrics into the Cosmos SDK with minimal friction.
- Operator configurability via application configuration.
- Use of battle-tested libraries (go-metrics, Prometheus).
template_adherence.decision: We will add an additional configuration block to `app.toml` that defines telemetry settings, supporting in-memory and Prometheus sinks. A `Metrics` type will be created to bootstrap metrics collection and expose metrics via an API endpoint `/metrics`. The system will support gathering metrics in different formats and allow operators to dump metrics on demand via signals. Application developers can easily instrument code with minimal effort.

- Provides exposure into the performance and behavior of the application.

Negative:
- None explicitly stated.

template_adherence.title: ADR 015: IBC Packet Receiver
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the implementation of the IBC packet receiving mechanism within the Cosmos SDK, referencing ICS 26 - Routing Module. It addresses the need to utilize existing routing functionality in baseapp.router, the verification and execution steps in routing module callbacks, and the handling of atomic multi-message transactions to preserve IBC-related state changes even if application state changes revert. The context also highlights the introduction of a new CodeType, CodeTxBreak, to handle transaction breaks without aborting the entire transaction.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for developer ergonomics by reducing boilerplate verification code, ensuring atomic multi-message transaction state preservation, safe and capability-restricted access to channels via PortKeeper, integration of proof verification at the application level to prevent misbehavior, and maintaining sequence integrity to prevent double execution. Additionally, the design aims to embed state change commitment logic into baseapp.runTx and provide an intuitive interface for developers.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement PortKeeper with capability keys restricting access to bound channels, modify baseapp.runMsgs to break message loops on non-OK results but persist state changes on CodeTxBreak, define an AnteDecorator (ProofVerificationDecorator) for IBC packet receiving to verify Merkle proofs, extract side effects into separate functions called by application handlers, introduce ChannelKeeper.CheckOpen for channel handshake validation, and embed the ProofVerificationDecorator into the top-level application AnteHandler chain. The ADR also specifies the creation of a Data field in Packet for dynamic IBC and outlines example application-side usage for channel checking and message handling.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include an intuitive interface for developers where IBC handlers do not need to manage authentication, and embedding state change commitment logic into baseapp.runTx. Negative consequences include the inability to support dynamic ports as routing is tied to the baseapp router. Neutral consequences involve the introduction of a new AnteHandler decorator and potential support for dynamic ports via hierarchical port identifiers.

alternatives.description: Implement a separate routing module as defined in ICS 26 instead of utilizing baseapp.router.
pros: Clear separation of routing logic from baseapp.
Potentially easier to maintain routing module independently.
cons: Increased complexity due to additional module.
More boilerplate code for verification and execution steps.
Less developer ergonomics.

alternatives.description: Do not introduce CodeTxBreak and abort entire transaction on any packet failure.
pros: Simpler transaction handling logic.
No need for special code types or breaking logic.
cons: State changes from previous successful packets would be reverted.
Channels could get stuck due to reverted sequences and commitments.
Less robust handling of atomic multi-message transactions.

alternatives.description: Let each application module handle proof verification individually without a centralized AnteDecorator.
pros: Modules have full control over their own verification logic.
Potentially more flexible for module-specific needs.
cons: Risk of inconsistent or incorrect proof verification.
Increased chance of application misbehavior violating IBC protocol.
More complex application logic.

template_adherence.title: ADR 016: Validator Consensus Key Rotation
template_adherence.context:
Validator consensus key rotation feature has been discussed and requested for a long time, for the sake of safer validator key management policy (e.g. https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1136). So, we suggest one of the simplest form of validator consensus key rotation implementation mostly onto Cosmos-SDK.

We don't need to make any update on consensus logic in Tendermint because Tendermint does not have any mapping information of consensus key and validator operator key, meaning that from Tendermint point of view, a consensus key rotation of a validator is simply a replacement of a consensus key to another.

Also, it should be noted that this ADR includes only the simplest form of consensus key rotation without considering multiple consensus keys concept. Such multiple consensus keys concept shall remain a long term goal of Tendermint and Cosmos-SDK.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for safer validator key management policy.
- Desire to implement simplest form of consensus key rotation without changing Tendermint consensus logic.
- Avoiding complexity of multiple consensus keys concept for now.
- Minimizing frequent key rotation to reduce burden on LCD and IBC.
- Governance control over rotation limits and fees.
- Compatibility with existing Tendermint ABCI ValidatorUpdate mechanism.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a simple validator consensus key rotation mechanism mostly on Cosmos-SDK without changing Tendermint consensus logic. The rotation involves creating a new consensus key, broadcasting a transaction to update the key mapping, and immediately disabling the old key. Limits on rotation frequency and fees are applied to prevent abuse. The implementation leverages existing Tendermint ABCI ValidatorUpdate capabilities and adds new parameters and tracking in the staking module.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Validators can rotate consensus keys immediately or periodically for better security.
- Improved security against Long-Range attacks by discarding old keys.

Negative:
- Increased computation in the slash module due to key lookups per height.
- Frequent rotations may reduce light client bisection efficiency.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but the ADR mentions the long-term goal of supporting multiple consensus keys per validator, which is not included in this ADR.
pros: Simpler implementation focusing on single consensus key rotation.
No changes needed in Tendermint consensus logic.
cons: Does not support multiple consensus keys, which may be a desired feature in the future.

template_adherence.title: ADR 17: Historical Header Module
template_adherence.context: In order for the Cosmos SDK to implement the IBC specification, modules within the SDK must have the ability to introspect recent consensus states (validator sets & commitment roots) as proofs of these values on other chains must be checked during the handshakes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to store recent headers for consensus state introspection, the requirement to make these headers available for querying by SDK modules, and considerations about storage methods and configuration parameters.
template_adherence.decision: The application must store the most recent n headers in a persistent store, initially possibly the current Merklised store, with alternatives considered. Headers are stored during handling of abci.RequestBeginBlock, and the data is made available via the Keeper's GetHistoricalInfo function. The parameter n may be configurable.
template_adherence.consequences: Requires changes to the Cosmos SDK but not Tendermint. Positive impacts include easy retrieval of headers and no need for RPC or ABCI changes. Negative impact includes data duplication and additional disk usage.

No RPC calls to Tendermint required.
No ABCI alterations required.
cons: Duplicates n headers data in Tendermint and the application, leading to additional disk usage.

alternatives.description: Use a non-Merklised store later as no proofs are necessary.
pros: Potentially simpler storage without Merklisation overhead.
cons: May lose some benefits of Merklised storage such as proof capabilities.

alternatives.description: Store only the hash of the validator set instead of full headers.
pros: Reduced storage requirements.
cons: May limit the ability to introspect full consensus state details.

template_adherence.title: Extendable Voting Periods
template_adherence.context: Currently the voting period for all governance proposals is the same.  However, this is suboptimal as all governance proposals do not require the same time period.  For more non-contentious proposals, they can be dealt with more efficently with a faster period, while more contentious or complex proposals may need a longer period for extended discussion/consideration.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have variable voting periods based on voter demand rather than proposer choice, avoiding a second voting process to determine voting period length, and handling complexities such as redelegation/unbonding during voting periods.

template_adherence.title: Protocol Buffer State Encoding
template_adherence.context: The Cosmos SDK currently uses go-amino for binary and JSON encoding, aiming for parity between logical and persistence objects. However, Amino does not fully meet goals such as language agnosticism, upgradeability, and performance, causing issues in cross-language support and acting as a performance bottleneck. Therefore, a new encoding protocol is needed that is language and platform agnostic, supports rich clients, offers high performance, minimal message size, codegen-based encoding, and backward/forward compatibility. This ADR focuses on state serialization in the Cosmos SDK state machine.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for a serialization protocol that is language and platform agnostic, has a thriving ecosystem, high performance, minimal encoded message size, codegen-based rather than reflection-based, and supports backward and forward compatibility. Additionally, the migration should allow coexistence with Amino during transition and provide a good developer experience.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt Protocol Buffers for serializing persisted structured data in the Cosmos SDK. Modules will accept a codec interface, Marshaler, with three implementations: AminoCodec, ProtoCodec, and HybridCodec. HybridCodec uses Amino for JSON and Protobuf for binary encoding, facilitating gradual migration. Modules that require interface serialization will define their own codec interfaces extending Marshaler. The use of google.protobuf.Any is chosen for encoding interfaces, with a type registration mechanism (InterfaceRegistry) to ensure safe decoding and prevent vulnerabilities. Additional mechanisms like UnpackInterfaces are introduced for interface unpacking during deserialization. Amino compatibility is maintained via LegacyAmino codec. Alternatives like Cap'n Proto and FlatBuffers were considered but rejected due to ecosystem maturity and complexity.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include significant performance gains, support for backward and forward compatibility, and better cross-language client support. Negative consequences include a learning curve for Protobuf and slightly larger message sizes due to Any usage, potentially mitigated by future compression. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using Amino encoding as is.
pros: Existing system with established usage.
No migration effort required.
cons: Does not fully meet goals of language/platform agnosticism.
Poor backward and forward compatibility.
Performance bottleneck.
Difficult cross-language support.

alternatives.description: Adopt Cap'n Proto as the serialization protocol.
pros: Native support for interfaces and generics.
Built-in canonicalization.
cons: Less mature ecosystem compared to Protobuf.
Smaller client ecosystem and tooling support.

alternatives.description: Adopt FlatBuffers as the serialization protocol.
pros: No parsing/unpacking step needed.
Efficient memory usage.
cons: Requires significant research and migration effort.
Not designed for untrusted inputs.
Smaller ecosystem compared to Protobuf.

template_adherence.title: Custom BaseApp panic handling
template_adherence.context: The current implementation of BaseApp does not allow developers to write custom error handlers during panic recovery in the runTx() method. The proposal is to introduce a middleware solution to allow more flexible and customizable panic handling, including special cases like sdk.ErrorOutOfGas, without rewriting the whole BaseApp.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for flexibility in panic recovery handling; ability to add custom error handlers; maintain compatibility with existing BaseApp flow; support for special error cases like OutOfGas; desire to avoid rewriting BaseApp; ensure deterministic node behavior in presence of panics.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a middleware-based design for panic recovery handling in BaseApp. Introduce RecoveryHandler and recoveryMiddleware types to build a chain of panic handlers. This approach allows multiple custom handlers, preserves existing behavior, and supports special cases like OutOfGas.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Enables custom panic handlers, preserves standard BaseApp usage, supports error context enrichment and passthrough panics. Negative: Changes execution model design. Neutral: OutOfGas and default panic handlers become middlewares.

template_adherence.title: ADR 024: Coin Metadata
template_adherence.context:
Assets in the Cosmos SDK are represented via a `Coins` type that consists of an `amount` and a `denom`, where the `amount` can be any arbitrarily large or small value. In addition, the Cosmos SDK uses an account-based model where there are two types of primary accounts -- basic accounts and module accounts. All account types have a set of balances that are composed of `Coins`. The `x/bank` module keeps track of all balances for all accounts and also keeps track of the total supply of balances in an application.

With regards to a balance `amount`, the Cosmos SDK assumes a static and fixed unit of denomination, regardless of the denomination itself. In other words, clients and apps built atop a Cosmos-SDK-based chain may choose to define and use arbitrary units of denomination to provide a richer UX, however, by the time a tx or operation reaches the Cosmos SDK state machine, the `amount` is treated as a single unit. For example, for the Cosmos Hub (Gaia), clients assume 1 ATOM = 10^6 uatom, and so all txs and operations in the Cosmos SDK work off of units of 10^6.

This clearly provides a poor and limited UX especially as interoperability of networks increases and as a result the total amount of asset types increases. We propose to have `x/bank` additionally keep track of metadata per `denom` in order to help clients, wallet providers, and explorers improve their UX and remove the requirement for making any assumptions on the unit of denomination.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve user experience (UX) by providing richer metadata about coin denominations.
- Current system assumes a fixed unit of denomination which limits UX.
- Desire to support multiple denominations and aliases for assets.
- Need for clients, wallets, and explorers to have reliable metadata without assumptions.
- Storage overhead should be minimal.
- Support for querying metadata via CLI and REST interfaces.
- Governance control over denomination metadata.
template_adherence.decision:
The `x/bank` module will be updated to store and index metadata by `denom`, specifically the "base" or smallest unit -- the unit the Cosmos SDK state-machine works with.

Metadata will include a list of denominations with their names, exponents relative to the base, and aliases. Important denominations such as `base` and `display` will be identified.

The metadata structure is defined with protobuf messages `DenomUnit` and `Metadata`.

Clients can use this metadata to convert and display balances appropriately.

Metadata will be included in the `GenesisState` of the `x/bank` module.

Query handlers will be added to CLI and REST interfaces to access and convert metadata.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides clients, wallet providers, and block explorers with additional data on asset denomination to improve UX and remove any need to make assumptions on denomination units.

Negative:
- A small amount of required additional storage in the `x/bank` module. The amount of additional storage should be minimal as the amount of total assets should not be large.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Do not add metadata tracking to the `x/bank` module and continue relying on clients to make assumptions about denomination units.
pros: No additional storage overhead in the `x/bank` module.
Simpler implementation without changes to existing modules.
cons: Poor user experience due to lack of standardized metadata.
Clients and wallets must make assumptions which can lead to errors.
Does not scale well with increasing asset types and interoperability.

alternatives.description: Add metadata tracking but do not expose it via CLI and REST interfaces, limiting usage to internal module logic.
pros: Improves internal handling of denominations.
Minimal exposure reduces API complexity.
cons: Clients and wallets cannot leverage metadata for improved UX.
Limits usefulness of metadata to internal processes only.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025: IBC Passive Channels
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to expand the naive IBC relayer strategy to a passive one that can detect and relay channel handshake messages and packets without prior knowledge of channels.
- Desire to expose comprehensive events to capture channel metadata for passive relayers.
- Allow application modules to control channel open attempts.
- Maintain compatibility with existing naive relayer implementations.
- Avoid constraining app modules to complete handling of channel open try messages within a single transaction or block.
template_adherence.decision:
- Expose events to allow "passive" connection relayers.
- Enable application-initiated channels via such passive relayers.
- Allow port modules to control how to handle open-try messages.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Makes channels into a complete application-level abstraction.
- Applications have full control over initiating and accepting channels, rather than expecting a relayer to tell them when to do so.
- A passive relayer does not have to know what kind of channel (version string, ordering constraints, firewalling logic) the application supports. These are negotiated directly between applications.

Negative:
- Increased event size for IBC messages.

Neutral:
- More IBC events are exposed.

alternatives.description: Continue using the naive relayer strategy that requires predetermined channels and explicit knowledge of channels to relay packets.
pros: Simplicity in relayer implementation.
Less event data emitted, potentially smaller message sizes.
cons: Relayer must know channels in advance.
Less flexible, cannot handle dynamic channel openings.
Does not support application-initiated channels effectively.

alternatives.description: Implement a fully structured negotiation protocol between relayer and application modules for channel opening, requiring synchronous handling within transactions.
pros: Explicit negotiation and version control.
Potentially more robust channel opening process.
cons: Increased complexity in app modules.
Constraints on app modules to complete handling within transactions or blocks.
Less flexible for asynchronous or delayed handling.

template_adherence.title: ADR 026: IBC Client Recovery Mechanisms
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the challenge of client expiry or misbehaviour in the IBC protocol, where it is difficult to distinguish between genuine faults and user mistakes. Without a recovery mechanism, funds in affected channels become permanently locked. The ADR aims to provide a safe recovery mechanism for exceptional cases where clients can no longer be updated.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to handle client expiry and misbehaviour safely, the inability to distinguish between Byzantine faults and user errors at the protocol layer, and the security implications of allowing governance to override client state. The desire to avoid recovery in cases of chain halting (Byzantine behavior) and to maintain security by requiring governance approval are key drivers.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement governance-based recovery mechanisms for clients that have expired or been frozen due to misbehaviour, with specific flags and functions added to Tendermint and solo machine clients. Chains that have halted are excluded from recovery. Governance proposals can update clients under controlled conditions, and clients can opt out of this recovery mechanism.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include establishing recovery mechanisms for expiry and misbehaviour and allowing clients to opt out. Negative consequences include added complexity for users and governance participants needing to select new headers. Neutral consequences are explicitly stated as none.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative is to not provide any recovery mechanism, leading to permanently locked funds in cases of client expiry or misbehaviour.
pros: Simplicity, no added complexity or governance overhead.
cons: Funds remain permanently locked in affected channels.
No recovery options for users in exceptional cases.

template_adherence.title: Use NX
template_adherence.context: We want a monorepo tool to help us to scale development up for multiple projects and teams. It should not be too much in the way, but help us manage code, dependencies and CI/CD.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Low complexity and overhead in development.
* Fit for our stack.
* Optimize CI/CD with dependency graphs and/or caching.
* Flexible.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Nx", because:

* It's specially designed around our stack (TypeScript, React, Node.JS, NPM, ESLint, Prettier, Cypress, Jest, NextJS).
* It's relatively easy to learn with focused documentation.
* It has schematics to generate apps, libraries and components that includes all of our tools.
* It is opinionated, which gives us a good base to start developing faster. Many things can still be configured or extended.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to use Nx will provide a monorepo tool that fits well with our technology stack and development practices, enabling easier scaling of multiple projects and teams. It offers benefits such as optimized CI/CD, code generation, and opinionated defaults to speed up development. However, being opinionated and maintained by an agency may have some downsides.

template_adherence.title: CSS
template_adherence.context: We're building websites and web applications that share a common design system with reusable components. How do we write CSS styles in a way that is performant and safe?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Should be performant, with code splitting, caching and minimal runtime overhead.
- Needs to have easy access to our design system constants. These should optimally be shared with JS logic.
- Should be type-safe to catch issues when refactoring.
- Reusable components should be closed, not accepting arbitrary styles/classes.
- We want a pattern for responsive props with atomic layout components.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: Treat, because it combines the best of both worlds from CSS-in-JS and CSS modules.

We'll create shared components that have responsive props, but are otherwise closed for modifications. Theme variables are defined in a shared library with TypeScript.

Example:

```typescript jsx
// Good:
<Box padding"small" />
<Box padding={{xs: 'small', md: 'medium'}} />
<Input large />
<Text preset="heading3" as="p" />

// Bad:
<Box className={customLayout} />
<Input style={{ height: 50, padding: 16 }} />
<Text className={styles.heading} />
```
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Treat is statically extracted at build time, so it has minimal runtime.
- Styles load in parallel with JS, also when code splitting.
- Styles are written in TypeScript which gives us type safety when referring to shared variables, styles and helpers.
- Styles are in special files, separate from markup and components giving us clear separation with good visibility into the rendered markup.
- We can pull in responsive layout component patterns from [Braid], which gives us a good base to lay out components and pages.

Negative Consequences:
- We are choosing a pretty new framework, so it may 1) have bugs or issues, 2) be an obstacle for new developers or 3) be discontinued.
- When we're generating responsive styles at build time we need to be mindful at how many variations we allow (eg media queries, columns, whitespace), since they can easily bloat our CSS with unused styles.

template_adherence.title: Branching and release strategy
template_adherence.context: How do we want to organise work in branches and how should changes be released? How should different branches be continuously deployed for QA?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* We need to have confidence in our releases.
* We want more structured releases while we're still getting our footing in a shared monorepo.
* We need simplicity and clear [takt time] so different teams can plan for what is going out the door from them.
* It should work well with our agile work environment.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "OneFlow" because it provides a single eternal branch with well structured releases.

We'll implement OneFlow with these details:

* Release branches are set up the Monday after each sprint. This is sometimes called release trains, where features line up for different release trains.
* Release and quality managers from each team are responsible for reviewing and approving releases.
* Releases apply to all apps in the monorepo.
* Releases are versioned like this: `{cycle}.{sprint}.{hotfix}`. So version 3.1.2 is the release after cycle 3, sprint 1 with two hot fixes applied.
* Feature branches are merged using "Squash and merge", so they can be easily reverted.
* There are two ways to build larger features.
* If the feature is isolated and not likely to cause conflicts, they can stay on long-living feature branches until they are ready to be released.
* If the feature touches many parts of the codebase, it can be useful to merge changes more often but hide the feature in production with feature flags.
* If a project needs to deploy updates outside of the sprint rhythm, they should use hotfix branches.

### Future strategy

With time, we expect to build up better testing capabilities which gives us more confidence in the health of our monorepo. Then we can move quicker, with a simpler GitHub Flow branching strategy and continuous delivery into production.

### Hosting environments

We'll set up continuous delivery to different hosting environments:

Environment | Git source            | Databases/services | Features
------------|-----------------------|--------------------|----------
sandbox     | feature branch        | Test               | All
dev         | master                | Test               | All
staging     | master                | Prod               | All
pre-prod    | release/hotfix branch | Prod               | Finished
prod        | latest release tag    | Prod               | Finished

We'll probably start with dev, staging, pre-prod and prod environments, since feature branch deployments are more dynamic and difficult to manage.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to adopt OneFlow with a structured release process and feature branch management will provide a clean git history and structured releases, improving confidence and planning. However, it may make continuous integration more difficult. The future strategy allows for evolution towards simpler branching and continuous delivery as testing improves. The hosting environment setup supports continuous delivery to multiple environments, facilitating QA and release management.

template_adherence.title: Unified naming strategy for files and directories
template_adherence.context: As of the date of this writing, there are multiple different naming styles used in the monorepo, mostly because NX has defaults that differ between schematic types. In order for navigating the monorepo in a consistent rational manner, we should align on naming strategy for files and directories.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Provide consistency when navigating the codebase
* The earlier we decide on this, the better
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: Name files after their default export. If that default export is a React Component, or a class, then the file name should be in PascalCase. Otherwise, the filename should be in camelCase. Basically, for naming files avoid using kebab-case and snake_case and make sure the name follows the default export of the file.

Naming directories should follow these guidelines:
Only use kebab-case when naming NX apps and libraries, or folders containing apps and libraries, e.g. `island-ui` instead of `islandUi`:
`import { Box } from '@island.is/island-ui/core'`

Use PascalCase for directories only containing React components:
````
components/CtaButton/index.ts
import 'components/CtaButton'
````
or:
````
components/CtaButton/CtaButton.tsx
import 'components/CtaButton/CtaButton'
````
rather than
````
components/cta-button/CtaButton.tsx
````

In all other cases, use camelCase.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Easier to navigate the codebase
* File names are more readable, and developers know what to expect
* This approach is the most common practice, and something most JS and TS developers are familiar with.

alternatives.description:

* kebab-case
* PascalCase
* camelCase
* snake_case

template_adherence.title: Open Source License
template_adherence.context:
It is the offical policy of the Digital Iceland and stated in the Techical Direction that it is to be implemented as free and open source. Open source software by definition is open to anyone to use, modify, distribute and study. These permissions are enforced an open source license. There are a number of well-known and widely used open source licenses available and we need to choose a license that best fits the goals of digital iceland.

There are two main types of open source licences:  more permissive licences that confer broad freedoms and minimal obligations (e.g., the MIT, BSD and the Apache 2.0 licences); and sharealike licences that require licensing adaptations with the same licence if they distribute them (e.g., the GNU GPL).

Development for Digital Iceland will be open and free with minimum complications for development for all involved. Reuse and transparency will be promoted.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* The primary motivation is to encourage, co-development, collabiration, transparency and reuse of the software.
* It is important to build on the experience of similar government led inititives in other countries.
* Digital Iceland has no patents or intellecatual property that needs to be protected or guarded by the license chosen.
* It is not a concern for Digital Iceland that the license restricts usage in other projects, be it open or closed source.
template_adherence.decision:
The MIT license was chosen, for the following reasons:

* It is the least restrictive of the licenses.
* It is very consise, simple and easy to understand and therefore should be clear to users and developers.
* Digital Iceland does not require protection of patents or existing intelletual property.
* Well known government lead initiatives like uk.gov and X-Road use the MIT license.
* The MIT license is the best known and most widely used free and open-source license in the world.
template_adherence.consequences: Choosing the MIT license means the software will be licensed under a very permissive, simple, and widely recognized license that encourages reuse, collaboration, and transparency. It aligns with Digital Iceland's goals and experiences from similar initiatives. However, the ADR does not explicitly discuss potential negative consequences or trade-offs of this choice.

alternatives.description: Apache license
pros: Good, because is well known and very permissive like the MIT license.
cons: It has restrictions around redistribution that do not apply for Digital Iceland.
It is very long and wordy and therefore requires more effort to understand.

alternatives.description: BSD license
pros: Good, because is well known and very permissive like the MIT license.
cons: It has restrictions about using the names of the copyright holder which is not a concern for Digital Iceland.

alternatives.description: GNU GPL license
pros: It is very well known.
cons: It is not permissive and requires derived software to adopt the license as well.

template_adherence.title: Form field groups and variations
template_adherence.context: All form fields are statically bound, limiting flexibility in form building. For example, the 'Name' field cannot distinguish firstname, middlename, and lastname. There is a need for form field variations to allow more flexible form construction.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support alternative storage and presentation of form fields, such as adding an 'Other' input to radio/checkbox fields and grouping address components. The solution should preserve existing functionality, allow pre-made templates, and avoid database changes.
template_adherence.decision: Create additional versions for each individual form field, introducing a 'version' attribute while keeping 'formtype' and other JSON attributes the same. Add a 'groupid' attribute to group fields dynamically. Form groups will be non-editable but appear as regular fields in JSON. Also, create a helper listing of form group templates in JSON format to define group membership.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Flat JSON object simplifies handling, reuses existing form fields flexibly, enforces best practices via non-editable groups, and requires no database changes. Negative: Harder syntax to read/edit compared to full HTML templates, increased initial development effort, and limitation on nesting form groups infinitely.

alternatives.description: Create additional versions of the form field, treating each version as a new form field type.
pros: Allows explicit versioning of form fields.
Preserves existing form field types.
cons: May increase the number of form field types to manage.
Could complicate form field handling logic.

alternatives.description: Create alternative(s) under each form field.
pros: Keeps alternatives grouped under the same form field.
Potentially more organized structure.
cons: Optional consideration, not fully detailed.
May complicate JSON structure and processing.

template_adherence.title: Translations
template_adherence.context: The Form Builder must support multiple languages, allowing custom human translations, pre-translated common fields, and fallback to machine translation services.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for multi-language support, ease of updating translations without code access, leveraging existing frameworks and packages, and ensuring a fallback mechanism for translations.
template_adherence.decision: Use a translation loader to store human translated language lines in the database, use the file system for pre-translated templates, and fallback to machine translation services. The fetching order will be human translated (database) -> pre-translated (file template) -> machine translated (cached, database) -> machine translated (API). MVP will only require human and pre-translated layers.
template_adherence.consequences: This approach allows form authors to update translations without code access, supports multiple translation sources, and provides a fallback mechanism. However, it introduces complexity in managing multiple translation layers and syncing language lines when forms change.

alternatives.description: Leverage Lumen/Laravel localization features out of the box using template files.

No need for additional database or packages.
cons: Requires code access to update translations.
Editing PHP translation files is complex and error-prone.
Does not support dynamic translation updates through the app.

alternatives.description: Use Lumen/Laravel default file system with a file uploader to manage translation files.
pros: Allows uploading translation files without code deployment.
Leverages existing file system localization.
cons: Editing files requires correct PHP syntax.
Still complex to manage and update translations dynamically.

alternatives.description: Use a package to load and override file translations from the database (e.g., spatie/laravel-translation-loader).
pros: Enables storing translations in the database for dynamic updates.
Supports overriding file translations.
Facilitates translation management through the app.
cons: Adds dependency on external package.
Requires database schema changes and syncing logic.

template_adherence.title: No Terraform Backend in Module
template_adherence.context:
Terraform requires a `backend` for state file storage. Most existing Terraform modules within LIC have this `backend` set in the Terrform configuration in `main.tf`.

Having the `backend` configured in the module means that consumers can't overwrite the configuration. When building and testing modules it is useful to be able to use a "local" `backend`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly state decision drivers as a separate section or content. However, the context implies drivers such as flexibility for consumers to override backend configuration and ease of testing modules locally.
template_adherence.decision: We have not set the `backend` configuration in the `main.tf`.
template_adherence.consequences:
When running locally, such as when using the examples, the consumer can set the `backend`. This enables the `backend` to be decided by the consumer rather than the module.

When running in labelled environments the configuration will need to be set up to use the appropriate backend. In most cases this will be the `s3` backend.

alternatives.description: Set the `backend` configuration inside the module's `main.tf` file.
pros: Ensures consistent backend configuration across all consumers of the module.
Simplifies module usage by embedding backend setup.
cons: Prevents consumers from overriding backend configuration, reducing flexibility.
Makes local testing and development harder as backend is fixed.

alternatives.description: Do not set the `backend` configuration in the module, allowing consumers to configure it.
pros: Allows consumers to choose and override backend configuration as needed.
Facilitates local testing with different backends, such as local backend.
Increases module flexibility and reusability.
cons: Requires consumers to manage backend configuration themselves, which may lead to inconsistencies.
Potentially more setup required by consumers.

The range/hash key will be added automatically to the additional attributes by the module, reducing the load on the consumer with implementation detail.

template_adherence.title: Use Clean Architecture
template_adherence.context:
All applications inevitably have some form of "design" applied to them, whether it be an ugly bag of mostly functions, or a disciplined model developed by a group of software design experts. A good design can have a dramatic effect on the quality of an application, enabling a developer to quickly become familiar with the existing code, and knowing where new functionality would fit into the big picture.

One simple and yet effective design is called the Clean Architecture, as described by Robert Martin in a blog post from 2012 (see references below). The application is divided into several layers, with dependencies between layers going in only one direction. This encourages loose coupling and enables thorough unit testing through isolation of units via mocking. The Clean Architecture builds on earlier models, including Hexagonal Architecture and the Onion Architecture, which similarly break up the application into layers, with dependencies flowing in one direction.

A [tutorial](https://resocoder.com/2019/08/27/flutter-tdd-clean-architecture-course-1-explanation-project-structure/) by Matt Rešetá on Dart and Flutter uses a version of the Clean Architecture in which the domain layer defines the interface for one or more repositories, whose implementation lives in the data layer. This separation is often not covered in other depictions of Clean Architecture, but is helpful for understanding how best to keep dependencies unidirectional, as well as encouraging loose coupling and easier testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a clear, maintainable, and testable application design.
- Desire to use a proven architectural pattern that encourages loose coupling and unidirectional dependencies.
- Importance of enabling easy unit testing and separation of concerns.
- Preference for a version of Clean Architecture that clearly separates domain and data layers with repository interfaces.
template_adherence.decision:
The version of Clean Architecture described by Matt Rešetá will be used.

Additionally, dependency injection (a.k.a. inversion of control) will be used to maintain a clean separation between layers and permit easy unit testing.
template_adherence.consequences: This design has been used in this application for several months, and it has proven to be very helpful. Testing is easier, knowing where to find code is easier, and knowing where to fit new code is straightforward. By starting with use cases, and working from there, the code practically designs itself, and discourages writing unnecessary things.

template_adherence.context:
The authentication service serves multiple products, none of which is quite like the other. As such, the interface for the service should be as easy as possible to use from anywhere. In short that means accessing it over the network, as the client application will likely live on a different system. What's more, the protocol should be one so common that every system can support it.

As you may have guessed that would be HTTP/S. It is easy to understand, debug, is supported by basically everything, and trivial to implement (via readily available libraries). Alternatives could include GraphQL, which is fancy, but adds complexity that is unnecessary for this simple application, and a hand-written protocol, but that only creates more work for the client with no benefit.

template_adherence.title: Support External Data Store
template_adherence.context:
This application handles several important pieces of information, including the request/user mapping, and the session state for each browser connection. By default this information is stored in memory within the application process. However, if the application fails and another instance begins to process requests (e.g. via a load balancer), then any login requests that are still in progress will be lost (the user will get an error and have to try again).

To enable smooth failover and ensure high availability, an external data store option should be provided, in which both the request/user mapping and the session state will be stored. This store would be configured like any other aspect of the application, via environment variables. If not so configured, the existing in-memory data store should be used; this should be the default behavior.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for high availability and smooth failover; current in-memory storage leads to loss of in-progress login requests on failover; desire for configurable external data store; preference for popular, mature, well-maintained key/value store with Node.js client and easy cloud setup.
template_adherence.decision: The application will support the Redis key/value store as the external data store. Redis is chosen because it is popular, well supported, maintained for over 10 years, configurable for memory or file-based storage, and widely available on cloud providers.
template_adherence.consequences: During development, the Docker-based Redis container has worked well for enabling failover of the application. This choice enables reliable data storage across multiple instances and supports high availability.

template_adherence.title: Use ECMAScript Modules
template_adherence.context:
Since 2015 JavaScript has had a standard for defining and importing modules, as defined in chapter 15 of the ECMAScript 2015 Language Specification (also known as ECMAScript 6). Node.js introduced support for ECMAScript Modules (ESM) in late 2020, with all major supported versions providing ESM support.

Prior to the use of ECMAScript Modules, this application was using the `require()` functionality provided by Node.js to import modules. While this worked without any issue, the dawn of a major problem appeared on the horizon: third party libraries started using ESM. The old `require()` module system cannot import modules defined using the new ECMAScript 6 syntax. While ESM is backward compatible, it is not forward compatible. As more libraries migrate to this standard, the application will gradually go stale, using old versions of libraries.

As such, switching the entire application to ESM has become a necessity.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to keep the application up-to-date with third party libraries migrating to ECMAScript Modules, the incompatibility of the old `require()` system with ESM, and the necessity to adopt the modern standard for module definition and import in JavaScript.
template_adherence.decision: This application will use ECMAScript Modules because it is the only sensible choice going forward.
template_adherence.consequences:
Using `import` instead of `require()` brought about several other changes, including the need to remove the `include` hack that was used to deal with long import paths. In a similar vein, the use of `dotenv` had to be managed by the use of `import` of a new `env.js` module. The format of the shallow "modules" for configuring logging and the internal SAML IdP functionality required a minor change to use the ESM syntax.

Of more signifcance is that the single binary build produced by the `pkg` tool may be unavailable, at least temporarily, as it seems that `pkg` has several issues with ESM.

alternatives.description: Continue using the old `require()` module system and not switch to ECMAScript Modules.
pros: No immediate changes needed to the existing codebase.
Avoids potential issues with tools like `pkg` that have problems with ESM.
cons: Incompatibility with third party libraries that use ESM.
Application will gradually use outdated versions of libraries.
Not future-proof as the ecosystem moves towards ESM.
