template_adherence.title: Per namespace istio gateways
template_adherence.context:
Different tenant applications have differing ingress and egress requirements. Examples include:

* mutual TLS
* egress controls (e.g. limiting what can egress from a namespace / cluster)
* certificate operations (renewal etc.)

There is also the vision of the GSP that provides a common platform for all tenants based off a shared codebase. This platform allows suitable customisations to be suitable for the tenants running on it and, where possible, those customisations are controlled via kube-yaml.

At present, a single ingress gateway and egress gateway are defined by the GSP. In the case of the ingress gateway, all ingress traffic is routed through this which creates a range of difficulties:

* secrets relating to TLS certs (mutual or otherwise) have to be stored in `istio-system`
* having some endpoints use mutual TLS and others using non-mutual TLS is difficult/awkward/impossible on a single gateway
* a gateway is able to load certificates from a single secret (by default) so different applications in different namespaces will inevitably conflict
* different tenants in the same cluster will need to make changes to common "system" parts of the code (i.e. `istio-system`)
* controlling DNS entries and TLS configuration per tenant is difficult/awkward/impossible
* DNS is currently controlled via terraform in the GSP codebase (a single "*." record for the domain for the cluster provided as a convenience).
* TLS is currently terminated outside the cluter in an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in AWS, which doesn't suit all tenants

Other, indirect features:

* istio routing rules for single gateways in `istio-system` are:
* difficult to reason about and become quite brittle as a result
* don't align very well with istio's documentation
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to support different tenant ingress and egress requirements such as mutual TLS, egress controls, and certificate operations. The vision of a shared platform that allows tenant customizations via kube-yaml is important. Current single ingress/egress gateways cause difficulties in secret management, TLS configurations, routing complexity, and tenant isolation. Desired qualities include improved certificate and DNS management, better ingress control, alignment with Istio documentation, and tenant autonomy.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to create an ingress gateway and an egress gateway in each tenant ("managed") namespace, corresponding to option 4 in the alternatives list.
template_adherence.consequences: Tenants will have control over ingress rules including TLS, mutual TLS, secrets, routing, certificates, and DNS. There will be an increase in route53 records and AWS load balancer provisions. The change may cause some downtime during the initial migration.

alternatives.description: "Snowflake" load balancers and DNS records in tenant-specific terraform, bypass the `istio-system` ingress gateway as needed
pros: Quick
Relatively easy & familar
cons: Custom terraform for a tenant for something likely to be common (e.g. managing TLS termination and DNS ingress)
Doesn't make istio routing easier to work with
Doesn't improve certificate management (provisioning, renewing etc.)

alternatives.description: Allow tenants to configure multiple secrets on the `istio-system` ingress gateways
pros: Addresses the single-secret certificate problem
cons: Tenants need to know about gateway configuration
Tenants still manipulating shared namespaces & resources
Doesn't make istio routing easier to work with
Doesn't improve certificate management (provisioning, renewing etc.)

alternatives.description: Cert-manager and external-dns with single `istio-system` gateways
pros: Certificate management
DNS management (potentially)
cons: Tenants still manipulating shared namespaces & resources
Doesn't make istio routing easier to work with

alternatives.description: Per-namespace gateways with cert-manager and external-dns
pros: Certificate management
DNS management
Ingress control
Improves istio routing management (as it aligns more with the docs)
Alows tenants direct control (hence it's more inline with the vision)
cons: A complex change

template_adherence.title: Restricting CloudHSM network access to particular namespaces
template_adherence.context:
[ADR036](ADR036-hsm-isolation-in-detail.md) described the network and credential isolation we use to ensure that unauthorised users cannot access the CloudHSM.

Recently in 3ea9de2ff, we introduced a GlobalNetworkPolicy object, which is a Calico feature that allows a cluster-wide network policy to be imposed.  This allows us to control network access to and from particular namespaces in a way which cannot be overridden by tenants.

In particular, currently access to the HSM is only allowed from pods annotated with a `talksToHsm=true` label.

When working in their own namespace, a developer has full control over what labels they put on their pods, so they can still choose to put the `talksToHsm=true` label on their pods.  But they do not have control over what labels the namespace itself has; to change this would require a change to the `gsp` or appropriate `cluster-config` repository, which would make such a change visible to many more people.

Therefore, if we extend the GlobalNetworkPolicy to require a `talksToHsm=true` label on *both* the pod *and* the namespace, we will prevent tenants from unilaterally opening up network access to the HSM from their namespaces.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to ensure unauthorized users cannot access CloudHSM.
- Existing network and credential isolation mechanisms.
- Introduction of GlobalNetworkPolicy to enforce cluster-wide network policies.
- Current limitation that developers can label pods but not namespaces.
- Desire to prevent tenants from unilaterally opening network access to HSM from their namespaces.
- Maintain control over which namespaces can access HSM via labels managed in cluster-config repositories.
template_adherence.decision:
We will augment the GlobalNetworkPolicy (previously described in ADR036) by:

- setting a `GlobalNetworkPolicy` that denies access to the CloudHSM's IP address unless the pod carries a label (`talksToHsm=true`) and the namespace also carries a label (`talksToHsm=true`) and allows all other egress traffic
template_adherence.consequences:
Control of which namespaces get the `talksToHsm=true` label will be via the appropriate `-cluster-config` repo.  If a developer wants to allow a new namespace to talk to the HSM, they will need to issue a PR against that repo.

If we are confident in the GlobalNetworkPolicy's control of HSM access, we could consider reducing the technical controls required on non-HSM namespaces.  For example, we could consider allowing developers to run plain `kubectl apply` in unprivileged namespaces, for fast-feedback learning.

template_adherence.title: Kubernetes resource access rules
template_adherence.context: Several different levels of access are required within a kubernetes cluster. The GSP uses role based access control so these levels are granted to users and groups via roles.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to define clear access levels within each namespace to balance operational effectiveness and security, allowing developers and SREs appropriate permissions without risking major production outages.
template_adherence.decision: We will create two levels of access within each namespace: Operator and Auditor. The Operator role is a relatively permissive read-write role for developers and in-cluster concourse teams. The Auditor role is given to all authenticated users for debugging and basic remedial actions without formal escalation.
template_adherence.consequences: Site Reliability Engineers can operate the GSP effectively with reduced need for admin access. Service team members can iterate changes quickly in specific namespaces. Restrictions prevent interference with other namespaces and major production outages, though some degradation is possible but fixable via deployment pipelines.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but alternatives could include having a single access level or more granular roles beyond Operator and Auditor.
pros: Simpler role management if only one role is used.
More granular control if multiple roles are defined.
cons: Single role may lead to excessive permissions for some users.
Too many roles can complicate management and understanding.

template_adherence.title: ADR044: Security improvements
template_adherence.context: Currently there are no restrictions on what options a service team puts into pod specifications. This means that a pod in a tenant namespace could escalate its privileges to access resources that it should not have access to. Examples include host namespaces, privileged containers, host networking, arbitrary host volume mounts. Currently, our defence against this is that we enforce deploying infrastructure as code, and we require 2-eyes review on every code change. However, kubernetes offers pod security policies as an extra layer of defence.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to restrict pod specifications to prevent privilege escalation and unauthorized access to resources, while allowing system namespaces to have less restrictive policies to function properly. The desire to add an extra layer of defense beyond code review and infrastructure as code.
template_adherence.decision: Implement pod security policies with specific configurations: a restrictive default policy for tenant namespaces disallowing privileged containers, host networking, and other risky options; and a less restrictive policy for system namespaces such as gsp-system, kube-system, and istio-system to allow necessary privileges.
template_adherence.consequences: System services will have the access they need (privileged, host networking, etc.), while tenant service teams will be restricted in their capabilities. Tenant teams can still run container processes as root but cannot escalate privileges to access host parts. This improves security by limiting privilege escalation risks.

alternatives.description: Continue relying solely on infrastructure as code and 2-eyes review without implementing pod security policies.
pros: No additional configuration or maintenance overhead.
No changes to existing deployment processes.
cons: Higher risk of privilege escalation by tenant pods.
Lack of automated enforcement of security policies.

alternatives.description: Implement pod security policies with different configurations or use alternative Kubernetes security mechanisms.
pros: Potentially more tailored security policies.
Use of newer or more flexible security features.
cons: Increased complexity in policy management.
Possible compatibility issues or learning curve.

template_adherence.title: Replacing harbor with ECR
template_adherence.context:
[Harbor][] has proved itself to be rather unstable (causing several incidents from various root causes). We have also been gradually rolling back our usage within GSP of the various tools that Harbor provides:

* we are not using notary for signing (image provenance); this is now being handled using image digests instead of tags, enforced by gatekeeper
* we haven't yet implemented anything using Clair
* we no longer have a requirement for anonymous public access of docker repositories

It is also worth noting that some of these (e.g. "Clair") have been integrated into AWS ECR since we last looked.

In order to implement the decisions in [ADR045 dev namespaces][ADR045] we must ensure that each namespace has its own place to store docker images, and that one namespace cannot overwrite another namespace's docker images. This would be very fiddly to achieve with Harbor because it would require interactions with the Harbor API which doesn't fit very well with "desired state configuration".
However with ECR we can more easily leverage IAM and the existing Service Operator patterns to allow tenants to provision their own ECR repositories with their own credentials.

See also [ADR012][].
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Harbor has been unstable causing incidents.
- Gradual rollback of Harbor features in use.
- Need for namespace isolation for docker images.
- Desire to leverage AWS ECR features like IAM and Service Operator.
- Simplify management by using yaml for repository existence.
- Integration of security features (like Clair) into ECR.
- Avoid fiddly interactions with Harbor API that don't fit desired state configuration.
template_adherence.decision: We will replace the Harbor registry (the last Harbor component in use in GSP at time of writing) with AWS ECR with "push" credentials managed by the [Service Operator][].
template_adherence.consequences:
- Ability to deliver namespace-isolated repositories for pushing images.
- Private repositories only.
- Stability improvements to the GSP by removing Harbor completely.
- Repository existence in ECR managed by yaml.
- Simplified management and better integration with AWS services.

alternatives.description: Continue using Harbor despite its instability and limitations.
pros: Harbor is already in use and familiar to the team.
Existing workflows and integrations remain unchanged.
cons: Harbor has proven unstable causing incidents.
Requires fiddly interactions with Harbor API for namespace isolation.
Does not leverage newer AWS ECR features and integrations.

alternatives.description: Use another container registry solution other than Harbor or ECR.
pros: Potentially find a more stable or feature-rich solution.
Could better fit specific organizational needs.
cons: Requires evaluation and integration effort.
May lack existing integrations like Service Operator.
Uncertainty about stability and support.

template_adherence.title: Replace Kiam with IAM Roles for Service Accounts
template_adherence.context: The ADR explains the current use of Kiam in the GSP cluster to restrict IAM role access at Pod and Namespace level, its benefits, and operational problems experienced. It also introduces the AWS-managed alternative, IAM Roles for Service Accounts, and the considerations around migrating to it, including compatibility issues with Grafana and the approach to block direct access to the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to restrict IAM role access at Pod and Namespace level, operational reliability issues with Kiam, availability of AWS-managed IAM Roles for Service Accounts, compatibility with existing software (Grafana), and security concerns about direct IMDS access.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to replace Kiam with IAM Roles for Service Accounts, grant nodes read-only CloudWatch metrics access for Grafana, block IMDS access from non-gsp-system namespaces, allow IMDS access only from specifically annotated pods in gsp-system, and remove Kiam.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include nodes having read-only access to CloudWatch metrics roles, with restricted Pod access outside gsp-system, and presumably improved reliability and security by removing Kiam and using AWS-managed IAM Roles for Service Accounts.

alternatives.description: Continue using Kiam as is.
pros: Existing system already in place.
Provides Pod and Namespace level IAM role restriction.
Blocks access to IMDS as required.
cons: Operational problems causing Pod IAM role assumption failures.
Opaque failure modes leading to downtime.
Maintenance overhead of running Kiam agents and servers.

alternatives.description: Use IAM Roles for Service Accounts without additional network policies.
pros: AWS-managed solution, likely more reliable.
Simplifies architecture by removing Kiam.
Native integration with EKS.
cons: Does not block direct access to IMDS by default.
Grafana compatibility issues requiring workaround.
Potential security concerns if IMDS access is not restricted.

template_adherence.title: 2. Export ASRSnippet Metadata for Snippet Metrics Processing
template_adherence.context:
Data Engineers are building performance dashboards for Snippets using the metrics we collect from Firefox Telemetry. Telemetry pings include only basic information about the Snippet, like Snippet ID.

For better to understand and more complete dashboards, we want to enhance the Telemetry received information with more Snippet metadata, like campaign information, included URL, main message used and others.

To achieve this we will export the metadata from the Snippets Service in a machine readable format and make the file available in a Cloud Storage Provider. Then Data Engineers will import the metadata and combine them Telemetry data in unified dashboards.

template_adherence.title: 3. Convert Templates to Database Models
template_adherence.context:
Snippet Templates have been historically a combination of HTML, CSS and Javascript with Jinja2 variables. Template is saved in the database, through the `SnippetTemplate` Django Model. Upon save Django would extract the Jinja2 variables and use this list to auto-generate the Snippet Admin UI.

In the Snippet Admin UI, the users would select from a drop-down a Template and then a list of Inputs, Images, Textareas and Booleans would appear to represent the Jinja2 variables of the selected template.

Upon save the values of those inputs would be combined into a JSON blob and saved in the database in the Snippets Django Model.

This system allowed for fast iteration on templates without the need of redeploying the application. It served us well for all these years but imposes a large number of limitations and shortcomings like:

- The template forms are dynamic and not real Django forms. Thus we cannot take benefit of the excellent Django form validation. Bogus input is a daily problem Snippet Editors fight with reviews.

Converting Templates to real models would allow us to:

- Validate type of input: text, link, URLs.

- Enforce secure links.

- For icons validate, type, size and dimensions of the image and thus increase the quality of the snippet.

- Have complex validations like require an input when another input is set.

- Give better error messages.

- Have an overall better Admin UI.

- Snippet Editors have to re-upload icons over and over again since all images are saved as part of a blob and not in a gallery.

- Snippet Bundles are huge because they include the full blobs. Moving images outside of the bundle would drastically decrease the bundle size and reduce the CDN transfer costs. We also expect benefits on the CPU and Memory requirements on the server side and faster Activity Stream page on the client side due to the reduced size of IndexedDB.

### Why is this now possible?

- Deploys used to be painful and now are not.
- Also the template code is now part of Firefox and don't change that often.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve validation of inputs (type, secure links, image properties).
- Desire to improve Admin UI and user experience for Snippet Editors.
- Reduce bundle size and CDN transfer costs.
- Reduce server CPU and memory requirements.
- Faster client-side performance due to smaller IndexedDB size.
- Deployment process has improved, making this change feasible.
- Template code stability in Firefox reduces frequency of changes.
template_adherence.decision:
We decide to move templates into real Django models. Each ASR Template will get its own Django Model and entry in the Django Admin.

Similarly, images will be moved to a new Django model named `Icons` and templates will link to those icons.

Each `ASRSnippet` will link to one `Template` object using Django's model inheritance.

This change will affect only the `ASRSnippet` models; the pre-ASR and `JSONSnippet` implementations will remain the same until decommissioned.

Scripts to migrate from the current system to the new system for all `ASRSnippets` will be created.
template_adherence.consequences:
New templates will now require more work to get integrated into the system. Since they also have to get coded into Firefox and ride the trains, this does not impose a real problem.

Better experience for the Snippet Editors, more Snippets, less costs and many many happy faces.

alternatives.description: Keep the current system of dynamic template forms with Jinja2 variables and JSON blobs.
pros: Allows fast iteration on templates without redeploying the application.
No immediate need to change existing infrastructure.
cons: Dynamic forms lack real Django form validation, leading to bogus input issues.
No type validation or complex validation capabilities.
Poor Admin UI experience.
Large snippet bundles increase CDN transfer costs and server resource usage.

alternatives.description: Convert templates to real Django models and move images to a separate model.
pros: Enables validation of input types and secure links.
Improves Admin UI and user experience.
Reduces snippet bundle size and CDN costs.
Reduces server CPU and memory requirements.
Enables complex validations and better error messages.
Improves client-side performance.
cons: New templates require more work to integrate.
Requires migration scripts and changes to existing models.
Template code must be maintained in Firefox, adding coordination overhead.

template_adherence.title: 3. AWX For Infrastructure Automation
template_adherence.context: The Middleware team has strived to practice Infrastructure-As-Code, meaning DLP's AWS account should be reflected entirely within GitHub. This has mostly been accomplished but Ansible playbooks are currently run in Ansible Core on individual laptops of the Middleware team. The eventual goal should be GitOps, automated infrastructure changes triggered by a commit. For that purpose we will need a platform capable of running playbooks automatically. This platform would need to be able to run the playbooks on demand or scheduled. RedHat provides two solutions: AWX and Ansible Tower. AWX is the upline of Ansible Tower, meaning it is a more advanced version that lacks official support.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for automated infrastructure changes triggered by commits (GitOps). Requirement for a platform to run Ansible playbooks automatically, on demand or scheduled. Consideration of RedHat solutions (AWX and Ansible Tower) and their support/licensing. Desire to reduce dependency on individual laptops and increase automation capabilities.
template_adherence.decision: The Middleware team will use AWX to manage DLP's infrastructure automation needs. A different tool may be used for application automation.

Shibboleth integration will be needed. Additionally the creation of LDAP groups to manage access to AWX for administrators and developers is required, and LDAP groups require group managers.

template_adherence.title: 4. IIIF Manifest Caching
template_adherence.context: Hyrax by default does not cache IIIF manifests, which take a considerable about of time to create. The amount of time depends on the number of filesets present in the work, because Hyrax queries Fedora for each of them. For our books, there could be hundreds of pages, meaning the manifest will take minutes to generate. Lux however, does not have minutes to wait for a manifest, and will time out before the manifest is ready.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce manifest generation time to prevent timeouts in Lux, the cost and complexity of caching, and the maintainability and performance trade-offs of alternatives.
template_adherence.decision: We will save manifests as they are generated with the id of the work and the datetime the last time the work was updated to a folder that will persist through deployments to a given environment. The location of the folder will be controlled by ENV variable, and should have a sensible default. This cache will be queried before generating the manifest again, and if one is found, the cached version will be served. Additionally, we will create a rake task to generate manifests for works that do not have them. Finally, we will create another rake task to delete manifests that are no longer needed, so the cache does not grow unbounded.
template_adherence.consequences: We will know this is successful if book objects in Lux do not timeout when fetching the manifest from Curate. One drawback to this approach is that we will have to pay for the disk space that the manifests take up. However, implementing this solution should be quicker and more straight-forward than the alternatives. Taking this approach does not stop us from refactoring manifest generation code in the future.

alternatives.description: No Caching
pros: We would not have to pay to store manifests.
We would not have to clean up stale manifests.
cons: No refactoring would match the speed of caching.
We would be responsible for the new code, greatly increasing the area of code we have to maintain.
May complicate upgrades.
Rewriting that much functionality would take longer than the solution above.

alternatives.description: ETags
pros: We would not have to clean up stale manifests
cons: Caching with Apache is less well understood to implementing the caching rules ourselves.
It is unclear if we could prepopulate this.

template_adherence.title: 5. Route 53 Hosted Zone
template_adherence.context:
Servers are often destroyed and rebuilt with a new private IP address, so a block of IP addresses is added into the `/etc/hosts` file of each server in a group when one is provisioned.
This was an extension of work done for Solr Cloud that writes the IPs of the other Solr Cloud instances of a group.
Recently, a Solr server experienced corruption of it's `/etc/hosts` file, which caused the instance to drop out of the cluster.

Fedora produces 503 errors when under load, primarily during Curate imports.
This causes the background jobs associated with the imports to go into retries, and sends error notifications to Honeybadger.
Sometimes, the jobs do not succeed when they are retried, causing DPS team members to have to fix the affected works manually.

Our theory at the moment is that something about using `/etc/hosts` (rather than a centralized DNS solution like AWS's Route 53) is the cause of Fedora's errors.

Route 53, was blocked by AWS@Emory at the time the DLP project started, but has since been enabled.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section, but the context implies drivers such as reliability issues with `/etc/hosts`, the need for a centralized DNS solution, and the enabling of Route 53 by AWS@Emory.
template_adherence.decision:
Avoid using `/etc/hosts` for server-to-server communication by setting up DNS for our servers, using a Route 53 private hosted zone (.internal.emory.edu).
Point the .env files of Curate to the internal.emory.edu address for Fedora and IIIF.
Add <service>.internal.emory.edu as a ServerAlias for Fedora, IIIF, and Solr.
Change the SOLR_HOST and ZK_HOST variables for Solr instances.
Use the internal.emory.edu hostname for Zookeeper config, instead of an IP address value.
template_adherence.consequences: All EC2s must re-register their new A-record in Route 53 when they are created, so that Route 53 always has the latest IP address.

alternatives.description: Continue using hosts file
pros: Arguably simpler setup because it avoid the need to use another AWS service.
cons: Vulnerable to hosts file corruption or changes.
Complicates new EC2 creation.

template_adherence.title: Use the ADR slug as its unique ID
template_adherence.context:
Currently, ADR files follow this format: `NNNN-adr-title.md`, with NNNN being an incremental number from `0000` to `9999`.
It causes an issue during a `git merge` when two developers have created a new ADR on their respective branch.
There is a conflict because [an ADR number must be unique](20200926-use-the-adr-number-as-its-unique-id.md).
template_adherence.decision:
From now on, we won't use ADR numbers anymore.
An ADR will be uniquely identified by its slug (ie. its filename without the extension), and its filename will have the following format: `YYYYMMDD-adr-title.md`, with `YYYYMMDD` being the date of creation of the file.

As a result, there won't have conflicts anymore and the files will still be correctly sorted in the IDE thanks to the date.

Finally, the ADRs will be sorted with these rules (ordered by priority):

1. By Date field, in the markdown file (if present)
2. By Git creation date (does not follow renames)
3. By file creation date if no versioned yet
4. By slug

The core library is responsible for sorting.

template_adherence.title: ADR 2: Event Subscription
template_adherence.context: In the light client (or any other client), the user may want to subscribe to a subset of transactions (rather than all of them) using `/subscribe?event=X`. For example, I want to subscribe for all transactions associated with a particular account. Same for fetching. The user may want to fetch transactions based on some filter (rather than fetching all the blocks). For example, I want to get all transactions for a particular account in the last two weeks (`tx's block time >= '2017-06-05'`). Now you can't even subscribe to "all txs" in Tendermint. The goal is a simple and easy to use API for doing that.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow users to subscribe to a subset of transactions or fetch transactions based on filters rather than all transactions. The desire for a simple and easy to use API. The need to support powerful and flexible queries for event notifications and search APIs. Consideration of performance issues with matching functions and database size. The need to support multiple indexers with different APIs for historic queries.
template_adherence.decision: The ABCI app will return tags with a `DeliverTx` response inside the `data` field (for now, possibly a separate field later). Tags are a list of key-value pairs, protobuf encoded. Subscribers can query these tags to receive only a subset of transactions matching their queries. A new package will be developed to replace the current `events` package to allow clients to subscribe to different types of events. For fetching transactions, queries will be supported with indexing storage (e.g., Postgres, SQLite) for historic queries.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include having the same format for event notifications and search APIs and a powerful enough query system. Negative consequences include potential performance issues with the match function when there are many queries/subscribers and issues with too many transactions in the database. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR, but implied alternatives include: 1) Not supporting filtered subscriptions and fetching (current state), 2) Using a different mechanism than tags in DeliverTx responses, 3) Not developing a new package for event subscriptions.
pros: Current state is simpler and requires no changes.
Avoids complexity of new package and tag-based filtering.
cons: Does not meet user needs for filtered subscriptions and fetching.
Less flexible and powerful querying capabilities.

template_adherence.title: Must an ABCI-app have an RPC server?
template_adherence.context:
ABCI-server could expose its own RPC-server and act as a proxy to Tendermint.

The idea was for the Tendermint RPC to just be a transparent proxy to the app.
Clients need to talk to Tendermint for proofs, unless we burden all app devs
with exposing Tendermint proof stuff. Also seems less complex to lock down one
server than two, but granted it makes querying a bit more kludgy since it needs
to be passed as a `Query`. Also, **having a very standard rpc interface means
the light-client can work with all apps and handle proofs**. The only
app-specific logic is decoding the binary data to a more readable form (eg.
json). This is a huge advantage for code-reuse and standardization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a unified and standard RPC interface for all apps.
- Desire to avoid burdening app developers with exposing Tendermint proof logic.
- Complexity considerations in managing one server versus two.
- Importance of code reuse and standardization for light-client compatibility.
template_adherence.decision: We dont expose an RPC server on any of our ABCI-apps.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Unified interface for all apps

### Negative

- `Query` interface

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Historical Validators
template_adherence.context:
Right now, we can query the present validator set, but there is no history.
If you were offline for a long time, there is no way to reconstruct past validators. This is needed for the light client and we agreed needs enhancement of the API.
template_adherence.decision:
For every block, store a new structure that contains either the latest validator set,
or the height of the last block for which the validator set changed. Note this is not
the height of the block which returned the validator set change itself, but the next block,
ie. the first block it comes into effect for.

Storing the validators will be handled by the `state` package.

At some point in the future, we may consider more efficient storage in the case where the validators
are updated frequently - for instance by only saving the diffs, rather than the whole set.

An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Can query old validator sets, with proof.

### Negative

- Writes an extra structure to disk with every block.

### Neutral

alternatives.description:
An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
pros: Cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed.
cons: More complex implementation.

template_adherence.title: ADR 005: Consensus Params
template_adherence.context: Consensus critical parameters controlling blockchain capacity have until now been hard coded, loaded from a local config, or neglected. Since they may be need to be different in different networks, and potentially to evolve over time within networks, we seek to initialize them in a genesis file, and expose them through the ABCI. While we have some specific parameters now, like maximum block and transaction size, we expect to have more in the future, such as a period over which evidence is valid, or the frequency of checkpoints.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have consensus critical parameters configurable per network and evolvable over time, to avoid hard coding or local config limitations. The desire to have parameters initialized in genesis and exposed through ABCI, and to maintain sanity checks and flexibility for future parameters.
template_adherence.decision: Consensus critical parameters should not be in the config.toml but optionally included in the genesis.json file and loaded into the State. Parameters not included get default values; 0 means undefined, -1 means not applicable. Parameters determine block and transaction validity. The ConsensusParams struct can evolve by adding new structs. Certain parameters must be greater than 0 for sanity. ABCI's InitChain and EndBlock are extended to handle ConsensusParams appropriately, with updates applied for the next block.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Allows specifying alternative capacity limits and consensus parameters without recompiling software; parameters can change over time under application control. Negative: More exposed parameters increase complexity; different rules at different blockchain heights complicate fast sync. Neutral: Potential conflicts between TxSize validity checks and config's max_block_size_tx proposal sizes.

alternatives.description: Keep consensus parameters hard coded or loaded from local config only.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need to extend genesis or ABCI interfaces.
cons: Lack of flexibility for different networks.
Cannot evolve parameters over time easily.
Requires recompilation for changes.

alternatives.description: Include all consensus parameters in the entire genesis file and pass it to InitChain.
pros: Complete initialization of all parameters at chain start.
Simplifies parameter management in one place.
cons: May expose parameters to the app that it shouldn't know about.
Less modular and flexible.
Potentially more complex genesis structure.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: PeerTransport
template_adherence.context: One of the more apparent problems with the current architecture in the p2p package is that there is no clear separation of concerns between different components. Most notably the `Switch` is currently doing physical connection handling. An artifact is the dependency of the Switch on `config.P2PConfig`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate concerns between components, reduce dependencies (especially the Switch's dependency on P2PConfig), simplify the Switch implementation, and allow pluggable transport implementations for easier testing and flexibility.
template_adherence.decision: Transport concerns will be handled by a new component (`PeerTransport`) which will provide Peers at its boundary to the caller. The Switch will use this new component to accept new Peers and dial them based on NetAddress, thus removing transport concerns from the Switch and its dependency on P2PConfig.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include freeing the Switch from transport concerns, enabling pluggable transport implementations, and removing the Switch's dependency on P2PConfig, making testing easier. Negative consequences include more setup required for tests depending on Switches. Neutral consequence is that multiplexed transport will be the default implementation.

alternatives.description: Keep the current architecture where the Switch handles physical connection handling and depends on P2PConfig.
pros: No additional component or interface needed.

cons: Switch remains complex and tightly coupled to transport concerns.
Testing is harder due to dependencies.
Less modular and flexible architecture.

alternatives.description: Introduce PeerTransport as a separate component to handle transport concerns, as chosen in the decision.
pros: Clear separation of concerns.

cons: Requires additional setup for tests depending on Switches.

template_adherence.title: Secp256k1 Signature Malleability
template_adherence.context:
Secp256k1 has two layers of malleability. The signer has a random nonce, and thus can produce many different valid signatures. This ADR is not concerned with that. The second layer of malleability basically allows one who is given a signature to produce exactly one more valid signature for the same message from the same public key. (They don't even have to know the message!) The math behind this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Note that in many downstream applications, signatures will appear in a transaction, and therefore in the tx hash. This means that if someone broadcasts a transaction with secp256k1 signature, the signature can be altered into the other form by anyone in the p2p network. Thus the tx hash will change, and this altered tx hash may be committed instead. This breaks the assumption that you can broadcast a valid transaction and just wait for its hash to be included on chain. One example is if you are broadcasting a tx in cosmos, and you wait for it to appear on chain before incrementing your sequence number. You may never increment your sequence number if a different tx hash got committed. Removing this second layer of signature malleability concerns could ease downstream development.

### ECDSA context

Secp256k1 is ECDSA over a particular curve. The signature is of the form `(r, s)`, where `s` is a field element. (The particular field is the `Z_n`, where the elliptic curve has order `n`) However `(r, -s)` is also another valid solution. Note that anyone can negate a group element, and therefore can get this second signature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to remove the second layer of signature malleability to ease downstream development.
- Desire to maintain the ability to expect a transaction hash to appear in the blockchain.
- Simplicity and ease of checking the canonical form.
- Alignment with existing solutions like Ethereum's approach.
- Consideration of implementation effort and maintenance overhead (forking a library).
template_adherence.decision:
We can just distinguish a canonical form for the ECDSA signatures. Then we require that all ECDSA signatures be in the form which we defined as canonical. We reject signatures in non-canonical form.

A canonical form is rather easy to define and check. It would just be the smaller of the two values for `s`, defined lexicographically. This is a simple check, instead of checking if `s < n`, instead check `s <= (n - 1)/2`. An example of another cryptosystem using this is the parity definition here https://github.com/zkcrypto/pairing/pull/30#issuecomment-372910663.

This is the same solution Ethereum has chosen for solving secp malleability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Lets us maintain the ability to expect a tx hash to appear in the blockchain.

Negative:
- More work in all future implementations (Though this is a very simple check)
- Requires us to maintain another fork

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated)

template_adherence.title: ADR 015: Crypto encoding
template_adherence.context: We must standardize our method for encoding public keys and signatures on chain. Currently we amino encode the public keys and signatures. The reason we are using amino here is primarily due to ease of support in parsing for other languages. We don't need its upgradability properties in cryptosystems, as a change in the crypto that requires adapting the encoding, likely warrants being deemed a new cryptosystem. (I.e. using new public parameters)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for ease of support in multiple languages, space efficiency especially for signatures due to gas cost and throughput impact, compatibility with existing APIs, and the trade-offs between amino encoding's upgradability and overhead versus simpler encoding methods.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to continue using amino encoding for public keys due to ease of support and existing libraries, despite its drawbacks in space efficiency and complexity. For signatures, the decision is to switch to using a primitive []byte type for better space efficiency, as signatures do not need to encode their type. Specific canonical representations are defined for Ed25519 and Secp256k1 signatures.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include more space efficient signatures. Negative consequences include maintaining an amino dependency for cryptography. Neutral consequences include no change to public keys encoding.

pros: Potentially more space efficient by removing protobuf overhead.

template_adherence.title: Limiting txs size inside a block
template_adherence.context: We currently use MaxTxs to reap txs from the mempool when proposing a block, but enforce MaxBytes when unmarshaling a block, so we could easily propose a block thats too large to be valid. We should just remove MaxTxs all together and stick with MaxBytes, and have a `mempool.ReapMaxBytes`. But we can't just reap BlockSize.MaxBytes, since MaxBytes is for the entire block, not for the txs inside the block. There's extra amino overhead + the actual headers on top of the actual transactions + evidence + last commit. We could also consider using a MaxDataBytes instead of or in addition to MaxBytes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid proposing blocks that are too large to be valid.
- Desire to simplify configuration by removing MaxTxs.
- Need to account for overhead beyond just transaction bytes (headers, evidence, last commit).
- Consideration of MaxBytes vs MaxDataBytes for block size limits.
- Maintainability concerns regarding constants if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove MaxTxs and rename MaxTxsBytes to MaxBytes. When reaping transactions from the mempool, calculate the upper bound for transaction bytes by subtracting overheads (amino overhead, last commit bytes, evidence bytes, header bytes) from MaxBytes. Constants for overhead sizes are defined in the types package. ChainID is bounded to 50 symbols max. A test should be written to ensure constants remain accurate if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a clear way to limit block size.
- Reduces the number of configuration variables.
Negative:

template_adherence.title: ADR 024: SignBytes and validator types in privval
template_adherence.context: Currently, the messages exchanged between tendermint and a (potentially remote) signer/validator, namely votes, proposals, and heartbeats, are encoded as a JSON string (e.g., via `Vote.SignBytes(...)`) and then signed. JSON encoding is sub-optimal for both hardware wallets and for usage in ethereum smart contracts. Both issues are detailed in issue#1622. Also, there are currently no differences between sign-request and -replies, and no possibility for a remote signer to include an error code or message in case something went wrong. The messages exchanged between tendermint and a remote signer currently live in privval/socket.go and encapsulate the corresponding types in types.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a binary encoding format easily parseable by hardware devices and smart contracts.
- Clear separation between sign-requests and sign-replies.
- Ability to include error codes and messages in responses.
- Compatibility with existing code and interfaces.
- Consideration of future KMS (Key Management System) use cases.
template_adherence.decision:
- Restructure vote, proposal, and heartbeat messages to use a binary encoding format (amino).
- Split messages exchanged between tendermint and remote signers into requests and responses.
- Include an error type in responses.
- Remove ChainID parameter from SignBytes method and include ChainID directly in vote message.
- Define new protobuf-like message structures for Vote, Proposal, Heartbeat, and their corresponding sign request and reply messages.
- Postpone decisions regarding PubKey handling for KMS to future discussions.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Signing bytes can be easily parsed by hardware modules and smart contracts.
- Clearer separation between requests and responses.
- Added error messages enable better error handling.

Negative:
- Relatively large refactoring affecting significant code areas.
- Many places assume a Vote with a signature included; interfaces will need modification.

Neutral:
- No neutral consequences explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSON encoding for messages and keep the current message structure without separating requests and responses or including error codes.
pros: No changes required to existing codebase.
No need to refactor interfaces or message handling.
cons: JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and smart contracts.
No ability to include error codes or messages in responses.
No clear separation between requests and responses, leading to potential confusion and error handling difficulties.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025 Commit
template_adherence.context:
Currently the `Commit` structure contains a lot of potentially redundant or unnecessary data. It contains a list of precommits from every validator, where the precommit includes the whole `Vote` structure. Thus each of the commit height, round, type, and blockID are repeated for every validator, and could be deduplicated, leading to very significant savings in block size.

The original tracking issue for this is #1648. Discussions include replacing the `Vote` type in `Commit` with a new `CommitSig` type, which includes at minimum the vote signature. The `Vote` type will continue to be used in the consensus reactor and elsewhere.

Primary questions include what should be included in the `CommitSig` beyond the signature, with constraints such as including a timestamp for BFT time calculation. Other concerns include whether to include the validator address, how to represent absent votes, and how to represent votes for nil and other block IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce redundancy and block size by deduplicating repeated fields in commits.
- Maintain necessary information for BFT time calculation (timestamp).
- Consider ergonomic and debugging advantages of including validator address.
- Handle absent votes and serialization issues.
- Protocol constraints disallow votes for conflicting block IDs in the same round.
- Desire to keep the commit structure consistent with Tendermint protocol assumptions.
- Potential future changes to remove timestamp or validator address.
- Trade-offs between block size savings and complexity in code handling Vote vs CommitSig.
template_adherence.decision:
Deduplicate the fields in the `Commit` structure by introducing a new `CommitSig` type that includes only necessary fields: BlockIDFlag, ValidatorAddress, Timestamp, and Signature. The `Commit` struct will have Height, Round, BlockID, and a slice of `CommitSig` as Precommits.

Timestamp is retained for now to support BFT time calculation, with plans to revisit in the future.

ValidatorAddress is included for ergonomic and debugging benefits despite increasing block size.

Absent votes are explicitly included with no Signature or Timestamp but with ValidatorAddress to resolve serialization issues.

Votes for other block IDs are not allowed; only Absent, Nil, or Commit flags are used to indicate vote status.

Future considerations include possibly supporting other block IDs and revisiting the inclusion of timestamp and validator address.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Significant block size savings (up to ~8kB per block for 100 validators) by removing redundant fields.

Negative:
- Large breaking change to block and commit structure.
- Added complexity in code to differentiate between Vote and CommitSig objects.

Neutral:
- Commit.Precommits no longer contains nil values, improving serialization and clarity.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing `Commit` structure with full `Vote` objects for each precommit.
pros: No breaking changes to block and commit structure.
No need to differentiate between Vote and CommitSig in code.
cons: High redundancy leading to larger block sizes.
Inefficient serialization and network usage.

alternatives.description: Remove timestamp from `CommitSig` to further reduce size.
pros: Further block size reduction.
Simplifies `CommitSig` structure.
cons: Requires more analysis and work to switch to proposer based time.
Potentially breaks BFT time calculation assumptions.

alternatives.description: Exclude ValidatorAddress from `CommitSig` to save space.
pros: Reduces block size by 20 bytes per validator.
Smaller commit size.
cons: Loses ergonomic and debugging advantages.
Lite clients need to fetch validator set to verify commits.
Commit does not contain all info to reconstruct votes independently.

template_adherence.title: ADR 029: Check block txs before prevote
template_adherence.context:
We currently check a tx's validity through 2 ways.

1. Through checkTx in mempool connection.
2. Through deliverTx in consensus connection.

The 1st is called when external tx comes in, so the node should be a proposer this time. The 2nd is called when external block comes in and reach the commit phase, the node doesn't need to be the proposer of the block, however it should check the txs in that block.

In the 2nd situation, if there are many invalid txs in the block, it would be too late for all nodes to discover that most txs in the block are invalid, and we'd better not record invalid txs in the blockchain too.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to detect invalid transactions earlier in the consensus process to avoid committing invalid txs.
- Maintain consistency and correctness of the blockchain.
- Minimize performance impact and avoid redundant validations.
- Ensure application logic can adapt to new interface methods.
- Consider network overhead of sending tx data multiple times.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to reject the proposed solution of checking block transactions before prevote due to the performance impact being too great, as referenced in issue #2384.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- More robust defense against adversaries proposing blocks full of invalid transactions.

Negative:
- Requires adding a new interface method, necessitating changes in application logic.
- Increases network load by sending all transaction data twice over ABCI.
- Causes potentially redundant validations (e.g., signature checks in both CheckBlock and DeliverTx).

Neutral:
- No additional neutral consequences explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Implement a method in BlockExecutor to check all transactions' validity in a block before sending out a prevote, using CheckTxAsync for each transaction.
pros: Allows early detection of invalid transactions before consensus prevote.
Improves robustness against invalid blocks.
cons: May cause performance degradation due to repeated transaction checks.
CheckTx shares state with mempool, which may cause inconsistencies.

alternatives.description: Define a new interface method checkBlock in Application to check block validity using the same state as deliverTx.
pros: Ensures consistency by using the same state as deliverTx.
Allows applications to implement block-level transaction validation.
Improves early detection of invalid transactions.
cons: Requires all applications to implement a new interface method.
Adds complexity to application logic.
Potentially doubles transaction validation work, impacting performance.

alternatives.description: Optimize by altering deliverTx to deliverBlock, caching the block after checkBlock validation to avoid redundant checks.
pros: Saves network and computation resources by caching validated blocks.
Reduces redundant transaction validation during deliverTx phase.
cons: Adds complexity to application logic and state management.
Requires careful handling of cached state to avoid inconsistencies.

template_adherence.title: ADR 033: pubsub 2.0
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses issues with the initial pubsub design, including problems with synchronous vs asynchronous message publishing, blocking vs non-blocking sends, and the choice between channels and callbacks for message transmission. It highlights the need for strict ordering of events and addresses the "slow client problem" where slow subscribers can block the system.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include ensuring strict ordering of events, avoiding deadlocks caused by slow subscribers, providing subscribers with information about message tags, and improving the interface to be more idiomatic and informative about subscription cancellation reasons.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a MsgAndTags struct for messages, change Subscribe() to return a Subscription struct with methods Out(), Canceled(), and Err(), make Out() channel buffered by default with capacity 1, provide a separate SubscribeUnbuffered() function for unbuffered channels, and treat buffered and unbuffered channels differently in the publisher to avoid blocking on buffered channels. Slow subscribers on buffered channels are terminated to prevent blocking.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a more idiomatic interface, subscribers knowing message tags, and awareness of subscription cancellation reasons. Negative consequences include no concurrency in publishing messages since version 1. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use synchronous publishing with goroutines per subscriber or per message.
pros: Allows concurrency and performance improvements.
Avoids slow client problem by using goroutines.
cons: Difficult to maintain strict ordering of events.
Potential uncontrolled memory growth due to many goroutines.
Complex implementation and unclear benefits with many subscribers.

alternatives.description: Use non-blocking sends with select default case to skip slow subscribers.
pros: Prevents system blocking due to slow subscribers.
Simplifies handling slow clients.
cons: Slow clients may miss messages without notification.
Requires developers to ensure subscriber code does not block, which is difficult.

alternatives.description: Use callback functions instead of channels for message transmission.
pros: Gives subscribers more flexibility in handling messages.
Allows use of mutexes, channels, goroutines as needed.
cons: Callbacks carry local scope, risking memory leaks or increased memory usage.
Less idiomatic in Go compared to channels.

template_adherence.title: ADR 034: PrivValidator file structure
template_adherence.context:
For now, the PrivValidator file `priv_validator.json` contains mutable and immutable parts. Even in an insecure mode which does not encrypt private key on disk, it is reasonable to separate the mutable part and immutable part.

References:
[#1181](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1181)
[#2657](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2657)
[#2313](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2313)
template_adherence.decision: We can split mutable and immutable parts with two structs: FilePVKey (immutable) and FilePVLastSignState (mutable), then combine them into FilePV. FilePV should be located in config, and FilePVLastSignState in data, with store paths specified in config.yml. Methods of FilePV need to be changed accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- separate the mutable and immutable of PrivValidator

Negative:
- need to add more config for file path

Neutral: (no content)

template_adherence.title: ADR 035: Documentation
template_adherence.context: The Tendermint documentation has undergone several changes until settling on the current model. Originally, the documentation was hosted on the website and had to be updated asynchronously from the code. Along with the other repositories requiring documentation, the whole stack moved to using Read The Docs to automatically generate, publish, and host the documentation. This, however, was insufficient; the RTD site had advertisement, it wasn't easily accessible to devs, didn't collect metrics, was another set of external links, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for better documentation hosting that is accessible to developers, collects metrics, and integrates well with the website. The previous solution (Read The Docs) was insufficient due to ads, accessibility issues, lack of metrics, and external links.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was made to use VuePress for documentation because it allows for metrics collection (Google Analytics) and hosting the documentation on the website as a `/docs` endpoint, maintaining synchrony between docs and code.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: The architecture is largely positive relative to prior documentation arrangements.
Negative: A significant portion of the docs automation/build process is in private repos with limited access/visibility to developers, handled by the SRE team.
Neutral: There is a challenge of "what goes where" for documentation aspects due to organizational separation between Tendermint & Cosmos.

alternatives.description: Continue using Read The Docs (RTD) for documentation hosting.
pros: Automatic generation, publishing, and hosting of documentation.
Existing setup familiar to the team.
cons: RTD site had advertisements.
Not easily accessible to developers.
Did not collect metrics.
Added another set of external links.

alternatives.description: Host documentation directly on the website without VuePress.
pros: Potentially simpler hosting setup.
No dependency on external documentation generators.
cons: Might lack features like metrics collection.
Could require more manual synchronization between docs and code.
Less automation and integration compared to VuePress.

template_adherence.title: Deliver Block
template_adherence.context:
Initial conversation: https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2901

Some applications can handle transactions in parallel, or at least some
part of tx processing can be parallelized. Now it is not possible for developer
to execute txs in parallel because Tendermint delivers them consequentially.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to allow applications to execute transactions in parallel or at least partially parallelize tx processing.
- Current Tendermint delivers transactions sequentially, limiting performance.
- Desire to simplify and speed up communication between application and Tendermint.
- Consideration that not all applications will benefit; some may slow down.
- Need to support both current and new ABCI application types to avoid forcing all apps to change.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to merge the existing `BeginBlock`, `EndBlock`, `Commit`, and `DeliverTx` steps into a single `DeliverBlock` step. This new step allows application developers to decide how to execute transactions (in parallel or sequentially) and simplifies the interface and communication. Additionally, a new ABCI application type will be introduced to support this change alongside the existing one.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Simpler introduction and tutorials for new developers (only 3 methods to implement instead of 5).
- Transactions can be handled in parallel.
- Simpler interface.
- Faster communications between Tendermint and application.

Negative consequences:
- Tendermint must support two kinds of ABCI applications, increasing complexity.

alternatives.description: Keep the current ABCI interface with separate BeginBlock, DeliverTx, EndBlock, and Commit steps.
pros: No changes required to existing applications.
No need to support multiple ABCI types.
cons: Does not allow parallel transaction processing.
More complex interface for developers.
Slower communication between Tendermint and application.

alternatives.description: Introduce a new ABCI type with DeliverBlock step while keeping the existing ABCI interface for backward compatibility.
pros: Allows parallel transaction processing.
Simplifies interface for new applications.
Supports both old and new applications during transition.
cons: Increases complexity by supporting two ABCI types.
Requires applications to change implementation if they want to use the new interface.

template_adherence.title: ADR 039: Peer Behaviour Interface
template_adherence.context: The responsibility for signaling and acting upon peer behaviour lacks a single owning component and is heavily coupled with the network stack. Reactors maintain a reference to the `p2p.Switch` which they use to call `switch.StopPeerForError(...)` when a peer misbehaves and `switch.MarkAsGood(...)` when a peer contributes in some meaningful way. While the switch handles `StopPeerForError` internally, the `MarkAsGood` method delegates to another component, `p2p.AddrBook`. This scheme of delegation across Switch obscures the responsibility for handling peer behaviour and ties up the reactors in a larger dependency graph when testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decouple signaling peer behaviour from acting upon it.
- Reduce coupling between reactors and the network stack.
- Improve testability by reducing dependencies.
- Centralize responsibility for managing peer behaviour.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a `PeerBehaviour` interface and concrete implementations which provide methods for reactors to signal peer behaviour without direct coupling to `p2p.Switch`. Introduce `ErrorBehaviourPeer` and `GoodBehaviourPeer` types to provide concrete reasons for stopping peers and ways peers contribute, respectively. Provide a concrete implementation wrapping the switch and another for testing purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Decouples signaling from acting upon peer behaviour.
- Reduces coupling of reactors and the Switch and network stack.
- Centralizes responsibility for managing peer behaviour.

Negative:
- Initial implementation adds a level of indirection by wrapping the Switch.

Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing approach where reactors directly call methods on `p2p.Switch` and `p2p.AddrBook` to signal peer behaviour.
pros: No additional abstraction or interface needed.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: High coupling between reactors and network stack.
Responsibility for peer behaviour is split and unclear.
Difficult to test reactors due to large dependency graph.

alternatives.description: Introduce a different interface or mechanism for signaling peer behaviour, possibly event-driven or using callbacks.
pros: Could provide more flexible or decoupled design.
May allow asynchronous handling of peer behaviour.
cons: More complex implementation.
Potentially harder to understand and maintain.
Not chosen due to complexity and current needs.

template_adherence.title: ADR 042: State Sync Design
template_adherence.context: StateSync is a feature which would allow a new node to receive a snapshot of the application state without downloading blocks or going through consensus. Once downloaded, the node could switch to FastSync and eventually participate in consensus. The goal of StateSync is to facilitate setting up a new node as quickly as possible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include performance (speed of snapshot production and consumption), safety (cost of pushing invalid snapshots), liveness (cost of preventing snapshot construction), and engineering effort. Security models such as light client validation versus majority of peer validation are also key drivers. The need for parallelizability, validation, and efficient snapshot formats are also considered.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt an eager StateSync approach with per chunk light client validation. This approach pre-computes efficient snapshots served sequentially to new nodes and validates each chunk on receipt to avoid eclipse attacks associated with majority peer validation.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a safe and performant state sync design with real-world implementation experience, general interfaces for application-specific innovation, and a parallelizable implementation path with reasonable engineering effort. Negative consequences include static scheduling lacking real-time chunk availability optimizations.

alternatives.description: Lazy StateSync: Snapshots are produced dynamically at request time using existing data structures, with chunking done lazily and dynamically. Validation tends to be per chunk using existing tree structures.
pros: Uses existing data structures without auxiliary data structures
Per chunk validation aligns naturally with existing tree structures
cons: Performance concerns with random reads and iterating to determine element numbers
Potentially less efficient compression and snapshot serving
Validation and chunking complexity

alternatives.description: Eager StateSync: Snapshots are produced periodically and served from disk at request time using auxiliary data structures optimized for batch read/writes. Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation.
pros: Efficient compression and serving of snapshots
Sequential IO optimized
Can serve many new peers efficiently
cons: Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation, vulnerable to eclipse attacks
Potential burden on block proposers if snapshot data included in block headers

template_adherence.title: Lite Client with Weak Subjectivity
template_adherence.context:
The concept of light clients was introduced in the Bitcoin white paper. It describes a watcher of distributed consensus process that only validates the consensus algorithm and not the state machine transactions within.

Tendermint light clients allow bandwidth & compute-constrained devices, such as smartphones, low-power embedded chips, or other blockchains to efficiently verify the consensus of a Tendermint blockchain. This forms the basis of safe and efficient state synchronization for new network nodes and inter-blockchain communication (where a light client of one Tendermint instance runs in another chain's state machine).

In a network that is expected to reliably punish validators for misbehavior by slashing bonded stake and where the validator set changes infrequently, clients can take advantage of this assumption to safely synchronize a lite client without downloading the intervening headers.

Light clients (and full nodes) operating in the Proof Of Stake context need a trusted block height from a trusted source that is no older than 1 unbonding window plus a configurable evidence submission synchrony bound. This is called “weak subjectivity”.

Weak subjectivity is required in Proof of Stake blockchains because it is costless for an attacker to buy up voting keys that are no longer bonded and fork the network at some point in its prior history. See Vitalik’s post at Proof of Stake: How I Learned to Love Weak Subjectivity.

Currently, Tendermint provides a lite client implementation in the light package. This lite client implements a bisection algorithm that tries to use a binary search to find the minimum number of block headers where the validator set voting power changes are less than < 1/3rd. This interface does not support weak subjectivity at this time. The Cosmos SDK also does not support counterfactual slashing, nor does the lite client have any capacity to report evidence making these systems theoretically unsafe.

NOTE: Tendermint provides a somewhat different (stronger) light client model than Bitcoin under eclipse, since the eclipsing node(s) can only fool the light client if they have two-thirds of the private keys from the last root-of-trust.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to support light clients in a Proof of Stake blockchain context.
- Requirement for a trusted block height (weak subjectivity) to prevent attacks.
- Desire to improve safety and efficiency of light client synchronization.
- Limitations of current Tendermint light client implementation (no weak subjectivity support).
- Trade-offs between bandwidth/computation and security in verification algorithms.
- User experience considerations for trust initialization.
- Potential for evidence reporting and slashing to enhance security.
template_adherence.decision: Add the weak subjectivity interface for new or offline light clients, requiring initialization of TrustOptions with trust period, height, and hash or a callback for confirmation. Implement linear verification by downloading all headers between TrustHeight and LatestHeight. Implement bisecting verification to optimize bandwidth and computation by recursively verifying mid-point headers until synchronization is achieved. Include mechanisms to submit evidence of misbehavior and cache trusted headers to minimize network usage. Plan for future user-friendly trust establishment methods such as HTTPS endpoints or on-chain registries.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Light client is safe to use, tolerating offline periods within limits.

Negative:
- Increased complexity due to bisection algorithm.

Neutral:
- Social consensus mechanisms for trust initialization can be error-prone.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing Tendermint light client without weak subjectivity support.
pros: Simplicity of implementation.
No changes to existing client behavior.
cons: The client is theoretically unsafe in Proof of Stake contexts.
No support for evidence reporting or counterfactual slashing.
Vulnerable to attacks exploiting lack of weak subjectivity.

alternatives.description: Implement only linear verification without bisecting verification.
pros: Simpler verification algorithm.

cons: Higher bandwidth and computation costs due to downloading all headers between trust and latest heights.

cons: Requires additional on-chain infrastructure and governance.

template_adherence.title: ABCI Evidence Handling
template_adherence.context:
Evidence is a distinct component in a Tendermint block and has its own reactor for high priority gossipping. Currently, Tendermint supports only a single form of evidence, an explicit equivocation, where a validator signs conflicting blocks at the same height/round. It is detected in real-time in the consensus reactor, and gossiped through the evidence reactor. Evidence can also be submitted through the RPC.

Currently, Tendermint does not gracefully handle a fork on the main chain. If a fork is detected, the node panics. At this point manual intervention and social consensus are required to reconfigure. We'd like to do something more graceful here, but that's for another day.

It's possible to fool lite clients without there being a fork on the main chain - so called Fork-Lite. See the fork accountability document for more details. For a sequential lite client, this can happen via equivocation or amnesia attacks. For a skipping lite client this can also happen via lunatic validator attacks. There must be some way for applications to punish all forms of misbehaviour.

The essential question is whether Tendermint should manage the evidence verification, or whether it should treat evidence more like a transaction (ie. arbitrary bytes) and let the application handle it (including all the signature checking).

Currently, evidence verification is handled by Tendermint. Once committed, evidence is passed over ABCI in BeginBlock in a reduced form that includes only the type of evidence, its height and timestamp, the validator it's from, and the total voting power of the validator set at the height. The app trusts Tendermint to perform the evidence verification, as the ABCI evidence does not contain the signatures and additional data for the app to verify itself.

Arguments in favor of leaving evidence handling in Tendermint:
1) Attacks on full nodes must be detectable by full nodes in real time, ie. within the consensus reactor.
2) Amensia attacks require an interactive protocol among all validators and are specific to Tendermint.
3) Evidence gossipping is higher priority and distinct from normal transactions.
4) ABCI application frameworks benefit from Tendermint handling evidence verification.

Arguments in favor of moving evidence handling to the application:
5) Skipping lite clients require tracking historical validator sets, which the app already manages.
6) Cross-chain validation requires apps to process evidence from other chains.
7) Evidence from lite clients may be large and could be a DoS vector; handling as transactions allows fee mechanisms to mitigate this.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for real-time detection of attacks on full nodes, complexity of amnesia attacks requiring interactive protocols, prioritization of evidence gossipping, benefits of centralized evidence verification in Tendermint, the need to track historical validator sets for skipping lite clients, cross-chain validation requirements, and potential DoS vectors from large evidence submissions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is that evidence detection belongs in Tendermint. Points (5) and (6) do not impose large obligations on Tendermint, and (7) is a concern but can be mitigated by out-of-band mechanisms such as payment channels or banning client IPs. The burden of large data submissions is on the client. A separate ADR will describe how Tendermint will handle new forms of evidence, including monitoring protocols, tracking past validators, and managing DoS issues.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include no real changes to ABCI and Tendermint handling evidence for all apps. Neutral consequences include the need to be careful about denial of service on the Tendermint RPC. Negative consequences include Tendermint duplicating data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period.

alternatives.description: Leave evidence handling in Tendermint.
pros: Real-time detection of attacks within consensus reactor.
Handles complex amnesia attacks specific to Tendermint.
Supports high priority evidence gossipping.
Centralizes evidence verification logic benefiting all ABCI apps.
cons: Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys during unbonding period.
Potential DoS vectors from large evidence submissions.

alternatives.description: Move evidence handling to the application.
pros: Avoids redundant management of historical validator set data in Tendermint.
Supports cross-chain validation by processing evidence as transactions.
Engages application's fee mechanism to mitigate DoS attacks.
cons: Requires each app to implement evidence verification logic.
May complicate real-time detection of attacks on full nodes.
Needs significant changes to ABCI to support evidence as transactions.

template_adherence.title: ADR 50: Improved Trusted Peering
template_adherence.context:
When `max-num-inbound-peers` or `max-num-outbound-peers` of a node is reached, the node cannot spare more slots to any peer by inbound or outbound. Therefore, after a certain period of disconnection, any important peering can be lost indefinitely because all slots are consumed by other peers, and the node stops trying to dial the peer anymore.

This is happening because of two reasons, exponential backoff and absence of unconditional peering feature for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain stable and persistent peering connections despite limits on inbound and outbound peer slots, and to overcome issues caused by exponential backoff and lack of unconditional peering for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce two new parameters in `config.toml`: `unconditional-peer-ids` to allow certain peers to connect regardless of max inbound/outbound limits, and `persistent-peers-max-dial-period` to limit the dial period during exponential backoff for persistent peers. This approach was chosen over modifying existing persistent-peers due to complexity and to cover both inbound and outbound cases.
