template_adherence.title: 12. Generalized Randomness for Holochain applications
template_adherence.context:
Distributed applications, like centralized ones, often need a source of randomness.  Having confidence and verifiability of that randomness poses particular challenges in the the distributed context. Specifically, we need a source of randomness with some of the following properties:
1. It is outside their control or influence so it can be used for a dice roll, card deck shuffle, or something where they may have an interest in skewing the results.
2. It is predictably reproducable, so that other nodes, whether players in a game, or validating nodes later, can reproduce the SAME random seed to reach the same random output for purposes of validation.
3. It is generalizable. Ideally, every application won't have to build their own approach to randomness, but can take advantage of a useful underlying convention. There are pitfalls we want to help them avoid in a distributed, eventually consistent system.
4. It doesn't require specific parties to be online to access the randomness data, so that later validators can confirm it even if parties with private entries are not online or no longer part of the network.

In the case of multiple parties wanting to generate randomness together, [cointoss](https://github.com/holochain/cointoss) provides an example of sharing of the hash of a secret which when later revealed can be combined to create a random number seed.  This method can be generalized into storing a bunch of private secrets, and publishing the hashes of those secrets, and then later revealing the secret to be combined with another party doing the same.  In cointoss this revelation happens via node-to-node communication, but in the general case it doesn't have to work that way.

Our application environment includes interactions (gossip and validation)  the combination of which are highly unpredicable (they include things like network latency, and timestamps) but verifiable after the fact. So for example, using the "first" four validation signatures on your opponent's last move as a random seed, could be one approach.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a source of randomness that is outside control, reproducible, generalizable, and accessible without specific parties online; challenges of distributed environment; desire to provide reusable randomness generation methods for applications; need for verifiability and security.
template_adherence.decision:
We will:
1. Implement mixins to provide randomness generation for some usecases using the cointoss combined secret method (both n2n for single events, and dht pushed for multiple events)
2. Provide app level access to unpredictable gossip/validation events for explicit use as seeds for random number generators.
template_adherence.consequences:
- We will want to have our approach reviewed as proof of the validity of these approaches  (i.e. this should get included in the security review(s))
- We need to add protocol/calls/callbacks in the network abstraction layer (See ADR 7) to gain access to this randomness.

template_adherence.title: 13. Signal/Listener model and API
template_adherence.context:
In the go code we used polling from the UI to discover local state changes, be they in the source-chain or in the DHT.  We want to change this to an event based model where UI (or other clients, like bridged apps) can become listeners to signals.  Additionally there are system level signals (like warrants) as well as other app level definable signals that we want consumers of exposed holochain app APIs to be able to access on a push (i.e. listening) basis.

Note that this is only about signals that can be listened to by conductor context, i.e. by the client of the core_api, NOT by the app nodes themselves.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to move from a polling model to an event-based model for UI and other clients.
The requirement to support system level and app level signals accessible via push.
Clarification that signals are for conductor context clients, not app nodes.
Desire to follow a known pattern (Signal-slot) for API design.
template_adherence.decision:
We will extend the API in a way roughly equivalent to the Signal-slot pattern, including:
- Declaring observable signals in the DNA similar to function declarations.
- Allowing app developers to emit signals via a new emit() function.
- Providing core_api methods to register and unregister listeners (listen() and unlisten()).
template_adherence.consequences:
- Need to clarify when emit() calls are valid (e.g., during validations and genesis).
- Ensure app developers understand signals are client-specific, not global.
- Consider which system signals to emit.
- Create a separate ADR for signals between nodes at the DHT level.
- Enforce permission checks for listeners based on capability access.
- Decide between full pub/sub model or signal/slot pattern with direct references.

template_adherence.title: 14. P2P - IPC Abstraction
template_adherence.context:
Rust as a language, in my opinion, does not lend itself to rapid prototyping. Writing efficient Rust code, while absolutely possible, is a problem domain unto itself, and takes time. E.g. Is it worth returning borrowed references in this case to save memory? Am I able to craft the lifetimes appropriately given all the other api usages of my struct? What about synchronization? These questions are implementation details, not architectural. If we are still working out the details with the underlying architecture, we don't want to be spending brainpower on * how * we accomplish our experiments.

In this prototyping / proof-of-concept phase, I don't want to take the time to write efficient rust code, but I don't want to leave us with a bunch of unmaintainable inefficient spaghetti if we *do* decide to go forward with the prototype.
template_adherence.decision:
Abstract the p2p library at the process level.

- The P2P process will host a [ZeroMQ](http://zeromq.org/) ROUTER socket. This process can be in any language that supports zmq, and using any of the transports it supports. (Likely start with unix domain sockets for their high throughput).
- The holochain rust code will connect to the P2P process with a ROUTER socket using the [zmq](https://crates.io/crates/zmq) crate.
- The holochain rust code will access this ipc abstraction through the [network-abstraction](0007-abstraction-for-network-layer.md) framework allowing the option to implement, for example, the rust version of libp2p both internally, and as a separate process.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Pros
* Ability to prototype and experiment with p2p solutions in other languages (including the more mature nodejs version of [libp2p](https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p)).
* Separation of concerns in terms of security and stability.
* Multiple Holochain processes can share the overhead (cpu, memory, bandwidth) of a single p2p network connection.

### Cons
* Work overhead for creation of additional abstraction layer.
* Additional complexity for system setup / maintanence for both developers and end-users. That is, they will have to start up / configure two processes instead of one.

template_adherence.title: Capabilities & Security ADR
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need for a unified security model for Holochain applications, emphasizing that each zome should enforce its own security model, allowing granular and revokable access control, and distinguishing between application-level and architectural security concerns.

template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt a variant of the capability-based security model where Holochain DNA instances grant revokable, cryptographic capability tokens as access credentials. template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include the implementation of capability grants as private entries on the chain, the need for mechanisms to handle capability requests and validation, and the impact on zome function calls, bridging, and genesis processes. It also affects how tokens are exposed and managed, and introduces considerations for intra-membrane security for cross-zome calls.

template_adherence.title: 3. Generate Schema variants from a data source + manifest
template_adherence.context:
Form variations are tackled through a mixture of routing rules (go here if...), skip conditions (skip this if...) and splitting of schemas into "form types" (e.g. Retail Sales Index (RSI) form types 0102, 0112 are survey runner schemas 1_0102.json and 1_0112.json). Compared to existing surveys Monthly Business Survey (MBS) has a large number of form types which makes splitting and maintaining them by hand too onerous. The Author service is the long term solution but we need something more manageable in the interim for the MBS.

We need a solution that lightens the load of authoring form variations.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Not explicitly stated as a separate section, but can be inferred from the context and decision sections: the need to manage a large number of form types more easily, reduce manual maintenance, and provide an interim solution before the Author service is ready.
template_adherence.decision:
We will spilt schemas into manifests and blocks and generate the survey runner JSON at build time.

- Each manifest file will represent a form type. A manifest will define the survey metadata, one or more groups and the block ids that each group composes. Manifests will be stored in YAML.

- A block file will define a single survey runner block and the question it contains. Blocks which have different metadata but contain the same question will duplicate the question. Blocks which contain the same question should have the same file name with a suffix that makes identifying potential duplicate/similar questions easy, e.g. for RSI `total-internet-sales-0102`, `total-internet-sales-0112`. Blocks will be stored in YAML.

- The following directory structure will be used

```
data/
sources/
blocks/
rsi/
introduction-0102.yaml
introduction-0112.yaml
summary.yaml
...
mci/
introduction-0203.yaml
internet-sales.yaml
...
...
manifests/
rsi/
0102.manifest.yaml
0112.manifest.yaml
...
mci/
0203.manifest.yaml
0213.manifest.yaml
...
...
```

- The scripts which aid the build process and other useful tasks will live in the `scripts/` folder.

- The json files produced by the manifests will continue to be tested by the test_schema_validation.py suite.

- This solution is temporary and will be superseded once Author goes live.
template_adherence.consequences:
Authors will switch from creating a whole schema for each form type to creating a manifest for each form type and any blocks they require.

Block definitions will no longer be duplicated across multiple form variations/types.

Questions do not have a single source of truth. A question can appear in many blocks, where typically the blocks have different routing and/or skip conditions. As questions are embedded in block files they are effectively duplicated. Authors who are updating a question, e.g. a guidance change, will have to bear this in mind. They will have to identify the blocks that contain the question and update each of them.

Authors will need to remember to run the build and the schemas unit test suite (test_schema_validation.py) before they submit a pull request to make sure any changes they have made don't violate Runners schema. If they don't the Travis build will fail.

No impact on survey runner code, it doesn't care where the json comes from as long as it conforms to its schema.

template_adherence.title: Simplify URLs and extend to support repeating effectively
template_adherence.context: The current URL structure used in runner is too long and overloaded. The URL should be as clean and readable as possible. The existing URL includes unnecessary parameters such as eq_id, survey_id, collection_exercise_id, group_id, and group_instance, which can be derived from the session or schema. The goal is to simplify the URL structure by removing these redundant parts.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is driven by the need for cleaner, more readable URLs, simpler routing and piping, and the ability to support repeating blocks effectively. The current complexity and redundancy in URLs make them cumbersome and less maintainable. The solution should also consider the uniqueness of block IDs and the handling of repeating list items.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to simplify the URL structure by making block IDs the root URLs, removing group IDs and unnecessary group instances. For blocks that drive repeats (list creators), URLs will include list identifiers and repeat identifiers. For blocks that repeat from a listing, URLs will include list identifiers, list item IDs, and block IDs. This approach reduces URL length and complexity while supporting repeating blocks effectively.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include cleaner and more readable URLs, simpler routing and piping, and a limitation that repeats based on anything other than a list will not be possible currently. template_adherence.title: 6. Make named lists a first class construct
template_adherence.context:
The current approach to collecting a list of things e.g. people that live in a household, and asking questions for each thing in that list, is more complex than it needs to be.

Collecting a list of things is currently achieved using repeat until logic with a confirmation question to get out of the repeat - something like "Is this everyone that lives at ...?". While the happy path journey is acceptable, it soon falls apart when a user attempts to do something else, for example editing or removing a list item. This also means that every time we evaluate the routing path, we need to follow the list item entry and confirmation combination for every item in the list. Attempting to fit creation of a list of things into the standard question per block model is wrong, as the add/edit/remove journeys are not relevant outside of the list creation.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Simplify the process of collecting lists of items.
- Improve handling of add/edit/remove journeys for list items.
- Simplify routing path evaluation.
- Remove unnecessary and complex repeat functionality.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to make named lists a first class construct by:

- Defining list creation explicitly in the schema with a new block type (ListCollector).
- Storing lists and answers within the context of a list using a new structure in the questionnaire store.
- Removing all unnecessary repeat functionality and moving repeat out of routing_rules.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Routing and piping become simpler.
- Related answers in the answer store are more clearly identified.
- Repeats based on anything other than a list will no longer be possible.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing repeat until logic with confirmation questions for list collection.
pros: No changes to existing schema or runner logic.
Familiar to current users and developers.
cons: Complex handling of add/edit/remove journeys.
Routing path evaluation is complicated and inefficient.
Not scalable or maintainable for complex list operations.

alternatives.description: Use a generic question per block model for list creation and management.
pros: Uniform approach to question handling.
Leverages existing question block types.
cons: Does not handle add/edit/remove journeys well.
Forces complex logic into standard question blocks.
Leads to complicated routing and state management.

template_adherence.title: 6. Use row-level-security in Postgres to implement multitenancy
template_adherence.context:
Multitenancy is required because we are now deploying openchs-server on the cloud. This can be achieved by
1. Multiple databases
2. Multiple schemas
3. Same database with a discriminator column

Constraints:
1. An organisation should not be able to view or update another organisation's data
2. There is common metadata for forms, concepts that organisations can override

Other concerns/requirements:
1. The architecture should prevent mistakes in code to leak data from one organisation to another
2. Maintaining multiple copies of metadata (if using multiple dbs/schemas) is hard
3. Data per organisation is low
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to implement multitenancy for cloud deployment
- Data isolation between organisations
- Ease of maintenance for metadata
- Prevention of data leakage between organisations
- Low data volume per organisation
template_adherence.decision:
- Use discriminators to achieve multitenancy.
- Enforce multitenancy using Postgres RLS policies
- Create a hierarchical organisation structure where organisations can read metadata from current or parent organisations, and read/write data for their own organisation
- Use OpenCHS as the grandparent organisation. It will hold the default program metadata
template_adherence.consequences:
- Additions a form element to an organisation can be done through a new row. But deletion cannot be. So, for each table that needs deletion of rows per organisation, there will be a non_applicable_table that handles organisation specific deletes
- Any change to OpenCHS organisation will automatically propagate to all organisations. This might not be desirable in the future

alternatives.description: Multiple databases
pros: Strong isolation between organisations
Easy to backup and restore per organisation
cons: High maintenance overhead
Difficult to share common metadata

alternatives.description: Multiple schemas
pros: Better isolation than single schema
Can share some metadata
cons: Still some maintenance overhead
Complexity in managing schemas

alternatives.description: Same database with a discriminator column
pros: Simpler to maintain
Easier to share metadata
cons: Risk of data leakage if discriminator is not enforced properly

template_adherence.title: 13. Handling change of catchments in the client
template_adherence.context:
A change in catchment in a device can be caused by two reasons.
1. The user-catchment assignment has changed in the server
2. A new user has logged in.

In both these conditions,
- It is possible that there is unsynced data in the device
- The new user might not have control over old data

A new catchment means that the last update date times are wrong, and the data is also wrong on the device, so this means a full sync from the server. We should do this, but not allow existing unsynced data to be wiped out.

Also note that the catchment an individual belongs to is set when he/she is created. Therefore, a sync of data will not affect any unsynced data.
template_adherence.decision: When a change in catchment is detected by openchs-client, existing unsynced data will be synced to the server, all data deleted, and a fresh sync started.
template_adherence.consequences: If a user needs to discard existing unsynced data on the client, he/she needs to remove them manually.

template_adherence.title: 5. Store invalid data in a column against ApplyApplication
template_adherence.context:
We are importing applications from apply into register by using the `ApplyApplication` model as an intermediate datastore. Since these applications might contain data that is not understood by register, we need a way to handle such attributes, so that they can be prompted back to the user managing the trainee in register.

We spiked a couple of approaches; option 1, [to add accessor methods to ApplyApplication](https://github.com/DFE-Digital/register-trainee-teachers/pull/1149), and option 2, [storing invalid data on the ApplyApplication model](https://github.com/DFE-Digital/register-trainee-teachers/pull/1147).

Consensus was for option 2, but there were mixed opinions about where it should live. Some felt it should be on the relevant model, eg, invalid trainee data should be on the `Trainee` model, and invalid degree data on the `Degree` model.

On the other hand, if we did move it to `Trainee`, it could get confusing, since it can be argued that `trainee.invalid_data` should account for all fields on the trainee and we already have validations to check the state of the trainee data entered in our system before submission.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to handle invalid data from Apply applications effectively, the desire to have a single source of truth for invalid data, the complexity of managing invalid data across multiple models, and minimizing risk of losing original context by not polluting the original application dump.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to keep the invalid data on the `ApplyApplication` model and wipe it out on successful submission of a TRN.
template_adherence.consequences: The advantage is that `ApplyApplication` becomes a single source of truth for invalid data from Apply. Introducing a new column avoids polluting the original application dump, minimizing risk of losing original context. Managing invalid data across multiple models would be cumbersome and error-prone, especially as more unique sections might be handled in the future.

alternatives.description: Add accessor methods to ApplyApplication to handle invalid data.
pros: Keeps invalid data handling within the ApplyApplication model.
May provide more direct access methods for invalid data.
cons: Possibly more complex to implement and maintain.
Consensus was not in favor of this approach.

alternatives.description: Store invalid data on the relevant models, e.g., `Trainee` or `Degree`.
pros: Invalid data is closer to the relevant domain model.
May align with domain-driven design principles.
cons: Could be confusing as `trainee.invalid_data` might need to account for all trainee fields.
Would require managing invalid data across multiple models, increasing complexity.

template_adherence.title: Use NX
template_adherence.context: We want a monorepo tool to help us to scale development up for multiple projects and teams. It should not be too much in the way, but help us manage code, dependencies and CI/CD.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Low complexity and overhead in development.
* Fit for our stack.
* Optimize CI/CD with dependency graphs and/or caching.
* Flexible.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "Nx", because:

* It's specially designed around our stack (TypeScript, React, Node.JS, NPM, ESLint, Prettier, Cypress, Jest, NextJS).
* It's relatively easy to learn with focused documentation.
* It has schematics to generate apps, libraries and components that includes all of our tools.
* It is opinionated, which gives us a good base to start developing faster. Many things can still be configured or extended.
template_adherence.consequences: The ADR does not explicitly state consequences, but by choosing Nx, the team will benefit from a tool tailored to their stack, with good documentation and tooling support, at the cost of some opinionation and reliance on an open source project maintained by an agency.

template_adherence.title: CSS
template_adherence.context: We're building websites and web applications that share a common design system with reusable components. How do we write CSS styles in a way that is performant and safe?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Should be performant, with code splitting, caching and minimal runtime overhead.
- Needs to have easy access to our design system constants. These should optimally be shared with JS logic.
- Should be type-safe to catch issues when refactoring.
- Reusable components should be closed, not accepting arbitrary styles/classes.
- We want a pattern for responsive props with atomic layout components.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: Treat, because it combines the best of both worlds from CSS-in-JS and CSS modules.

We'll create shared components that have responsive props, but are otherwise closed for modifications. Theme variables are defined in a shared library with TypeScript.

Example:

```typescript jsx
// Good:
<Box padding"small" />
<Box padding={{xs: 'small', md: 'medium'}} />
<Input large />
<Text preset="heading3" as="p" />

// Bad:
<Box className={customLayout} />
<Input style={{ height: 50, padding: 16 }} />
<Text className={styles.heading} />
```
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Treat is statically extracted at build time, so it has minimal runtime.
- Styles load in parallel with JS, also when code splitting.
- Styles are written in TypeScript which gives us type safety when referring to shared variables, styles and helpers.
- Styles are in special files, separate from markup and components giving us clear separation with good visibility into the rendered markup.
- We can pull in responsive layout component patterns from [Braid], which gives us a good base to lay out components and pages.

Negative Consequences:
- We are choosing a pretty new framework, so it may 1) have bugs or issues, 2) be an obstacle for new developers or 3) be discontinued.
- When we're generating responsive styles at build time we need to be mindful at how many variations we allow (eg media queries, columns, whitespace), since they can easily bloat our CSS with unused styles.

template_adherence.title: Branching and release strategy
template_adherence.context: How do we want to organise work in branches and how should changes be released? How should different branches be continuously deployed for QA?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
We need to have confidence in our releases.
We want more structured releases while we're still getting our footing in a shared monorepo.
We need simplicity and clear [takt time] so different teams can plan for what is going out the door from them.
It should work well with our agile work environment.
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option: "OneFlow" because it provides a single eternal branch with well structured releases.

We'll implement OneFlow with these details:

* Release branches are set up the Monday after each sprint. This is sometimes called release trains, where features line up for different release trains.
* Release and quality managers from each team are responsible for reviewing and approving releases.
* Releases apply to all apps in the monorepo.
* Releases are versioned like this: `{cycle}.{sprint}.{hotfix}`. So version 3.1.2 is the release after cycle 3, sprint 1 with two hot fixes applied.
* Feature branches are merged using "Squash and merge", so they can be easily reverted.
* There are two ways to build larger features.
* If the feature is isolated and not likely to cause conflicts, they can stay on long-living feature branches until they are ready to be released.
* If the feature touches many parts of the codebase, it can be useful to merge changes more often but hide the feature in production with feature flags.
* If a project needs to deploy updates outside of the sprint rhythm, they should use hotfix branches.

### Future strategy

With time, we expect to build up better testing capabilities which gives us more confidence in the health of our monorepo. Then we can move quicker, with a simpler GitHub Flow branching strategy and continuous delivery into production.

### Hosting environments

We'll set up continuous delivery to different hosting environments:

Environment | Git source            | Databases/services | Features
------------|-----------------------|--------------------|----------
sandbox     | feature branch        | Test               | All
dev         | master                | Test               | All
staging     | master                | Prod               | All
pre-prod    | release/hotfix branch | Prod               | Finished
prod        | latest release tag    | Prod               | Finished

We'll probably start with dev, staging, pre-prod and prod environments, since feature branch deployments are more dynamic and difficult to manage.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision leads to a structured release process with a single eternal branch and release trains, improving confidence and planning in releases. It also allows for flexibility in feature development and hotfixes. However, it may increase complexity in continuous integration and requires good testing capabilities to move towards simpler strategies in the future.

It would be supported by our new centralized authority server and should be implemented in all new clients and resource systems needing authentication or authorization. A requirement might be made that the authority service need to support other protocols for legacy systems but all new systems should be encourage to use the same protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Secure
- Well defined and well reviewed standard
- Easy to implement by client and resource systems
- Support for non web client systems i.e. mobile devices
template_adherence.decision: Chosen option: "OAuth 2.0 + OpenID Connect", because it is secure and well examined and and has support libraries for our tech stack.
template_adherence.consequences: The ADR does not explicitly state consequences, but from the decision and pros/cons, the impact includes adopting a secure, well-supported protocol that fits new systems and tech stack, while potentially dealing with token size and complexity issues.

alternatives.description: OAuth 2.0 + OpenID Connect
pros: The authentication protocol is designed specifically to work with the authorization protocol.
Supports non web clients i.e. native apps.
Has certified, open source libraries for relying parties for OpenID authentication that match our tech stack (javascript with typescript definitions).
cons: Could require large tokens for authorization for multiple services, or split up tokens complicating the process.

alternatives.description: SAML 2.0
pros: It is the currently used standard for legacy systems.
cons: Doesn't have good support for non web clients.
Main focus is on enterprise SSO, not centralized authorization.

template_adherence.title: CMS
template_adherence.context:
island.is will be maintaining and publishing content from many different government agencies and institutions. Their technical skill may vary a great deal, the content skill may also be lacking, therefore it is paramount for the system to be user friendly and intuitive.

Agencies and institutions should have enough autonomy with regards to editing content they are responsible for, to minimise the manual labour required by the island.is editors.

Which CMS system would best suit the needs of island.is?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Content needs to be editable by non technical users

- Content needs to be accessible across multiple domains and platforms

- Setup should be simple for developers new to the project

- The system should manage flexible content structures to limit systems impact on design

- The system should be user friendly and easy to use for a non technical person

- The system needs to offer a suitable workflow option to ease content management once multiple agencies start to contribute
template_adherence.decision:
Devs narrowed the choice down to two options Contentful and Contentstack.

Both systems meet the required featureset.

A decision from management was made to use Contentful.
Contentful is deemed to have a larger presence in the Icelandic dev community.
Contentful is also believed to have a stronger funding base.
Contentful is already implemented in some of our projects.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision to use Contentful means the project benefits from a CMS with a strong API, a large user ecosystem, and existing local community support. However, it may introduce complexity for new users due to its generic structure and complex billing. The choice also leverages existing implementations, potentially reducing integration effort.

template_adherence.title: Open Source License
template_adherence.context:
It is the offical policy of the Digital Iceland and stated in the Techical Direction that it is to be implemented as free and open source. Open source software by definition is open to anyone to use, modify, distribute and study. These permissions are enforced an open source license. There are a number of well-known and widely used open source licenses available and we need to choose a license that best fits the goals of digital iceland.

There are two main types of open source licences:  more permissive licences that confer broad freedoms and minimal obligations (e.g., the MIT, BSD and the Apache 2.0 licences); and sharealike licences that require licensing adaptations with the same licence if they distribute them (e.g., the GNU GPL).

Development for Digital Iceland will be open and free with minimum complications for development for all involved. Reuse and transparency will be promoted.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* The primary motivation is to encourage, co-development, collabiration, transparency and reuse of the software.
* It is important to build on the experience of similar government led inititives in other countries.
* Digital Iceland has no patents or intellecatual property that needs to be protected or guarded by the license chosen.
* It is not a concern for Digital Iceland that the license restricts usage in other projects, be it open or closed source.
template_adherence.decision:
The MIT license was chosen, for the following reasons:

* It is the least restrictive of the licenses.
* It is very consise, simple and easy to understand and therefore should be clear to users and developers.
* Digital Iceland does not require protection of patents or existing intelletual property.
* Well known government lead initiatives like uk.gov and X-Road use the MIT license.
* The MIT license is the best known and most widely used free and open-source license in the world.
template_adherence.consequences: Choosing the MIT license promotes minimal restrictions, ease of understanding, and aligns with other government initiatives, encouraging reuse and transparency. However, it does not protect patents or intellectual property, which is acceptable for Digital Iceland.

alternatives.description: Apache license
pros: Good, because is well known and very permissive like the MIT license.
cons: It has restrictions around redistribution that do not apply for Digital Iceland.
It is very long and wordy and therefore requires more effort to understand.

alternatives.description: BSD license
pros: Good, because is well known and very permissive like the MIT license.
cons: It has restrictions about using the names of the copyright holder which is not a concern for Digital Iceland.

alternatives.description: GNU GPL license
pros: It is very well known.
cons: It is not permissive and requires derived software to adopt the license as well.

template_adherence.title: Use Terraform across multiple AWS accounts
template_adherence.context: We have created multiple AWS accounts to host the different TDR environments, and we're happy with the decision we made during the Alpha to use Terraform to configure the infrastructure. The Alpha only ran in one AWS account using Terraform workspaces, but for Beta, we prefer to run Terraform in a controlled environment like Jenkins to improve access control, deployment process, and auditing. However, there is a challenge in bootstrapping Jenkins infrastructure using Terraform itself.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts
- Desire to use Terraform for infrastructure as code
- Preference to run Terraform in a controlled environment (Jenkins) rather than developer machines
- Security concerns about AWS credentials management
- Need for a bootstrapping process for Jenkins infrastructure
- Desire for controlled deployment and auditability
template_adherence.decision: Create multiple Terraform projects run in different stages: a backend project run from a development machine to bootstrap infrastructure and create IAM roles and Terraform state storage; a CI project run from a development machine using the backend's state storage; and an environment project run from Jenkins against each environment account. Use IAM roles to allow Jenkins to run Terraform without AWS secret keys.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved security by avoiding AWS secret keys in Jenkins, better control over deployment processes, and auditability of Terraform runs. Negative consequences include increased complexity in managing multiple Terraform projects and the bootstrapping process.

alternatives.description: Run Terraform scripts directly from developer machines for all environments.
pros: Simpler setup without need for bootstrapping Jenkins infrastructure.
No need to manage IAM roles for Jenkins.
cons: Less control over who can deploy to production.
No centralized audit trail of Terraform runs.
Security risk of AWS credentials on developer machines.

alternatives.description: Use Terraform workspaces within a single AWS account to manage multiple environments.
pros: Simpler Terraform state management.
No need to manage multiple AWS accounts.
cons: Does not align with organizational decision to use multiple AWS accounts.
Less isolation between environments.
Potential security and compliance issues.

template_adherence.title: Versioning and deployments
template_adherence.context: TDR will have multiple deployment environments: integration, staging and production. We want to be able to deploy new versions of our services to each environment in turn.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to deploy new versions of services to multiple environments in a controlled and automated manner. The desire to have an auto-incrementing version number generated by Jenkins rather than manual semantic versioning. The need to handle Docker image tagging and deployment efficiently. The constraints of current Docker Hub capabilities and potential future improvements with AWS ECR.
template_adherence.decision: Configure each project's build and Jenkinsfile to automate version tagging, Docker image building and tagging, and deployment to environments in sequence. Use Jenkins build numbers for versioning. Implement a deployment process that retags Docker images per environment and triggers AWS ECS service updates accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: Automated and consistent versioning and deployment process across environments. Reduced manual intervention and errors. Some inefficiency in Docker image retagging due to Docker Hub limitations, which may be improved in the future with AWS ECR. Reliance on Jenkins build numbers for versioning, which requires management if build numbers reset.

alternatives.description: Use semantic versioning instead of Jenkins build numbers for versioning.
pros: Semantic versioning is a widely recognized standard.
Versions convey meaning about changes (major, minor, patch).
cons: Requires manual version number updates by developers.
Less practical for applications compared to libraries in this context.

alternatives.description: Manually deploy to each environment without automation.
pros: Simple to implement initially.
No need to configure complex CI/CD pipelines.
cons: Prone to human error.
Slower deployment process.
Inconsistent deployments across environments.

alternatives.description: Use Docker Hub's tagging capabilities if supported to avoid retagging inefficiencies.
pros: More efficient deployment process.
Reduces network and storage overhead.
cons: Currently not supported by Docker Hub.
Dependent on future Docker Hub features or migration to AWS ECR.

template_adherence.title: 3. TDR frontend framework
template_adherence.context: Transfer Digital Records needs a web interface to allow government users to upload files to be transferred to The National Archives. There are many frameworks to choose from when building user interfaces for the web, including server-side frameworks like Rails, Node.js, Spring, and client-side JavaScript frameworks like React, Vue, or Angular, optimized for dynamic content updates without full page reloads.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The main drivers include ease of development and maintenance by a team familiar with Java and Scala, preference for Scala as the default language, familiarity with JavaScript for client-side development, and the need to support progressive enhancement so the site is usable without JavaScript where possible, except for the file upload page which requires JavaScript for client-side file analysis.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use Scala Play framework. Play was chosen over other MVC frameworks to continue development in Scala. A server-side MVC framework was preferred over Next.js to better support progressive enhancement, as Play's main purpose is server-side rendering. Next.js, while supporting server-side rendering, primarily enhances client-side JavaScript and is less suited for scenarios where JavaScript is unavailable or fails to load.
template_adherence.consequences: By choosing Scala Play, the team leverages their existing Scala expertise and supports progressive enhancement effectively, ensuring usability even when JavaScript is disabled or fails. This may limit the use of some client-side JavaScript enhancements that frameworks like Next.js facilitate, but aligns with the project's accessibility goals.

cons: Primarily designed to enhance client-side JavaScript rather than support progressive enhancement.
Less suitable when JavaScript is unavailable or fails to load.
Team less familiar with JavaScript compared to Scala.

alternatives.description: Use other server-side MVC frameworks like Rails (Ruby) or Spring (Java).
pros: Mature frameworks with strong community support.
Support server-side rendering and progressive enhancement.
cons: Team less familiar with Ruby or Java compared to Scala.
May require additional learning and maintenance overhead.

template_adherence.title: Restricting User Access To S3 Objects
template_adherence.context:
Ensure that TDR users are not able to overwrite/view another user’s objects in the TDR AWS S3 upload bucket.

Potential options to resolve the problem are to use:
* AWS Cognito;
* Signed URLS.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include security concerns to prevent users from accessing or overwriting other users' S3 objects, the advantages and disadvantages of AWS Cognito versus signed URLs, and integration with existing authentication providers like Keycloak.
template_adherence.decision:
Decided to go with AWS Cognito, with Keycloak as an OpenId authentication provider, using IAM policy to restrict access to a user's objects.

AWS Cognito was chosen over signed URLs due to better security (less risk of eavesdropping), compatibility with AWS KMS encrypted S3, and scalability (avoiding generating thousands of signed URLs).
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include improved security by restricting user access to their own S3 objects, integration with Keycloak for authentication, and scalable access control via IAM policies.

Negative consequences include the complexity of setting up AWS Cognito with Keycloak and managing IAM policies, as well as the need to maintain this infrastructure.

alternatives.description: Use AWS Cognito with Keycloak as an OpenId authentication provider and IAM policies to restrict access to user-specific S3 objects.
pros: Better security by avoiding risks associated with signed URLs.
Works with AWS KMS encrypted S3 buckets.
Scalable as it avoids generating many signed URLs.
Standards-based authentication with OpenId.
cons: Requires integration between Keycloak and AWS Cognito.
More complex setup and maintenance.

alternatives.description: Use signed URLs to grant access to S3 objects.
pros: Simpler to implement initially.
No need for complex IAM policies or identity pools.
cons: Risk that signed URLs can be intercepted and used until they expire.
Need to generate a separate signed URL for each file, which can be cumbersome for large consignments.
Less integration with AWS KMS encrypted buckets.

template_adherence.title: 8. Keycloak User Administrators Configuration
template_adherence.context:
Keycloak provides a flexible way to organise access for users to its administration functions.

TDR requires user configuration that allows the following:
* Set of users permission to manage transferring body users, ie the users of the TDR application.
* Set of users permission to manage keycloak users, ie those internal TNA users who can administer Keycloak itself, including setting up TDR application users.

The configuration needs to consider the following principles:
* *Least privilege*: only allow the user the minimum level of permissions to perform the requires operations
* *Elevated privileges*: prevent a user accruing additional permissions above what they require
* *User data protection*: ensure user data is secure
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to manage user permissions for transferring body users and internal TNA users.
- Principles of least privilege, elevated privileges prevention, and user data protection.
- Clear demarcation between transferring body users and internal users.
- Ease of administration and permission management.
template_adherence.decision:
Decided on Option 2: Define TDR user administrators in top level realm.

Rationale: Having user administrators in the top level realm provides a clear demarcation between transferring body users (defined in the TDR realm) and internal users, offering additional protection against inadvertently giving incorrect permissions.
template_adherence.consequences:
- User administrators are managed in the top level realm, simplifying permission boundaries.
- Clear separation reduces risk of permission errors.
- Administration is streamlined by using groups to define permissions.
- The decision is superseded by a later ADR (0009).

cons: Potentially less clear separation between user types.
May increase risk of permission misconfiguration.

alternatives.description: Define TDR user administrators in top level realm.
pros: Clear demarcation between transferring body users and internal users.
Additional protection against incorrect permissions.
Simplifies administration by centralizing user administrators.

template_adherence.title: base25 encoding for consignment references
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need for a user-friendly consignment reference to replace the difficult-to-use UUID currently generated by the TDR system. template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include usability for end users, consistency with other projects, the need for an incremental ID to encode, customizability of the ID generation, maintainability of encoding methods, and the ability to handle long numeric identifiers in a readable format.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to use a PostgreSQL sequence for generating the incremental ID due to its customizability and ability to start from a specific value with no cycling. template_adherence.consequences: The chosen approach allows for a consistent, user-friendly consignment reference that can be generated reliably and encoded efficiently. It leverages existing tools and database features, reducing custom development effort. However, reliance on an open-source library introduces some risk if the project changes. template_adherence.title: Use queues and Lambdas to run backend file checks
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need to run multiple backend file checks (antivirus scan, SHA-256 checksum, file format ID) on files uploaded to an S3 bucket as part of a TDR consignment. The system must handle potentially thousands of files of varying sizes, provide timely results, and be flexible for future additions or removals of checks.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The architecture must support parallel processing of many files, handle large file sizes, provide timely feedback to users, be scalable without managing servers, and be flexible for future changes. It must also handle AWS Lambda execution time limits and concurrency constraints.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use AWS Lambda functions to run the file checks and AWS SQS queues to coordinate the workflow steps. Files are uploaded to S3, triggering events that send messages through SNS and SQS queues. Lambdas process these messages, download files to EFS for checks, and send results back via SQS to a final Lambda that updates the API. This serverless approach allows parallel processing, scalability, and easier maintenance. Alternatives like AWS Step Functions were rejected due to concurrency limits encountered in prototypes.
template_adherence.consequences: The chosen architecture enables scalable, parallel processing of file checks without managing servers, improving user experience by providing timely results. It leverages AWS serverless services, reducing operational overhead. However, there are current limitations such as lack of systematic load testing, potential slow file format identification, concurrency issues with metadata updates and temporary file storage, and no explicit mechanism to mark all checks as complete. These will require future refinements.

cons: Failed under Lambda concurrent usage limits in prototype testing.

pros: No execution time limits like Lambda's 15 minutes.

template_adherence.title: 20. Increase message visibility timeout in file check queues
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes an issue with file check Lambda functions coordinated by SQS queues, where messages are sometimes sent to a failure queue even though the Lambda eventually succeeded. This is problematic for monitoring and is suspected to be caused by the SQS message visibility timeout being too short relative to Lambda execution time, including initialization delays.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to prevent premature message retries that cause false failure reports, the desire to maintain efficient processing without excessive retry delays, and the operational constraints of Lambda initialization and execution times.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to set the SQS message visibility timeout to three times the Lambda timeout for all file check Lambdas, and to add error handling in Lambdas to immediately retry failed messages by setting visibility timeout to zero. Batch size is also set to 1 to facilitate testing and debugging.
template_adherence.consequences: This change will reduce false failure messages by preventing premature retries, but will increase retry delays if the error handling does not trigger. It also adds complexity by requiring additional error handling logic and tuning of timeout values.

alternatives.description: Keep current visibility timeout equal to Lambda timeout.
pros: Simplicity, no configuration changes needed.
No increase in retry delays.
cons: Causes premature retries leading to false failure messages.
Failure queue becomes unreliable for monitoring.

alternatives.description: Set visibility timeout to 6 times Lambda timeout as per AWS recommendation.
pros: Maximizes safety against premature retries.
Aligns with AWS official guidance.
cons: Longer retry delays, potentially slowing down error recovery.
May be unnecessarily conservative, increasing latency.

template_adherence.title: Proxy S3 uploads through CloudFront
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the current problem where users upload files directly from their browsers to AWS S3, causing issues for users on restricted networks that block requests to amazonaws.com domains. The goal is to proxy these uploads through a domain under tdr.nationalarchives.gov.uk to avoid network restrictions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to maintain integration with existing S3-based workflows, support for multipart uploads via the AWS JavaScript SDK, network restrictions blocking direct S3 access, authorization mechanisms compatible with the SDK, minimizing additional service maintenance, and security considerations such as restricting upload permissions and cookie security.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to proxy requests to S3 through CloudFront, using signed cookies for authorization. Uploads will be directed to a CloudFront domain (e.g., upload.tdr.nationalarchives.gov.uk) which proxies to the S3 bucket. Signed cookies will be generated by a Lambda function behind the same CloudFront instance, with API Gateway bridging CloudFront and Lambda. The AWS JavaScript SDK will be configured to use the CloudFront endpoint for uploads.
template_adherence.consequences: The new architecture routes uploads through CloudFront, enabling users on restricted networks to upload files. Authorization is handled via signed cookies, improving security with IP restrictions and short-lived cookies. The approach maintains compatibility with the AWS SDK and existing workflows. There is minimal expected cost increase, and an additional certificate for signing cookies must be securely managed.

alternatives.description: Run a proxy service (e.g., NGINX in ECS or Lambda) to forward requests to S3 and handle authorization.
pros: Allows full control over proxy logic and authorization.
Can integrate with existing token systems.
cons: Requires maintaining an additional service.
Would need to proxy Cognito and STS requests or modify SDK usage.
Increases operational complexity.

alternatives.description: Use S3 website endpoints with a custom domain.
pros: Simple to set up with Route 53.
Uses custom domain for uploads.
cons: Only supports HTTP, not HTTPS.
No SSL termination, insecure for uploads.

alternatives.description: Use API Gateway as a proxy for uploads.
pros: Managed service, no server maintenance.
Can integrate with Lambda authorizers.
cons: 30-second maximum request time, problematic for large uploads.
Would require chunk size adjustments.
Might need to proxy Cognito and STS or modify SDK usage.

alternatives.description: Use CloudFront signed URLs for authorization.
pros: Built-in CloudFront feature.
Fine-grained per-file authorization.
cons: Inconvenient for thousands of files due to per-file URL generation.
Not compatible with AWS JavaScript SDK which requires domain-level configuration.

alternatives.description: Use Keycloak tokens directly for authorization with custom edge functions.
pros: Simplifies token management by using Keycloak tokens only.
Potentially reduces token exchange complexity.
cons: Not obviously compatible with AWS JavaScript SDK.
Requires custom client-side JavaScript for multipart uploads.
Increases client complexity.

template_adherence.decision: All schema mutations will globally synchronize via a check-and-set operation on a specific cell in a lock table.
template_adherence.consequences:

- The lock table must be created synchronously to avoid the bug.
- Client startup will be slower due to linearization of part of the startup process.

template_adherence.title: Create schema lock table via a one off CLI command

- Have Atlas clients refuse to start if the _locks table is missing and provide a CLI to create it.

- Is very, very hard to get wrong
- Should be easily automatable in most setups, removing the manual step

- Use the lock service for locking rather than the _locks table, then we don't have to create it.
- Completely automatic and removes code
- Leaves open the possibility of locks failing and operations never realising that the issue has been triggered

- Have each node create a unique table, then run paxos to decide which one is the winner
- This requires a bunch of extra, error prone code

template_adherence.title: Stop allowing embedded lock and timestamp services in production
template_adherence.context:
Currently a completely normal way to set up AtlasDB is to run an embedded lock and timestamp service that only your atlas client talks to in Java. If this happens with 2 different clients, then they can easily clash with each other and cause undefined issues in the KVS. It also stops CLIs that require knowledge of lock and timestamp being able to run against these atlas clients.

There is no reason for this situation to arise in production. Lock and Timestamp services can still be deployed in a sensible fashion without spinning up a separate service by registering the lock and timestamp server endpoints in your application, and having your own nodes act as the servers. Alternatively, you can spin up an completely external lock and timestamp service whose whole reason for existence is to perform these roles.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly list decision drivers as a separate section or clearly articulated list. However, from the context and decision sections, the drivers can be inferred as preventing clashes between clients using embedded lock and timestamp services, enabling CLI compatibility, and promoting sensible deployment of lock and timestamp services in production.
template_adherence.decision:
1. Remove the ability to run embedded lock and timestamp services in configuration
2. Provide an easy to run Timelock Server which provides lock and timestamp services to applications
3. Provide a sensible development story for testing against a TimelockServer that can be started from Java.
template_adherence.consequences: 1. We have to support a new, standalone server and all related considerations (e.g. versioning, healthchecks)

template_adherence.title: Create schema lock table using configuration
template_adherence.context:
Due to table creation issue we need to be able to safely create _lock table as a one off operation for each keyspace that atlas uses. The discussed options include:

- Have Atlas clients refuse to start if the _locks table is missing and provide a CLI to create it.
- This does require manual interview for whoever is handling operations
- Is very, very hard to get wrong
- Should be easily automatable in most setups, removing the manual step

- Use the lock service for locking rather than the _locks table, then we don't have to create it.
- Completely automatic and removes code
- Leaves open the possibility of locks failing and operations never realising that the issue has been triggered

- Have each node create a unique table, then run paxos to decide which one is the winner
- This requires a bunch of extra, error prone code

- Create an additional entry in the configuration, lockLeader, to denote which host is responsible for creating the locks table.
- The host whose name is the same as lockLeader will create the lock table, others will wait until the lockLeader is up.
- Requires all hosts to have the same configuration for lock leader
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need for safe creation of the _lock table without manual intervention, minimizing complexity, ensuring consistent configuration across nodes, and avoiding error-prone code. Desired qualities include automation, simplicity, and reliability.
template_adherence.decision:
We decided to use an extra item of configuration, because:
1. Internal tools enable us to be confident that different Atlas servers on the same cluster are configured consistently.
2. Running paxos to decide which table is the winner was more complex than anticipated.
template_adherence.consequences:
On first-time startup, servers can now be started concurrently, but they must have consistent configuration.
There are two failure modes that can be caused by inconsistent configuration or failure of the lock leader:
1. No node believes that it is the lock leader - then all nodes will wait forever.
2. More than one node believes itself to be the lock table - then we will have duplicate lock tables and still be vulnerable to the initial issue.

alternatives.description: Have Atlas clients refuse to start if the _locks table is missing and provide a CLI to create it.
pros: Very hard to get wrong
Easily automatable in most setups, removing the manual step
cons: Requires manual intervention for whoever is handling operations

alternatives.description: Use the lock service for locking rather than the _locks table, then we don't have to create it.
pros: Completely automatic
Removes code
cons: Leaves open the possibility of locks failing and operations never realizing that the issue has been triggered

alternatives.description: Have each node create a unique table, then run paxos to decide which one is the winner.
cons: Requires a bunch of extra, error prone code

alternatives.description: Create an additional entry in the configuration, lockLeader, to denote which host is responsible for creating the locks table.
pros: Enables confident consistent configuration across servers
cons: Requires all hosts to have the same configuration for lock leader

template_adherence.title: Use CQL for column paging for sweep
template_adherence.context:
As of version 0.12.0, our implementation of sweep for Cassandra relied upon the getPageWithRangeCreator method of CassandraKeyValueService, which fetches values for all columns and timestamps from Cassandra. In cases where a cell with a large value was overwritten (with other large values) many times, this caused Cassandra to run out of memory, even if only a single row was fetched. (internal issue 44272).

We needed a way to run sweep without Cassandra running out of memory in such cases.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid Cassandra running out of memory when fetching large overwritten cells during sweep, the desire to fetch only a certain number of cells at once, and the preference for simpler and higher throughput queries (CQL over thrift).
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a more granular batching solution by paging through columns for each row using CQL queries with limits, adding an optional parameter timestampsGetterBatchSize in CassandraKVSConfig to enable this behavior only if set, and choosing CQL over thrift due to simplicity and higher throughput.
template_adherence.consequences: An additional parameter timestampsGetterBatchSize is added to CassandraKVSConfig. When set, sweep pages through columns of each row while searching for timestamps, which may be less efficient but more flexible and less likely to cause Cassandra to run out of memory.

alternatives.description: Continue using getPageWithRangeCreator method fetching all columns and timestamps at once.
pros: Simplicity: no changes needed to existing implementation.
cons: Causes Cassandra to run out of memory when cells with large values are overwritten many times.
Not scalable for large data sets with large overwritten cells.

alternatives.description: Use thrift protocol for fetching columns and timestamps with paging.
pros: Potentially could be used for paging columns.
cons: More complex to write queries compared to CQL.
Empirically shown to have lower throughput than CQL.

template_adherence.title: Adding Heartbeat for Schema Lock Holders
template_adherence.context:
As of version 0.16.0, anyone trying to acquire the a schema mutation lock that is already held by someone else would keep trying to acquire the lock until a fixed timeout threshold. Once that threshold was reached, we would stop trying to acquire the lock and throw a timeout exception. This would effectively kill the client trying to grab the lock and necessitate a restart. We have a timeout threshold instead of retrying indefinitely to handle cases where the lock holder dies without releasing the lock.

However, we think this has caused a lot of unnecessary exceptions since the threshold is static. We believe we could avoid a lot of timeouts if we have some way of informing anyone trying to acquire the lock if the lock holder is alive or dead. Once we have that information, we can keep retrying as long as we know that the lock holder is alive without timing out needlessly.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce unnecessary timeout exceptions caused by static timeout threshold.
- Desire to inform lock acquirers about the health (alive/dead) of the lock holder.
- Avoid data corruption by not allowing overridable locks.
- Provide better exception information to users.
- Maintain manual intervention for dead lock holders to ensure safety.
template_adherence.decision:
To inform anyone trying to acquire the lock if the lock holder is dead or alive, we decided to have the lock holder periodically update its lock (heartbeat) in the locks table while its still holding the lock. That way, anyone else trying to acquire the lock can see the updates to the lock and keep retrying as long as the updates continue.

Currently, the lock value in the locks table consists of a randomly generated identifier. To incorporate the heartbeat updates into the same value, we decided to change the lock value to following format: `<randomly generated id>_<heartbeat value>`. The heartbeat value would essentially be incremented by 1 for every "heartbeat" by the lock holder.

For example, a lock with identifier `123456789` and heartbeat value `23` would have `123456789_23` as its lock value.

Once we had the heartbeat mechanism in place, we needed to decide whether to allow someone waiting on a lock to override the lock and grab it once it detects that the lock holder is dead (via its heartbeat). Allowing locks that could be overridden weakened the guarantee provided by the lock and could cause corruption in rare situations. On the plus side, overridable locks would minimize human intervention when dealing with dead lock holders.

However, it was decided that we should avoid the possibility of data corruption as much as possible. Therefore, we won't have overridable locks for now and simply use the information about the health of the lock holder to better inform the exception we throw when we timeout on the lock. This will still require manual intervention (truncating the locks table) when a lock holder dies without releasing the lock but provides a better picture of the situation to the human user.
template_adherence.consequences:
There should be significantly lower instances of schema mutation lock timeouts. The only cases where we should have timeouts should be:

1. When someone holding the lock dies, we throw an informative exception mentioning that we suspect the lock holder is dead and recommend cleaning the locks table.

2. When someone continues holding the lock for an **unreasonable** amount of time (default: 10 mins, is configurable)

template_adherence.title: 9. Load and Read Streams in the Same Transaction
template_adherence.context:
Reading streams from within the same transaction that calls loadStream() must be supported. There are a number of benefits to doing this rather than reading streams outside the transaction.

1. If the transaction that calls loadStream() is run with retry, you risk leaking resources because multiple streams may be created that never get returned to the caller (so the caller has no opportunity to close them). The stream can not only be read (entirely) inside the transaction, but also closed inside the transaction. This makes it safe to run with retries (since the retries can also close the stream they load).

2. When the actual stream data is read outside of the transaction, that read can fail (for example if the stream was then deleted). If instead the read is performed inside the transaction, any failed reads would also cause the transaction to fail, which could be desired. For example, if as a result of reading the stream you want to perform some writes based on the read data, it makes sense to perform all of that in a single transaction.
template_adherence.decision: Reading from a stream inside the same transaction that calls loadStream() should be the preferred method unless you have a specific reason that the reads must be performed later outside the transaction. Reading from a stream should be supported both inside the same transaction where it was loaded and outside (after the transaction commits or aborts).
template_adherence.consequences: Internal products currently rely on being able to read streams in the same transaction that loadStream() is called. This must be supported unless you first ensure that all internal products have been rewritten to never read from a stream in the same transaction that loads it.

template_adherence.title: Use partial row complete cell batching in getTimestampsByCell
template_adherence.context: As of version 0.35.0 , our implementation of `DbKvs.getTimestampsByCell` was creating a MultiMap with all pairs of (Cell, timestamp) from the range determined by the row batch size. In case of wide rows, or simply a row batch size that is too large, this could cause us to run out of memory; see issue #982.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid running out of memory when processing wide rows or large row batch sizes, and to ensure correctness and parallelization in sweep processing.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to use a block (a triple of row name, column name, and timestamp) batch size, defaulting to 1000000 to avoid loading too many blocks into memory. The algorithm fetches blocks by row, column, and increasing timestamp until the batch size is met, with specific handling depending on whether rows are fully processed or not.
template_adherence.consequences: For rows wider than the value of the batch size, `DbKvs.getTimestampsByCell` may split them into several RowResults.

alternatives.description: Partial row batching: fetch up to 1000000 blocks. If the block batch size is hit, stop immediately (cells can be split across multiple batches).
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Hard to reason about for sweep correctness.
Requires repeating last block or keeping it in memory, reducing parallelization and risking correctness bugs.

alternatives.description: Full row batching: fetch up to 1000000 blocks. If the block batch size is hit in the middle of a row, continue fetching until the row is exhausted.
pros: Ensures full rows are processed.
cons: Does not guard well against wide rows with many overwrites.

alternatives.description: No batching, but throw an error when the block batch hint is reached.
pros: Simple error handling.
cons: Relies on caller retry logic to reduce batch size.
Less robust and more error-prone.

template_adherence.title: Retry long-running locks via BlockingTimeoutException
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes a problem where the TimeLock server experiences thread buildups due to long-running lock requests exceeding the Jetty idle timeout, causing resource leaks and leader election issues. This is detailed with a concrete example and root cause analysis.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include preventing idle timeouts from occurring, ensuring resources are freed if timeouts happen, maintaining compatibility with existing clients, and minimizing changes to the lock service API. Concerns about resource management, client-server interaction, and system stability are highlighted.
template_adherence.decision: The chosen decision is to introduce a blocking timeout for lock requests, set lower than the Jetty idle timeout, to interrupt and notify clients when exceeded. This uses Guava's TimeLimiter and serializes exceptions to inform clients to retry appropriately, balancing resource management and client behavior.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include changes in lock request behavior for long blocks, exception serialization changes, potential starvation due to timeouts, and additional configuration parameters. The ADR discusses impacts on fairness, client retry logic, and system robustness.

alternatives.description: Significantly increase the Jetty idle timeout to a large value like 1 day.
pros: Simple to implement.
Avoids changing client or server logic.
cons: Long resource allocation in case of failures.
Requires client-side idle timeout increase.
Does not fully solve the problem.

alternatives.description: Convert the lock service to a non-blocking API with tokens and polling or server push.
pros: Likely best long-term solution.
Avoids blocking requests.
cons: Significant API change.
Not preferred at this time.

alternatives.description: Implement connection keep-alives or heartbeats to reset idle timeout.
pros: Reasonable approach to keep connections alive.
cons: Not readily supported by Jetty.
Adds complexity.

alternatives.description: Send a last-gasp message to free resources before stream closes.
pros: Clean resource freeing approach.
cons: Not supported by Jetty yet (issue #824).

alternatives.description: Have clients truncate requests to the idle timeout length.
pros: Similar to implemented solution.
cons: Requires clients to know server idle timeout.
Not appropriate as timeout is server-configured.

alternatives.description: Use a custom HTTP status code or header to signal retry.
pros: Simpler than serializing exceptions.
Existing error decoder can handle status codes.
cons: Clients unlikely to understand custom codes.
Prefer to avoid custom codes and headers.

template_adherence.title: Batch timestamp requests on the client side
template_adherence.context:
A TimeLock cluster can serve multiple services. Under these circumstances, each TimeLock client node can separately open connections to TimeLock and request timestamps and locks. As timestamp and lock requests are typically very common (for instance, a single write transaction needs to contact TimeLock multiple times), TimeLock tends to experience relatively heavy loads. This affects overall throughput, as TimeLock takes longer to respond to requests.

The `PersistentTimestampService` supports querying for a contiguous range of timestamps. This functionality has already been used in production, in Palantir's large internal product.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce load on TimeLock servers due to frequent timestamp and lock requests from multiple services. The desire to improve throughput and reduce response times. The trade-off between batching requests to reduce load and the potential increase in latency for clients, especially under light load conditions. The requirement to maintain the ability to disable batching for applications requiring real-time responses.
template_adherence.decision: Use the `RequestBatchingTimestampService` to coalesce timestamp requests to TimeLock, enabling it by default. Configure it with a zero millisecond delay interval to dispatch requests immediately after the previous completes. Maintain the ability to disable request batching to accommodate applications sensitive to latency.
template_adherence.consequences: Load on TimeLock servers should be reduced due to fewer network calls for timestamps. Clients may experience increased latency, particularly if TimeLock was not heavily loaded before. Users should monitor `TimestampService.getFreshTimestamps` metrics rather than `TimelockService.getFreshTimestamp` to accurately assess timestamp serving performance. Lock requests and compound operations are not batched, so their performance remains unaffected.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text, but implied alternatives include: not batching requests at all, or batching with different delay intervals.
pros: No added latency from batching.
Simpler client implementation.
cons: Higher load on TimeLock servers due to many individual requests.
Potential throughput bottlenecks.

alternatives.description: Batching with a non-zero delay interval to accumulate more requests before sending.
pros: Potentially greater load reduction on TimeLock servers.
More efficient batching.
cons: Increased latency due to waiting for batch accumulation.
Complexity in tuning delay interval.

template_adherence.title: Assessment of ADR 'Write Cassandra tombstones and sentinels with a fresh Cassandra timestamp' adherence to MADR template
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the problem of timestamp handling for Cassandra tombstones and sentinels in AtlasDB, explaining the current issues and the need for a change in timestamp assignment to preserve key invariants and improve tombstone droppability.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include preserving key invariants related to timestamp ordering, improving tombstone droppability during compaction, avoiding reliance on wall-clock time for transactional tables, and minimizing performance impact on critical path operations.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to change the timestamps for sweep sentinels, tombstones, and range tombstones to use fresh timestamps from the timestamp service, while keeping cell write timestamps unchanged. This involves an additional RPC call for these operations but does not affect normal client read/write transactions.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include the need for a fresh timestamp supplier during key-value service initialization, an additional RPC overhead for sentinel and tombstone writes (not on critical paths), and improved tombstone droppability. Memoization approaches were considered but rejected due to correctness risks.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing timestamp scheme with fixed or derived timestamps for sentinels and tombstones.
pros: No additional RPC overhead.
No changes to existing timestamp service usage.
cons: Does not satisfy all key invariants, especially the third invariant.
Leads to issues with tombstone visibility and compaction effectiveness.

alternatives.description: Make the fresh timestamp supplier optional, falling back to legacy mode if not provided.
pros: Backward compatibility for services not providing fresh timestamp supplier.
Less immediate disruption to existing systems.
cons: Reduced benefits in tombstone droppability.
Increased complexity in supporting two modes.

alternatives.description: Use memoization to reduce RPC calls for fresh timestamps.
pros: Potentially reduces RPC overhead.
May improve performance for multiple tombstone writes in a batch.
cons: Risk of incorrect timestamp ordering leading to live data visibility issues.
Increased complexity and potential correctness bugs.
