template_adherence.title: 0007. Feature toggles development
template_adherence.context:
This change describes a methodology of development which we believe will help us increase the confidence and speed in the development process.

What problem are we trying to solve

Currently the time between a PR is sent and the code gets merged is between 1 day to in some case 4 to 5 days.

This has some disadvantages:

1) This workflow incentivises developers to make large PRs, as building incrementally but having to wait 2 to 3 days for the code to be merged at each step is not desirable and results in loss of context.

2) If a bug is introduced it is harder to fix, as the longer it takes to integrate code the more likely the developer has lost familiarity with the code.

3) Constant rebases introduce an overhead for the developer and can introduce subtle bugs, as rebased code is not thoroughly reviewed.

4) Code review is only performed once, but during the manual QA step significant changes might be added, which are not reviewed anymore.

How are we going to address it

We believe feature toggles development https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html is a step in the right direction.

The way it would work is:

A developer starts working on a new feature.
Any new code will be scoped behind a feature flag and:

1) no significant changes are made to the existing codebase
2) no changes are visible to the user when the feature flag is off

In this case the manual QA step can be skipped, and the code can be integrated as soon as the review step is done.

Clojure reviewers can object if they think the changes are so significant that manual QA is required.

This process should ease some workload on the QA team and move some of the responsibilities on clojure developers.

What needs to change

To improve no bugs are introduced, there needs to be a concerted effort in improving the current test suites, both e2e and clojure, and ensure new code is sufficiently covered.
The shape/type of tests needed is open to discussion, but generally light integration tests + light e2e tests are a good approach for this kind of workflow.

Also manual smoke testing of the images generated is necessary, until we are more confident on our test suites.

Once the feature is to be toggled, a PR will be sent changing the config, at which point manual QA will be required before merging.

If fixes are to be applied, they can be made in a separate PR, which can skip manual QA, but will not skip code review, ensuring that subsequent changes are reviewed. Once those are merged into develop, the PR that changes the feature toggle will resume testing.

How far we want to go

At the most extreme, this workflow allows push-to-master, with multiple commits a day being integrated, but this would hardly fit with the code-review process.

The idea is to add some rigour to the process so that the review step is meaningful, essentially at any point it could be toggled on and it should provide **value** to the end user.

This means that PRs that will skip manual QA need to be deliverables and presentable to an end-user (no incomplete implementations), i.e. features need to be split into meaningful chunks.

Not all code contributions will want to use this workflow, it is up to the developer to decide.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to increase confidence and speed in the development process.
- Current PR merge delays cause large PRs, loss of context, harder bug fixes, overhead from rebases, and insufficient review of changes made during manual QA.
- Desire to reduce manual QA workload and shift some responsibility to developers.
- Need for improved test coverage and quality assurance.
- Maintain meaningful code review and deliverable increments.
template_adherence.decision:
Adopt feature toggles development methodology where new code is scoped behind feature flags, allowing code integration immediately after review without manual QA if the feature flag is off and no significant changes are made to existing codebase.

Manual QA is required only when toggling the feature on.

Improve test suites and maintain code review rigor.

Allow developers to decide whether to use this workflow.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Faster integration of code changes.
- Reduced manual QA workload.
- Smaller, incremental, deliverable PRs.
- Maintains code review quality.

Negative:
- Requires improved test coverage and discipline.
- Some developers may choose not to use this workflow.
- Potential risk if feature toggles are misused or tests are insufficient.

alternatives.description: Continue with the current development and PR process without feature toggles.
pros: No change to existing workflow, so no learning curve.
Maintains current manual QA process which may catch issues.
cons: Longer PR merge times (1-5 days).
Incentivizes large PRs, causing loss of context.
Harder bug fixes due to delayed integration.
Overhead from rebases and potential subtle bugs.
Manual QA changes are not reviewed again.

template_adherence.title: 0010. Remove jail and Status API
template_adherence.context:
Originally, we supported 3rd party status extensions in form of javascript jailed execution environment (eq Jail) + small js library exposing chat commands API to js code.

While neat in theory, it has some serious downsides:

- Design of the API was quite poor, preferring mutable semantics over stateless API leveraging strength of the host application (cljs/re-frame).
As a result of that, more dynamic/state requiring things (like the live tx detail in `/send` command messages) were very hard to do,
so instead of "eating our own dogfood", we decided to side-step the API and implement such things as hard-coded logic in the app, while partly
retaining the js code for "easier" things (like parameter declaration).
Needles to say, such efforts produced code of very poor quality, riddling our app with hard-coded "magic" everywhere in the codebase, completly
defeating the point of "dogfooding" while still requiring more effort and being much more error prone (no way to unit test jail logic) because
of the need to asynchronously communicate with jail for leftover logic in command messages (the parts not hardcoded in app).

- We were in a state where there was not even one command defined completely in jail, with all of them requiring custom hardcoded logic in app to
actually work.
Due to numerous changes and rush to get things working, half of the API was obsolete and was not working/working differently then described in
the API documentation.

- We are quite tight stretched regarding performance and the Jail didn't particularly help with that - whenever some command message was defined in
Jail, it required constant RN Bridge "ping-pong" whenever sending the message or receiving the message, eating more resources + breaking otherwise
quite simple logic into harder to reason asynchronous call chains (execute method defined in Jail, wait for the result, execute next method in Jail...).

- Till now, there was no real interest in 3rd party bots anyway - the only "real" DAPPs submitted to status were "normal" DAPPs utilising just the `web3.js`
API and built on top of regular web technologies, so they could be ran in any Ethereum client like Metamask or Mist, besides Status.

- There is a very promising new concept of extensions (project pluto), which will enable to extend status with much nicer and declarative extension
definitions.
Such extensions will not be able to only hook-in into the command messages logic, but also other application (host) hooks, like wallet assets/collectibles,
chat contacts, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Poor design of the existing Jail API preferring mutable semantics over stateless API.
- Difficulty in implementing dynamic/state requiring features.
- Poor code quality and hard-coded logic due to API limitations.
- Obsolete and inconsistent API documentation.
- Performance issues caused by Jail's asynchronous communication.
- Lack of real interest in 3rd party bots using the Jail.
- Emergence of a better extension concept (project pluto) offering more capabilities.
template_adherence.decision: Remove Jail and `Status.js` API from the application and rework command messages into nicely encapsulated app level protocols. Command related logic will be centralized, leveraging the platform's strengths, enabling faster and more pleasant development. The 3rd party code issue will be addressed separately by extensions.
template_adherence.consequences: `Status.js` is deprecated and there is no way to define custom commands using javascript only.

alternatives.description: Continue using the Jail and Status.js API with improvements.
pros: Maintain backward compatibility.
Leverage existing codebase and knowledge.
cons: Poor API design is hard to fix.
Performance issues remain.
Hard-coded logic and poor code quality persist.
No guarantee of increased interest in 3rd party bots.

alternatives.description: Replace Jail with a new extension system (project pluto) without removing Jail immediately.
pros: Allows gradual transition.
New extension system offers better capabilities.
Avoids immediate disruption.
cons: Maintains complexity temporarily.
Requires supporting two systems simultaneously.
Delays removal of problematic Jail API.

template_adherence.title: Arrays
template_adherence.context: Currently it is inefficient to detect the length of an array and it is impossible to know if a key (without subkeys) should be an array or not.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for efficient detection of array length and clear identification of array keys; compatibility with existing metadata conventions; ensuring plugins can rely on correct array metadata early; handling of overrides and cascading lookups; validation of array structure.
template_adherence.decision: Store length in metadata 'array' of key, or keep metadata 'array' empty if empty array. Only children with '#'-syntax are allowed in a valid array, with indices starting at '#0'. Both 'keyAddName("#12")' and 'keyAddBaseName("#_12")' are allowed. The 'spec' plugin will add the 'array' marker with correct length early to ensure plugin reliability. Arrays are validated by the 'spec' plugin to ensure correct metadata and structure.
template_adherence.consequences: Requires fixes and adaptations in yajl, metadata library, and spec plugin. Significant work needed to detect misstructured nested arrays. Potential semantic changes if user or dir keys override system arrays. Documentation must note that mixing array and non-array keys is unsupported and suggest moving array parts to separate child keys.

alternatives.description: Metadata arrays work by convention without special serialization or validation.
pros: Simple to implement
No changes to serialization or validation needed
cons: Inefficient detection of array length
Ambiguity in identifying arrays

alternatives.description: Use '###empty_array' as in yajl.
pros: Existing convention in yajl
cons: Does not allow efficient access to first element

alternatives.description: Store length (not last element) with prepending '#_...'.
pros: Explicit length storage
cons: Needs prepending which complicates key naming

alternatives.description: Store element after last element (C++-style).
pros: Familiar to C++ developers
cons: Does not fit well with key-value structure

alternatives.description: Use value and not metadata 'array'.
pros: Simplifies metadata usage
cons: Ambiguous representation

alternatives.description: Use metadata on all children.
pros: Explicit metadata for each child
cons: Increased metadata overhead

template_adherence.title: Bootstrap
template_adherence.context: Currently, the default backend (default.ecf) is also used for bootstrapping, which causes two problems: 1) The default backend is read with different parentKeys requiring absolute paths, which is incompatible with most plugins except dump. 2) When 'system:' is large without mount points, everything is reread twice during bootstrapping.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for a fast bootstrap process that does not unnecessarily read large files, and the problems caused by the current approach of using the default backend for bootstrapping.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to split the concepts of default (default.ecf) and bootstrap (elektra.ecf) backends. During bootstrap, only elektra.ecf is read. The default backend reading default.ecf is only relevant when no root backend is mounted. The algorithm involves trying to get system:/elektra using the file elektra.ecf (KDB_DB_INIT) and mounting the init backend to system:/elektra.
template_adherence.consequences: The new approach avoids rereading large files unnecessarily and resolves the issues with absolute paths and plugin compatibility during bootstrapping. Migration scripts are provided to upgrade from previous setups, though some old mount points may be lost if not properly exported and imported.

template_adherence.title: Deferred Plugin Calls
template_adherence.context: Calling exported functions is a primary way for coordinating plugins in Elektra. Since some plugins encapsulate other plugins, exported functions from encapsulated plugins become unavailable. Encapsulating plugins cannot implement and forward calls for every function exported by encapsulated plugins, so a generic mechanism for function calls to these encapsulated plugins is needed. Additionally, some plugins lazy-load encapsulated plugins, requiring the call mechanism to defer calls until the plugins are loaded.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
1. Plugins encapsulating other plugins shall be able to lazy-load them.
2. Callers shall not be entangled in encapsulating plugin details.
3. The encapsulation of the plugins shall not be broken.
4. The mechanism shall be generic.
template_adherence.decision: Encapsulating plugins export a function called `deferredCall` with the declaration `void elektraDeferredCall (Plugin * plugin, char * name, KeySet * parameters)`. Encapsulating plugins shall save multiple deferred calls and call the exported functions specified by `name` passing the `parameters` KeySet when a plugin is initialized in the same order as received. Plugins that support deferred calls shall have the following declaration for their functions `void somePluginFunction (Plugin * plugin, KeySet * parameters)`. The calling developer is responsible for ensuring that the called functions have a compatible declaration. Encapsulated plugins that do not export a specified function name are omitted.
template_adherence.consequences: The solution allows changing encapsulating plugin implementations without breaking callers. The called functions receive their parameters via a KeySet. While called functions could return data using the `parameters` KeySet (or a separate KeySet), there is no defined moment when the data can be collected, and defining such a moment would break the lazy-loading constraint. It is recommended to use callbacks passed as `parameters`. Callback function declarations are not limited by this decision. Functions supporting deferred calls should allow for multiple calls (i.e., they should be idempotent), leaving state at affected plugins and avoiding duplicating state in encapsulating plugins.

alternatives.description: Encapsulating plugins export a function called `getEncapsulatedPlugins`. This would break encapsulation and break lazy-loading since to return the encapsulated plugin handles they have to be loaded.
pros: Simple to implement.
cons: Breaks encapsulation.

template_adherence.title: Error Code Implementation
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of implementing error codes in a way that is suitable for cross compilation and maintainability. The problem is to find a better approach to error code implementation that balances ease of maintenance and cross-language support.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the frequency of error code changes (assumed to be rare), the need to support multiple compiled languages (C, C++, Java, Rust, Go), the complexity of code generation tools (mustache templates, CMake, Ruby scripts), and the desire to minimize effort and maintainability overhead.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to write the few macros manually and also manually write exceptions for the language bindings and mappings from Elektra's internal errors to language-specific errors. The existing code will be refactored so that error macros directly call macros. When adding a new error code, language bindings must be adapted accordingly.
template_adherence.consequences: The current bindings remain untouched, and a tutorial on how to write a binding should be written. Updates to error codes will require syncing every binding, but this should be rare. The approach minimizes effort and complexity but requires manual maintenance when error codes change.

template_adherence.title: Holes and Non-leaf values in KeySets

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support strongly hierarchical structured data, the behavior of underlying formats (some supporting holes and non-leaf values, others not), and the usefulness for migration purposes.
template_adherence.decision: Support holes and values for non-leaves in a KeySet if the underlying format allows it. If the format does not support it and no obvious workaround exists (e.g., JSON), support holes and values in non-leaves with key names starting with ®elektra.
template_adherence.consequences: Allows flexibility in key-value representation fitting the idea of key-value pairs, supports formats that allow such structures, and aids migration scenarios. However, it implies complexity in handling formats that do not natively support holes or non-leaf values.

alternatives.description: Require the data structure to always be complete, disallowing holes and non-leaf values.
pros: Ensures consistency and completeness of data structures.
Simplifies processing and validation.
cons: May not be compatible with all underlying formats.
Limits flexibility and migration capabilities.

alternatives.description: Prohibit non-leaf values entirely.
pros: Simplifies the data model.
Avoids ambiguity in key-value representation.
cons: Not all formats support this restriction.
Reduces flexibility and may complicate migration.

template_adherence.title: Logging
template_adherence.context: Both code comments and assertions are unfortunately not very popular. A quite efficient way to still get some documentation about the code are logging statements. In Elektra they are currently inconsistent and unusable. Thus there is an urge for this decision.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Logging must be disabled by default.
- Should completely compile away with ENABLE_LOGGER=OFF.
- Should support minimalistic, compile-time filtering (per modules and verbosity level?) and some sinks (stderr, syslog or files).
- Run-time problems are checked via assertions, not logged.
- Opinions about if logging should be to stderr or files differ.
- Filtering with grep is not enough.
- By default there should be no output.
- With ENABLE_LOGGER=ON only warnings and errors should be shown on stderr.
- Other sinks like syslog and file may log more (they are not immediately visible and distracting).
- Performance is not so important (because logging is usually turned off anyway).
template_adherence.decision:
Provide a Macro

```c
ELEKTRA_LOG (int module, const char *msg, ...);
```

that calls

```c
elektraLog ([as above], const char * function, const char * file,
const int line, ...);
```

and adds current function, file and line to `elektraLog`'s arguments.

`elektraLog` is implemented in a separate `log.c` file. If someone needs filtering, logging to different sources or similar, he/she simply modifies `log.c`.

Severity levels and module definitions are also specified to support structured logging.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The current VERBOSE would be turned off forever and the code within VERBOSE needs to be migrated to `ELEKTRA_LOG`.
- Logging is easy to use and flexible.
- Logger can be changed by modifying only `log.c` without recompiling other files.
- Removes dependency of `stdio.h` from every individual file to a single place.

template_adherence.title: Lookup Every Key
template_adherence.context: On structures like maps or arrays there are different possibilities which keys are looked up in the KeySet and which are simply iterated. Without any guidelines, applications would provide arbitrary inconsistent behavior.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for consistent behavior in key lookup on data structures; simplicity and ease of understanding; performance considerations; allowance for exceptions when justified.
template_adherence.decision: Every key that an application wants to use, must be looked up with `ksLookup` using a cascading lookup key.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision provides a very simple and consistent rule that is easy to understand and follow. It ensures that the `spec` is always honored. However, it requires some helper functions or support in bindings as it can be tricky to implement, for example, for arrays.

template_adherence.title: Plugin Variants
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem that some plugins cannot fully define their contract statically and their contract depends on configuration, leading to the concept of plugin variants. The issue is the lack of a way to enumerate possible plugin variants to list all functionality of Elektra.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need for user customizability (adding and suppressing plugin variants), modularity (plugins yield their own variants), performance optimization (avoid reopening plugins multiple times), and the requirement that the number of variants be bounded and fully enumerable.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to delay implementation until after version 1.0. The best candidate implementation involves providing a function `genconf` that lists all variants with essential configuration and contract changes, with mechanisms for overriding and disabling variants via keys. This approach aligns with existing APIs and allows extensibility and customizability.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision requires implementing `genconf` for several plugins, extending the PluginDatabase to list all variants, and enhancing the `kdb plugin-list` command to show variants. Currently, only configuration overrides are possible, and adding additional information to variants is not yet supported. This approach provides a consistent and extensible way to enumerate plugin variants but delays immediate implementation.

pros: Potentially comprehensive enumeration of configurations.
cons: Plugins might need to self-reference, complicating enumeration.
Elektra's specification language was incomplete and inconsistent at the time.
Does not fit with the `checkconf` approach.

template_adherence.title: Reference Counting
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses issues related to reference counting in the Key and KeySet APIs, including problems with locking not resetting when reference count reaches zero and inconsistencies in C++ API behavior. It aims to improve reference counting mechanisms to handle these problems.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to fix locking issues when reference counts reach zero, unify reference counting behavior across APIs, ensure thread safety, manage reference count limits, and optimize memory usage.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to add a second counter to Key objects: one for references and one for locking the keyname, protected by a re-entrant lock. A reference counter is also introduced for KeySets. Limits on reference counts are set with error handling on overflow, and fixed-size types are used for counters. Reference increments/decrements are managed around plugin interactions.
template_adherence.consequences: The new approach saves memory by using two smaller counters instead of one large one, adds complexity in maintaining two counters, and improves functionality and consistency. Some features are not yet implemented, such as updating bindings and automatic keyname locking.

alternatives.description: Make reference counting thread safe, which could be useful for JNI.
pros: Improves thread safety.
Potentially useful for JNI integration.
cons: Does not address all issues with locking and API inconsistencies.
May add complexity without solving all problems.

alternatives.description: Start reference counting at 1 and let keyDecRef perform keyDel.
pros: Simplifies reference counting logic.
Aligns with some common reference counting patterns.
cons: May not address locking issues.
Could lead to unexpected behavior in current API usage.

template_adherence.title: Metadata in Spec Namespace
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the problem of making storage-plugins suitable for the 'spec' namespace by ensuring they can store all metadata as specified in METADATA.ini. It highlights issues with metadata merging across namespaces and the lack of support in most file formats.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to preserve configuration file structure metadata, avoid errors from storing unrelated metadata in wrong namespaces, and support different meanings of metadata like 'array' and 'type' in different namespaces. It also considers the usability of simple storage plugins and the clarity of metadata usage across namespaces.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to store metadata unrelated to configuration file structure only in the 'spec:/' namespace. Metadata designed for storage plugins to preserve configuration file structure can be stored in any namespace. Different storage plugins or configurations should be used for the 'spec:/' namespace, such as 'ni' or TOML with 'meta' configuration. The 'kdb mount' tool will add the 'meta' plugin configuration when mounting a storage plugin to 'spec:/'.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision requires different default plugins in 'spec:/' than in other namespaces, which may cause confusion due to differing meanings of metadata like 'array'. It prevents internal metadata from leaking into configuration files and allows the use of simple storage plugins with realistic specifications. The 'spec:/' meaning of 'array=' must be stored explicitly, while other meanings should be inferred by storage or spec plugins.

alternatives.description: Store metadata in comments like the 'ini' plugin.
pros: Simple to implement.

Comments should not be modified by parsers.

alternatives.description: Designate metadata only for 'spec:/' or only for restoring configuration file formats, renaming metadata types to clarify namespaces.
pros: No merging of metadata needed.

cons: Requires renaming metadata types.
May complicate metadata handling.

alternatives.description: Do not support 'array' or 'type' if the underlying configuration file format does not support it.
pros: Simplifies storage plugin requirements.
cons: Limits functionality.

template_adherence.title: Validation
template_adherence.context: Validation plugins operate as independent blackboxes. For every backend each mounted validation plugin iterates over the whole keyset, checks every key for its trigger metakey, and validates the key. Currently all needed validation plugins need to be specified at mount-time - if additional validation is required, the backend has to be remounted with the required plugins and plugin configuration. If validation of a key fails, each plugin decides on its own how to handle the issue and proceed in ways that might be different from what is expected or desired.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The forces influencing the decision include the need to handle validation failures consistently, the desire to support multiple validation plugins per key, and the requirement to specify behavior for validation failures without remounting backends. Desired qualities include extensibility, improved error handling, and centralized control over validation failure responses.
template_adherence.decision: Use a wrapper plugin to iterate over the keyset and delegate the validation of each key to the corresponding validation plugin.
template_adherence.consequences: Validation plugins have to export their validation routine `static int validateKey(const Key * key, const Key * errorKey)` returning 1 if validation succeeded, 0 on failure. This approach centralizes error handling, allows multiple validations per key, and simplifies implementation of different error handling strategies.

alternatives.description: Extend validation plugins to allow us to specify what should happen if a key fails to validate.
pros: Allows each plugin to handle failure behavior individually.
cons: Requires changes to all validation plugins.
May lead to inconsistent failure handling across plugins.

alternatives.description: Export a validation function that allows us to use an additional plugin to decide what should be done.
pros: Separates validation logic from failure handling.
Enables flexible failure handling strategies.
cons: Adds complexity by introducing additional plugins.
May complicate plugin management.

template_adherence.title: Use of ULIDs for Database Identifiers
template_adherence.context: Postgres can autoincrement identifiers for database tables. By default this is an integer.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for scalable and concurrent-friendly unique identifiers; desire for lexicographically sortable IDs; limitations of serial integers and UUIDs.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to use ULIDs for all database IDs because they are lexicographically sortable and contain a UNIX timestamp, addressing scaling and concurrency issues better than serial integers and UUIDs.
template_adherence.consequences: Requires more customization of Postgres schemas; potential drawbacks include exposure of timestamps, lack of sub-millisecond accuracy, and some ULID implementations may not be fully reliable.

alternatives.description: Use serial integers as default Postgres autoincrement IDs.
pros: Simple and default behavior in Postgres.
Easy to implement and understand.
cons: Potential problems with scaling and concurrency.
Not lexicographically sortable in a meaningful way.

alternatives.description: Use UUIDs for database IDs.
pros: Globally unique identifiers.
Widely supported and used.
cons: Not lexicographically sortable.
Larger size and less human-readable.

template_adherence.title: 15. Phoenix Context Organization
template_adherence.context: Our Phoenix Contexts are becoming bloated. We need some organizational pattern to keep things modular.
template_adherence.decision:
We've decided to use the rules described here: [A Proposal for Some New Rules for Phoenix Contexts](http://devonestes.herokuapp.com/a-proposal-for-context-rules)

1. Resources have Schema files, and those contain only schema definitions, type definitions, validations and changeset functions
2. Every Schema has its own Secondary Context
3. The only place you use your Repos is in a Secondary Context, and only for the associated resource
4. Primary Contexts define higher level ideas in your application, and most interactions between resources will take place there
template_adherence.consequences: We will need to refactor a bit right now but this should give us a good pattern moving forward.

template_adherence.title: 21. Elasticsearch indexing
template_adherence.context: We need to push our Meadow resources to the Elasticsearch `common` index so that they can be discovered on the Digital Collections website. We also want the ability to do full text searching and faceting from within the Meadow ingest application. We investigated using Postgres through our GraphQL API, but concluded there would potentially be performance issues at scale.
template_adherence.decision:
- Meadow will write to same `common` index that Donut does
- The `source.model.application` property exists to identify source application
- Items will be indexed with a `published` `true` or `false` flag
- Requests through the `elastic-proxy` will refuse to return any unpublished items.
- For Elasticsearch requests through from the Meadow front end, the Elixir app backend will provide a plug/route and add AWS signing credentials to the request as well as filter results limiting to Meadow items only.
template_adherence.consequences: Full text searching and faceting in Meadow will be easier but the front end will now have to make requests through more than one API, increasing the complexity somewhat.

template_adherence.title: 26. reentrant-processes
template_adherence.context: Elixir provides a very high level of fault tolerance and quick restarts of failed processes, but our code has to be written properly to take advantage of this restart capability. Work Queues are one solution, but not always feasible (because iterating over and queueing up thousands of tasks can be a long-running operation in itself).
template_adherence.decision: Avoid writing long-running, iterative operations – especially those that change data – as loops. Rather, use a single, atomic initialization task to record tasks to be done (and a way to track completion), and use a [`GenServer`](https://hexdocs.pm/elixir/GenServer.html) or [`GenStage`](https://hexdocs.pm/gen_stage/GenStage.html) to handle the task (and mark it done) in atomic, transactional pieces.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Tasks become more resilient and able to survive a process/server termination, crash, restart, or replacement
- Code becomes more complicated as loops needs to be broken out into init/process/sweep stages

template_adherence.title: Use Only FileSet Digest for Preservation Object Name

template_adherence.consequences: None for the time being – this decision merely documents how Meadow works in practice.

template_adherence.title: Consume content items only from the publishing API
template_adherence.context:
When we created the ETL pipeline we originally used the publishing API messages just to flag items as updated. Then we would fetch items from the content store overnight.

We now grow the `Item` dimension every time there is an update, instead of limiting it to one record per day. Now that we do this, we rely on two sources of truth for this data: the publishing API and the content store. We should not need to make requests to the content store at all, because the content store is intended to support the frontend architecture, not ETL/analytics.

We are addressing this now because we want to change the data warehouse to store individual parts of guides and travel advice, and this is difficult to implement due to the complexity of the message processing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid reliance on the content store for ETL/analytics, as it is intended for frontend support.
- Desire to simplify data warehouse to store individual parts of documents.
- Complexity of message processing with current approach.
- Need for predictable and easy to debug pipeline processing.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use the publishing API messages to extract all content, rather than issuing an additional request to the content store.

The decision includes refactoring the publishing API message handler to transform messages into a `ContentItem` class, processing synchronously for predictability, and handling multi-part items by creating multiple item records per message.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Enables easy implementation of multi-part documents.
- Removes dependency of data warehouse on frontend infrastructure.
- Pipeline becomes more predictable and easier to debug due to synchronous processing.
- Potentially more complex message handling logic within the ETL pipeline.

alternatives.description: Continue using the content store alongside publishing API messages for ETL processing.
pros: Leverages existing content store infrastructure.
May reduce complexity in message processing by fetching full content from content store.
cons: Maintains dependency on frontend infrastructure (content store).
Increases complexity by relying on two sources of truth.
Does not support multi-part document storage easily.

alternatives.description: Fetch all content directly from the content store, ignoring publishing API messages for content extraction.
pros: Simplifies ETL pipeline by relying on a single source for content.
Content store is designed to serve frontend, so content is readily available.
cons: Content store is not intended for ETL/analytics, leading to architectural mismatch.
Potentially slower or less efficient for ETL purposes.
Does not support multi-part document storage easily.

template_adherence.title: Create a new application for UI management
template_adherence.context:
We aim to provide Content Designers and Managing Editors with the data that they need to manage content at scale and make informed decisions around content; this implies providing them with a set of pages with time series of metrics, aggregated results, and other stats from the Data Warehouse.

It is not clear yet how big/complex the solution should be because we are still in early days, but as per user research, we have found out that:

1. Users are keen to have performance data about their content
2. Users will need an application to fulfil their content management needs.

So, it seems that the application will continue having its own line of development for more quarters while we actively do user research on it.

At this moment, the next step for the development team is to build the UI for the first iteration of the tool, so we would need to decide where this new functionality should live.

We are considering two options:

Option 1: Create a new application, and access the Data Warehouse via an API.

Option 2: Add the UI to the Data Warehouse application.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to provide Content Designers and Managing Editors with data to manage content at scale.
- Uncertainty about the size and complexity of the solution as it is early days.
- User research indicating demand for performance data and an application to manage content.
- Desire to decide where the new UI functionality should live.
- Consideration of maintainability, deployment, and architectural clarity.
- Consistency with existing GOV.UK application design conventions.
- Need for a stable API and ease of evolution without impacting other tools.
template_adherence.decision: Create a new application to host the UI for Content Management at scale.

template_adherence.title: Process each RabbitMQ message in a Sidekiq Job
template_adherence.context:
Content Performance Manager is subscribed to events in PublishingAPI via RabbitMQ. At the moment we process the events synchronously:

```
class Consumer
def process(rabbit_mq_message)
# preprocess
do_process(rabbit_mq_message)
# post-process
end
end
```

Each item should run within a transaction, so we effectively need to wrap it with:

```
ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
do_process(rabbit_mq_message)
end
```

With this configuration we have had unexpected side effects because the database seems to reject the connections via the following message:

```
`PG::ConnectionBad: PQsocket() can't get socket descriptor: BEGIN
```

We debugged the database for many hours, and we got the feeling that the connections might be shared among multiple threads, and this only happens in staging because we have more RabbitMQ workers / hosts.

In any case, we had already planned using Sidekiq for processing the messages because:

1. It allows us to reuse the existing monitoring capabilities in GOV.UK
2. It supports out-of-the-box exponential backoff algorithm for retries.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to handle RabbitMQ messages reliably without database connection issues.
- Desire to run each message processing within a transaction.
- Existing problems with synchronous processing causing connection errors.
- Sidekiq offers monitoring capabilities and retry mechanisms.
- The staging environment has more RabbitMQ workers causing concurrency issues.
template_adherence.decision: Process all the events from Publishing API in Sidekiq Jobs.
template_adherence.consequences: Define a new ActiveJob job to process each message.

alternatives.description: Continue processing messages synchronously within the current consumer class, wrapping each message processing in a database transaction.
pros: Simplicity: no new infrastructure or job system needed.
Immediate processing without queuing delay.
cons: Database connection issues due to concurrent threads sharing connections.
Lack of retry and backoff mechanisms.
Harder to monitor and manage processing failures.

alternatives.description: Process messages asynchronously using Sidekiq jobs.
pros: Reuses existing monitoring capabilities in GOV.UK.
Supports exponential backoff for retries out-of-the-box.
Isolates message processing in separate jobs, reducing connection sharing issues.
cons: Requires defining new ActiveJob jobs.
Adds complexity of asynchronous processing and job management.

template_adherence.title: Store Content Item JSON that makes the dimensions grow
template_adherence.context: Each Content Item is defined by a JSON document that includes all the metadata, the links and the content details. Some days we had more than 4 million events, and each one of them implied a new version of a Content Item with no real changes. template_adherence.title: Track attribute changes through time for basepaths
template_adherence.context:
The Data Warehouse tracks changes to Content Items through time so, for example, if we change the organisation attached to a Content Item, we should know WHEN that change happened and WHAT changed.

Tracking changes not only applies to other entities associated to the Dimension Items, but also to core attributes like the `title`, `description`, `rendering-app`, or any other attribute. This is the foundation of our Data Warehouse: track changes and track performance at the same time.

In GOV.UK we can identify a Content Item on a unique way by their `content_id`.

It is the combination of a `content_id` and a `locale` what makes a Content Item unique. So on our first iteration of the DW, when we decided to use the Content Item as the `grain`, hoping to be able to track all our changes by `content_id`.

Shortly after we noticed that most of our metrics are not related to a Content Item but the `base_path` of the item; the is due to some Content Items like Guides or Travel Advice, has multiple `base_paths` and we need to track metrics at that level (sub item). This was a business requirement driven by user research.

So we decided to reduce the scope of the `grain` to the `base_path` of the Content Item, which simplified and fulfilled our user needs. It was accepted by the business that if the `base_path` changes, then we won't be able to track the series backwards. We decided to postpone dealing with this issue when we had more information about it.

As of today, we have learned more about our real needs for querying metrics. Aggregating metrics through time for a Content Item with a base_path, need to be done via its `content_id`, and there some edge cases to handle to be accurate. Unfortunately, to address this issues, we need to make our queries more complex, and the codebase is way more complicated to maintain and reason about.

The underlying problem is that we don't have a way to track our grain (base_path) through time because all the attributes can be changed, and overcoming this limitation using `content_id` and `locales` it is just not worth the effort.

In summary, we would need to provide an efficient way to:

Given a `base_path` in their latest version, select all the metrics through time, regardless of the changes to the item.

At the very end, what we are asking for is for a real unique identifier for the item, because we actually don't have it, because the `content_id` is not playing that role.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to track changes to Content Items and their attributes over time.
- Business requirement to track metrics at the `base_path` level rather than just `content_id`.
- Complexity and maintainability issues arising from current approach using `content_id` and `locale`.
- Requirement for an efficient way to query metrics through time regardless of changes.
- Need for a real unique identifier for the item to enable accurate tracking.
template_adherence.decision:
Associate a unique identifier to each item that is tracked in the dimensions item.

Each `base_path`, which represents the grain of Data Warehouse, will have a unique identifier that will never change. This ID will allow us to perform queries through time in an efficient way, and also to be accurate with our results.

On the same go, all the Content Items that share a locale will also be uniquely referenced in the Data Warehouse.

Note: We would not need to add this unique identifier if:
1. The sub-items for Content with multiple paths have a unique UID for each `base_path`. However, implementing this would require modifying each publishing application, impacting immediate delivery.
2. All the content items that have different locales but same ID have a different `content_id`.
template_adherence.consequences: It has a low impact in our codebase; we only need to generate it once (on creation), then it will be cloned with each version, so at the very end, a few lines of code with an important impact in our delivery.

alternatives.description: Not adding a unique identifier and relying on existing `content_id` and `locale` combinations.
pros: No changes needed to existing publishing applications.
Immediate delivery without additional development overhead.
cons: Cannot efficiently track metrics through time at the `base_path` level.
Queries become more complex and codebase harder to maintain.
Does not fulfill business requirements for accurate tracking.

alternatives.description: Modify publishing applications to assign unique UID for each `base_path` sub-item.
pros: Provides unique identifiers at the sub-item level.
Enables accurate tracking and querying through time.
cons: Requires modification of each publishing application.
Impacts immediate delivery timelines.
Needs wider conversation and coordination.

template_adherence.title: 5. Implement Minimal API Abstracting Grimoire
template_adherence.context:
Grimoire is great as a single source of truth due do it's well designed data-model. The APIs Grimoire exposes have the following drawbacks however:

- Clojure specific
- other languages will need to reimplement storage abstractions, which is tedious work and bug-prone
- Slightly unwieldy for the use case that seems most common for tooling authors that want to build on top of Grimoire data:
- "Give me all information about an `artifact`" (namespaces, defs, version, etc.)
- `artifact` could be something like `[bidi "2.1.3"]` here
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to make Grimoire data easy to use from multiple languages
- Current APIs are Clojure specific and require reimplementation in other languages
- Desire to provide a minimal API that abstracts Grimoire data for common tooling use cases
- Maintainability and ease of use for tooling authors
template_adherence.decision:
Implement a minimal "cache" API on top of Grimoire data with the following properties:
- File-based with single files containing different "bundles" of Grimoire data
- Files encoded in Transit format to reduce duplication
- Files can be regenerated at any time

An initial implementation exists in `cljdoc.cache` and `cljdoc.spec`. The cache structure is a map with `:cache-id` and `:cache-contents` keys.

Storage could also be implemented as a Grimoire storage implementation, but this was rejected due to the desire for a minimal API for multiple languages.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The cache map may be extended in the future, e.g., adding timestamps for validation
- Versioning of the cache format should be considered to handle changes over time
- The cache becomes a primary API, so stability and versioning are important
- Positive: Easier multi-language access to Grimoire data
- Negative: Need to maintain cache format and versioning

alternatives.description: Implement the cache storage as a storage implementation for Grimoire, supporting all Grimoire operations.
pros: Supports all Grimoire operations
Unified storage approach
cons: API would not be minimal
Less suitable for multiple languages
More complex to maintain

template_adherence.title: 8. Use CircleCI as Analysis Sandbox
template_adherence.context:
Analyzing untrusted Clojure code means loading it which should only be done in some kind of sandboxed environment. A Docker image has been created to help with this but this still requires us to run and monitor job execution. Bad actors could still trigger many builds to run Bitcoin miners and other compute-stealing stuff.

Alternatives to running Docker ourselves are AWS Lambda (probably similar compute-stealing issues) and "hacking" a continous integration service to do the job for us. More detail can be found in the [notes on Isolation](https://github.com/martinklepsch/cljdoc/blob/72da65055ab94942f33fb63b29b732e81b559508/doc/isolation.md)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to safely analyze untrusted Clojure code in a sandboxed environment to prevent misuse of compute resources, and the desire to avoid running and monitoring Docker jobs ourselves due to potential abuse and operational overhead.
template_adherence.decision: For a first version of cljdoc we will use CircleCI to run analysis for us. The result of this analysis will be made available as a build artifact which can then be loaded in a trusted environment to import data into Grimoire and build HTML (or other) documentation frontends.
template_adherence.consequences: CircleCI's free tier comes with 1500 minutes of build-time. This will not be sufficient for building documentation for the entire Clojure ecosystem. For the first few dozens of projects we should probably be fine but at some point we'll reach the cap. At this point we might want to ask CircleCI for sponsorship or look for alternatives.

cons: Requires running and monitoring job execution ourselves.
Potential for abuse by bad actors triggering many builds for malicious purposes.

alternatives.description: Using AWS Lambda for sandboxing.
pros: Serverless, no need to manage infrastructure.

cons: Likely similar compute-stealing issues as running Docker ourselves.

alternatives.description: Using a continuous integration service (like CircleCI) to run analysis jobs.
pros: Leverages existing CI infrastructure.

Free tier available for initial usage.
cons: Limited build minutes on free tier.

template_adherence.title: 11. Use Tachyons As CSS Foundation
template_adherence.context:
A primary component of cljdoc is a web application. As part of our work on this web application we regularly need to implement new UI elements or flows to support overall product development. This frontend work requires usage of CSS to specify positioning, text styles and many more variables.

A common problem with CSS is that developers try to generalize CSS classes so that they can be reused (see e.g. BEM). Arguably the intention is great but inevitably the time will come when constraints change and so the component's CSS is modified. By that time other people may have used that component in other places relying on the current implementation.

In programming languages breaking a collaborator's expectation like this can be mitigated using assertions or automatic tests but this is less easily done when working with CSS.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid breaking collaborators' expectations when CSS classes are modified, the desire for reusable and immutable CSS classes, and the goal to enable contributors to move confidently and quickly in frontend development.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt the approach of using atomic, immutable utility classes as promoted by the Tachyons library, which provides safe-to-reuse, single-purpose classes that help with consistent scales of whitespace and font-sizes, avoiding modification of CSS class definitions.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Enables safe reuse of CSS classes at the component level, promoting consistency and confidence among contributors.
Negative: Tachyons' approach may be unfamiliar and require extra effort to get contributors to buy into it.

alternatives.description: Continue using generalized CSS classes with approaches like BEM.
pros: Familiar approach to many developers.
Allows reuse of CSS classes.
cons: Risk of breaking collaborators' expectations when CSS classes are modified.
Hard to maintain and refactor CSS over time.

alternatives.description: Use atomic, immutable utility classes as promoted by Tachyons.
pros: Safe-to-reuse, single-purpose classes.
Helps achieve consistent scales of whitespace and font-sizes.
Avoids breaking collaborators' expectations.
cons: May be unfamiliar and weird to developers initially.
Requires effort to get contributors to adopt the approach.

template_adherence.title: 12. Move Away From Static Site Approach
template_adherence.context:
When starting to build cljdoc I was somewhat reluctant to accept the idea of managing a service people would rely on in my spare time. This has lead to an architecture where all docs are built on an otherwise inaccessible server and then deployed to S3. This is great for uptime but the problem with that approach quickly became obvious: any time I made a tweak to how documentation is rendered I would have to rebuild all documentation.

This is a hard blocker given the current iteration speed.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve iteration speed and reduce the overhead of rebuilding all documentation whenever a rendering tweak is made. Also, considerations about uptime and performance when moving away from static hosting.
template_adherence.decision: Move away from rendering documentation to files and serving them via S3 to rendering HTML as it is requested.
template_adherence.consequences:
Uptime and performance were a key motivation for the decision to host docs statically. Rendering docs on a server may impact both of these and will probably require some work to ensure they are not affected too much.

Performance should be solvable by putting a CDN in front of the server but so far response times are reasonable.

A CDN may also improve uptime but this of course depends on it already being cached so there's no strict guarantees.

Overall moving towards rendering stuff dynamically will allow for much faster iteration speed and make it easier for contributors to get started locally.

template_adherence.title: 13. Move to SQLite for Storage
template_adherence.context: From the start cljdoc embraced a library called `lib-grimoire`, which is a filesystem-backed database to store information about Clojure code. This foundation allowed cljdoc to focus on automation and UI work. However, with adoption and new features that don't fit `lib-grimoire`'s data model, extending it is difficult. The current data model hierarchy is Groups → Artifacts → Versions → Namespaces → Vars, stored as `.edn` files.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a more flexible schema and query language to accommodate evolving domain model; performance improvements; ease of transition to more robust databases in the future; operational simplicity.
template_adherence.decision: Move data out of Grimoire into SQLite. SQLite offers low operational complexity, flexible schema, generic query language, and better performance (up to 15x faster in tests). Data will be stored mostly as BLOBs to keep close to Grimoire's model, with key fields in columns for querying and data validity.
template_adherence.consequences: Preparations have begun (issue 58). A one-off migration will be necessary. Running both backends simultaneously is possible but better suited for high availability scenarios.

pros: Robust, scalable, and feature-rich.

template_adherence.title: Don't Ship Examples Just Yet
template_adherence.context:
I'm having second thoughts on shipping examples as one of the next main things for cljdoc. Second to a clojure.spec integration it would be a huge feature but I'm no longer sure its impact will be proportional.

Many people suggested examples as a feature for cljdoc but I think this might be more due to their familiarity with them from sites like clojuredocs.org — rather than library authors actively looking for ways to add structured examples to their libraries.

Various hypothesis that would support the addition of examples haven't been tested or verified sufficiently:

- Are examples useful for libraries? Their usefulness is mostly proven with regards to standard library functions which are tiny in scope and mostly operate on plain data. Libraries often require more complex setup.
- Will library authors add examples to their libraries?
- Is a community-repository necessary? This has been mostly introduced to allow adding examples to Clojure itself.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Uncertainty about the proportional impact of shipping examples as a feature.
- Hypotheses about usefulness and adoption of examples by library authors are untested.
- Desire to focus on features that deliver value without requiring extra work from library authors.
- Need to prioritize development efforts that scale with user base rather than author effort.
template_adherence.decision:
Don't ship examples just yet.

cljdoc is great because library authors don't have to do anything to get great looking documentation, let's keep it that way and focus on broader adoption, i.e. features that deliver value without requiring extra work from library authors.
template_adherence.consequences:
No examples. Also some freed up time that can be directed towards other features that scale proportional to users rather than already-busy library authors doing even more work.

A few days of work sunk into this and the progress is preserved in the branch `70-examples` for now.

alternatives.description: Ship examples as a main feature for cljdoc immediately, despite uncertainties about their impact and adoption.
pros: Potentially adds a highly requested feature that users are familiar with from other sites.
Could enhance documentation richness if library authors adopt it.
cons: Uncertain if library authors will add examples.
May require extra work from library authors, reducing adoption.
Risk of investing effort into a feature with unproven value.

alternatives.description: Delay shipping examples until hypotheses about their usefulness and adoption are tested and verified.
pros: Avoids premature investment in a feature with uncertain impact.
Allows focus on features that require no extra work from library authors.
Preserves development resources for higher priority features.
cons: Delays availability of a potentially useful feature.
May disappoint users expecting examples soon.

template_adherence.title: Use Nomad For Deployment
template_adherence.context:
cljdoc's deployment story has been simplistic but effective. To recap:

- During CI a zip file is pushed to S3 that contains all files to run the application
- On the live server there is systemd service that will download an archive and run it. The
version of the downloaded archive is specified via a file on the server.

Updating simply required updating a file on the server and restarting the service.

The issue with this approach however is that every time a new release was pushed to the server
the restart of the systemd service would incur up to a minute of downtime. While this generally
isn't a huge deal it discourages certain development practices that may be desirable such as
Continuous Deployment.

Our existing deployment setup (and tools used by it) are poorly equipped to handle this kind of
deployment scenario. A large amount of bash scripts would be required to start a new cljdoc server,
wait for it to become available, update nginx's upstream port, and kill old cljdoc server instances
in a repeatable, automated manner. Likely these bash scripts would be error-prone and turn into
something nobody likes to touch.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce downtime during deployment
- Desire to enable Continuous Deployment practices
- Existing deployment tools are insufficient and complex to automate
- Need for automated, reliable deployment with health checks
- Simplify operational tasks and machine images
template_adherence.decision: Implement a canary deploy mechanism for the cljdoc server application using Nomad and Traefik. These tools provide automatic SSL certificates, declarative job specifications, APIs for scheduling and cycling deployments, health checks, and simpler machine images. This approach simplifies operations and enables Continuous Deployment.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Inefficient resource allocation due to running two sets of tasks side by side, leading to instances operating at half capacity, though not problematic in practice.
- Increased complexity for developers due to the use of complex tools like Nomad and Consul.
- Atypical usage of Nomad in a single node cluster may lead to limited support or future improvements.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing systemd and Nginx setup with bash scripts to automate deployment.
pros: Familiarity with existing tools and processes
No need to introduce new complex tools
cons: High downtime during deployment (up to a minute)
Error-prone and complex bash scripts
Discourages Continuous Deployment practices

alternatives.description: Use other deployment orchestration tools or platforms (not specified in ADR).
pros: Potentially better suited tools for deployment
May offer features similar to Nomad and Traefik
cons: Not evaluated or detailed in ADR
Uncertainty about integration and benefits

template_adherence.title: A caching layer based on memoized functions backed by sqlite
template_adherence.context:
Cljdoc needs to store ad-hoc data that doesn't directly fit in its data model.
For example: Project's download stats on Clojars, Projects contributors, stars on Github etc.
We need this data to show alongside project's documentation. The source of truth for this kind of data is a service across the network.
Clojars, Github, Maven Central etc. Making multiple network calls to render documentation for a projects deteriorates performance.
template_adherence.decision:
We decide to cache this data to avoid multiple network calls. We are using `clojure.core.memoize` to provide a layer over this cache.
It enables us to memoize functions that make network calls. `clojure.core.memoize` requires an implementation of `clojure.core.cache/CacheProtocol`
to memoize return values of a function. We provide an implementation of this protocol. Our cache has two important properties.
First, it is persistent (backed by cljdoc datastore), we don't want to loose cached data on server restart.
Second, it has a TTL functionality. Some data such as Github stars and Clojars download count etc should be refreshed timely.
TTL can be used to set expiry time for a cached item.
template_adherence.consequences:
##### Performance:
By avoiding multiple network calls to render a documentation we reduce the page load latency.

##### Debugging:
Memoized functions may return data from the original data source or from cache when there is a cache hit.
For debugging purpose sometimes it could be challenging to trace where the data is coming from.

##### Security:
This cache implementation is backed by sqlite to provide persistence. It runs some raw SQL queries that are prone to sql injection attacks.
As a safety measure any value that is received from the client should not be used as a parameter to initialize this cache.

template_adherence.title: Implement our own indexing and artifacts search
template_adherence.context:
We need to be able to search (documented) projects, whether they come from Clojars or Maven Central.

See https://github.com/cljdoc/cljdoc/issues/85
template_adherence.decision:
Implement our own search, using direct integration with Lucene. Download and index artifact list from Clojars and "org.clojure" artifacts from Maven Central.

We will use Lucene as that is the absolutely prevailing solution for search in Java. Direct Java interop is quite idiomatic in Clojure; it isn't too much work as we only need to implement the parts relevant for us and not a generic Lucene wrapper.
We avoid the risk of depending on incomplete and potentially abandoned library (as happend to Clojars with clucy). And to be able to use Lucene efficiently we need to understand it sufficiently anyway.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Our search results will be different from those you get from Clojars, we won't benefit from any improvements on Clojars' side
* We will be able to search also for non-Clojars projects (and thus also make their docset available in Dash)
* Cljdoc will become slightly more complex and possibly expensive to operate (due to downloading the ~10MB index from Clojars regularly)
* New projects will not appear immediately in the search until the next scheduled indexing (unless we mitigate that somehow)
* We can fine-tune the search to prioritize the results we want

template_adherence.title: 20. Support links from docs to SCM when testing locally
template_adherence.context:
Background

Cljdoc imports documentation from clojars artifacts and SCM (Source Code Management) repositories.
The SCM is a git repository and usually one hosted on GitHub.

Documentation is imported to cljdoc from 2 distinct sources:

1. API docstrings from sources in a clojars artifact
2. Stand-alone articles such as `README.md` and documentation under `doc/**` from an SCM repository.

It is not uncommon for documentation to contain links to other files under in the SCM repository.
In these cases, cljdoc automatically rewrites these links to target the correct resource.
If the SCM document is an article that has been imported to cljdoc, the link will target the imported article hosted by cljdoc,
otherwise the link will target the hosted SCM, which in most cases, is GitHub.

Issues with Testing Locally

Before a project is released to clojars and automatically imported to cljdoc, an author will often want to preview their
documentation by running cljdoc locally.

Because cljdoc works from the published artifact, when testing locally, authors will first publish their project to their local maven repository.
This will remain true for whatever solution we choose here.

A current limitation of running cljdoc locally, as directed by current guidance, is that direct links to SCM files cannot be previewed.
Concrete examples of non-functioning links are images, source code and articles.

These broken links make it difficult to get a real sense of how docs will appear and behave on cljdoc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The ADR is driven by the need to preview documentation locally with working SCM links, to improve the author experience.
Key drivers include:
- Ability to preview documentation locally with functional SCM links
- Avoiding complex local setups
- Reflecting production behavior accurately in previews
- Minimizing maintenance burden
- Accepting minor inconvenience of pushing to hosted SCM for preview
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to complement the guidance for running cljdoc locally by importing documentation from hosted SCM (e.g., GitHub) rather than the local file system.
This involves authors committing and pushing changes to a branch on hosted SCM and ingesting docs from that branch.
This approach requires no extra local setup and provides a preview that truly reflects production behavior.
The minor downside is the need for authors to push to hosted SCM for previewing.
template_adherence.consequences:
Library authors will have guidance on how to get a fuller preview of what their documentation will look like on cljdoc before officially releasing.
Since the change is documentation only (and minor fixes discovered while testing docs), the main maintenance burden is limited to the docs.

template_adherence.title: API-008: Multi State store API design
template_adherence.context:
This decision record is to support multiple state stores support in Dapr. We agreed on the decision to introduce the breaking change in API to support multi state store with no backward compatibility.

With this change , the state API allows the app to target a specific state store by store-name, for example:

v1.0/state/storeA/

v1.0/state/storeB/

Earlier this breaking change, the API is v1.0/state/`<key>`

We have reviewed multi storage API design for completeness and consistency.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support multiple state stores in Dapr, requiring a breaking API change with no backward compatibility. Ensuring clarity in API usage for targeting specific state stores. Handling actor state store configuration explicitly to avoid ambiguity. Maintaining consistency and completeness in multi storage API design.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to introduce a new state store API version v1.0/state/`<store-name>`/ to support multiple state stores. Users must specify actorStateStore: true in configuration YAML if using actors to persist state. Multiple YAML files with unique store names are required to provide multiple stores. The breaking change requires CLI updates and explicit actor state store specification.
template_adherence.consequences: The changes enable meeting multiple state stores requirements. However, it introduces a breaking change with no backward compatibility, requiring users to update their configurations and possibly CLI usage. Actor state store must now be explicitly specified, which may cause warnings or failures if misconfigured.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing single state store API without breaking changes.
pros: No breaking changes, preserving backward compatibility.
Simpler API usage for existing users.
cons: Does not support multiple state stores.
Limits flexibility and scalability.

alternatives.description: Introduce a new version of the API alongside the old one to support multiple state stores, maintaining backward compatibility.
pros: Supports multiple state stores.
Maintains backward compatibility for existing users.
cons: Increases API complexity and maintenance overhead.
May cause confusion about which API version to use.

- State Transaction API, if the key is "transaction"

template_adherence.title: gRPC and Protobuf message coding convention
template_adherence.context: We have defined gRPC services and protobuf messages without convention, which results in the duplicated protobuf definitions and inconsistent names of services and messages. Thus, this record defines the minimum-level coding convention for Protobuf message to improve the quality of grpc/protobuf message definitions.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to avoid duplicated protobuf definitions, ensure consistent naming of services and messages, and improve the quality and readability of gRPC/protobuf message definitions.
template_adherence.decision: Use `google.protobuf.Any` data field only if the message field conveys serialized protobuf message with type url. Otherwise, use the explicit data type or protobuf message. Use `Request` suffix for gRPC request message name and `Response` suffix for gRPC response message name. Do not use `Client` and `Service` suffix for gRPC service name. Avoid duplicated protobuf message definitions by defining the messages in shared proto. Define and use enum type if field accepts only predefined values.
template_adherence.consequences: This allows us to define the consistent, readable gRPC service and protobuf message.

template_adherence.title: CLI-002: Self-Hosted mode Init and Uninstall behaviours
template_adherence.context: Changes in behavior of `init` and `uninstall` on Self Hosted mode for. Discussed in this [issue](https://github.com/dapr/cli/issues/411).
template_adherence.decision:
* Calling `dapr init` will
* Install `daprd` binary in `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr\bin` for Windows.
* Set up the `dapr_placement`, `dapr_redis` and `dapr_zipkin` containers.
* Create the default `components` folder in `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS or `%USERPROFILE\.dapr\bin` for Windows.
* Create the default components configurations for `pubsub.yaml`, `statestore.yaml` and `zipkin.yaml` in the default `components` folder.
* Create a default configuration file in `$HOME/.dapr/config.yaml` for Linx/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr\config.yaml` for Windows for enabling tracing by default.
* Calling `dapr init --slim` will
* Install the binaries `daprd` and `placement` in `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr\bin` for Windows.
* Create an empty default `components` folder in `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS or `%USERPROFILE\.dapr\bin` for Windows.
* Calling `dapr uninstall` will
* Remove the folder containing binaries `bin` the default path `$HOME/.dapr` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr` for Windows.
* Remove the docker dapr_placement if Docker is installed.
* Calling `dapr uninstall --all`
* Remove the folder containing binaries `bin` the default path `$HOME/.dapr` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr` for Windows.
* Remove the docker containers dapr_placement, dapr_redis and dapr_zipkin if Docker is installed.
* Remove the default folder `$HOME/.dapr` in Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr` in Windows.
* CLI on the init command will fail if a prior installtion exists in the default path `$HOME/.dapr` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr` for Windows.
* **There will no longer be an option for `--install-path` during init or during uninstall.**
* The `dapr` CLI by default will expect the `daprd` in `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr\bin` for Windows. The command `dapr run` will not expect the `daprd` binary to be in the `PATH` variable, it will launch the binary from the default path.
template_adherence.consequences: All other binaries except `dapr` cli and configurations that dapr needs (on running `dapr init`)will be placed in the path  `$HOME/.dapr/bin` for Linux/MacOS and `%USERPROFILE%\.dapr\bin` for Windows.

template_adherence.title: ENG-003: Test infrastrcuture
template_adherence.context:
E2E tests ensure the functional correctness in an e2e environment in order to make sure Dapr works with the user code deployments. The tests will be run before / after PR is merged or by a scheduler.

Dapr E2E tests require the test infrastructure in order to not only test Dapr functionalities, but also show these test results in a consistent way. This document will decide how to bring up the test cluster, run the test, and report the test results.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to ensure functional correctness of Dapr with user code deployments via E2E tests.
Tests must run before/after PR merges or by scheduler.
Test infrastructure must support running tests and reporting results consistently.
Support for local and CI environments.
Avoid dependencies on third-party test frameworks and self-hosted CI/test report services.
Use Kubernetes environments for testing.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to run E2E tests under Kubernetes environments, supporting local machine (Minikube) and CI (Azure Kubernetes Service).
Manual instructions or simple scripts will be provided to bring up test infrastructure instead of using kubetest.
Azure Pipeline will be used for running tests and reporting results instead of Prow and Testgrid to avoid self-hosting.
Tests will clean up and revert configurations after completion.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences:
- Tests run on Minikube locally and Azure Kubernetes Service in CI, but compatible with any RBAC-enabled Kubernetes clusters.
- Manual instructions and scripts provided for building test Kubernetes cluster.
- Azure Pipeline used for running tests and reporting results without self-hosting.

Negative consequences:
- Not using kubetest or Kubernetes standard test frameworks may reduce integration with existing tools.
- Not using Prow/Testgrid may limit some community-standard CI/test reporting features.

alternatives.description: Use kubetest and Kubernetes standard test frameworks like ginkgo, gomega for bringing up test clusters and running tests.
pros: Leverages existing Kubernetes testing tools and frameworks.
Potentially better integration with Kubernetes community tools.
cons: Adds dependency on third-party test frameworks.
May complicate test setup and maintenance.

alternatives.description: Use Prow and Testgrid for CI and test result management.
pros: Standard Kubernetes CI and test reporting tools.
Community supported and widely used.
cons: Requires self-hosting on Google Cloud Platform.
Adds operational overhead.

template_adherence.title: SDK-001: SDK Releases
template_adherence.context: Dapr exposes APIs for building blocks which can be invoked over http/gRPC by the user code. Making raw http/gRPC calls from user code works but it doesn't provide a good strongly typed experience for developers.

For Actors, language specific SDKs are written as Actor specific handcrafted code is preferred since this greatly simplifies the user experience. e.g. The C# Actor SDK shipped with the 0.1.0 release.

There will be no auto-generated code for actor SDKs, which are also handcrafted to focus on API usability.

template_adherence.title: SDK-002: Java JDK Versions
template_adherence.context:
Dapr offers a Java SDK. Java 11 is the latest LTS version. Java 8 is the previous LTS version but still the mainly used version by the Java community in 2019. What should be the minimum Java version supported by Dapr's Java SDK?

See https://github.com/dapr/java-sdk/issues/17
template_adherence.decision:
* Java 8 should be the minimum version supported for Dapr's Java SDK.
* Java 11 should be used in samples and user documentation to encourage adoption.
* Java 8's commercial support ends in 2022. Dapr's Java SDK shoud migrate to Java 11 prior to that. The timeline still not decided.
template_adherence.consequences:
* Customers running with Java 7 or below cannot use Dapr's Java SDK.
* Customers running with Java 8 are still supported, even through Java 11 is the recommended version.
* Modern language features will not be available in Dapr's Java SDK code.
* Modern JVM features can still be used since the Java 11 JVM can run Java 8 bytecode.
