template_adherence.title: Keep Server and Frontend in Same Repository
template_adherence.context: Since server and frontend development will be split up with different technologies, we have the option of also splitting up their code repositories.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to balance low overhead for bootstrapping and developer onboarding against the potential benefits of separate development and deployment flows. Consideration of the anticipated coupling between frontend and server components and the complexity of managing multiple repositories.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to keep the server and frontend in one repository. This choice is justified by the benefits of having a single entry point for code, documentation, and build/CLI tools, which reduces overhead and simplifies developer onboarding. The anticipated lack of heavy decoupling between frontend and server supports this decision. The option to split into separate repositories remains if packaging as separate services becomes necessary.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include simplified developer environment setup, unified searchability of components, consolidated command line and deployment tools, and easier visibility of changes affecting both frontend and server. Negative consequences include challenges in tracking server and frontend development separately, difficulties in packaging or provisioning individual components, and potential root directory bloat due to multiple languages and package systems.

Mitigations include building command execution helpers and preferring Go packages over shell execution.

template_adherence.title: Mock third-party APIs in CI/CD integration tests
template_adherence.context:
When running integration tests in our CI environment, how will EASi test the calls to third-party APIs? Will those API calls be mocked or will they hit the live APIs? The main driver behind this ADR is CEDAR integration tests, and a desire to sufficiently test EASI-CEDAR integration while providing fast feedback in CI. Okta tests are out of scope.

In this context, "integration test" refers to either: (1) a Cypress test (frontend/backend integration/end-to-end test); or (2) the backend integration tests that run when invoking `easi test`. "CI environment" means the network in which our CircleCI containers run. "Deployed environment" means one of our AWS environments (development, implementation, production). The term "mock" is being used loosely here, and is meant to be inclusive of other testing terms such as stub, fake, spy, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the need to sufficiently test EASI-CEDAR integration while providing fast feedback in CI, reducing operational and networking overhead in the CI environment, ensuring tests run in a clean environment, and balancing the trade-offs between test speed, accuracy, and maintenance overhead.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to mock the API calls in the CI integration tests. This choice is made to speed up tests, reduce operational and networking overhead, and rely on health check tests in deployed environments to catch integration issues with the third-party API client.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include faster tests, reduced networking dependencies and traffic load on the third-party API, and tests running in a clean environment without needing to reset test data. Negative consequences include tests not fully matching the deployed environment behavior and the need to write additional mock code.

Adds traffic load on the third-party API
Adds networking dependencies to the CI test environment

alternatives.description: Mock the API calls
pros: Health check tests that run on server startup in deployed environments already test that the deployed environment is successfully integrated with the external API

Follows a design-by-contract methodology

cons: Tests do not fully match the code as it will run in deployed environments

template_adherence.title: Use 1Password for sharing secrets

template_adherence.title: CEDAR Data Model Definition
template_adherence.context: Data records from the EASi Governance workflow need to be pushed to CEDAR, which then processes and pushes data to Alfabet. The EASi data model is frequently changing, causing high coordination costs between EASi and CEDAR teams due to tightly coupled API specifications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need to reduce high coordination and cost between EASi and CEDAR teams caused by tightly coupled API specifications; desire for a flexible data model that can evolve independently; responsibility for schema definition and parsing; need for near real-time processing and queuing for unrecognized schemas.
template_adherence.decision: The CEDAR team published a new OpenAPI/Swagger API with a loosely defined JSON 'blob' field allowing EASi to define the schema. EASi communicates the schema name with each submission. CEDAR processes recognized schemas immediately and queues unrecognized ones until support is implemented. This shifts schema definition responsibility to EASi and reduces synchronous dependencies.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive: Reduced coordination overhead, flexible schema evolution, clear responsibility for schema definition, near real-time processing with queuing for unrecognized schemas. Negative: Requires EASi to manage and communicate schema changes effectively; potential delays in processing new schemas until CEDAR updates support.

alternatives.description: Continue with tightly coupled OpenAPI/Swagger specification synchronized between EASi and CEDAR teams.
pros: Clear, strict API contract.
Immediate understanding of data model changes by both teams.
cons: High coordination overhead.
Slow to adapt to changes.
High cost of synchronization.

alternatives.description: Use a loosely defined JSON 'blob' with no schema communication or queuing mechanism.
pros: Maximum flexibility for EASi.
Minimal upfront coordination.
cons: CEDAR team may struggle to parse data.
No clear responsibility for schema definition.
Potential data processing errors and delays.

template_adherence.title: Use react-testing-library in place of Enzyme
template_adherence.context: Currently, our frontend test coverage is abysmal. It's sitting right around 30%. As a team, we've talked about being more intentional about writing unit tests, but often times unit tests were taking longer than the feature themselves. We realized that writing tests with Enzyme was making testing harder and confusing. Enzyme was released in 2016 by AirBnb. At the time, it was the gold standard for testing in the React ecosystem. However by 2019, the React API has changed dramatically and support for Enzyme has decreased with react-testing-library picking up the market share.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve frontend test coverage and make testing easier.
- Desire for better support and resources in the testing library.
- Importance of accessibility in testing.
- Avoiding confusion caused by Enzyme's shallow vs. deep rendering.
- Industry trend moving away from Enzyme towards react-testing-library.
template_adherence.decision: We decided to go with React Testing Library for all of the reasons above. We believe that it will encourage us to write more unit tests by making testing easier.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include better support and resources, easier and more accessible testing, and alignment with industry standards. Negative consequences include the need to learn a new library/API and a potentially messy transition period with tests using two different libraries.

alternatives.description: Use react-testing-library as the testing library.
pros: It has the most support in the industry, providing better resources.
Uses the DOM, eliminating confusion around shallow vs. deep rendering.
Accessibility first: provides simple ways to target elements by role or accessible name.
Developer friendly ways to test keyboard actions and focus.
Easy to use selectors.
cons: Another library/API to learn.
Transition from Enzyme to RTL might get messy with tests using two different libraries.

alternatives.description: Stick with Enzyme as the testing library.
pros: It's currently in use with existing examples.
Lots of resources online.
cons: Tests are hard to setup/write.
Online resources are outdated since RTL is preferred.
Not the recommended testing suite by React.
Selectors don't account for accessibility.

template_adherence.title: Router Configurations Storage
template_adherence.context:
The router will use some sort of configuration to decide what events are to be sent to what consumers and how. These configurations can be defined for each partner/enterprise so we could end up having 20-50 configurations.

We have these two options for storing these configurations:

-  Store configurations in Django settings (YAML configuration files).

-  Store configurations in some Django model (database).
template_adherence.decision: Keeping in mind a large number of enterprise clients, we will store router configurations in `Django configuration models <https://github.com/openedx/django-config-models>`__.
template_adherence.consequences:
Storing configurations in `Django configuration models <https://github.com/openedx/django-config-models>`__ will keep the settings files cleaner.

Django configuration models have built-in caching support which would help us address performance-related challenges.

Since enterprise customer management might be done by teams other than operators, putting these configurations in database will allow us to let customer support teams manage the settings or could also make make it self service in future.

alternatives.description: Store configurations in Django settings
cons: Having too many settings can clutter app settings and would be difficult to manage.

template_adherence.title: Transformers Architecture
template_adherence.context:
We can develop event transformers either using the “Backend” architecture or “Processor” architecture. Making the transformers “backends” will result in relatively more nesting in the configurations as this “backend” will have its own configurations.

If we decide to develop the event transformers as “processors”, it will result in less complexity in the code since the transformer can be easily appended in any backend’s (router or logger) processors’ pipeline.
template_adherence.decision: Transformers will be developed as event processors that can be added in any backend’s pipeline. Then the transformed events can be used for any purpose, either for simply logging using the LoggerBackend or to route events using EventRoutingBackend.
template_adherence.consequences: Developing transformers as processors will result in relatively less complex configurations and it would provide us wider range of use cases for the transformers.

template_adherence.title: Versioning of event transformers
template_adherence.context: Event transformers may undergo modification in future in response to consumer request, change in specification, bug fixes etc.
template_adherence.decision: Versions of event transformers will be maintained and emitted as part of xAPI and Caliper events. The "transformer version" will be a concatenation of the name of the transformer ("event-routing-backends"), an @ symbol, and the semantic version of the event-routing-backends package used to generate the event. This combined version "event-routing-backends@v(X.Y.Z)" can be found in context [ extensions [ https://w3id.org/xapi/openedx/extension/transformer-version ] ] for xAPI statement and in extensions [ transformerVersion ] for Caliper event. Transformer version number will be the semantic version of the event-routing-backends package. The event-routing-backends major version will be incremented when: Transformer is changed due to update in original specification (xAPI or Caliper); A key is removed from or renamed in the existing transformer; Value of a key is updated in the existing transformer. The event-routing-backends minor version will be incremented when: A key is added to an existing transformer; A new event is added for transformation. Minor version (Z) will be incremented when: A bug is fixed. Change logs of transformers will be maintained for both xAPI and Caliper.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include clear versioning strategy for event transformers, enabling consumers to track changes and compatibility. Negative consequences are not explicitly stated but may include overhead in maintaining versions and changelogs.

template_adherence.title: Access control of events
template_adherence.context: `event-routing-backends` can transform filtered edX events in xAPI and Caliper format which can then be routed to configured URLs. Procedure for configuring URLs of learning record consumers can be found in the :ref:`Installation`. List of supported edX events can be accessed `here`_. A method is required to filter edX events based on event name, course id, organisation id etc. or on any combination of these properties.
template_adherence.decision:
#. A method will be created that filters events that match the criteria specified in `match_params` in router configurations.

#. `match_params` is a dict comprising of one or more key value pairs.

#. A key in `match_params` need to be an exact match of a key in edX event where hierarchy levels can be separated by '.' (dot).

#. Value of a key in `match_params` can ONLY be a string or a list of strings.

#. Strings in value can be a regular expression. This regular expression will be compared with value of corresponding key in edX event to find a match.

#. `AND` relationship will be assumed between keys a for successful comparison, if more than one key is specified in `match_params`.

#. `OR` relationship will be assumed between entries of a list in value of a key, for a successful comparison.

template_adherence.title: Copy Liberator data from sftp to s3 - ADR 007
template_adherence.context:
An SQL dump of the liberator database is put in a SFTP server as a zip file by a supplier. This data is important to the parking team so we need to ingest it into the platform. In order to do this we first need to move the data from the SFTP server into the landing zone S3 bucket.

There was also the option to pay for the supplier to directly drop the file into S3.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use a lambda function to achieve this. The function will run at 06:00 UTC, triggered by a cloudwatch event, finding the file date stamped for that day then streaming it into the given S3 bucket.

It finds the file by searching for a filename pattern, if there is more than one file that matches then it will get all of them.

The connection details for the SFTP server are stored in ssm parameter store.
template_adherence.consequences: This lambda function is not currenlty reusable as we need to search for the correct file in the server before retrieving it, which is not generic. Further work could be done to seperate this out, if required.

template_adherence.title: Using Clojure functions for ETL
template_adherence.context: Akvo DASH is a system that allows the user to connect to different data sources and import the data. After that user must be able to transform it (clean, aggregate, etc). We have been looking at different open source ETL frameworks like Pentaho Data Integration, Clover ETL, Onyx Platform, Bubbles, and Kiba ETL. Some of them provide a GUI to build transformations, others require coding. There are other ones that are based on Hadoop ecosystem, which is really too much for our current needs: Luigi, Oozie, Azkaban.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the team's skills (Clojure expertise), the suitability of Clojure for data transformation, the complexity of existing ETL frameworks, and the current needs which do not require heavy Hadoop-based solutions.
template_adherence.decision: Based on the skills of the team (Clojure expertise) and the fact Clojure excels at data transformation, the decision is to use small ad-hoc functions for handling the import and transformation, which is enough for current needs. Scheduling libraries like Quartzite may be used depending on requirements.
template_adherence.consequences: The current approach will be to create ad-hoc functions to handle imports (extract) from different data sources. If a high availability (HA) setup is needed, there is an easy transition to Onyx Platform. This approach leverages team skills and keeps the solution lightweight but may require changes if needs grow.

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Formatting of response values
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need for a consistent and homogeneous solution for serializing increasingly complex response values. Historically, multiple values were separated by pipes or encoded as JSON in some cases. The current challenge is to add a new `code` property to some response types without introducing new properties as the response content grows.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The drivers include the increasing complexity of response values, the need for a scalable solution that avoids adding new properties, and the requirement to maintain consistency across different response types.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to extend the JSON-based schema and encode complex answers in a packed string format. The meaning of each response type will be reviewed to determine the encoding format (JSON, string, array, etc). Multiple responses will be encoded using a JSON array.
template_adherence.consequences: The consequences include all response types containing a single value property whose format depends on the question type, the need for processing response values in various components to visualize human-readable versions, ensuring backwards compatibility with existing responses, and potential adaptations needed for GAE test harnesses to support the new format.

alternatives.description: Continue using the historical approach of separating multiple values with pipes and JSON-encoded responses for complex types.
pros: Simple to implement for existing cases.
No immediate changes required to existing systems.
cons: Not scalable as response complexity grows.
Inconsistent encoding methods across response types.
Difficult to add new properties without complicating the format.

alternatives.description: Introduce new properties for each response type to handle additional data like `code`.
pros: Explicit representation of additional data.
Clear structure for each response type.
cons: Does not scale well as response content grows.
Increases complexity of response format.
May require significant changes in processing components.

template_adherence.title: ADR003: Avoid Default Exports and Prefer Named Exports
template_adherence.context:
When CommonJS was the primary authoring format, the best practice was to export only one thing from a module using the `module.exports = ...` format. This aligned with the UNIX philosophy of "Do one thing well". The module would be consumed (`const localName = require('the-module');`) without having to know the internal structure.

Now, ESModules are the primary authoring format. They have numerous benefits, such as compile-time verification of exports, and standards-defined semantics. They have a similar mechanism known as "default exports", which allows for a consumer to `import localName from 'the-module';`. This is implicitly the same as `import { default as localName } from 'the-module';`.

However, there are numerous reasons to avoid default exports, as documented by others before:

- https://humanwhocodes.com/blog/2019/01/stop-using-default-exports-javascript-module/

A summary:

- They add indirection by encouraging a developer to create local names for modules, increasing cognitive load and slowing down code comprehension: `import TheListThing from 'not-a-list-thing';`.
- They thwart tools, such as IDEs, that can automatically rename and refactor code.
- They promote typos and mistakes, as the imported member is completely up to the consuming developer to define.
- They are ugly in CommonJS interop, as the default property must be manually specified by the consumer. This is often hidden by Babel's module interop.
- They break re-exports due to name conflicts, forcing the developer to manually name each.

Using named exports helps prevent needing to rename symbols, which has myriad benefits. A few are:

- IDE tools like "Find All References" and "Go To Definition" function
- Manual codebase searching ("grep", etc) is easier with a unique symbol
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve code comprehension and reduce cognitive load
- Desire to leverage IDE and tooling benefits such as rename and refactor
- Avoid errors and typos caused by ambiguous default exports
- Improve interoperability with CommonJS and re-export scenarios
- Align with modern ESModules best practices
template_adherence.decision: We will stop using default exports except when absolutely necessary (such as `React.lazy` modules). A workaround exists for those that would prefer to never use `default` by using a dynamic import with a manual default assignment.
template_adherence.consequences: We will actively work to remove default exports from our codebases, being as explicit as possible. For example, connected components will be explicitly named exports. We will add tools, such as lint rules, to help migrate away from default exports.

alternatives.description: Continue using default exports as the primary export mechanism.
pros: Aligns with some existing codebases and developer habits
Simplifies import syntax in some cases
cons: Increases cognitive load due to local renaming
Thwarts IDE refactoring and rename tools
Promotes typos and mistakes
Complicates CommonJS interop
Breaks re-exports due to name conflicts

alternatives.description: Use only named exports and avoid default exports entirely.
pros: Improves code comprehension and tooling support
Reduces errors and typos
Better interoperability and re-export handling
cons: May require more verbose import syntax
Some libraries and tools expect default exports

template_adherence.title: ADR004: Module Export Structure
template_adherence.context: With a growing number of exports of packages like `@backstage/core`, it is becoming more and more difficult to answer questions such as whether an export in a module is also exported by the package, or what is exported from a directory. Currently, there is no consistent pattern for structuring exports, resulting in a mix of package-level re-exports deep in the directory tree, shallow re-exports for each directory, exports using `*`, and explicit lists of each symbol. This lack of predictability makes it difficult to reason about module boundaries and the safety of exporting symbols in given files.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need for a predictable and traceable export structure to easily determine if a symbol is publicly exported by the package, to improve maintainability and clarity of module boundaries, and to enforce consistent export patterns across the codebase.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to make each exported symbol traceable through index files down to the root of the package (`src/index.ts`). Each index file will only re-export from its immediate directory children, and only index files will have re-exports. Index files re-exporting other index files will use wildcard exports (`export * from ...`), while index files re-exporting symbols from non-index files will enumerate all exports explicitly. Internal cross-directory imports from non-index to index modules are allowed, while imports bypassing index files are discouraged but sometimes necessary.
template_adherence.consequences: The export structure in the codebase will be actively reworked, prioritizing key library packages. Tools such as lint rules may be added to help enforce the export structure. This will improve the traceability and predictability of exports but requires effort to refactor existing code and maintain discipline in following the export rules.

alternatives.description: Continue with the current mixed export patterns without enforcing a consistent structure.
pros: No immediate refactoring effort required.
Flexibility in how exports are structured.
cons: Difficult to reason about module boundaries.
Hard to determine if a symbol is publicly exported.
Increased maintenance complexity and potential for errors.

alternatives.description: Enforce a flat export structure where all exports are declared only at the root index file.
pros: Simplifies understanding of what is exported by the package.
Single point of export declaration.
cons: May lead to very large and unwieldy root index files.
Less modular and harder to maintain as the codebase grows.

template_adherence.title: ADR006: Avoid React.FC and React.SFC
template_adherence.context:
Facebook has removed `React.FC` from their base template for a TypeScript project. The reason for this was that it was found to be an unnecessary feature with next to no benefits in combination with a few downsides.

The main reasons were:

- **children props** were implicitly added
- **Generic Type** was not supported on children

Read more about the removal in [this PR](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/pull/8177).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need to keep the codebase up to date with best practices, avoid implicit children props that may cause confusion, and handle generic types properly in React components.
template_adherence.decision: To keep our codebase up to date, we have decided that `React.FC` and `React.SFC` should be avoided in our codebase when adding new code. This is supported by examples showing the preferred way to type React components without using `React.FC` or `React.SFC`.
template_adherence.consequences: We will gradually remove the current usage of `React.FC` and `React.SFC` from our codebase.

alternatives.description: Continue using React.FC and React.SFC as is.
pros: Familiar to many developers.
Simplifies typing of functional components by implicitly adding children props.
cons: Implicit children props can lead to unintended usage.
Generic types are not supported on children, limiting flexibility.
Facebook has removed React.FC from their base template, indicating it is not best practice.

alternatives.description: Avoid using React.FC and React.SFC and explicitly type props including children.
pros: More explicit and clear typing of props.
Avoids implicit children props issues.
Supports generic types properly.
cons: Requires more verbose typing in some cases.
May require developers to learn new patterns.

template_adherence.title: ADR010: Use the Luxon Date Library
template_adherence.context: Date formatting (e.g. `a day ago`) and calculations are common within Backstage. Some of these useful features are not supported by the standard JavaScript `Date` object. The popular Moment.js library has been commonly used to fill this gap but suffers from large bundle sizes and mutable state issues. On top of this, momentjs is being sunset and the project recommends using one of the more modern alternative libraries. See [RFC] Standardized Date & Time Library.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a modern date library to replace Moment.js due to its large bundle size and mutable state issues.
- Desire for immutability and usage of modern JavaScript APIs.
- Need to reduce bundle sizes and avoid multiple date libraries.
- Maintain a full feature set for date and time tasks.
template_adherence.decision: We will use Luxon as the standard date library within Backstage. Luxon provides a similar feature set and API to Moment.js but improves on its design through immutability and the usage of modern JavaScript APIs (e.g. Intl). This results in smaller bundle sizes while providing a full feature set and avoids the need for using additional libraries for common date & time tasks.
template_adherence.consequences:
- All core packages and plugins within Backstage should use Luxon for any date manipulation or formatting that cannot be easily accomplished with the native JavaScript Date object.
- Using a single date library avoids having to learn multiple library APIs.
- Having a single date library will reduce bundle sizes.

template_adherence.title: ADR011: Plugin Package Structure
template_adherence.context:
A core feature of Backstage is the extensibility via plugins. The Backstage repository is open for contributions of plugins. Even most of the core features are implemented as plugins. A plugin consists of one or multiple packages in the `plugins/` directory. Up till now, we have a simple conventions for naming plugin packages: Plugins are named `x`, with the option of having a related backend plugin called `x-backend` (where `x` is the plugin name, like `catalog` or `techdocs`). There is a need for sharing code between the frontend and backend of a plugin, between backend plugins, or components and hooks between different frontend plugins ([some examples](https://github.com/backstage/backstage/issues/3655#issuecomment-758166746)). This results in emerging plugin packages with shared code, like `packages/catalog-client` or `packages/techdocs-common`.

> There is a common phrase in software development:
> [Naming things is hard](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TwoHardThings.html)

To keep the contributed plugins consistent, this Architecture Decision Record provides rules for naming plugin packages.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for consistent naming conventions for plugin packages.
- Requirement to share code between frontend and backend of plugins.
- Distinction between core packages and plugin packages.
- Desire to maintain repository structure clarity and ownership.
- Anticipation of future needs for additional package types or rules.
- Potential tooling support to enforce naming and dependencies.
template_adherence.decision:
We will place all plugin related code in the `plugins/` directory. The `packages/` directory is reserved for core package of Backstage.

We follow this structure for plugin packages (where `x` is the plugin name, for example `catalog` or `techdocs`):

- `x`: Contains the main frontend code of the plugin.
- `x-backend`: Contains the main backend code of the plugin.
- `x-react`: Contains shared widgets, hooks and similar that both the plugin itself (`x`) and third-party frontend plugins can depend on.
- `x-node`: Contains utilities for backends that both the plugin backend itself (`x-backend`) and third-party backend plugins can depend on.
- `x-common`: An isomorphic package with platform agnostic models, clients, and utilities that all packages above or any third-party plugin package can depend on.

We prefix the package names with `@backstage/plugin-`.

This structure is based on a [suggestion in issue #3655](https://github.com/backstage/backstage/issues/3655#issuecomment-758166746).
template_adherence.consequences:
We will actively migrate existing packages that are part of a plugin to the `plugins/` folder. This affects packages like:

- `packages/techdocs-common` which should be moved to `plugins/techdocs-node` and named `@backstage/plugin-techdocs-node`.
- `packages/catalog-client` which will be part of a future `plugins/catalog-common` and named `@backstage/plugin-catalog-common`.
- While the new location of `packages/catalog-model` should be `plugins/catalog-common` we might want to do an exception here, as it's a very central package.

The limited set of rules might not be sufficient in the future. If additional packages are required, we will revisit this decision and extend the pattern.

If possible, we will add tools, such as lint rules, to help enforce the package names and dependencies between them or CLI commands to generate these packages.

The distinction between core packages and plugins helps us to setup [CODEOWNERS](https://docs.github.com/en/github/creating-cloning-and-archiving-repositories/about-code-owners) in the repository. We can set the code owners for the `packages/` folder to the core team and create additional rules (like `plugins/x*`) for plugin maintainers.

alternatives.description: Continue with the existing loose conventions without formalizing package structure or naming rules.
pros: No immediate effort required to define or enforce new rules.
Flexibility for plugin authors to organize packages as they see fit.
cons: Inconsistent package naming and structure across plugins.
Harder to share code and maintain consistency.
Potential confusion for contributors and maintainers.

alternatives.description: Adopt a different directory structure, such as placing all plugin packages under `packages/plugins/` instead of `plugins/`.
pros: Keeps all packages under a single top-level directory.
May align better with existing tooling expecting packages under `packages/`.
cons: Less clear separation between core packages and plugins.
May complicate ownership and code owner rules.
Could cause confusion about the distinction between core and plugin packages.

template_adherence.title: ADR 001: Erasure Coding Block Propagation
template_adherence.context:
Block propagation is currently done by splitting the block into arbitrary chunks and gossiping them to validators via a gossip routine. While this does not have downsides it does not meet the needs of the Celestia chain. The celestia chain requires blocks to be encoded in a different way and for the proposer to not propagate the chunks to peers.

Celestia wants validators to pull the block from a IPFS network. What does this mean? As I touched on earlier the proposer pushes the block to the network, this in turn means that each validator downloads and reconstructs the block each time to verify it. Instead Celestia will encode and split up the block via erasure codes, stored locally in the nodes IPFS daemon. After the proposer has sent the block to IPFS and received the CIDs it will include them into the proposal. This proposal will be gossiped to other validators, once a validator receives the proposal it will begin requesting the CIDs included in the proposal.

There are two forms of a validator, one that downloads the block and one that samples it. What does sampling mean? Sampling is the act of checking that a portion or entire block is available for download.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to change block propagation to meet Celestia chain requirements.
- Desire to have validators pull blocks from IPFS network rather than proposer pushing chunks.
- Need to reduce storage requirements by storing only headers within unbonding period.
- Maintain minimal breakage to public interface.
- Reduce storage interface complexity.
- Potential increase in user request processing time.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement erasure coding for block propagation, where the proposer encodes and splits the block via erasure codes and stores them in the node's IPFS daemon. The proposer includes the CIDs in the proposal which is gossiped to validators, who then request the CIDs. The proposal and vote message types are updated to include header hashes and additional fields. Disk storage is modified to store only headers within the unbonding period, with pruning options. The RPC layer will redirect block queries through IPFS. This approach reduces storage needs and aligns with Celestia's design goals, while maintaining minimal breakage to the public interface.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include minimal breakage to the public interface, storing blocks in a single place (IPFS), and reducing the storage interface complexity within Celestia. Negative consequences include potentially longer user request processing times. The design changes require updates to proposal and vote message types, disk storage interfaces, and RPC query handling. This approach may require further adjustments to maintain the public RPC interface unchanged.

alternatives.description: Continue using the current block propagation method by splitting blocks into arbitrary chunks and gossiping them to validators.
pros: No changes required to existing block propagation mechanism.
No impact on current storage or RPC interfaces.
cons: Does not meet the needs of the Celestia chain.
Proposer pushes chunks to peers, which is not desired.
Higher storage requirements as full blocks are stored.
Less efficient block verification process.

alternatives.description: Modify the block propagation to push chunks to peers but optimize chunking or encoding differently.
pros: Potentially improved performance over current method.
May require less drastic changes than full IPFS integration.
cons: Still involves proposer pushing chunks, which Celestia wants to avoid.
May not fully leverage IPFS benefits.
Storage and interface changes still needed.

template_adherence.title: ADR 1: Logging
template_adherence.context:
Current logging system in Tendermint is very static and not flexible enough.

Issues: [358](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/358), [375](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/375).

What we want from the new system:

- per package dynamic log levels
- dynamic logger setting (logger tied to the processing struct)
- conventions
- be more visually appealing

"dynamic" here means the ability to set smth in runtime.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a flexible, dynamic logging system that supports per-package log levels, dynamic logger settings, and better visual appeal. Compatibility with existing libraries and ease of use are also important.
template_adherence.decision: Adopt a new logging interface inspired by go-kit Logger interface but tailored to Tendermint's needs, implement a stdout logger with current formatting style, enable dynamic logger setting tied to processing structs, and establish conventions for key-value ordering in logs.

template_adherence.context: In the light client (or any other client), the user may want to subscribe to a subset of transactions (rather than all of them) using `/subscribe?event=X`. For example, I want to subscribe for all transactions associated with a particular account. Same for fetching. The user may want to fetch transactions based on some filter (rather than fetching all the blocks). For example, I want to get all transactions for a particular account in the last two weeks (`tx's block time >= '2017-06-05'`). Now you can't even subscribe to "all txs" in Tendermint. The goal is a simple and easy to use API for doing that.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for users to subscribe to a subset of transactions rather than all.
- Desire for a simple and easy to use API.
- Support for filtering and fetching transactions based on queries.
- Performance considerations with many queries/subscribers.
- Support for historic queries requiring indexing storage.
template_adherence.decision: ABCI app returns tags with a `DeliverTx` response inside the `data` field (for now). Tags are a list of key-value pairs, protobuf encoded. These tags are parsed and matched with current queries (subscribers). If the query matches the tags, the subscriber receives the transaction event. A new package will replace the current `events` package to allow clients to subscribe to different types of events. For fetching transactions, queries are supported but require indexing storage for historic queries.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Same format for event notifications and search APIs.
- Powerful enough query capabilities.

Negative:
- Performance issues with the `match` function when there are too many queries/subscribers.
- Potential issues with too many transactions in the database.

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated)

alternatives.description: Not explicitly stated in the ADR, but alternatives could include not supporting filtered subscriptions or using a different mechanism for event subscription and fetching.
pros: Simpler implementation.
cons: Less flexible for users.
Does not meet user needs for filtered subscriptions.

template_adherence.title: Must an ABCI-app have an RPC server?
template_adherence.context:
ABCI-server could expose its own RPC-server and act as a proxy to Tendermint.

The idea was for the Tendermint RPC to just be a transparent proxy to the app.
Clients need to talk to Tendermint for proofs, unless we burden all app devs
with exposing Tendermint proof stuff. Also seems less complex to lock down one
server than two, but granted it makes querying a bit more kludgy since it needs
to be passed as a `Query`. Also, **having a very standard rpc interface means
the light-client can work with all apps and handle proofs**. The only
app-specific logic is decoding the binary data to a more readable form (eg.
json). This is a huge advantage for code-reuse and standardization.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a unified and standard RPC interface for all apps.
- Desire to avoid burdening app developers with exposing Tendermint proof logic.
- Complexity considerations in managing one server versus two.
- Importance of code reuse and standardization for light-client compatibility.
template_adherence.decision: We dont expose an RPC server on any of our ABCI-apps.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Unified interface for all apps

### Negative

- `Query` interface

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 004: Historical Validators
template_adherence.context:
Right now, we can query the present validator set, but there is no history.
If you were offline for a long time, there is no way to reconstruct past validators. This is needed for the light client and we agreed needs enhancement of the API.
template_adherence.decision:
For every block, store a new structure that contains either the latest validator set,
or the height of the last block for which the validator set changed. Note this is not
the height of the block which returned the validator set change itself, but the next block,
ie. the first block it comes into effect for.

Storing the validators will be handled by the `state` package.

At some point in the future, we may consider more efficient storage in the case where the validators
are updated frequently - for instance by only saving the diffs, rather than the whole set.

An alternative approach suggested keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
While it might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed, it would be more complex,
and likely less efficient.
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Can query old validator sets, with proof.

### Negative

- Writes an extra structure to disk with every block.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: Keeping the validator set, or diffs of it, in a merkle IAVL tree.
pros: Might afford cheaper proofs that a validator set has not changed.
cons: More complex.
Likely less efficient.

template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to have consensus critical parameters configurable per network and evolvable over time, to avoid hard coding or local config limitations. The desire to have parameters initialized in genesis and exposed through ABCI, and to maintain sanity checks and defaults for parameters.
template_adherence.decision: No consensus critical parameters should ever be found in the `config.toml`. A new `ConsensusParams` is optionally included in the `genesis.json` file, and loaded into the `State`. Any items not included are set to their default value. A value of 0 is undefined, and -1 indicates the parameter does not apply. The parameters determine block and transaction validity via the union of all relevant parameters. The `ConsensusParams` can evolve over time by adding new structs. Specific parameters like `BlockPartSizeBytes` and `BlockSize.MaxBytes` are enforced to be greater than 0. The ABCI's InitChain and EndBlock are extended to handle these parameters appropriately.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to specify alternative capacity limits and consensus parameters without recompiling software, and the ability to change them over time under application control. Negative consequences include increased complexity due to more exposed parameters and complications in fast sync due to different rules at different blockchain heights. Neutral consequences include potential conflicts between TxSize validity checks and config's proposal size limits.

alternatives.description: Keep consensus parameters hard coded or loaded from local config only.
pros: Simplicity in implementation.
No need to extend genesis or ABCI interfaces.
cons: Lack of flexibility to change parameters per network or over time.
Requires recompilation or manual config changes for parameter updates.

alternatives.description: Load all consensus parameters from the entire genesis file without selective exposure.
pros: All parameters centralized in genesis.
Simplifies parameter management in one place.
cons: May expose parameters that the application shouldn't know about.

template_adherence.title: Decouple the PartSetHeader from the BlockID
template_adherence.context: Celestia has multiple commits to the block data via the `DataHash` and the `PartSetHeader` in the `BlockID`. As stated in the #184 issue, the `PartSetHeader` is no longer needed for this additional commitment to the block's data. However, it will still be used for block propagation during consensus in the short-medium term. Therefore, the plan is to remove the `PartSetHeader` from as many places as possible, but keep it in the `Proposal` struct.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to reduce redundant commitments to block data.
- Maintain block propagation functionality during consensus.
- Conservative approach preferred to avoid widespread bugs due to `BlockID` usage.
- Desire to enable use of well-tested 64kb sized chunks.
- Stepping stone towards better designs.
template_adherence.decision: Continue implementing the conservative design that decouples the `PartSetHeader` from the `BlockID` while retaining it in the `Proposal` struct, as described in the linked PR comment. This approach is not orthogonal to other designs and serves as an interim solution while better designs are developed.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Conservative and easy to implement.
- Acts as a stepping stone for other better designs.
- Allows use of 64kb sized chunks, which are well tested.

Negative:
- Not an ideal design as it still requires including an extra commitment to the block's data in the proposal.

Overall, this decision balances immediate implementation feasibility with future improvements.

alternatives.description: Remove the `PartSetHeader` entirely and use the existing `DataAvailabilityHeader` for block propagation during consensus, enabling parallel block propagation.
pros: Potentially cleaner design by removing redundant commitments.
Enables parallel block propagation during consensus.
cons: Requires significant changes due to widespread `BlockID` usage.
Risk of bugs when removing `PartSetHeader` from many places.
More experimental and less conservative approach.

template_adherence.context: The proposed trust metric will allow Tendermint to maintain local trust rankings for peers it has directly interacted with, which can then be used to implement soft security controls. The calculations were obtained from the TrustGuard project. Background information explains the need for tracking peer trustworthiness to improve security and reliability, and discusses challenges such as strategic oscillation by malicious nodes and the use of fading memories to balance adaptability and resilience.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to improve Tendermint security and reliability by tracking peer behavior over time, the challenge of malicious nodes adapting their behavior, the desire to maintain a history of trust data efficiently, and the requirement to preserve interval values across node executions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a trust metric that counts good and bad events over intervals, calculates a trust value using a PID-controller-like equation combining proportional, integral, and derivative components, employs fading memories for efficient history data management, and provides a trust metric store and interface for managing and querying trust metrics. The design includes configurable parameters and persistence of trust history across node executions.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling non-binary security decisions, implementing soft security controls, and providing profiling information for peer interactions. Negative consequences include the requirement to save trust metric history data across node executions. Neutral notes emphasize the need to record both good and bad events.

cons: Less nuanced security decisions

template_adherence.title: ADR 007: From Ukraine, with Love
template_adherence.context:
Currently, our fork of tendermint includes changes to how to erasure block data, minor changes to the header to commit to that data, additions to serve data availability sampling, along with some miscellaneous modification to adhere to the spec. Instead of incorporating all of these changes into our fork of tendermint, we will only make the strictly necessary changes and the other services and their code to the new celestia-node repo. Notably, we will also refactor some of the remaining necessary changes to be more isolated from the rest of the tendermint codebase. Both of these strategies should significantly streamline pulling updates from upstream, and allow us to iterate faster since most changes will be isolated to celestia-node.

Update: many of the changes described below have since been minimized or removed. Please see ADR 008 for a summarized list of changes. Notably, we removed intermediate state roots, adopted two new methods from ABCI++ instead of PreprocessTxs, and are still signing over the PartSetHeader.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to minimize changes to the tendermint fork to ease upstream updates
- Desire to isolate Celestia-specific logic to a separate process (celestia-node)
- Improve iteration speed by separating concerns
- Maintain compatibility with upstream tendermint changes
- Refactor to isolate changes and reduce coupling
- Prepare for future design changes and scalability
template_adherence.decision: Treat tendermint more as a "black box" by keeping minimal necessary changes in the tendermint fork (celestia-core) and moving other Celestia-specific logic to a separate process (celestia-node) communicating via RPC. Refactor additions to tendermint into their own packages to ease future updates and maintain separation of concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Streamlined pulling changes from upstream
- Faster iteration due to separation of functionality
- Opportunity to reconsider past design choices without starting from scratch
- Preparation for future designs
- Avoid having two p2p stacks in a single repo

Negative:
- Some computations may be performed multiple times
- Running multiple nodes instead of a single node is less convenient for node operators if full celestia-node participates in consensus

alternatives.description: Incorporate all changes directly into the tendermint fork without separation.
pros: Simpler deployment with a single node/process
No need for inter-process communication
cons: Harder to pull updates from upstream tendermint
Slower iteration due to tightly coupled code
More complex codebase with mixed concerns

alternatives.description: Use a monolithic approach with heavy modifications to tendermint and no separate process.
pros: All logic in one place
Potentially better performance without RPC overhead
cons: Difficult to maintain and update
High risk of merge conflicts with upstream
Less modular and flexible

template_adherence.title: ADR 010: Crypto Changes
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint is a cryptographic protocol that uses and composes a variety of cryptographic primitives.

After nearly 4 years of development, Tendermint has recently undergone multiple security reviews to search for vulnerabilities and to assess the the use and composition of cryptographic primitives.

### Hash Functions

Tendermint uses RIPEMD160 universally as a hash function, most notably in its Merkle tree implementation.

RIPEMD160 was chosen because it provides the shortest fingerprint that is long enough to be considered secure (ie. birthday bound of 80-bits).
It was also developed in the open academic community, unlike NSA-designed algorithms like SHA256.

That said, the cryptographic community appears to unanimously agree on the security of SHA256. It has become a universal standard, especially now that SHA1 is broken, being required in TLS connections and having optimized support in hardware.

### Merkle Trees

Tendermint uses a simple Merkle tree to compute digests of large structures like transaction batches
and even blockchain headers. The Merkle tree length prefixes byte arrays before concatenating and hashing them.
It uses RIPEMD160.

### Addresses

ED25519 addresses are computed using the RIPEMD160 of the Amino encoding of the public key.
RIPEMD160 is generally considered an outdated hash function, and is much slower
than more modern functions like SHA256 or Blake2.

### Authenticated Encryption

Tendermint P2P connections use authenticated encryption to provide privacy and authentication in the communications.
This is done using the simple Station-to-Station protocol with the NaCL Ed25519 library.

While there have been no vulnerabilities found in the implementation, there are some concerns:

- NaCL uses Salsa20, a not-widely used and relatively out-dated stream cipher that has been obsoleted by ChaCha20
- Connections use RIPEMD160 to compute a value that is used for the encryption nonce with subtle requirements on how it's used
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly have a section titled 'Decision Drivers'. However, the context and concerns raised about the current cryptographic primitives (e.g., RIPEMD160 being outdated, Salsa20 being obsolete, SHA256 being a universal standard with hardware acceleration) imply the drivers are security, modernity, performance, and standardization of cryptographic functions.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is clearly stated under the 'Decision' section with subsections for each cryptographic primitive:

- Hash Functions: Use the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 hash instead of RIPEMD160 for everything
- Merkle Trees: TODO (no decision yet)
- Addresses: Compute ED25519 addresses as the first 20-bytes of the SHA256 of the raw 32-byte public key
- Authenticated Encryption: Use xChaCha20 instead of xSalsa20 and use an HKDF instead of RIPEMD160 to compute nonces

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: PeerTransport
template_adherence.context: One of the more apparent problems with the current architecture in the p2p package is that there is no clear separation of concerns between different components. Most notably the `Switch` is currently doing physical connection handling. An artifact is the dependency of the Switch on `config.P2PConfig`.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate concerns between components, reduce dependencies of Switch on configuration, simplify implementation and testing, and allow pluggable transport implementations.
template_adherence.decision: Transport concerns will be handled by a new component (`PeerTransport`) which will provide Peers at its boundary to the caller. The Switch will use this new component to accept new Peers and dial them based on NetAddress, removing its dependency on P2PConfig.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include freeing Switch from transport concerns, enabling pluggable transport implementations, and removing Switch dependency on P2PConfig, making testing easier. Negative consequences include more setup required for tests depending on Switch. Neutral consequence is that multiplexed transport will be the default implementation.

alternatives.description: Keep the current architecture where Switch handles physical connection and depends on P2PConfig.
pros: Simpler initial setup as no new component is introduced.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: Switch is burdened with multiple responsibilities violating separation of concerns.
Harder to test Switch independently due to dependency on P2PConfig.
Less flexible transport implementations.

alternatives.description: Introduce PeerTransport component to handle transport concerns separately from Switch.
pros: Clear separation of concerns.
Switch no longer depends on P2PConfig, simplifying testing.
Allows pluggable transport implementations.
Simpler Switch implementation.
cons: Requires additional setup for tests involving Switch.
Increased complexity in initial implementation.

template_adherence.title: Secp256k1 Signature Malleability
template_adherence.context:
Secp256k1 has two layers of malleability. The signer has a random nonce, and thus can produce many different valid signatures. This ADR is not concerned with that. The second layer of malleability basically allows one who is given a signature to produce exactly one more valid signature for the same message from the same public key. (They don't even have to know the message!) The math behind this will be explained in the subsequent section.

Note that in many downstream applications, signatures will appear in a transaction, and therefore in the tx hash. This means that if someone broadcasts a transaction with secp256k1 signature, the signature can be altered into the other form by anyone in the p2p network. Thus the tx hash will change, and this altered tx hash may be committed instead. This breaks the assumption that you can broadcast a valid transaction and just wait for its hash to be included on chain. One example is if you are broadcasting a tx in cosmos, and you wait for it to appear on chain before incrementing your sequence number. You may never increment your sequence number if a different tx hash got committed. Removing this second layer of signature malleability concerns could ease downstream development.

### ECDSA context

Secp256k1 is ECDSA over a particular curve. The signature is of the form `(r, s)`, where `s` is a field element. (The particular field is the `Z_n`, where the elliptic curve has order `n`) However `(r, -s)` is also another valid solution. Note that anyone can negate a group element, and therefore can get this second signature.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to remove the second layer of signature malleability to ease downstream development.
- Desire to maintain the ability to expect a transaction hash to appear in the blockchain.
- Simplicity and ease of checking the canonical form.
- Alignment with existing solutions such as Ethereum's approach.
- Consideration of implementation effort and maintenance overhead (forking a library).
template_adherence.decision:
We can just distinguish a canonical form for the ECDSA signatures. Then we require that all ECDSA signatures be in the form which we defined as canonical. We reject signatures in non-canonical form.

A canonical form is rather easy to define and check. It would just be the smaller of the two values for `s`, defined lexicographically. This is a simple check, instead of checking if `s < n`, instead check `s <= (n - 1)/2`. An example of another cryptosystem using this is the parity definition here https://github.com/zkcrypto/pairing/pull/30#issuecomment-372910663.

This is the same solution Ethereum has chosen for solving secp malleability.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Lets us maintain the ability to expect a tx hash to appear in the blockchain.

Negative:
- More work in all future implementations (Though this is a very simple check)
- Requires us to maintain another fork

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated)

template_adherence.title: Limiting txs size inside a block
template_adherence.context: We currently use MaxTxs to reap txs from the mempool when proposing a block, but enforce MaxBytes when unmarshaling a block, so we could easily propose a block thats too large to be valid. We should just remove MaxTxs all together and stick with MaxBytes, and have a `mempool.ReapMaxBytes`. But we can't just reap BlockSize.MaxBytes, since MaxBytes is for the entire block, not for the txs inside the block. There's extra amino overhead + the actual headers on top of the actual transactions + evidence + last commit. We could also consider using a MaxDataBytes instead of or in addition to MaxBytes.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to avoid proposing blocks that are too large to be valid.
- Desire to simplify configuration by removing MaxTxs.
- Need to account for overhead beyond just transaction bytes (headers, evidence, last commit).
- Consideration of MaxBytes vs MaxDataBytes for block size limits.
- Maintainability and clarity in block size limits.
- Ensuring resource usage bounds are clear and enforceable.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to remove MaxTxs entirely and rely solely on MaxBytes for limiting block size. MaxTxsBytes is renamed to MaxBytes. When reaping transactions from the mempool, the upper bound is calculated by subtracting known overheads (amino overhead, last commit bytes, evidence bytes, header bytes) from MaxBytes. Constants for overhead sizes are defined in the types package. ChainID length is bounded to 50 symbols. A test should be written to ensure constants remain accurate if underlying structs change.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Provides a clear and singular way to limit block size.
- Reduces the number of configuration variables.
Negative:
- Requires maintenance of constants that represent overhead sizes; these must be updated if underlying data structures change.
Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using MaxTxs to limit the number of transactions in a block.
pros: Simple to understand as it limits transaction count directly.
May be easier to implement initially.
cons: Does not account for transaction size variability, potentially leading to blocks that are too large.
Leads to inconsistency between proposing and unmarshaling blocks.
Less precise control over block size.

alternatives.description: Use both MaxBytes and MaxDataBytes to limit block size and transaction data size respectively.
pros: Provides fine-grained control over total block size and transaction data size.
Can optimize resource usage more precisely.
cons: Adds complexity to configuration and understanding.
Requires additional calculations and maintenance.
May be confusing to users and developers.

template_adherence.title: ADR 012: ABCI Events
template_adherence.context: ABCI tags were first described in ADR 002. They are key-value pairs used to index transactions. Currently, ABCI messages return a list of tags describing an event during Check/DeliverTx/Begin/EndBlock, with each tag referring to a property of the event. Since there is only one list of tags, recording data for multiple events in a single message must be done using prefixes in the key space. Alternatively, groups of tags constituting an event can be separated by a special tag denoting a break between events, allowing straightforward encoding of multiple events into a single list without prefixing, at the cost of special tags to separate events. template_adherence.title: ADR 024: SignBytes and validator types in privval
template_adherence.context: Currently, the messages exchanged between tendermint and a (potentially remote) signer/validator, namely votes, proposals, and heartbeats, are encoded as a JSON string and then signed. JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and ethereum smart contracts. There are no differences between sign-request and -replies, and no possibility for a remote signer to include error codes or messages. The messages currently live in privval/socket.go and encapsulate corresponding types in types.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a binary encoding format easily parseable by hardware devices and smart contracts; need to separate sign-requests and responses; need to include error types in responses; compatibility with existing code and interfaces; clarity and maintainability of message types.
template_adherence.decision: Restructure vote, proposal, and heartbeat messages to use a binary encoding format (amino); split messages into requests and responses; include an error type in responses; remove ChainID parameter from SignBytes; implement SignBytes method returning binary marshaled bytes; further considerations for PubKey handling deferred.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: easier parsing by hardware and smart contracts, clearer separation of requests and responses, better error handling.
Negative: large refactoring, interfaces need modification, assumptions about Vote with signature need adjustment.
Neutral: none explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Continue using JSON encoding for messages and keep current message structure without separating requests and responses or including error codes.
pros: No major refactoring needed.
Maintains backward compatibility with existing code and interfaces.
cons: JSON encoding is sub-optimal for hardware wallets and smart contracts.
No error codes or messages in responses, limiting error handling.
No clear separation between requests and responses, reducing clarity.

alternatives.description: Use a different binary encoding format other than amino, such as protobuf or flatbuffers.

template_adherence.title: ADR 025 Commit
template_adherence.context:
Currently the `Commit` structure contains a lot of potentially redundant or unnecessary data. It contains a list of precommits from every validator, where the precommit includes the whole `Vote` structure. Thus each of the commit height, round, type, and blockID are repeated for every validator, and could be deduplicated, leading to very significant savings in block size.

The original tracking issue for this is #1648. We have discussed replacing the `Vote` type in `Commit` with a new `CommitSig` type, which includes at minimum the vote signature. The `Vote` type will continue to be used in the consensus reactor and elsewhere.

A primary question is what should be included in the `CommitSig` beyond the signature. One current constraint is that we must include a timestamp, since this is how we calculuate BFT time, though we may be able to change this in the future.

Other concerns include whether to include the validator address, how to represent absent votes, and how to represent votes for nil and other block IDs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include reducing redundancy and block size by deduplicating repeated fields in the `Commit` structure, maintaining necessary information for BFT time calculation (timestamp), ergonomic and debugging advantages of including validator address, handling absent votes explicitly to resolve serialization issues, and clarifying representation of votes for nil and other block IDs. Also, the need to maintain compatibility and consider future breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to deduplicate the fields and introduce a new `CommitSig` type in the `Commit` structure. The `Commit` struct will include Height, Round, BlockID, and a slice of `CommitSig` for Precommits. The `CommitSig` struct includes BlockIDFlag, ValidatorAddress, Timestamp, and Signature.

Timestamp is retained for now to avoid breaking changes. ValidatorAddress is included for ergonomic and debugging benefits despite increasing block size. Absent votes are included explicitly with no Signature or Timestamp but with ValidatorAddress to resolve serialization issues. Votes for other block IDs besides Absent, Nil, and Commit are not allowed currently, but future support may be considered.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive consequences include significant savings in block size (up to 8kB per block for 100 validators) by removing redundant fields.

Negative consequences include a large breaking change to the block and commit structure and added complexity in code to differentiate between Vote and CommitSig objects.

Neutral consequence is that Commit.Precommits no longer contains nil values.

alternatives.description: Keep the existing `Commit` structure with the full `Vote` type for each precommit, accepting the redundancy and larger block size.
pros: No breaking changes to the block and commit structure.
Simpler code as only one Vote type is used.
cons: Significant redundancy leading to larger block sizes.
Inefficient serialization and bandwidth usage.

alternatives.description: Remove the timestamp from `CommitSig` to further reduce size and complexity.
pros: Smaller commit size.
Simplifies the `CommitSig` structure.
cons: Requires more analysis and work to switch to proposer based time.
Potentially breaks BFT time calculation and consensus assumptions.

alternatives.description: Exclude ValidatorAddress from `CommitSig` to reduce block size.
pros: Reduces block size by 20 bytes per validator.
Aligns with minimal necessary data in commit.
cons: Loses ergonomic and debugging advantages.
Lite clients cannot verify commits without downloading validator set.
Requires additional access to ValidatorSet to reconstruct votes.

template_adherence.title: ADR 026: General Merkle Proof
template_adherence.context:
We are using raw `[]byte` for merkle proofs in `abci.ResponseQuery`. It makes hard to handle multilayer merkle proofs and general cases. Here, new interface `ProofOperator` is defined. The users can defines their own Merkle proof format and layer them easily.

Goals:
- Layer Merkle proofs without decoding/reencoding
- Provide general way to chain proofs
- Make the proof format extensible, allowing thirdparty proof types
template_adherence.decision: The ADR decides to introduce a new interface `ProofOperator` for Merkle proofs, allowing users to define their own Merkle proof formats and layer them easily. This interface supports handling various data types and chaining proofs without decoding/reencoding. Additionally, a protobuf message `ProofOp` is defined to interconvert with `ProofOperator` for encoding schemes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Layering becomes easier (no encoding/decoding at each step)
- Thirdparty proof format is available

Negative:
- Larger size for abci.ResponseQuery
- Unintuitive proof chaining (it is not clear what `Run()` is doing)
- Additional codes for registering `OpDecoder`s

template_adherence.title: ADR 029: Check block txs before prevote
template_adherence.context:
We currently check a tx's validity through 2 ways.

1. Through checkTx in mempool connection.
2. Through deliverTx in consensus connection.

The 1st is called when external tx comes in, so the node should be a proposer this time. The 2nd is called when external block comes in and reach the commit phase, the node doesn't need to be the proposer of the block, however it should check the txs in that block.

In the 2nd situation, if there are many invalid txs in the block, it would be too late for all nodes to discover that most txs in the block are invalid, and we'd better not record invalid txs in the blockchain too.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to check transaction validity earlier in the consensus process to avoid committing invalid transactions.
- Avoid recording invalid transactions in the blockchain.
- Maintain application state consistency.
- Minimize performance impact and redundant validations.
- Ensure compatibility with existing application logic.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to reject the proposed solution of adding a new CheckBlock method to the Application interface to validate all transactions before prevote, due to the performance impact being too great. This is documented in the Decision section with a reference to issue #2384.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- More robust defense against adversaries proposing blocks full of invalid transactions.

Negative:
- Requires adding a new interface method, necessitating changes in application logic.
- Involves sending all transaction data over ABCI twice.
- Potentially redundant validations (e.g., signature checks in both CheckBlock and DeliverTx).

Neutral:
- (No neutral consequences explicitly stated.)

alternatives.description: Implement the CheckBlock method in the Application interface to validate all transactions in a block before sending a prevote.
pros: Allows early detection of invalid transactions before consensus prevote phase.
Prevents committing invalid transactions to the blockchain.
Improves robustness against adversarial blocks.
cons: Adds a new interface method requiring application changes.
Increases performance overhead due to double validation.
Sends all transaction data twice over ABCI.
May cause redundant validations (e.g., signature checks).

template_adherence.title: ADR 033: pubsub 2.0
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses issues with the initial pubsub design, including problems with synchronous vs asynchronous message publishing, blocking vs non-blocking sends, and the choice between channels and callbacks for message transmission. It outlines the challenges of ensuring strict event ordering, handling slow subscribers, and interface design concerns.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for strict ordering of events, avoiding deadlocks caused by slow subscribers, providing an idiomatic and flexible interface for subscribers, and ensuring subscribers are aware of subscription cancellation reasons. Performance, memory usage, and ease of use are also considered.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a MsgAndTags struct for messages, change Subscribe() to return a Subscription struct with Out(), Canceled(), and Err() methods, make Out() channel buffered by default with capacity 1, provide a separate SubscribeUnbuffered() for unbuffered channels, and treat buffered and unbuffered channels differently in the publisher to avoid blocking on buffered channels. Slow subscribers on buffered channels are terminated to prevent system halts.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a more idiomatic interface, subscribers knowing message tags, and awareness of subscription cancellation reasons. Negative consequences include no concurrency in publishing messages since version 1. Neutral consequences are not explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Use synchronous publishing with goroutines per subscriber to avoid slow client problems but maintain strict ordering.
pros: Maintains strict ordering of events.
Avoids slow client problem by using goroutines.
cons: More complex implementation.
Potentially high resource usage with many subscribers.

alternatives.description: Use non-blocking sends with select and default case to skip slow subscribers.
pros: Prevents system from blocking due to slow subscribers.
Simpler implementation.
cons: Slow subscribers may miss messages without notification.
Subscribers may not know if they missed messages.

alternatives.description: Use callback functions instead of channels for message transmission.
pros: More flexibility for subscribers.
Subscribers can implement custom handling including mutexes and goroutines.
cons: Risk of memory leaks due to local scope.
Less idiomatic in Go compared to channels.

template_adherence.title: ADR 034: PrivValidator file structure
template_adherence.context:
For now, the PrivValidator file `priv_validator.json` contains mutable and immutable parts. Even in an insecure mode which does not encrypt private key on disk, it is reasonable to separate the mutable part and immutable part.

References:
[#1181](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/1181)
[#2657](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2657)
[#2313](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2313)
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to separate mutable and immutable parts of the PrivValidator file for better structure and security, and to specify store paths in configuration.
template_adherence.decision: Split the PrivValidator file into two structs: `FilePVKey` for immutable parts and `FilePVLastSignState` for mutable parts, then combine them into `FilePV`. Store `FilePV` in `config` and `FilePVLastSignState` in `data`, with file paths specified in `config.yml`.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Separation of mutable and immutable parts of PrivValidator.
Negative:
- Additional configuration needed for file paths.
Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Keep the PrivValidator file as a single structure without separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Simpler file structure.
No need to change existing methods or add configuration.
cons: Less clear separation of concerns.
Potential security and maintainability issues.

alternatives.description: Encrypt the private key on disk instead of separating mutable and immutable parts.
pros: Improved security by encrypting sensitive data.
cons: Increased complexity in handling encryption/decryption.
Does not address separation of mutable and immutable data.

template_adherence.title: ADR 035: Documentation
template_adherence.context: The Tendermint documentation has undergone several changes until settling on the current model. Originally, the documentation was hosted on the website and had to be updated asynchronously from the code. Along with the other repositories requiring documentation, the whole stack moved to using Read The Docs to automatically generate, publish, and host the documentation. This, however, was insufficient; the RTD site had advertisement, it wasn't easily accessible to devs, didn't collect metrics, was another set of external links, etc.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for better documentation hosting that is accessible to developers, collects metrics, and integrates well with the codebase. The existing Read The Docs solution was insufficient due to ads, accessibility issues, lack of metrics, and external linking.
template_adherence.decision: Use VuePress for documentation to enable metrics collection and host documentation on the website as a `/docs` endpoint, maintaining synchrony between docs and code by building the website whenever docs are updated.

Positive: The architecture is largely positive relative to prior documentation arrangements.
Negative: A significant portion of the docs automation/build process is in private repos with limited access/visibility to developers, handled by the SRE team.
Neutral: Organizational separation between Tendermint & Cosmos creates challenges about documentation placement.

alternatives.description: Continue using Read The Docs (RTD) for documentation hosting.
pros: Automatic generation, publishing, and hosting of documentation.
Existing setup familiar to the team.
cons: Contains advertisements.

Does not collect metrics.
Requires external links, causing fragmentation.

alternatives.description: Host documentation directly on the website without VuePress.
pros: Potentially simpler setup.
Direct control over hosting.
cons: May lack features like metrics collection.
