template_adherence.title: ADR 037: Deliver Block
template_adherence.context: Some applications can handle transactions in parallel, or at least some part of tx processing can be parallelized. Now it is not possible for developer to execute txs in parallel because Tendermint delivers them consequentially.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to allow applications to decide how to execute transactions (in parallel or consequentially), simplify and speed up communications between application and Tendermint, and the consideration that not all applications will benefit from the new approach and may require complete changes to their implementation.

template_adherence.title: ADR 039: Peer Behaviour Interface
template_adherence.context: The responsibility for signaling and acting upon peer behaviour lacks a single owning component and is heavily coupled with the network stack. Reactors maintain a reference to the `p2p.Switch` which they use to call `switch.StopPeerForError(...)` when a peer misbehaves and `switch.MarkAsGood(...)` when a peer contributes in some meaningful way. While the switch handles `StopPeerForError` internally, the `MarkAsGood` method delegates to another component, `p2p.AddrBook`. This scheme of delegation across Switch obscures the responsibility for handling peer behaviour and ties up the reactors in a larger dependency graph when testing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to decouple signaling peer behaviour from acting upon it.
- Reduce coupling between reactors and the network stack.
- Improve testability by reducing dependencies.
- Centralize responsibility for managing peer behaviour.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce a `PeerBehaviour` interface and concrete implementations which provide methods for reactors to signal peer behaviour without direct coupling to `p2p.Switch`. Introduce `ErrorBehaviourPeer` and `GoodBehaviourPeer` types to provide concrete reasons for stopping peers and ways peers contribute, respectively. Provide a concrete implementation wrapping the switch and another for testing purposes.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Decouples signaling from acting upon peer behaviour.
- Reduces coupling of reactors and the Switch and network stack.
- Centralizes responsibility for managing peer behaviour.

Negative:
- Initial iteration adds a level of indirection by wrapping the Switch.

Neutral:
- None specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using the existing approach where reactors directly call methods on `p2p.Switch` and `p2p.AddrBook` to signal peer behaviour.
pros: No additional abstraction or interface needed.
No changes to existing codebase structure.
cons: High coupling between reactors and network stack.
Responsibility for peer behaviour is split and unclear.
Difficult to test reactors due to large dependency graph.

alternatives.description: Introduce a different interface or pattern other than `PeerBehaviour` to decouple signalling, such as event-driven or observer pattern.
pros: Potentially more flexible or extensible.
May better suit asynchronous or event-based architectures.
cons: More complex implementation.
May require significant refactoring.
Not explored in this ADR.

template_adherence.title: ADR 042: State Sync Design
template_adherence.context: StateSync is a feature which would allow a new node to receive a snapshot of the application state without downloading blocks or going through consensus. Once downloaded, the node could switch to FastSync and eventually participate in consensus. The goal of StateSync is to facilitate setting up a new node as quickly as possible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include performance (speed of snapshot production and consumption), safety (cost of pushing invalid snapshots), liveness (cost of preventing snapshot construction), and engineering effort. Security models such as light client validation versus majority of peer validation are also key drivers. Implementation considerations include snapshot format, validation methods, and performance characteristics like random vs sequential reads and parallelizability.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to adopt an eager StateSync approach with per chunk light client validation. This approach pre-computes efficient snapshots served on demand using sequential IO and validates each chunk on receipt to avoid eclipse attacks associated with majority peer validation.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include a safe and performant state sync design supported by real-world implementation experience, general interfaces for application-specific innovation, and a parallelizable implementation path with reasonable engineering effort. Negative consequences include static scheduling lacking opportunities for real-time chunk availability optimizations.

alternatives.description: Lazy StateSync: Snapshots are produced dynamically at request time using existing data structures, with chunking done lazily and dynamically. Validation tends to be per chunk using existing tree structures. Concerns include performance of random reads and iteration.
pros: Uses existing data structures without auxiliary data structures
Per chunk validation aligns naturally with existing tree structures
cons: Performance issues with random reads and iteration
Potentially less efficient compression and snapshot serving
Validation may be less robust compared to eager approach

alternatives.description: Eager StateSync: Snapshots are produced periodically and served from disk at request time using auxiliary data structures optimized for batch read/writes. Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation.
pros: Efficient compression and serving of snapshots
Sequential IO optimizations
Supports parallelization and batch processing
cons: Requires honest majority of peers for manifest validation, vulnerable to eclipse attacks
Potentially higher storage overhead for auxiliary data structures

template_adherence.title: ABCI Evidence Handling
template_adherence.context:
Evidence is a distinct component in a Tendermint block and has its own reactor for high priority gossipping. Currently, Tendermint supports only a single form of evidence, an explicit equivocation, where a validator signs conflicting blocks at the same height/round. It is detected in real-time in the consensus reactor, and gossiped through the evidence reactor. Evidence can also be submitted through the RPC.

Currently, Tendermint does not gracefully handle a fork on the main chain. If a fork is detected, the node panics. At this point manual intervention and social consensus are required to reconfigure. We'd like to do something more graceful here, but that's for another day.

It's possible to fool lite clients without there being a fork on the main chain - so called Fork-Lite. See the fork accountability document for more details. For a sequential lite client, this can happen via equivocation or amnesia attacks. For a skipping lite client this can also happen via lunatic validator attacks. There must be some way for applications to punish all forms of misbehaviour.

The essential question is whether Tendermint should manage the evidence verification, or whether it should treat evidence more like a transaction (ie. arbitrary bytes) and let the application handle it (including all the signature checking).

Currently, evidence verification is handled by Tendermint. Once committed, evidence is passed over ABCI in BeginBlock in a reduced form that includes only the type of evidence, its height and timestamp, the validator it's from, and the total voting power of the validator set at the height. The app trusts Tendermint to perform the evidence verification, as the ABCI evidence does not contain the signatures and additional data for the app to verify itself.

Arguments in favor of leaving evidence handling in Tendermint:
1) Attacks on full nodes must be detectable by full nodes in real time, ie. within the consensus reactor.
2) Amensia attacks require an interactive protocol among all validators and are specific to Tendermint protocol.
3) Evidence gossipping is higher priority and currently handled by a distinct Evidence reactor.
4) ABCI application frameworks benefit from Tendermint handling evidence verification.

Arguments in favor of moving evidence handling to the application:
5) Skipping lite clients require tracking of all validators bonded over some period, which the app tracks.
6) Applications supporting cross-chain validation will process evidence from other chains as transactions.
7) Evidence from lite clients may be large and a DoS vector; putting it in transactions allows fee mechanisms to mitigate this.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for real-time detection of attacks on full nodes, complexity of amnesia attacks requiring protocol-specific handling, prioritization of evidence gossipping, benefits of centralized evidence verification in Tendermint, the need for historical validator set tracking for skipping lite clients, cross-chain validation requirements, and potential DoS vectors from large evidence submissions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is that evidence detection belongs in Tendermint. Points (5) and (6) do not impose large obligations on Tendermint and can be handled by the app using Tendermint libraries. Point (7) is a concern but can be mitigated by out-of-band mechanisms such as payment channels or banning client IPs sending bad data. The burden of sending large data lies on the client. A separate ADR will describe how Tendermint will handle new forms of evidence, including monitoring protocols, tracking past validators, and managing DoS issues.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- No real changes to ABCI
- Tendermint handles evidence for all apps

Neutral:
- Need to be careful about denial of service on the Tendermint RPC

Negative:
- Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during the unbonding period

alternatives.description: Leave evidence handling in Tendermint.
pros: Real-time detection of attacks on full nodes within consensus reactor.
Handles complex amnesia attacks specific to Tendermint protocol.
Supports high priority evidence gossipping via distinct Evidence reactor.
Reduces duplication of evidence verification logic across ABCI application frameworks.
cons: Tendermint duplicates data by tracking all pubkeys that were validators during unbonding period.
Potential DoS vectors from large evidence submissions that need mitigation.

alternatives.description: Move evidence handling to the application.
pros: Avoids redundant management of historical validator set data in Tendermint.
Supports cross-chain validation by processing evidence as transactions.
Engages application's fee mechanism to mitigate DoS from large evidence submissions.
cons: Complex amnesia attacks require protocol-specific handling awkward to coordinate from the app.
Evidence gossipping priority is harder to manage without Tendermint support.
Requires more changes to ABCI to support evidence as transactions.

template_adherence.title: Improved Trusted Peering
template_adherence.context:
When `max-num-inbound-peers` or `max-num-outbound-peers` of a node is reached, the node cannot spare more slots to any peer by inbound or outbound. Therefore, after a certain period of disconnection, any important peering can be lost indefinitely because all slots are consumed by other peers, and the node stops trying to dial the peer anymore.

This is happening because of two reasons, exponential backoff and absence of unconditional peering feature for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to maintain important peer connections despite reaching maximum inbound or outbound peer limits, and to overcome issues caused by exponential backoff and lack of unconditional peering for trusted peers.
template_adherence.decision: Introduce two new parameters in `config.toml`: `unconditional-peer-ids` to allow certain peers to connect regardless of max inbound/outbound limits, and `persistent-peers-max-dial-period` to limit the dial period during exponential backoff for persistent peers. This approach was chosen over modifying persistent-peers due to complexity.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Allows node operators to ensure stable and persistent connections with trusted peers by configuring new parameters.
Negative: Introduces new configuration parameters that require explanation to node operators.
Neutral: None specified.

alternatives.description: Use only persistent-peers for outbound connections and handle id-only items as unconditional peers within persistent-peers.
pros: Simplifies configuration by using existing persistent-peers structure.
cons: Requires complicated structural exceptions due to different item structures in persistent-peers.
Does not cover full utility of unconditional-peer-ids, especially for inbound connections.

template_adherence.decision: We would like to suggest a double signing risk reduction method. - Methodology : query recent consensus results to find out whether node's consensus key is used on consensus recently or not - When to check - When the state machine starts `ConsensusReactor` after fully synced - When the node is validator ( with privValidator ) - When `cs.config.DoubleSignCheckHeight > 0` - How to check 1. When a validator is transformed from syncing status to fully synced status, the state machine check recent N blocks (`latest_height - double_sign_check_height`) to find out whether there exists consensus votes using the validator's consensus key 2. If there exists votes from the validator's consensus key, exit state machine program - Configuration - We would like to suggest by introducing `double_sign_check_height` parameter in `config.toml` and cli, how many blocks state machine looks back to check votes - `double_sign_check_height = {{ .Consensus.DoubleSignCheckHeight }}` in `config.toml` - `tendermint node --consensus.double_sign_check_height` in cli - State machine ignore checking procedure when `double_sign_check_height == 0`
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Validators can avoid double signing incident by mistakes. (eg. If another validator node is voting on consensus, starting new validator node with same consensus key will cause panic stop of the state machine because consensus votes with the consensus key are found in recent blocks)
- We expect this method will prevent majority of double signing incident by mistakes.

### Negative

- When the risk reduction method is on, restarting a validator node will panic because the node itself voted on consensus with the same consensus key. So, validators should stop the state machine, wait for some blocks, and then restart the state machine to avoid panic stop.

### Neutral

alternatives.description: No explicit alternatives are discussed in the ADR text, but the changelog mentions splitting the ADR into two parts, with ADR-052 handling Tendermint Mode, implying an alternative approach to handling double signing risk reduction.
pros: Separation of concerns by splitting ADRs
cons: No detailed alternative risk reduction methods discussed

template_adherence.title: ADR 052: Tendermint Mode
template_adherence.context:
- Full mode: full mode does not have the capability to become a validator.
- Validator mode : this mode is exactly same as existing state machine behavior. sync without voting on consensus, and participate consensus when fully synced
- Seed mode : lightweight seed node maintaining an address book, p2p like TenderSeed
template_adherence.decision:
We would like to suggest a simple Tendermint mode abstraction. These modes will live under one binary, and when initializing a node the user will be able to specify which node they would like to create.

- Which reactor, component to include for each node
- full
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- *~~no privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)~~*
- validator
- switch, transport
- reactors
- mempool
- consensus
- evidence
- blockchain
- p2p/pex
- statesync
- rpc (safe connections only)
- with privValidator(priv_validator_key.json, priv_validator_state.json)
- seed
- switch, transport
- reactor
- p2p/pex
- Configuration, cli command
- We would like to suggest by introducing `mode` parameter in `config.toml` and cli
- `mode = "{{ .BaseConfig.Mode }}"` in `config.toml`
- `tendermint start --mode validator`  in cli
- full | validator | seednode
- There will be no default. Users will need to specify when they run `tendermint init`
- RPC modification
- `host:26657/status`
- return empty `validator_info` when in full mode
- no rpc server in seednode
- Where to modify in codebase
- Add  switch for `config.Mode` on `node/node.go:DefaultNewNode`
- If `config.Mode==validator`, call default `NewNode` (current logic)
- If `config.Mode==full`, call `NewNode` with `nil` `privValidator` (do not load or generation)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `privValidator` to related functions
- If `config.Mode==seed`, call `NewSeedNode` (seed node version of `node/node.go:NewNode`)
- Need to add exception routine for `nil` `reactor`, `component` to related functions
template_adherence.consequences:
### Positive

- Node operators can choose mode when they run state machine according to the purpose of the node.
- Mode can prevent mistakes because users have to specify which mode they want to run via flag. (eg. If a user want to run a validator node, she/he should explicitly write down validator as mode)
- Different mode needs different reactors, resulting in efficient resource usage.

### Negative

- Users need to study how each mode operate and which capability it has.

### Neutral

template_adherence.title: ADR 053: State Sync Prototype
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the plan and design for an initial state sync prototype in Tendermint, allowing new nodes to bootstrap faster by receiving application state snapshots instead of replaying blocks. It references background information in ADR-042 and details the snapshot data structures, ABCI interface, snapshot taking and restoring processes, and specific implementation details for the Gaia application.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for faster node bootstrap, consistency and determinism of snapshots, parallel chunk downloads, verification against trusted app hashes, compatibility with existing Tendermint and Gaia systems, and simplicity of the ABCI interface.
template_adherence.decision: The ADR chooses to implement a mandatory ABCI interface for state sync snapshots, with snapshots taken periodically, split into verifiable chunks, and restored by downloading and applying chunks sequentially. The design balances flexibility for applications with a small, general interface, and starts with a simple prototype without incremental chunk verification.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision enables faster node bootstrap and state sync, but requires applications to implement snapshotting and chunk verification. The mandatory ABCI interface is a breaking change but simplifies the design. The approach may lead to truncated block histories for state synced nodes and requires garbage collection of snapshots. The prototype approach allows future enhancements such as chunk verification and snapshot manifest on blockchain.

No changes to ABCI interface required.
cons: Slower node bootstrap.
Higher resource usage for new nodes.

pros: Less breaking change impact.

template_adherence.title: ADR 054: Crypto encoding (part 2)
template_adherence.context:
Amino has been a pain point of many users in the ecosystem. While Tendermint does not suffer greatly from the performance degradation introduced by amino, we are making an effort in moving the encoding format to a widely adopted format, Protocol Buffers. With this migration a new standard is needed for the encoding of keys. This will cause ecosystem wide breaking changes.

Currently amino encodes keys as <PrefixBytes> <Length> <ByteArray>.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to move away from amino encoding due to user pain points and performance degradation, the desire to adopt a widely used encoding format (Protocol Buffers), the requirement to define a new standard for encoding keys, and the impact of ecosystem-wide breaking changes.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to have the Cosmos-SDK define its own protobuf type for keys, allowing Tendermint to define only the keys used in its codebase (ed25519). The approach involves shifting all key encoding to protobuf, with custom marshal and unmarshal functions for amino encoding where backward compatibility is needed. This will require a hardfork upgrade and will be implemented in multiple PRs merged into a proto-breakage branch.
template_adherence.consequences: Keys will move to protobuf encoding, with amino marshal and unmarshal functions used where backward compatibility is necessary. Positive consequences include stable protocol buffer encoding, reduced amino overhead, and a large ecosystem of supported languages. Negative consequence is the requirement of a hardfork to integrate changes. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Continue using amino encoding without migrating to Protocol Buffers.
pros: No breaking changes to the ecosystem.
No need for a hardfork upgrade.
cons: Continued performance degradation and user pain points.
Lack of adoption of a widely used encoding format.
Missed opportunity to standardize key encoding.

alternatives.description: Define all key types in Tendermint instead of Cosmos-SDK.
pros: Centralized key type definitions.
Potentially simpler for Tendermint codebase.
cons: Less flexibility for Cosmos-SDK.
May not align with ecosystem needs.
Could increase maintenance burden on Tendermint.

template_adherence.title: ADR 055: Protobuf Design
template_adherence.context: Currently we use go-amino throughout Tendermint. Amino is not being maintained anymore (April 15, 2020) by the Tendermint team and has been found to have issues. Amino enables quick prototyping and development of features but does not provide the performance and developer convenience that is expected. For Tendermint to see wider adoption as a BFT protocol engine a transition to an adopted encoding format is needed. Several options are considered including Protobuf, FlatBuffers, and CapnProto.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for better performance, developer convenience, wider adoption, and support for multiple languages. The current solution (Amino) is unmaintained and has known issues. The ecosystem and tooling support are important factors.
template_adherence.decision: Transition Tendermint to Protobuf because of its performance and tooling. The ecosystem behind Protobuf is vast and has outstanding support for many languages. The design involves keeping current handwritten types and creating a /proto directory for .proto files, with utility functions to transition between handwritten Go types and protobuf generated types. This aligns with recommended file structures and enables future modularity.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include modular types in the future, less refactoring, ability to pull proto files into the spec repo, improved performance, and tooling support in multiple languages. Negative consequence is the need for developers to update proto types when updating types. Neutral consequences are not specified.

alternatives.description: Use Protobuf as the serialization format.
pros: Widely adopted and supported in many languages.
Good performance and tooling.
Proven in production for many years.
cons: Requires maintaining proto files alongside handwritten types.

alternatives.description: Use FlatBuffers as the serialization format.
pros: More efficient than Protobuf due to no parsing/unpacking step.
Tested and used in production.
cons: Not widely adopted.

alternatives.description: Use CapnProto as the serialization format.
pros: Very fast data interchange format.
Supports random access and canonical form useful for determinism.
cons: Not widely adopted in the industry.

template_adherence.title: ADR 058: Event hashing
template_adherence.context: The ADR discusses the problem of proving that certain events are part of the result in Tendermint's consensus mechanism. Before PR#4845, only certain fields were included in the Merkle tree for DeliverTx results, excluding non-deterministic fields and events. The addition of events to ResponseBeginBlock, ResponseEndBlock, and ResponseDeliverTx introduced challenges in proving their inclusion without hard-forks, which is undesirable for evolving applications.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to prove event inclusion in the consensus state without requiring hard-forks when events are added, removed, or updated. The desire to maintain application flexibility and avoid breaking changes. The need for a solution that can be upgraded via governance and is explicit rather than implicit.
template_adherence.decision: The decision was to add a new consensus parameter, Block#LastResultsEvents, which is a list of event types to be hashed into the LastResultsHash. This list can be updated via InitChain or EndBlock, allowing networks to manage event hashing without hard-forks. The initial list is empty, and applications must include events in this list to have them hashed.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include the ability to update the list of hashed events via parameter changes, avoiding hard-forks, and allowing applications to add events without breaking consensus. Negative consequences include adding another consensus parameter and increased state tracking complexity in Tendermint.

alternatives.description: Add a 'Hash bool' flag to each Event to indicate whether it should be hashed into LastResultsEvents.
pros: Makes event hashing explicit at the event level.
Allows node operators to decide which events to hash.
cons: Logic is implicit and depends on node operator's choice of application code.
Less explicit and harder to upgrade via governance compared to the chosen approach.

template_adherence.title: ADR 061: P2P Refactor Scope
template_adherence.context:
The `p2p` package responsible for peer-to-peer networking is rather old and has a number of weaknesses, including tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilites, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior. A refactor has been discussed for several years ([#2067](https://github.com/tendermint/tendermint/issues/2067)).

Informal Systems are also building a Rust implementation of Tendermint, [Tendermint-rs](https://github.com/informalsystems/tendermint-rs), and plan to implement P2P networking support over the next year. As part of this work, they have requested adopting e.g. [QUIC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-quic-transport/) as a transport protocol instead of implementing the custom application-level `MConnection` stream multiplexing protocol that Tendermint currently uses.

This ADR summarizes recent discussion with stakeholders on the scope of a P2P refactor. Specific designs and implementations will be submitted as separate ADRs.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to address multiple weaknesses in the current P2P package such as tight coupling, leaky abstractions, lack of tests, DoS vulnerabilities, poor performance, custom protocols, and incorrect behavior.
- Desire to maintain protocol compatibility initially while improving code and API.
- Interest in adopting modern transport protocols like QUIC and Noise.
- Concerns about breaking changes and resource intensity of maintaining own P2P stack.
- Stakeholder input including Informal Systems' plans and requests.
- Incremental and phased approach to refactor to manage risk and complexity.
template_adherence.decision:
The P2P stack will be refactored and improved iteratively, in several phases:

* Phase 1: code and API refactoring, maintaining protocol compatibility as far as possible.

* Phase 2: additional transports and incremental protocol improvements.

* Phase 3: disruptive protocol changes.

The scope of phases 2 and 3 is still uncertain, and will be revisited once the preceding phases have been completed as we'll have a better sense of requirements and challenges.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:

* Cleaner, simpler architecture that's easier to reason about and test, and thus hopefully less buggy.

* Improved performance and robustness.

* Reduced maintenance burden and increased interoperability by the possible adoption of standardized protocols such as QUIC and Noise.

* Improved usability, with better observability, simpler configuration, and more automation (e.g. peer/service/address discovery, rate-limiting, and backpressure).

Negative:

* Maintaining our own P2P networking stack is resource-intensive.

* Abstracting away the underlying transport may prevent usage of advanced transport features.

* Breaking changes to APIs and protocols are disruptive to users.

alternatives.description: Adopt LibP2P instead of maintaining our own P2P networking stack.
pros: Potentially good idea in principle.
Could leverage a widely used P2P networking stack.
cons: Highly breaking protocol change.
Might require forking and modifying LibP2P.
Concerns about the abstractions used.

alternatives.description: Incremental improvements to the current P2P stack, add support for pluggable transports, and gradually experiment with LibP2P as a transport layer.
pros: Allows gradual transition and experimentation.
Maintains compatibility initially.
Reduces risk of disruptive changes.
cons: Longer timeline for full adoption of new technologies.
May require maintaining legacy code longer.

template_adherence.title: ADR 063: Privval gRPC
template_adherence.context:
Validators use remote signers to help secure their keys. This system is Tendermint's recommended way to secure validators, but the path to integration with Tendermint's private validator client is plagued with custom protocols.

Tendermint uses its own custom secure connection protocol (`SecretConnection`) and a raw tcp/unix socket connection protocol. The secure connection protocol until recently was exposed to man in the middle attacks and can take longer to integrate if not using Golang. The raw tcp connection protocol is less custom, but has been causing minute issues with users.

Migrating Tendermint's private validator client to a widely adopted protocol, gRPC, will ease the current maintenance and integration burden experienced with the current protocol.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for a widely adopted, secure, and maintainable communication protocol.
- Existing use of protobuf in Tendermint making gRPC a natural fit.
- Desire to simplify integration and reduce custom protocol maintenance.
- Security concerns with previous protocols (man in the middle attacks).
- Need for language agnostic implementation.
- Upgrade path considerations for validator operators.
template_adherence.decision: After discussing with multiple stake holders, gRPC was decided on to replace the current private validator protocol. gRPC is a widely adopted protocol in the micro-service and cloud infrastructure world. gRPC uses protocol-buffers to describe its services, providing a language agnostic implementation. Tendermint uses protobuf for on disk and over the wire encoding already making the integration with gRPC simpler.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Use of an adopted standard for secure communication (TLS).
- Use of an adopted communication protocol (gRPC).
- Requests multiplexed onto the TCP connection (HTTP/2).
- Language agnostic service definition.

Negative:
- Users need to generate certificates to use TLS (added step).
- Users need to find a supported gRPC key management system.

Neutral:
- Not explicitly detailed in the ADR.

Additional consequences include a largely breaking change for validator operators requiring a coordinated upgrade path, and improved metrics and security features.

alternatives.description: JSON-RPC: Not considered because Tendermint uses protobuf extensively making gRPC a natural choice.
pros: JSON-RPC is a simpler and widely known protocol.
cons: Not aligned with Tendermint's existing protobuf usage.
Less efficient and less feature rich compared to gRPC.

template_adherence.title: ADR 064: Batch Verification
template_adherence.context:
Tendermint uses public private key cryptography for validator signing. When a block is proposed and voted on validators sign a message representing acceptance of a block, rejection is signaled via a nil vote. These signatures are also used to verify previous blocks are correct if a node is syncing. Currently, Tendermint requires each signature to be verified individually, this leads to a slow down of block times.

Batch Verification is the process of taking many messages, keys, and signatures adding them together and verifying them all at once. The public key can be the same in which case it would mean a single user is signing many messages. In our case each public key is unique, each validator has their own and contribute a unique message. The algorithm can vary from curve to curve but the performance benefit, over single verifying messages, public keys and signatures is shared.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to improve verification speed of signatures in Tendermint.
- Current individual signature verification slows down block times.
- Desire to leverage batch verification to improve performance.
- Consideration of alternative approaches like signature aggregation.
- Compatibility with existing validator signing behavior (unique messages per validator).
- Minimizing user errors in verification API usage.
- Support for curves that allow batch verification (starting with ed25519).
template_adherence.decision: Adopt Batch Verification by introducing a new interface with methods to add entries and verify them in batch. This approach improves verification speed while minimizing user errors. The batch verification will be used in consensus and block syncing, falling back to single verification if batch verification fails. Signature aggregation was considered but rejected due to unique messages per validator preventing aggregation benefits.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Positive: Faster verification times for curves that support batch verification.
- Negative: No way to identify which specific key failed verification in batch mode.
- Negative: On batch verification failure, must revert to single signature verification, potentially impacting performance.
- Neutral: No impact on users other than improved verification speed.
- Implementation complexity added by new interface and batch verification logic.
- Initial support limited to ed25519 curve.

alternatives.description: Signature aggregation as an alternative to batch verification.
pros: Leads to fast verification and smaller block sizes.
cons: At the time of writing, ongoing work to enable signature aggregation in Tendermint.
Every validator signs a unique message, preventing aggregation before verification.
Implementing signature aggregation with BLS could cause a potential slow down of 10x-100x in verification speeds due to unique messages.

template_adherence.title: ADR 66: End-to-End Testing
template_adherence.context:
The current set of end-to-end tests under `test/` are very limited, mostly focusing on P2P testing in a standard configuration. They do not test various configurations (e.g. fast sync reactor versions, state sync, block pruning, genesis vs InitChain setup), nor do they test various network topologies (e.g. sentry node architecture). This leads to poor test coverage, which has caused several serious bugs to go unnoticed.

We need an end-to-end test suite that can run a large number of combinations of configuration options, genesis settings, network topologies, ABCI interactions, and failure scenarios and check that the network is still functional. This ADR outlines the basic requirements and design for such a system.

This ADR will not cover comprehensive chaos testing, only a few simple scenarios (e.g. abrupt process termination and network partitioning). Chaos testing of the core consensus algorithm should be implemented e.g. via Jepsen tests or a similar framework, or alternatively be added to these end-to-end tests at a later time. Similarly, malicious or adversarial behavior is out of scope for the first implementation, but may be added later.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for comprehensive end-to-end test coverage across multiple configurations and network topologies.
- Limitations of current test coverage leading to unnoticed serious bugs.
- Feasibility constraints due to the large number of possible test combinations.
- Desire to have reproducible test environments locally and in CI.
- Scope limitations excluding comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing initially.
- Engineering resource considerations for building a custom test framework.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to implement a comprehensive end-to-end test suite that covers a broad range of configurations, network topologies, and failure scenarios. The test suite will be designed to run in Docker Compose environments for reproducibility and ease of debugging. It will focus on black-box testing via RPC interfaces, avoiding internal implementation details. The testnets will be configured via YAML files, and a custom test runner will orchestrate the tests. Comprehensive chaos and adversarial testing are out of scope for the initial implementation but may be added later.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Comprehensive end-to-end test coverage of basic Tendermint functionality, exercising common code paths as users would.
- Test environments can be easily reproduced locally and debugged with standard tooling.

Negative:
- Limited coverage of consensus correctness testing (e.g., Jepsen).
- No coverage of malicious or adversarial behavior initially.
- Need to develop a custom test framework, requiring engineering resources.
- Potentially slower CI times depending on tests run.
- Operational costs and overhead (infrastructure and maintenance).

Neutral:
- No support for alternative infrastructure platforms like Kubernetes or VMs initially.

template_adherence.title: ADR 067: Mempool Refactor
template_adherence.context: The ADR describes the need to refactor the Tendermint Core mempool to support prioritized transaction handling rather than the current FIFO queue. It outlines the challenges with the current design and the desired properties for the new mempool design, including application-determined priority, efficient concurrent access, eviction policies, and extensibility.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include the need for transaction prioritization by applications, efficient concurrent reads and writes, efficient transaction selection by priority for block proposals, fixed mempool capacity with eviction of lower priority transactions, efficient gossiping by priority, operator-configurable TTL for transactions, and extensibility for future features like replace-by-priority and multiple pending transactions per sender.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to introduce new fields `priority` and `sender` in the `ResponseCheckTx` type and implement a new versioned mempool reactor `v1` that maintains a mapping from senders to transactions and indexes transactions by priority using a thread-safe priority queue (max heap). The existing FIFO linked list is kept for gossiping. Eviction of lower priority transactions is implemented when the mempool is full.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enabling transaction prioritization by applications. Negative consequences include increased size of the `ResponseCheckTx` type, loss of causal ordering, and potential transaction failures due to priority-based reordering. Neutral consequences include possible eviction of transactions that passed `CheckTx` if higher priority transactions arrive later.

template_adherence.title: ADR 068: Reverse Sync
template_adherence.context:
The advent of state sync and block pruning gave rise to the opportunity for full nodes to participate in consensus without needing complete block history. This also introduced a problem with respect to evidence handling. Nodes that didn't have all the blocks within the evidence age were incapable of validating evidence, thus halting if that evidence was committed on chain.

[RFC005](https://github.com/tendermint/spec/blob/master/rfc/005-reverse-sync.md) was published in response to this problem and modified the spec to add a minimum block history invariant. This predominantly sought to extend state sync so that it was capable of fetching and storing the `Header`, `Commit` and `ValidatorSet` (essentially a `LightBlock`) of the last `n` heights, where `n` was calculated based from the evidence age.

This ADR sets out to describe the design of this state sync extension as well as modifications to the light client provider and the merging of tm store.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to allow full nodes to participate in consensus without complete block history, specifically to handle evidence validation properly.
The requirement to extend state sync to fetch and store recent light blocks to cover the evidence age.
The desire to integrate reverse sync into the state sync reactor and provide a P2P light client provider.
Maintainability concerns due to added code complexity.
The need to prevent pruning of blocks within the evidence age.
template_adherence.decision:
The state sync reactor will be extended by introducing two new P2P messages (LightBlockRequest and LightBlockResponse) and a new channel to support a "reverse sync" protocol that fetches, verifies, and stores prior light blocks.
This enables nodes to safely participate in consensus and validate evidence.
A new light client provider will be implemented to use the P2P stack instead of RPC.
Integration with state sync will involve giving state sync access to StateStore and BlockStore for persistence.
The design includes components like Dispatcher and BlockQueue to manage concurrent requests and serialization.
Pruning will be restricted for blocks within the evidence age.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive:
- Nodes have sufficient history to validate all types of evidence.
- State syncing nodes can use the P2P layer for light client verification, potentially improving UX and speed.

Negative:
- Increased code complexity and maintenance burden.

Neutral:
- None explicitly stated.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly discussed in the ADR, but implicitly the alternative would be to not implement reverse sync and continue with existing state sync mechanisms, which leads to nodes being unable to validate evidence if they lack block history.
pros: Simplicity, no additional code or protocol changes.
cons: Nodes cannot validate evidence without full block history, leading to halting consensus.
Does not solve the problem introduced by state sync and block pruning.

template_adherence.title: ADR 069: Flexible Node Initialization
template_adherence.context: The ADR addresses the need to support more flexible node initialization in the Tendermint project, particularly to reduce API surface area and internalize interfaces while still allowing operational patterns such as introspection and component replacement. The current tightly coupled node implementation limits modularity and maintainability, motivating a redesign of node initialization to be more flexible and less hard-coded.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is driven by the need to reduce coupling between components, improve maintainability, support future extensibility for component replacement, and avoid breaking existing user-facing APIs. Constraints include minimizing complexity, not requiring a full generic service orchestration framework, and maintaining backward compatibility for users.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to refactor the node package so that packages are responsible for their own initialization, minimize code in the node package, reduce direct coupling, and iterate on a flexible internal framework for node initialization. Reactors should not expose interfaces within the node implementation. The refactoring should be opaque to users and not require reevaluation of the service.Service framework. No proactive system for injecting components is provided, but future retrofit is possible. Priority is given to implementing p2p-based statesync reactor to avoid custom state-sync injection.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved maintainability, easier addition of services, ability to replace default components without vendoring, and thorough testing. Negative consequences include increased reliance on the service.Service interface, which has limitations, and a minimal scope that leaves many features for future work. template_adherence.title: Constructs and Patterns
template_adherence.context:
The AWS CDK provides components with two levels of abstraction. CfnComponents map directly to cloudformation resources whilst constructs are a higher abstraction which may create multiple related resources. For example, the `AutoScalingGroup` construct will also create `LaunchConfig` and `SecurityGroup` resources. This is a useful abstraction as it allows you to define all the components required for a particular concept in one place.

Further to this, various patterns are available - both AWS supported and open source. These patterns define an entire stack, based around common template. For example, a `EC2App` pattern might provide an `AutoScalingGroup`, `LoadBalancer` and the required `Roles` and `SecurityGroups`. These patterns are likely composed of multiple constrcuts (rather than CfnComponents) under-the-hood.

This library aims to standardise and simplify the process of setting up Guardian stacks by providing reusable components but what level(s) of abstraction should be provided?
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision is influenced by the need to provide reusable components with sensible defaults, flexibility for teams to architect their stacks, standardisation, ease of use for common stack types, and maintenance complexity.
template_adherence.decision:
This library should define a number of Guardian flavoured constructs which extend those provided by the AWS CDK library with Guardian defaults baked in. For example, a `GuAutoScalingGroup` and `GuApplicationLoadBalancer`.

Where those constructs are used in multiple ways, it should provide utlity classes for any common usages. For example, for the `Policy` constructs: `GuSSMPolicy`, `GuLogShippingPolicy` and `GuGetS3ObjectPolicy`

Built on top of those, it should also provide a number of patterns to cover common Guardian stack architectures. For example, `GuEC2App` and `GuLambdaApp` patterns. These patterns should be the encouraged entry point to the library, with the constructs only used outside of standard cases.
template_adherence.consequences: Providing patterns makes the developer experience far quicker and simpler in cases where developers are standing up standard stack types. From a maintainence viewpoint, it adds some complexity in designing, building and maintaing the patterns.

alternatives.description: Provide Constructs only
pros: Gives teams components with sensible Guardian settings by default.
Allows flexibility to architect stacks as teams choose.
cons: Teams must architect stacks themselves, potentially more effort.
Less standardisation compared to providing patterns.

alternatives.description: Provide both Constructs and Patterns
pros: Gives teams flexibility to use constructs or stand up standard stacks quickly.
Brings greater standardisation.
Allows more complex features to be built in "for free".
cons: Adds complexity in designing, building, and maintaining patterns.

template_adherence.title: Package Manager
template_adherence.context:
The project can either use `npm` or `yarn` as the package manager. This should be an either/or situation but a number of issues have been encountered when using `yarn` including:

- `yarn login` still prompts for a password at release time which doesn't work with `np`
- publishing with `yarn` leaves only the `index.js` file in the `lib` directory
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers are implied through the context and positions sections: the need for a consistent package manager choice, issues encountered with `yarn`, the wider use of `yarn` in the department, and the desire to abstract package manager usage to improve developer experience and consistency.
template_adherence.decision:
Use npm with the script pattern.

Any common tasks (e.g. `lint`, `test`, `build`) should have a script defined in the `script` directory. Any scripts run by CI should also be stored in this directory.
template_adherence.consequences:
Using the script pattern allows us to present a consistent interface whilst using whichever tool works best. Further to that, it makes it easier for new developers coming to a project as they don't have to know the specific commands to perform each task. Instead, they can easily see the available commands and run them simply by name.

This pattern becomes increasingly useful the more projects it is used in as developers get used to going to the `./script` directory rather than running command directly. Without common usage across the team it risks becoming a third standard rather than a replacement for the previous two ([Relevant XKCD](https://xkcd.com/927/)).

alternatives.description: Use `yarn` and fix the existing issues
pros: `Yarn` is more widely used across the team's, and wider department's, projects so it would present a more consistent approach.
There are more examples of common tasks written in `yarn` from our existing projects.
Developers are more likely to default to running `yarn` commands.
cons: Issues exist such as `yarn login` prompting for a password at release time which doesn't work with `np`.
Publishing with `yarn` leaves only the `index.js` file in the `lib` directory.

alternatives.description: Use `npm`
pros: `npm` provides a working alternative with no obvious drawbacks besides less common use in the department.
cons: Less common use of `npm` in the department compared to `yarn`.

alternatives.description: Use `npm` but use the script pattern to make it (more) opaque to the user
pros: Abstracts the choice of package manager away from the user.
Allows whichever tool is best fit to be used across projects.
Maintains a consistent experience for developers.

template_adherence.title: Testing
template_adherence.context:
One of the benefits of writing our infrastructure in a fully fledged programming language is the ability to write reusable components which can be tested. This library defines those components, both in the form of constructs and patterns (see [001-constructs-and-patterns](./001-constructs-and-patterns.md) for more details).

There are two main strategies that can be used to unit test these components.

Snapshot tests synthesise a given stack and compare the output to a previous version that has been verified by the user and checked into the repository. If there are any changes, the test fails and the user is displayed the diff to either fix or update the stored snapshot.

[+] Quick and easy to write

[+] Pick up any changes to the output cloudformation (particularly useful for unintended side effects)

[-] A change to the component may cause many unrelated tests to also fail

[-] When testing different permutations of a component, a number of snapshots will be created, each of which contains a certain amount of information which is irrelevant to the particular test. This adds some extra effort to understand what is relevant to the test which you're looking at

[-] Snapshots are easy to update which, especially when multiple are affected by a change, makes it easy to accidentally update them incorrectly. Further to this, as the snapshot (which is essentially the assertion) is stored in a different file, it's not immediately obvious if the assertions are valid

Direct Assertions use the different assertions provided by the test framework to test specific functionality. For example, asserting that a property exists or that an array contains a particular value.

[+] Each test only contains the relevant assertions for the test, making it easier to understand the consequence of settings certain props

[+] Changes will only fail tests that cover that particular area

[-] More complex and time consuming to write
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need for reusable components that can be tested
- Desire to have effective unit testing strategies
- Trade-offs between snapshot tests and direct assertions in terms of ease of writing, maintenance, and test relevance
- Need for a consistent testing style to improve maintainability and understanding
template_adherence.decision:
Use direct assertions for constructs and snapshots for patterns (and stacks).

This decision is a recommendation for the general approach. There may be some cases where using a different approach is more applicable for a given test.
template_adherence.consequences:
Having a consistent style for tests makes it easier to decide what and how to test each component. This approach should ensure that the unit tests provide good coverage whilst being easy to understand and maintain.

As direct assertion tests are more time consuming and complex to write than snapshots, this will create some additional work.

alternatives.description: Use snapshots for everything
pros: Quick and easy to write
Pick up any changes to the output cloudformation (particularly useful for unintended side effects)
cons: A change to the component may cause many unrelated tests to also fail

When testing different permutations of a component, a number of snapshots will be created, each of which contains a certain amount of information which is irrelevant to the particular test. This adds some extra effort to understand what is relevant to the test which you're looking at

Snapshots are easy to update which, especially when multiple are affected by a change, makes it easy to accidentally update them incorrectly. Further to this, as the snapshot (which is essentially the assertion) is stored in a different file, it's not immediately obvious if the assertions are valid

alternatives.description: Use direct assertions for everything
pros: Each test only contains the relevant assertions for the test, making it easier to understand the consequence of settings certain props
Changes will only fail tests that cover that particular area
cons: More complex and time consuming to write

alternatives.description: Use a combination of both for everything
Use direct assertions for constructs and snapshots for patterns (and stacks)

template_adherence.title: ADR 1: Decide Tech Stack
template_adherence.context: CodeCharta needs to analyze and visualize code to facilitate code audits. Many great tools exist that do one of these or both. template_adherence.decision_drivers:

- Desire to incorporate existing analysis tools

template_adherence.decision: CodeCharta will be divided into two tech stacks and also folders for `analysis/` and `visualization/` that only communicate via .json files. The runtime for the analysis is the JVM because Java is the main language audited and many Java metric tools exist. The runtime for visualization is the web browser for flexibility and ease of use. The interchange file format is `.cc.json` JSON files, supported by both environments.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include flexibility, leveraging existing tools, ease of use, and integration with other tools. Negative consequences include maintaining two different programming languages, JVM limitations for some languages, potential performance issues in the web for visualization, and less user-friendliness compared to a single program.

template_adherence.title: ADR 8: Angular Migration
template_adherence.context:
According to official version-support-status AngularJS will have end of life with the end of this year 2021. Therefore we need to migrate away from it, to maintain the following goals:

-   Stay browser compatible with new browser versions.
-   Continue to get security updates.
-   Continue to stay in sync with best practice regarding tooling support, dependencies and community support.
-   Keep being an attractive project for developers and community to contribute.

Migration to Angular, which can be done component wise, has already started via #2318.

Following two questions arose from the start of the migration:

1. Some shared state is not in redux store, but handled via broadcasting through $rootScope, like the currently selected building in visualization/app/codeCharta/ui/codeMap/threeViewer/threeSceneService.ts. $rootScope is AngularJS specific and cannot be used in new Angular components. We could:
1. Use Event Emitters in an Angular Service and temporarily upgrade $rootScope to sync between both worlds.
2. Move this and similar shared state into existing redux store. This would align with our docs, that the redux store is the only single state.
2. Do we continue to use plain redux, or do we migrate to Angular's NgRx?
- Advantage of plain redux:
- New developers don't need to learn concepts of NgRx and RxJs's Observables.
- Example of a migrated component and a template
- Advantage of NgRx:
- Angular community strongly recommends the use of NgRx and RxJs's Observables. Therefore better tooling and Angular support is to be expected.
- It fits naturally into Angular's internal update model. That makes it more performant and less likely to memory leaks / endless cyclic update loops.
- Example of a migrated component and a template
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to migrate away from AngularJS due to end of life in 2021.
- Maintain browser compatibility, security updates, tooling and community support.
- Desire to have a single source of truth for global state.
- Consideration between continuing with plain redux or migrating to NgRx.
- Developer learning curve and community recommendations.
- Performance and memory leak considerations.
template_adherence.decision:
1. We move all global state into the store, to have one single place and only one mechanism for global state.
2. We favor to migrate to NgRx.
template_adherence.consequences:
- All AngularJS components, services etc need to be migrated (see #2318 for progress).
- All AngularJS dependencies should be removed like angular, @types/angular (Angular has built-in type definitions), babel-plugin-angularjs-annotate, etc.

alternatives.description: Use Event Emitters in an Angular Service and temporarily upgrade $rootScope to sync between both worlds.
pros: Allows gradual migration without immediate full state store refactor.
Maintains existing broadcasting mechanism temporarily.
cons: Temporary solution adds complexity.
$rootScope is AngularJS specific and not ideal for new Angular components.

alternatives.description: Move shared state into existing redux store.
pros: Aligns with documentation that redux store is the single source of truth.
Simplifies state management by having one mechanism.
cons: Requires refactoring existing code to use redux store.
May require learning redux patterns for some developers.

alternatives.description: Continue to use plain redux.
pros: New developers don't need to learn NgRx and RxJs Observables.
Existing redux knowledge can be leveraged.
cons: Less integration with Angular's internal update model.
May miss out on tooling and community support advantages of NgRx.

alternatives.description: Migrate to Angular's NgRx.
pros: Strongly recommended by Angular community.
Better tooling and Angular support expected.
Fits naturally into Angular's update model, improving performance and reducing memory leaks.
cons: Requires learning NgRx and RxJs Observables.
Potentially steeper learning curve for developers.

template_adherence.title: Architecture Security
template_adherence.context: These are notes based on the InfoSec meeting held on the 30th of May 2019.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Ease of use for journalists when system authenticates them
* Security levels (public, protect, or restrict)
* Data retention based on inactivity
* Complexity
template_adherence.decision:
We are going with Option 2 as this provides us with security, while providing a simpler way to set up access for journalists.

Ben Thornton has agreed to this.

The benefits of this approach means that we will be using existing BBC services to implement security, rather than implementing our own servers. A single VPC is sufficient for **protected** levels of service, and we can apply SecurityGroups in between to have added security.

The downside of this approach is that it is not using SSO but we can add that later on.

In terms of data retention, we will go with the recommended 90 days.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include improved security using existing BBC services, simpler setup for journalists, and appropriate data retention period. Negative consequences include not using SSO initially, which may be added later.

alternatives.description: Cert-based authentication is fine for now. We might want to move to BBC Login (SSO). This will make it easier for journalists to access the system. When there's a mobile version of the application, it will simplify accessing the system, as people will have to follow an additional step to enrol their devices into MDM if using a cert-based authenticator.
pros: Cert-based authentication is currently sufficient.
Potential future move to SSO for easier access.
cons: Cert-based authentication requires device enrolment for mobile.
SSO not currently implemented.

alternatives.description: Following the guidelines above to implement a protected level service, we can host the UI in EC2 instance in Cosmos. Cosmos will automatically give us the ELBs, and most importantly the automatic authentication capabilities. The UI and backend server (Express) can be both hosted on the same EC2 instance, which will reduce the APIs exposure only to the UI. The fronting UI will have its own Express server. This means that the UI Express will communicate with the API Express via localhost. The backend server will only be on localhost and won't be exposed to the wider world. Although the UI and Express server live in the same box, they are still both in the Cosmos VPC, with cert authentication. We can use SecurityGroups between ELBs to restrict communication between each AWS service.
pros: Provides security while simplifying access setup.
Uses existing BBC services.
Single VPC sufficient for protected level.
SecurityGroups add security between services.
cons: Does not use SSO initially.

alternatives.description: Suggested by Ben: adding a load balancer or Cloudfront in front of EC2 that serves React, then adding VPCs. The VPC can be singular or multiple. Within these VPCs use different subnets for the components to talk to each other.
pros: Potentially more secure with multiple VPCs and subnets.
Examples and guidelines provided by Ben.
cons: Requires keeping web endpoint open to public and authenticating via proxy server in Apache, which may require custom development.
May need EC2 or Lambda instance to do redirects.
More complex setup than static web hosting.

template_adherence.title: Short title of solved problem and solution
template_adherence.context:
This addresses the fact that we could not configure different environments to point to different API URLs as necessary (across Int, Test, and Live envs in Cosmos).

At the point of deployment, `npm run build` is called in Jenkins to build the static  bundle and minify etc. Environment config (`REACT_APP_SERVER_URL` etc. variables declared in `.env`) get baked into the bundle and obfuscated at this point.

We would need different Jenkins jobs or parameters to bake in the environment config (eg. the correct server URL) multiple times, which goes against the idea of having an _unconfigured / environment agnostic_ RPM in Cosmos.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Avoiding too much extra code overhead
* Trying to avoid security converns with proxy solutions (injection / DB manipulations)
* Avoiding having to re-build in Cosmos or on the box
template_adherence.decision:
This is a common problem with create-react-app and the need to configure it. We came across [this solution](https://github.com/facebook/create-react-app/issues/578#issuecomment-277843310) which detailed a simple way of consuming config with the `window` global.

In source code this remains localhost:8080 as a local development fallback and it is passed in via Cosmos environment config.

alternatives.description:
The react app is build / bundled and served statically as usual
It continues to make API requests to localhost:8080
An additional express server acts as a proxy and passes on these requests to the correct API_URL, according to NODE_ENV config which is passed to the proxy server at runtime
pros: Good - it aligns initial idea that client could be pulled in _unconfigured_ via NPM.
Good - no additional rebuilds required
cons: Bad - additional server config and boilerplate required
Bad - additional issues and concerns around CORS, security and injection required
Bad - Not hugely replicable

alternatives.description:
There is environment configuration
The RPM used for the EC2 contains a script that performs a rebuild when on the box
cons: Bad, because of the release not mapping accurately to the system on the EC2

alternatives.description: Using the NODE_ENV config to configure the server and URL, without build / bundling
pros: Good, because can use environment config easily
cons: Bad, not a typical pattern
Bad, security concerns

template_adherence.title: Firebase infrastructure
template_adherence.context:
We have quite a few components to build up in the backend to get DPE to a stable point. Although initially decided to do development in AWS, working on AWS had been quite challenging with a steep learning curve. In a single project cycle, we've reached a point where we had infrastructures of most microservices setup. Unfortunately resources were removed from the project and priorities shifted to UX research, while back-end development halted. Picking these development tasks from half baked microservices is difficult. We now have to relearn what we've developed and complete integration. In order to simplify back-end development, we are looking at Firebase (Google Cloud Platform). Since Firebase is a plaftorm that targets development for startups and R&D, it provides many features out of the box. This could speed up developing the backend, namely the realtime database, authentication, while keeping possibilities open for offline, mobile, and multi-user solutions. We must consider technical (security, development, transfer, upfront learning) and non-technical (legal) cost.

Since we've designed the React components to be reusable, there is a question of whether AWS vs GCP makes it easier for transfer. Previous projects had all been rebuilt from scratch, including the infrastructure. Realistically, does it matter which Cloud provider we go with?
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Security (Authentication, PSTT integration)
- Legal
- Transfer
- Technical feasibility of DPE only
- Technical feasibility of CI, reproduceability
- Cost (time, money, engineering, opportunity)
template_adherence.decision: Firebase and AWS combined as PSTT integration is feasible to do, even with cross acount complications. Features such as authentication, user specific data retrieval, integration with database without migrations is already completed. Firebase provides abstractions around security and integrations with the database, as well as Functions. To save time around the project with features such as realtime database and easy API use, let's progress with Firebase. There are still some things such as CI, Deployment management that can be worked on, but this is a stretch goal for now. All in all, I believe that it will save time, and simply the overall architecture and code.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
- Faster turnaround for development
- Authentication
- Realtime database beneficial for some of our DPE requirements
- Managed services with many abstractions

Secondary positive consequences:
- Growing knowledge of GCP
- BBC Login (stretch goal)
- monitoring given out of the box (console.log maps to logging to GCP Logging Console)

Negative consequences:
- Upfront cost of learning for developers and there are many unknowns, until looked into
- Security concerns
- Redesigning architecture
- Redesigning database model
- Transfer not possible with infrastructure (?)

template_adherence.title: Architecture Security
template_adherence.context: These are notes based on the InfoSec meeting held on the 30th of May 2019.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Ease of use for journalists when system authenticates them
* Security levels (public, protect, or restrict)
* Data retention based on inactivity
* Complexity
template_adherence.decision:
We are going with Option 2 as this provides us with security, while providing a simpler way to set up access for journalists.

Ben Thornton has agreed to this.

The benefits of this approach means that we will be using existing BBC services to implement security, rather than implementing our own servers. A single VPC is sufficient for **protected** levels of service, and we can apply SecurityGroups in between to have added security.

The downside of this approach is that it is not using SSO but we can add that later on.

In terms of data retention, we will go with the recommended 90 days.
template_adherence.consequences: Positive consequences include enhanced security using existing BBC services, simpler setup for journalists, and appropriate data retention period. Negative consequences include not using SSO initially, which may be added later.

alternatives.description: Cert-based authentication is fine for now. We might want to move to BBC Login (SSO). This will make it easier for journalists to access the system. When there's a mobile version of the application, it will simplify accessing the system, as people will have to follow an additional step to enrol their devices into MDM if using a cert-based authenticator.
pros: Cert-based authentication is currently sufficient.
Potential future move to SSO for easier access.
cons: Cert-based authentication requires device enrolment for mobile.
SSO not currently implemented.

alternatives.description: Following the guidelines above to implement a protected level service, we can host the UI in EC2 instance in Cosmos. Cosmos will automatically give us the ELBs, and most importantly the automatic authentication capabilities. The UI and backend server (Express) can be both hosted on the same EC2 instance, which will reduce the APIs exposure only to the UI. The fronting UI will have its own Express server. This means that the UI Express will communicate with the API Express via localhost. The backend server will only be on localhost and won't be exposed to the wider world. Although the UI and Express server live in the same box, they are still both in the Cosmos VPC, with cert authentication. We can use SecurityGroups between ELBs to restrict communication between each AWS service.
pros: Provides security while simplifying access setup.
Uses existing BBC services.
Single VPC sufficient for protected level.
SecurityGroups add security between services.
cons: Does not use SSO initially.

alternatives.description: Suggested by Ben: adding a load balancer or Cloudfront in front of EC2 that serves React, then adding VPCs. The VPC can be singular or multiple. Within these VPCs use different subnets for the components to talk to each other.
pros: Potentially more secure with multiple VPCs and subnets.
Examples and guidelines provided by Ben.
cons: Requires keeping web endpoint open to public and authenticating via proxy server in Apache.
May require writing own Apache server; preference for Nginx.
Need EC2 or Lambda instance to do redirects.
More complex setup than static web hosting.

template_adherence.title: Modular Architecture (breaking down repositories and packages)
template_adherence.context: As this is an opensource project, we might want to separate out the projects so they are more digestible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* opensource means removing BBC specific code
* separating infrastructure
* electron and cep (future integration)
template_adherence.decision: We opted for Option 4 after another iteration of the architectual flow. Initially we went for option 3 because we wanted to have a uniform approach for possible future users. However, after much consideration, we collectively agreed to remove NPM packaging for the API (and the microservices). Similarly to option 3, we are still keeping the AWS stacks separate in the infrastructure repository. We will be using Travis CI for the NPM build. We will be using Jenkins (not publicly accessible) for the RPM build and releasing to Cosmos. We will be using Speculate, which is an open-source BBC project to generate SPEC files, which adds little overhead in the projects. We will not automate the release of NPM, but as a manual step which also does testing. We will retain the public state of each repository and not be concerned with "ready" state of our repositories.
template_adherence.consequences: The decision leads to a modular architecture with separate repositories and packages, using different packaging and deployment strategies (NPM for client, RPM for API). It supports open source goals by removing BBC-specific code and separating infrastructure. The approach balances uniformity and practical deployment considerations. However, some manual steps remain (e.g., manual NPM release), and the complexity of multiple repositories and deployment pipelines is introduced.

alternatives.description: Option 1 - bundle everything (UI, API, Infra) into an RPM.
pros: Simpler deployment as a single package.
cons: Less modular, harder to manage individual components.
Not aligned with open source goals of separation.

alternatives.description: Option 2 - separate the UI to a new github repository, bundle it as an NPM package. Keep infrastructure in the same repository as API. API will pull in UI as a dependency.
pros: Partial separation of concerns.
UI can be managed independently.
cons: Infrastructure and API remain coupled.
Less modular than full separation.

alternatives.description: Option 3 - separate the UI, API and infrastructure. Bundle UI and API separately as NPM packages. Infrastructure will have UI and API packages as dependencies.
pros: Full modularity.
Uniform packaging approach using NPM.
Simpler versioning and contribution per package.
cons: Using NPM for API packaging may be atypical.
Potential unknown benefits for external users.
More complex build and deployment.

alternatives.description: Option 4 - separate the UI, API and infrastructure. Bundle only UI as NPM package, and API will be bundled as RPM. Infrastructure repo will have UI as a dependency.
pros: Balances modularity with practical deployment.
API packaged as RPM aligns with deployment needs.
UI remains an NPM package for ease of use.
cons: More complex build pipeline with mixed packaging.
Manual steps in NPM release process.

template_adherence.title: Encapsulate SMA stack usage
template_adherence.context: Real world assembly programming exposes the stack pointer and the base pointer, allowing assembly code to directly mess with them, for example changing the stack pointer regardless of how `push` and `pop` instructions have been used. Despite allowing wild optimizations, this is really error prone and, if used extensively, makes programs very obscure: for these reasons, we don't want to support such things in our SMA architecture.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to prevent error-prone and obscure code caused by direct manipulation of stack and base pointers in assembly programming, while maintaining a consistent and simplified interface for stack usage in the SMA architecture.
template_adherence.decision: To prevent code from messing up the stack, we'll avoid adding public stack pointer and base pointer registers. Instead, these concepts will be encapsulated within the stack object implementation, exposing only `push` and `pop` interfaces to clients. Additional methods `pushFrame` and `popFrame` will abstract stack frame handling, and a new `call` instruction will support argument passing by managing the stack layout automatically.
template_adherence.consequences: Procedures become consistent by using only the stack for arguments and return values, avoiding direct register manipulation. However, it remains possible to corrupt the stack if misused, reflecting a partial implementation of the design goal to simplify stack usage. This approach balances simplicity with fidelity to real processor implementations, representing a compromise.

alternatives.description: Allow direct access to stack pointer and base pointer registers as in real assembly programming.
pros: Enables wild optimizations and maximum flexibility.
Closer to real assembly programming behavior.
cons: Highly error prone and leads to obscure code.
Increases complexity and risk of stack corruption.

alternatives.description: Provide only push and pop interfaces without additional abstractions for frames and calls.
pros: Simplifies the interface to basic stack operations.
Reduces exposure to direct pointer manipulation.
cons: Does not address the complexity of stack frame handling.
Requires manual boilerplate code for procedure calls and argument passing.
