template_adherence.title: Stop using registers in processor
template_adherence.context:
Communication between processor and interpreter must go both ways: the processor needs to pass the interpreter the instruction to execute, and the interpreter is supposed to be able to update the Instruction Pointer (IP), and to tell the processor if the execution needs to stop, and with which exit status.

Currently we are using an intermediate component, registers, partially like how real processors work, containing both the IP and the information about the exit status. However, the communication between the processor and the interpreter is so straightforward that a much simpler solution would be to just use classical call argument, and call return value. Registers could be used as a mediator, but for this to have sense the processor and the interpreter would have to be unaware of each other, and registers should implement a mechanism to automatically notify involved parties when a change is made, which seems overkill.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The communication between processor and interpreter must be bidirectional and straightforward.
The current use of registers as an intermediate component is unnecessarily complex.
A simpler communication mechanism is desired to reduce complexity and improve clarity.
Avoid over-engineering with automatic notification mechanisms in registers.
template_adherence.decision: The interpreter will keep taking an instruction from the processor, but this time it will return a data structure, which tells if an exit has been triggered, and in this case what's the exit status.
template_adherence.consequences: The processor doesn't need to define an interface for registers, and interpreters don't need to implement it anymore. Communication is simplified.

alternatives.description: Continue using registers as an intermediate component between processor and interpreter.
pros: Mimics real processor behavior.
Registers can hold both IP and exit status information.
cons: Adds unnecessary complexity for straightforward communication.
Requires implementing notification mechanisms for changes.
Processor and interpreter remain coupled through registers.

alternatives.description: Use classical call arguments and return values for communication between processor and interpreter.
pros: Simplifies communication.
Removes need for register interface and implementation.
Reduces coupling between processor and interpreter.
cons: May diverge from real processor behavior.
Requires changing existing communication mechanism.

template_adherence.title: Monorepo and directory layout
template_adherence.context: Following from decision [2018120802](2018120802-implement-clean-architecture.md), we want to follow the tenet of screaming architecture, stating that the first level directories of the application's source tree should represent the use cases, or features, of the application. However, we cannot define domain modules inside application directories, because the domain cannot be mapped 1-to-1 to application features, since the domain is independent from the application. In practical terms, this means that it could happen that two different features will need the same domain module, and if this domain module is defined in feature A, and feature B requires those domain concepts as well, then feature B will have to know about feature A, even if this makes no sense as far as the semantic of those features are concerned. Additionally, we cannot define adapters, or infrastructure code, inside feature directories either, because application cannot know about adapters, and very often an adapter targets multiple features, like a Web adapter can target different features of a primary port, and even a secondary adapter could be the target of different features, if it acts like a mediator, for example with commands or events. We're currently using only one source code repository, and we don't want to go through the hassle of maintaining multiple repositories yet, because the project structure is still being actively changed. On top of that, we want to support a plugin architecture, where multiple different kinds of applications can be built by assembling together plugins. This is exactly the purpose of Clean Architecture, with maybe the only difference that the typical example of Clean Architecture is a Web application where there's only one application supporting different features, while we'll have different applications that can possibly be built from the same components: this, however, is just a deploying detail.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
- Need to follow the screaming architecture principle for directory layout.
- Domain modules cannot be tied 1-to-1 to application features.
- Adapters cannot be defined inside feature directories.
- Desire to maintain a single source code repository (monorepo) to avoid complexity.
- Support for plugin architecture with multiple applications built from plugins.
- Need to clearly express features and use cases in directory structure.
- Build system must support dependencies across multiple directories.
template_adherence.decision: To avoid dealing with multiple source code repositories, we'll use the monorepo approach, keeping everything inside a single source code repository. The directory structure will not display application use cases at the first level because multiple applications and plugins will be located there. Instead, the directory layout will reflect the features of the toolkit, showing multiple applications and plugins. Two kinds of plugins are recognized: those added during development necessary for structure, and mods added post-deployment to enhance functionality without rebuilding the application.
template_adherence.consequences:
- The application clearly states its intent, listing features and use cases in application/ while other modules are categorized by layer and abstraction level.
- The build system must support dependencies located in different directories rather than a single lib/ or vendor/ directory.
- The directory layout supports multiple applications and plugin architectures.
- Enables adding new architectures or features post-deployment without rebuilding the entire application.

alternatives.description: Use multiple source code repositories instead of a monorepo.
pros: Clear separation of applications and features.
Simpler repository management per application.
cons: Increased complexity in managing multiple repositories.
Harder to share code and plugins across applications.
More overhead in coordinating changes across repositories.

alternatives.description: Define domain modules inside application feature directories.
pros: Aligns with screaming architecture principle of features at top level.
Simplifies locating domain code per feature.
cons: Domain modules may be duplicated or tightly coupled to features.
Features may need to know about other features to share domain modules, breaking independence.

alternatives.description: Define adapters inside feature directories.
pros: Adapters are close to the features they serve.
Simplifies understanding feature-specific adapters.
cons: Adapters often target multiple features, so this creates coupling.
Violates Clean Architecture principle that application should not know about adapters.

template_adherence.title: Data unit is parameterized type
template_adherence.context:
Our model of data is based on the idea that data is always a sequences of *data units*, so that any data can always be *expanded* into a list of data units. However, data units are themselves data, so that expanding them will return a list with only one element, that data unit itself.

This poses the following problem: we need to define a `Data` type, and a `DataUnit` type, where `Data` knows about `DataUnit` (because the `expand()` method must return `DataUnit[]`), and `DataUnit` knows about `Data`, because it extends it. This is of course impossible to do because it creates a circular dependency.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to model data as sequences of data units, with the ability to expand data into data units, while avoiding circular dependencies between `Data` and `DataUnit` types. Also, the desire to use parameterized types (generics) to solve this problem, and consideration of language support for generics.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to allow the client to specify the concrete `Data` implementation to be used as `DataUnit` when `Data` is defined, using parameterized types (generics). This means defining `Data<T: Data>` with an `expand(): T[]` method, where `T` is the concrete type used as `DataUnit`.
template_adherence.consequences: This approach might be problematic to implement in programming languages that don't support generics natively. However, it works in languages like Java, as demonstrated by the provided example code. This solution resolves the circular dependency problem by using parameterized types.

alternatives.description: Not explicitly mentioned in the ADR text. The ADR focuses on the chosen solution using parameterized types to solve the circular dependency problem.
pros: N/A
cons: N/A

template_adherence.title: Multiple usages of the processor
template_adherence.context:
The domain our virtual machine is supporting is concerned with running programs: as such, how programs should be run is a business rule, and the Processor is the Domain Service encapsulating that rule.

At the application level, we can think of several features that can support this domain:
- classic virtual machine, running an entire program, perhaps loaded from a file, until its termination
- REPL, where instructions are loaded one at a time from an interactive prompt, and executed, printing some kind of output each time
- debug, where we still have an entire program, but this time we want to support debugging features, like running step-by-step

Of course there could be many others. Can we use the same definition of a Processor in the domain to support all this cases?
template_adherence.decision:
We will keep the Processor as a Domain Service, because the three different kinds of execution we want to support really only differ for how data is handled in memory, and the domain doesn't concern itself with what is contained in memory (it doesn't even mention memory, since it's a detail of the interpreter, and we might as well use interpreters that don't use any memory):
- in the classic virtual machine, the Program is the entire program, that is executed from start to end
- in the REPL situation, each time a new instruction is inserted at the prompt, it is added to the Program, which is then fed to the Processor: this is necessary because we might have defined procedures that we want to call in the future; the state of memory is saved between different executions (this doesn't concern the domain), and to make the program start at the latest instruction, we add a new unconditional jump instruction at the beginning of it: this actually means that we don't run the entire program again (it isn't necessary since memory is preserved), but only the last inserted instruction
- in the debug situation, the Interpreter implementation can avoid returning control back to the Processor until requested to: this still doesn't concern the Processor implementation in the domain
template_adherence.consequences: If the Processor definition in the domain stays abstract enough, only mentioning the real business needs, we can reuse it in different applications situations.

template_adherence.title: Local architecture interfaces
template_adherence.context:
Sloth machine applications need to support any type of processor architectures, that can be loaded and chosen by users when running the applications. The architecture with which to run the virtual machine will be selected at launch time: for example, a command-line application could be used like:
$ sm --arc=sma program_file
template_adherence.decision:
We will support adding new architectures as mods, or user-side plugins, that are provided by the user without needing to rebuild the application.

We won't provide integration tests with real code targeting specific architectures in any Sloth Machine suite, because they become actually independent from the architecture, and as such they cannot know about any specific architecture, not event in tests, where we might just use stubs instead. Integration tests for architectures must be included in the specific architecture packages.

Local architectures

The local architecture loader, which is selected by an adapter to load architectures from local files, will load an architecture object from the module file.

This architecture will implement the `<Architecture>` domain interface, thus providing a `getInterpreter(<System>)` method, taking a System to return an Interpreter for that specific architecture.

The module file must be named `lib`, and must be located directly inside a directory called with the name of the architecture.

The architecture module is only allowed to depend on the `smf`, and no other external packages, because the environment where the architecture module is loaded is controlled by the suite loading it, for example the Sloth Machine virtual machine.
template_adherence.consequences:
The architectures supported by any Sloth Machine suite are not limited to the ones built within the suite itself.

It's not necessary to change nor rebuild the application to add support to new architectures.

template_adherence.title: Concrete and generic domain data units
template_adherence.context:
We've been thinking of defining abstract concepts of `DataUnit` and `Data`, so that `DataUnit` shares the interface with `Data`, and this interface contains a lot of methods, for example for comparison, arithmetic, etc. However, upon reviewing the usage of these concepts in the other domain modules, it's been evident that all these complex features weren't actually needed.

In addition to this, the idea was that the domain defined only the interfaces for the data units, and then each architecture provided implementations for them. This introduced the annoying problem of having to let the architecture control the loading of programs, because programs would need to contain the actual data units defined by the architecture. This was leading to the definition of a `StringLoader` in the framework domain, where programs were considered just strings (so independent from the specific architecture), and then also of an architecture specific program loader, using the given string loader to translate string programs to data unit programs: this was making the domain, and both the logic and the structure of the system, quite complicated.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to simplify the domain model by avoiding unnecessary complex features like comparison and arithmetic on data units.
The desire to keep the domain independent from architecture-specific implementations to avoid complexity in program loading.
The requirement that data units be based on a fundamental concept (Byte) to unify implementations.
The need to simplify concepts like Size and Address for clarity and modularity.
template_adherence.decision:
The decision is to base all special data implementations on the concept of Byte, making the data unit a runtime-independent byte implementation.
Data will be defined simply as a list of DataUnit, without additional features like comparison or arithmetic.
The concept of Size will be simplified to an integer, and Address will be moved from the program module to the data module to better represent addressing within data chunks.
template_adherence.consequences:
Architectures retain freedom to define more specific data implementations (e.g., Words, Doubles), but these won't be used outside architecture code.
The data module becomes much simpler.
The program loader becomes completely independent from the architecture, greatly simplifying the overall design.

alternatives.description: Define abstract concepts of DataUnit and Data with rich interfaces including comparison, arithmetic, etc., and let each architecture provide implementations.
pros: Allows rich feature sets on data units.
Enables architecture-specific implementations with full capabilities.
cons: Complex features were not actually needed in practice.
Introduces complexity in domain and system structure.
Requires architecture to control program loading, complicating design.

alternatives.description: Keep programs as strings independent of architecture and use a StringLoader in the framework domain, then have architecture-specific program loaders translating strings to data units.
pros: Keeps programs architecture-independent at string level.
Separates concerns between framework and architecture.
cons: Leads to complicated domain logic and structure.
Requires multiple loaders and translations, increasing complexity.

template_adherence.context:
We want programs to always terminate with an explicit exit system call, instead of automatically exit with status 0 when the execution reaches the last program instruction, for better consistency and transparency.

In the current version of the Processor, we use unbounded Address values: this prevents us from recognizing that the program misses an exit instruction, because we will theoretically be able to increment the Address indefinitely. This is in contrast with the case where the Processor was reading directly from the Memory, that by definition had a limited size, so that when the Program tried to read an Address that was outside of the memory, it was the signal the the exit instruction was missing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section, nor does it explicitly list the forces influencing the decision. However, the 'Context' section implicitly contains some drivers such as the need for explicit program termination, consistency, transparency, and handling of invalid addresses.
template_adherence.decision: We will let the Program throw an Invalid Address exception when the given Address cannot be found in the Program. This will happen both when a jump instruction tries to jump to an invalid address, and when the execution reaches the end of the Program with no exit instruction having been provided, at which point the next address will naturally not be valid.
template_adherence.consequences: It won't be possible for the Processor to tell if the given Program is specifically missing an exit instruction, because that would look exactly like an invalid jump instruction. We accept this situation under the assumption that programs won't usually be written directly in hexadecimal, but using a compiler or at least an assembler, that can be designed to signal the absence of the required exit instruction.

template_adherence.title: System interface
template_adherence.context:
Any architecture must have a way to communicate with the system over which the virtual machine is running, otherwise it wouldn't be possible to do any kind of input/output, thus for a program to perform any meaningful work.

We want to support different kinds of system abstractions: for example the operating system where a command-line virtual machine is running, or a system emulation over the Web that does input/output with the Web page.

To support this, we need to define a common interface for the System component, so that all possible architecture mods will know what they can do with it.

The main problem is that certain operations like `read` needs the concept of memory buffer to work, because we need to provide a buffer to it, where the read data will be stored. However, we don't support any concept of "memory" in our domain, so we cannot use anything like that to implement a buffer.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to support different system abstractions (e.g., OS command-line VM, web-based system emulation) requiring a common interface.
The challenge of implementing operations like `read` without a memory buffer concept.
The desire to have a flexible interface that can adapt to various underlying system implementations.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to design the System interface to return a complex `Data` object containing both the data and its size, instead of using traditional buffer-based read calls. This allows the interface to be independent of memory buffer concepts and adaptable to different system implementations.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive: Enables use of generic systems with any architecture implementation.
Negative: The ADR does not explicitly discuss potential drawbacks or challenges of this approach.

alternatives.description: Use the traditional read interface with memory buffers passed by reference.
pros: Familiar interface consistent with many existing systems.
Direct control over memory buffers.
cons: Not compatible with the domain lacking a memory concept.
Less flexible for different system abstractions.

alternatives.description: Define a completely new interface unrelated to traditional read calls, possibly with different semantics.
pros: Potentially more tailored to specific needs.
Could optimize for particular use cases.
cons: May increase complexity.
Less standard, harder to integrate with existing systems.

template_adherence.title: Handling generic components communication
template_adherence.context: The easiest technical solution to let different layers communicate, for example adapters and application, is direct method calls, like injecting the presenter into the interactor, and let the interactor call methods on the presenter object. However, this is not the most generic case of communication, since it doesn't support the situation of concurrent components, or components running on different processes or address spaces.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to support concurrent components and components running on different processes or address spaces, the desire for a clean and generic communication solution, and the ability to handle multiple adapters connected to the same port simultaneously.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a messaging communication structure where ports represent sets of messages and adapters are message handlers registered to respond to those messages. Direct method calls are considered a special case of this more generic messaging communication. This approach naturally leads to a micro-services deployment strategy with an API gateway acting as a message bus and application API surface.
template_adherence.consequences: Communication between components happens via a message bus in the most generic design. Simplifications are possible in specific areas if certain conditions are met, such as components running in the same address space or no concurrency requirements.

template_adherence.title: Interactor handling concurrent requests
template_adherence.context:
An application can generally handle concurrent requests coming from different device adapters.

If the interactor's dependencies don't depend on the request parameters, the same interactor instance can be used for every request. In some cases, however, some of the interactor's dependencies depend on the details of the request, for example the concrete presenter to be injected in the interactor in place of the presenter interface depends on the output model of the specific request, i.e. on the specific device adapter that is handling the current connection.

In some cases interactor's dependencies might have an identity, for example services with a specific configuration, like loggers, database drivers, etc., that shouldn't be created anew every time they're injected into the interactor.

If the same instance of an interactor is shared, then, we'd also face concurrency issues, because different requests would be sharing the same resource.

Finally, different requests might be coming in parallel, and routing to the interactor should be handled in a proper manner.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
The need to handle concurrent requests properly without sharing state that causes concurrency issues.
The requirement that some interactor dependencies depend on request-specific parameters.
The desire to keep design concerns separate from performance concerns.
The need to share certain dependencies with identity (e.g., configured services) across interactors.
The goal to simplify design by avoiding a broker component and maintain a clear architecture.
template_adherence.decision:
Each request should have its own interactor instance to handle request-specific dependencies like concrete presenters.
Dependencies that have identity and should be shared can be managed via the DI container to provide the same instance across interactors.
Performance concerns (like expensive dependency construction) should be handled separately, e.g., via proxies or caching, without impacting the design.
This approach simplifies design and separates design from performance concerns.
template_adherence.consequences:
The design is simplified by removing the need for a unique application layer per connection and eliminating the need for a broker component.
Design and performance concerns are properly separated.
Service applications resemble native applications more closely in design, differing mainly in the number of application instances.
The high-level design structure remains consistent regardless of duplication.

alternatives.description: Use a single interactor instance shared across all requests regardless of request-specific dependencies.
pros: Simplifies instance management by having only one interactor instance.
Potentially reduces memory usage by sharing the same instance.
cons: Leads to concurrency issues due to shared mutable state.
Cannot handle request-specific dependencies properly.
Design becomes complicated due to shared state management.

alternatives.description: Duplicate all application components (controllers, presenters, views, interactors, dependencies) for each request without sharing any dependencies.
pros: Ensures complete isolation between requests.
Avoids concurrency issues by having separate instances for each request.
cons: High resource consumption due to duplication of all components.
Performance overhead in creating many instances.
Complexity in managing many duplicated components.

template_adherence.title: Choosing a Framework
template_adherence.context: While being a novice to C# and WPF, I thought it might be helpful to adopt a popular framework to make the development process easier and remove some of the unnecessary "gotchas" of writing in a new language. Using a framework might also quicken the pace of development and remove the need to write many helper classes.
template_adherence.decision: The Galaxy Zoo touch table app will not use a framework. Adopting a framework seems like a shortcut to learning the basics of C#, and I want to focus more on _how_ the language works rather than than simply getting something working. Also, a framework might cause a lot of overhead if only a few aspects of the framework are being used. Learning a new framework along with learning C# and .NET might be overwhelming.
template_adherence.consequences:
While some frameworks are well documented (MVVM Light), others are quickly becoming deprecated (Silverlight), so there is a worry that any framework could soon lose favor in the .NET community. By declining the use of a framework, there is the potential of adding more dev time that will be spent creating a messenger, view model base, and other components often found in a WPF framework.

_In Retrospect:_ After becoming more familiar with WPF, I wish I had chosen a framework (perhaps MVVM Light) to achieve some of my needs for this app. For example, although I created my own messenger based on a Stack Overflow post, I often ran into issues with the messenger and was unable to find advice on Stack Overflow as most of those answers reference the MVVM Light messenger. I don't think MVVM Light would've been a huge load on the code. It's likely using a framework could've cleaned up some sections of code. I can see the merits of declining a framework for novices to WPF, but I don't think much is gained from going without.

template_adherence.title: Using the Messenger
template_adherence.context: Given the unique use case of having six classifiers on a single interface, there will likely be times the classifiers will need to communicate with one another and the app on a global scale. This is most apparent when considering notifications: where one classifier will have to send messages, subjects, and answers to another classifier. It simply isn't enough to have one parent view model communicate with a child and vice-versa. There should be a pub/sub technology used to remove some of the complexity in architecture.
template_adherence.decision: Although some WPF frameworks come shipped with a messenger, I will build my own simple messenger to better understand what is happening behind the scenes with a messenger. Building a messenger from scratch while also remove some reliance on a third-party framework.
template_adherence.consequences:
While a messenger does fulfill some needs in the app (inter-classifier communication), it is easy to become too dependent on a messenger. That said, a messenger should be used sparingly and only when there is no other way for the view models (or other components) to communicate with one another.

_In Retrospect:_ The messenger is incredibly useful for a multi-touch table. While I initially relied too much on the messenger, some later refactoring removed that dependence in lieu of more parent-child communication in the view models. I also found the messenger was helpful when some of the view models needed to initiate animation in a view due to an event firing.

template_adherence.title: Publishing with ClickOnce
template_adherence.context: The app needs a convenient way to deploy to multiple devices. However this is done, installing and updating the app should be effortless for users. Ideally, the developer would make any necessary changes to the app, publish those changes to a location, and someone on the other end would only need to double click a download/update link.
template_adherence.decision:
Older WPF and WinForm applications used a separate setup application, which was responsible for guiding someone through the process of installing an app. A user first downloaded the setup application, which would be responsible for installing the separate application on a system. We abandoned this route early in the development process due to the frequent errors that occurred during the install process.

ClickOnce is the standard publishing method for WPF applications. Visual studio even references ClickOnce under the "Security" tab of the properties window. Documentation on ClickOnce is also quite robust. Because of this, we will accept ClickOnce as our method of choice when publishing.
template_adherence.consequences:
There aren't many options to choose from when it comes to deploying a WPF application. Unfortunately, if ClickOnce doesn't easily suit our needs, we'll likely have to spend a good bit of time troubleshooting.

_In Retrospect:_ Unfortunately, it is recommended that ClickOnce deploys to a CD-Rom, a website, or a file share/UNC path. This seems particularly dated, especially with the CD-Rom reference. Also, the Adler Planetarium is deprecating their local file share system in lieu of using Google Drive. This is why we use Google Drive File Stream (see wiki) when publishing, which works _fine_. As WPF isn't necessarily cutting-edge technology, I don't see the publishing process evolving much in the future. While ClickOnce _usually_ works well, we'll have to deal with any errors in deployment as we have our hands tied with using ClickOnce.

template_adherence.title: ADR 8: Relying on a Local DB
template_adherence.context: The application runs well when using Panoptes for subject retrieval and Caesar for classification counts. Although the touch table has never lost internet connection (using WiFi) and internet connection on the museum floor is quite reliable, we should be prepared for internet outages, however abrupt or short. Although Caesar works well as a new service, we should be prepared for a situation where Caesar is unresponsive.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to handle potential internet outages and unresponsiveness of external services (Panoptes and Caesar) to ensure the application continues to function properly.
template_adherence.decision: We will use a local database in the case our external dependencies (Panoptes and Caesar) are unresponsive. The local database will hold subject information from Panoptes and classification counts from Caesar, and subject images locally to avoid waiting for large arrays from the API. A classification queue will be used to queue new classifications if unable to be created through the Panoptes API due to lost internet connection.
template_adherence.consequences: This decision introduces overhead in choosing new technologies and writing logic to keep subjects locally, adding a new part of the app to maintain. It increases complexity, potentially making maintenance harder for new developers, requiring strong documentation. However, it improves app resilience to internet outages and external service failures, ensuring classification counts are tracked correctly and the app performs well even if local subject images aren't available.

template_adherence.title: Recursive lambda or CloudWatch-triggered lambda
template_adherence.context: When a schedule is in the delayer queue, messages become visible after delayed period. However, those messages must be published in corresponding action topic, and it cannot be done automatically, being needed to use a lambda function to do this publishing.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
This project is a scheduler, so the latency is an important concern
Flexibility: ability to be good enough in high or low concurrent executions
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option was to "Cloudwatch-triggered lambda".

Chaining lambda functions is a good solution when the volume of messages is flat or well known. In a scenario of a variable/high-volume of messages, the function would introduce some latency, due to the lack of paralelism of execution. To achieve paralelism, the solution would become much more complicated.

The chosen solution introduces the folowing concepts:
- lambda function timeout: configured time on when a function will be forcibly stopped by it's container
- lambda execution baseline: amount of time that a lambda function should be ideally working
- cloudwatch event timer: amount of time on cloudwatch event will call lambda function

The execution baseline and the event timer should have the same values, and timeout should be greater. Function starts executing and during the execution baseline, it waits for messages. If no messages arrives when this time finishes, the function stops itself. However, if there's more messages waiting in the queue, the function keeps consuming messages until 1. there's no more messages, 2. reach the function timeout. Whilst, the function will keep running and as new function are spawned by CW events, those function will run in parallel.
template_adherence.consequences:
Positive Consequences:
* Enable parallelism and, for instance, reduces latency. This is very important for a scheduler

Negative consequences:
* More effort in develop and maintain this lambda function

alternatives.description: Recursive lambdas do their jobs and at the end, they call recursively the same function.
pros: Good, by the simplicity
cons: An error could stop the chain of calls
Can introduce latency

alternatives.description: CloudWatch-triggered lambdas keep doing their jobs until some time before their configured timeouts while CloudWatch triggers new executions in some intervals.
pros: Provide reduced latency due to concurrency capability of lambdas
cons: Complicated

template_adherence.title: DynamoDB update strategy
template_adherence.context:
In order to maintain the serverless nature of the project, a DynamoDB table was chosen as main persistence mechanism, which means that a schedule is primarily stored in DynamoDB and then distributed to other components, which in turn goes back to DynamoDB to update state. So, DynamoDB holds both state and historical data.

The problem here is that both `task-1minute-enqueuer` and `task-1minute-sqs2sns` will concur by Dynamo resources and probably will be throttled (it's easy to reproduce this behavior only by setting Dynamo's read and write capacity to 1 and trying to send some hundreds of schedules while some other are being enqueued in delayer queue).
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Solution must kept as simple as possible
* Even it could delay the problem, increase read and write capacity of DynamoDB is not an architectural solution
template_adherence.decision:
Take the decision for the use of the DynamoDB introduced a new concept for the entire architecture: the layered concern.

The `delayer-aws` solution aims to provide a way to schedule future operations reliably. It's not part of this system store or ingest or even present information about these schedules. In this sense, the use of DynamoDB is needed only because there's a need of store schedules that could not be posted in delayer queue, and there's only 2 options for those records: or they are in the delayer queue, or they're not. That's why the "state" field is needed, but it will not hold the *entire* lifecycle of a schedule.

With this in mind, we realize that all 3 options will be considered, but in different contexts:

- Present data of scheduler is not `delayer-aws`'s concern, but it will be needed. So all the data events should be published by `delayer-aws` to be consumed by another "view" platform - this is a kind of *event driven approach*.
- In this sense, if another system will ingest all of this published data, state and historical data will be stored in different persistent stores;
template_adherence.consequences: The decision introduces a layered concern architecture where DynamoDB is used only for schedules that cannot be posted in the delayer queue. The state field is used but does not hold the entire lifecycle of a schedule. This approach simplifies updates and reduces DynamoDB costs but may limit information about past events. It also enables an event-driven approach for data consumption by other systems.

pros: Enables decoupled data consumption
Supports event-driven architecture
cons: May add complexity in event handling

alternatives.description: Use separated persistence stores for state and historical data
pros: Separation of concerns
Potentially better performance and scalability
cons: Increased system complexity
Data synchronization challenges

alternatives.description: Don't use state as a field in database
pros: Simplified update policy
Reduced DynamoDB costs
cons: No information about past events

template_adherence.title: Use of a logging framework
template_adherence.context: Use of a logging mechanism other than javascript's console.log should provide more feature in logging.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
`console.log` is default for aws lambda and is simple, however have no features other then plot a text to be viewed somewhere
Startup time and memory consumption are very important factors
Complete log solutions like `winston` provide a lot of features
template_adherence.decision:
Chosen option as for "wrapped `console.log` calls". Since `console.log` is just a simple way to log things, it doesn't meant for more advanced logging purposes. `winston` came to fill this gap with a complete logging solution for nodejs applications. However, in the scope of a lambda function, specially in a AWS environment, the major part of those features will not be used (for example the transports, coloring, advanced templating).

In this sense, wrap a `console.log` with some basic features like leveling, and basic templating can fit better to current context. Only for the sake of *futurism*, the wrapper must be implemented following the same interface of `winston` (eg: `logger.info(...)`, `logger.error(...)`, etc).

cons: Bad, lack of features like leveling and pattern

Good, needed features could be implemented on demand
cons: Bad, effort of implementation something that is not the core business of the application

alternatives.description: winston framework
pros: Good, *de-facto* default for node.js logging
Good, lots of features
cons: Bad, lots of features :-) which for a lambda context could bring unecessarly overhead

template_adherence.title: Schedule internal data structure
template_adherence.context: Define a default data structure for the schedule information within interal structures of delayer-aws. The outside schedule model was already defined.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
* Structure is an internal representation, and format should be concerned with it's interal functionalityes
* Could be used in future event dispatchers
template_adherence.decision:
The json structure of the schedule will be:

```javascript
{
scheduleId: "484a127d-6ce3-11e8-8fdd-fb8b5aab61ea",
pointInTime: 1528662600,
apiKey: "nVMIr6J5Do1qutXsZt1dhaaJfjyq4YgzThPQWkQ1",
topicArn: "arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:472249637553:http-request_action-topic",
actionConfig: '{ "method" : "GET", "url" : "https://google.com/" }',
context: '{ "headers" : [], "payload": "" }'
}
```

Where:

* `scheduleId`: unique identifier of the schedule - generated
* `pointInTime`: unix timestamp created in UTC basis to the exact time of the execution of the schedule - informed by the client in request body
* `apiKey`: if informed, the client's api key - informed by the client in headers
* `topicArn`: the Amazon Resource identifier of the action topic on where the schedule will be published. If only the topic name was provided, the current account and the region of the *api-schedule-post* currently in execution will be used to build the arn.
* `actionConfig`: config object provided by the user based on the type of the action
* `context`: the data that will be used as context in the actions

template_adherence.title: 2. Docker Registry for Internal and Protected Images
template_adherence.context:
As part of our efforts around containerized deployment of the Alfresco Digital Business Platform we need to standardize on a Docker Image Registry that Alfresco engineering teams, other internal groups in the organization, and customers and partners can use to publish and consume Docker images.  We can describe those as 'internal' and 'protected' tiers.

The Nexus3 implementation in use at the time of writing does not meet our requirements around access control, security scanning, scalability and global performance, usability, or maintainability.

Our IT resources are currently stretched very thin and we should avoid adding another system for them to deploy and maintain if possible.
template_adherence.decision_drivers:
Need to standardize on a Docker Image Registry for internal and protected tiers.
Existing Nexus3 implementation does not meet requirements for access control, security scanning, scalability, global performance, usability, or maintainability.
Limited IT resources to deploy and maintain additional systems.
Preference for SaaS solution to reduce maintenance overhead.
Desire for automation capabilities via REST API for user provisioning and management.
Commitment of vendors to their SaaS offerings.
Cost considerations.
template_adherence.decision:
We will use Quay.io for the internal and protected tiers of access and use Docker Hub for public repositories.
Preference for SaaS solution to limit IT maintenance.
Quay.io's REST API allows potential automation of user and group management.
Quay/CoreOS is strongly committed to their SaaS offering, unlike Docker's focus on on-premises enterprise product.
template_adherence.consequences:
Cost: Estimated initial expenditure of $100/month, increasing with adoption.
Managing Access Control: Need to define processes for customer account creation and employee onboarding/offboarding, potentially automated via Quay's REST APIs.
Limited Control Over Solution: As a hosted service, less control than self-managed deployment; however, Quay offers an Enterprise on-premises option for future needs.

alternatives.description: Continue using Nexus3 implementation.
pros: Already in use, so no immediate migration needed.
cons: Does not meet requirements for access control, security scanning, scalability, global performance, usability, or maintainability.

alternatives.description: Use Docker Cloud for internal and protected tiers.
pros: Docker Cloud is a known service for Docker images.
cons: Lacks REST API for user provisioning/invitation and user/group management, limiting automation capabilities.

alternatives.description: Deploy and manage own Docker Registry solution on-premises.
pros: Full control over the solution.
Potentially better integration with internal systems.
cons: Requires IT resources to deploy and maintain another system.
Increases operational overhead.

template_adherence.title: 8. Applying Extensions to Docker Images
template_adherence.context:
One of the main advantages of Docker images is their immutability. This means once an image has been tested and verified there is a high confidence it will work as intended in other environments as it doesn't change.

Alfresco allows the core product to the enhanced via external modules in the form of AMPs or simple JARs.

This results in two big problems, how do we release containers with every combination of AMP available and how do customers apply their own extensions?

We have three options; apply extensions at build time (thus retaining the immutability advantage), apply extensions at runtime using a mechanism that doesn't change the contents of the container or apply extensions as the container initializes (breaking immutability).

Applying extensions at build time means we will be forcing customers to build their own images depending on which official and custom extensions they require.

However, there are a number of disadvantages of applying extensions at runtime; The immutability advantage is lost (the WAR file is changed), an extension could fail to apply and prevent the container from starting, it has the potential to introduce performance issues as the AMP or JAR has to be fetched and applied and finally it opens a potential security hole as code can be applied to a container via a simple environment variable.

We investigated potential approaches to keep the main container immutable by using volumes and initContainers but this increases the complexity of the solution and doesn't resolve all the issues outlined above.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include maintaining the immutability advantage of Docker images, minimizing complexity for customers, avoiding runtime failures and security risks, and providing a manageable deployment mechanism for extensions.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to proceed with applying extensions at build time, releasing a small number of images with and without common AMPs applied, as this approach avoids the disadvantages of runtime extension application and aligns with customer expectations.
template_adherence.consequences: Only supporting extensions applied at build time requires customers to build their own images if they have custom extensions or if the required combination of extensions is not shipped. To mitigate complexity, scripts and clear documentation will be provided to assist customers in building their own images.

alternatives.description: Apply extensions at runtime using a mechanism that doesn't change the contents of the container.
pros: Does not require customers to build their own images.
Potentially more flexible for applying extensions dynamically.
cons: Loses immutability advantage as WAR file is changed.
Extension application could fail and prevent container startup.
Potential performance issues due to fetching and applying extensions at runtime.
Potential security holes as code can be applied via environment variables.

alternatives.description: Apply extensions as the container initializes (breaking immutability).
pros: Allows dynamic application of extensions during container initialization.
cons: Breaks immutability of Docker images.
Similar risks as runtime application including failures and security concerns.

template_adherence.title: 9. Using one database per service
template_adherence.context:
Many of the components the Digital Business Platform offers need a database for storing information. Currently Content Services, Process Services and Sync Service do this but there might be more to come in the future. All three are using the same version of the database so the obvious question was raised: Can we just use one database for all our services?

We identified several advantages of using one database per service over one for all the services.

Choosing one database per service would put us in line with the current best practices in the microservices world, as well as allowing us to change versions of the DB individually, and as an added benefit it kills off the possibility of one service being able to impact performance on other services.

If we would choose one database for all our components however we would have fewer components to configure, keep track of, monitor and backup.
template_adherence.decision: We will proceed with the one database per service for existing and future components as there are a number of advantages over having all our services fight over the same database.
template_adherence.consequences: With each new component that has the need for database storage, we would automatically have one more configuration to manage, monitor and backup.

template_adherence.title: 10. Managing secrets used by DBP within the Kubernetes deployment
template_adherence.context:
Many of the components the Digital Business Platform have files or credentials that should be protected within the Kubernetes deployment.

Kubernetes has the concept of secrets within the deployment however certain measures need to be applied to ensure the security of these objects.

There is no turn key solution for securing data within Kubernetes however there are several levels of security that can be applied.

Identification of Secrets: The first and most important issue to first solve is identifying what needs to be kept as a Secret from Kubernetes Users. This includes license files, credentials for databases, credentials for connecting to external service providers, encryption keys and other business related information that may be considered secrets. As an example, s3 connector credential setup for ACS would need to be stored as a Secret object in Kubernetes.

Kubernetes Best Practices: A second step in securing these elements would be to follow Kubernetes best practices on securing secrets. Following these concepts we identified several risks and practices that need to be addressed.

Role Based Access Control policies should be applied at the Application and Direct Kubernetes User levels.

Enabling Auditing at cluster level is another step to take in order to have a cronological set of records documenting user activities.

Applications should not expose any secret data through logging or transmitting them to an untrusted party.

Encryption at Rest (within Kubernetes etcd storage) should be enabled however this implementations is in alpha state in Kubernetes 1.10.

Secret Kubernetes Manifests should not be shared or checked in to a source repository with Base64 encoding. This security risk has multiple fixes in the Kubernetes community, out of which we believe sealed-secrets and helm-secrets are great candidates for resolving this.

Integration with External Providers: The third posible layer of security would be a Kubernetes integration with an external secret provider where only the pods using that secret will be able to see the secret data, the secret itself would not be saved as a Kubernetes object. For this layer the current solution on the market which we investigated would be the vault-operator as a Kubernetes implementation that connects to Hashicorp Vault to fetch secrets.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The ADR does not explicitly label a 'Decision Drivers' section. However, the context and rationale imply drivers such as the need to protect sensitive files and credentials, the lack of a turnkey solution for securing data in Kubernetes, the importance of following Kubernetes best practices, and the desire to integrate with external secret providers for enhanced security.
template_adherence.decision: We will be transforming all configuration and files that we believe that could hold secrets into Kubernetes secret objects. Aside from that, the helm charts that we produce will provision Role Based Access Control policies to control the components access to Kubernetes objects.
template_adherence.consequences: As a result of this decision the storage and associated level of security (for direct Kubernetes Users) of those secrets is the responsibility of the customer.

alternatives.description: Use Kubernetes native secrets with best practices such as RBAC, auditing, encryption at rest, and avoid sharing manifests in source control.
pros: Leverages built-in Kubernetes features.
Follows community best practices.
Relatively straightforward to implement.
cons: Kubernetes encryption at rest is in alpha state (Kubernetes 1.10).
Secrets are stored as Kubernetes objects which may be exposed if cluster is compromised.

alternatives.description: Integrate Kubernetes with external secret providers like Hashicorp Vault via vault-operator.
pros: Secrets are not stored as Kubernetes objects, reducing exposure risk.
Only pods using the secret can access it.
Leverages mature external secret management solutions.
cons: Adds complexity to deployment and management.
Requires integration and maintenance of external systems.

template_adherence.title: 2. Expose terraform outputs from Product infrastructure to Application pipelines
template_adherence.context: We raised spike-575 to explore alternatives to expose outputs from product infrastructure pipelines to application pipelines, necessary because application pipelines need to consume artifacts dynamically generated by other external pipelines (e.g., published URLs output by Product Infrastructure Pipelines).
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to securely expose Terraform outputs from product infrastructure pipelines to application pipelines, minimizing complexity and maintaining secure access. Considerations include available key/value stores, Terraform provider support, infrastructure overhead, and workflow simplicity.
template_adherence.decision: We chose Hashicorp Vault over Azure KeyVault because Vault allows populating the store with secrets using Terraform code, fitting better with our Terraform workflow. KeyVault requires additional steps outside Terraform, adding complexity. Vault's RESTful API also facilitates easy consumption of outputs.
template_adherence.consequences: Storing Terraform outputs in Vault simplifies secure consumption by application teams, reduces pipeline complexity, and establishes separation of concerns by avoiding running Terraform utilities in application pipelines. However, sensitive data is stored in cleartext in Terraform state and plan files, requiring protection of these artifacts.

alternatives.description: Use Azure KeyVault as the key/value store for Terraform outputs.
pros: Hosted cloud-native service integrated with Azure.
No additional infrastructure required.
cons: Terraform provider only allows creating KeyVault, not populating it with secrets via Terraform code.
Requires running terraform output command and parsing stdout outside Terraform workflow, adding complexity.

alternatives.description: Use Hashicorp Vault as the key/value store for Terraform outputs.
pros: Allows populating the store with secrets using Terraform code.
RESTful service enabling easy consumption of outputs via HTTP clients.
More extensive Terraform provider resource capabilities.
cons: Requires provisioning and managing additional infrastructure to run Vault service.

template_adherence.title: 6. Internal DNS Solution
template_adherence.context: In order to run webapps within a fully private and secure Application Service Environment we needed to come up with a DNS solution so that when web applications are put into service these should be discoverable and available for consumption by other INTERNAL services. The "Internal" part of the description is fundamental within this context and it defines the scope of this proposal. In this context we are also assuming that each web application will have it's own DNS name, which will be dynamically generated by convention meanind DNS records will need to be updated dinamically.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: Need for a DNS solution that supports dynamic updates of DNS records for internal web applications; requirement for service discovery within a private and secure environment; desire to leverage existing DNS infrastructure and simplify configuration; need for automation and API-driven updates; compatibility with Azure webapp naming conventions and best practices for service naming.
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to leverage Consul's DNS interface for dynamic service discovery and DNS record updates, forwarding internal domain DNS queries from a DNS server like dnsmasq or BIND to Consul. This approach simplifies DNS server configuration, reuses existing infrastructure, and allows dynamic updates via simple API calls. The solution includes using dnsmasq to forward queries to Consul, adopting Consul's standard service lookup method, and handling exceptions like Azure SCM naming by registering SCM as a service with appropriate tags in Consul.
template_adherence.consequences: Implementing the DNS forward solution with dnsmasq and Consul improves automation capabilities by enabling dynamic DNS record updates via API. Using dnsmasq avoids complexities of more comprehensive DNS servers like BIND and requires minimal configuration changes. High availability can be achieved by deploying dnsmasq in pairs with load balancing. template_adherence.title: Azure IaaS disk encryption and data loss prevention
template_adherence.context:
As per CNP-129: "Ensure no data loss for Jenkins down time", the requirements were to:

1.  Ensure no data loss for Jenkins down time
2.  Use a separate data drive for Jenkins
3.  Ensure that data drive has replication enabled
4.  Ensure that the data drive is backed up
5.  Ensure when the Jenkins box is rebuild, it mounts the (above) drive
6.  All data drives for IAAS should be encrypted
7.  manually Enable recovery VAULT for Jenkins
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The decision drivers include ensuring no data loss during Jenkins downtime, using separate data drives with replication and backup, encryption of data drives, and enabling recovery vaults. The solution must address these requirements while dealing with limitations in Azure services and tooling (e.g., Terraform support, Azure Files capabilities).
template_adherence.decision: The decision is to use a terraform script to create an additional volume as a Jenkins data volume, which partially meets the data loss and replication requirements using Locally Redundant Storage (LRS). Azure Files was considered but rejected due to lack of Zone-redundant storage (ZRS). For encryption, custom kernel modules and scripts are used, but there is a known issue with VM reboot after encryption. Backup is attempted via Recovery Vault and backup policy using ARM templates, but policy creation fails due to API regressions. Feedback from Microsoft is awaited to resolve these issues.
template_adherence.consequences: The current solution supports partial data loss prevention and data replication via LRS. Encryption and backup solutions are incomplete due to technical issues and await vendor feedback. This means some requirements are only partially met, and future decisions depend on external fixes or workarounds.

alternatives.description: Use Azure Files with NFS volume attached for Jenkins data.
pros: Eases migration to Jenkins PaaS offering.
cons: Does not provide Zone-redundant storage (ZRS), failing replication requirement.

alternatives.description: Use Locally Redundant Storage (LRS) with additional volume as Jenkins data volume.
pros: Data replicated to at least 3 places within the same data center.
Supported by terraform script for infrastructure creation.
cons: Only partially meets data loss requirement.
Does not provide zone redundancy.

alternatives.description: Encrypt data drives using custom kernel modules and Azure Linux Agent.
pros: Meets encryption requirement for IAAS data drives.
cons: VM does not come back online after reboot due to decryption method.
Requires custom scripts and kernel modules.

alternatives.description: Create Recovery Vault and backup policy using ARM templates.
pros: Achieves backup requirement in principle.
cons: Terraform does not support this natively.
Backup policy creation fails due to API regressions.
Requires manual intervention and awaiting vendor fixes.

template_adherence.title: Definition of 'environment'
template_adherence.context:
The term 'environment' is incredibly overloaded and means different things to different people even on the same team. In the context of CNP infrastructure and applications, one developer's environment might be another's Azure subscription, or might be another's demo application location.

In the Jenkins library code, the single variable `environment` (or `env`, etc) is passed around with different meanings at both the calling and receiving sites. This causes confusion and makes understanding and debugging the library difficult. Also, having 3 separate concepts represented by a single variable introduces a source of potential bugs and reduces the flexibility of the overall solution. E.g. at the moment we can only have one environment per subscription.

Where developers have realised this limitation, other terms and variable names have been used locally but there is no consistent, shared set of terms so different names have been used to represent the same concepts.
template_adherence.decision_drivers: The need to reduce confusion caused by the overloaded term 'environment' and the single variable usage in code, which leads to bugs and inflexibility. The desire for consistent terminology across the team and codebase to improve understanding, debugging, and flexibility.
template_adherence.decision: Use three terms consistently to distinguish between the subscription, environment and application context. The three terms are Subscription (`subscription`), Environment (`environment`), and Application Context (`application_context`), each with clear definitions and example values. These terms should have a consistent meaning across all method and function calls, and method and function definitions should use the convention above.
template_adherence.consequences:
- Method definitions need to be checked to ensure correct variable names are used.
- Code refactoring to use multiple, different, correctly-named variables where more than one concept is described, possibly modifying method signatures.
- Application infrastructure code must specify three variables instead of one to correctly identify state storage locations and name infrastructure components.
- Application pipeline must pass the three values to infrastructure code when building.
- Special rules for `environment` and `application_context` values apply as described.
